title: 🎃 SAD NEWS, MAINE! A Beloved Haunted House Is Gone for Good 👻
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Popular Maine Haunted House Has Closed for Good
With Halloween happening THIS SATURDAY, spooky season is almost here! But unfortunately, there's some sad news for Maine's haunted house fans.
After several seasons of screams, scares, and unforgettable nights in the dark, Farmington Fright Fest is closing its doors for good. That means its three haunted attractions will not be returning this year,or in the years to come.
The event was voted one of the scariest Halloween attractions in the state of Maine, earning a reputation for delivering plenty of frights and unforgettable nights for Halloween fans.
Since 2021, Farmington Fright Fest has brought three spine-tingling weekends of terror to western Maine, giving local thrill-seekers something to look forward to every fall. For many, it became a Halloween tradition and a must-visit destination for anyone looking to get their scare on.
Read More: Bucksport, Maine Is Home To A Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
Kind of a bummer, right? Especially with Halloween just days away!
Thankfully, there are still plenty of spooky spots throughout New England where you can get your fright fix, including some great options right here in the Bangor area.
Maineiac Manor is located in the former Hollister location in the Bangor Mall, directly across from Spencer's. The 6,500-square-foot attraction has become a destination for anyone looking for a good scare.
Its spooky fun doesn't stop when Halloween is over, either. Maineiac Manor has offered a Krampus-themed Christmas haunted house in December and plans to bring visitors a regular schedule of creepy events and seasonal fun throughout the year.
When you visit, you'll encounter mesmerizing sets, handmade props, and actors in killer costumes hiding in the shadows — and sometimes right out in plain sight, ready to make you jump out of your skin!
And don't sleep on New Hampshire!
Haunted Overload, located in Lee, is one of the most distinctive haunted attractions in New England. It's an enormous outdoor experience built directly into the landscape, featuring gigantic homemade monsters, elaborate structures, eerie lighting, and larger-than-life Halloween scenery.
It's a whole different experience from a traditional haunted house. Instead of walking from room to room, you'll make your way through an outdoor world filled with enormous creatures and elaborate sets. The sheer scale is part of what makes Haunted Overload so memorable, and worth the drive for serious Halloween fans.
So, while we're sad to see Farmington Fright Fest go, Halloween isn't over just yet. With the big night arriving this Saturday, there's still time to squeeze in one more spooky adventure!

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
It is with profound sadness that the family of Mary Gauntt announces her passing on Oct. 26, 2026 at the age of 70.
Mary was born on April 26, 1956 to James and Helen Milan. She grew up in Bangor and was a 1974 graduate of John Bapst High School. Mary received a Bachelor of Science degree in education from the University of Maine at Orono in 1978. In 1982 Mary received Special Education Certification from Glassboro State College in New Jersey. Throughout her life Mary was active in several sports including racquetball, softball, karate, volleyball, and golf.
She married Roy Gauntt in Bangor on Oct. 11, 1980. They spent five years living in New Jersey before returning to Pemaquid Point in 1986. There, they purchased a small seasonal cottage, turning it into their home over the next year and a half. In 1995 their daughter Tara was born. Mary was a devoted mother, following Tara’s athletic and academic pursuits closely and cheering her on throughout.
Mary continued her career in education teaching special education until 2011 when she retired. She then enjoyed working for Bristol Parks at Pemaquid Point Lighthouse for the next 15 years. Mary was always finding ways to give to her community including volunteering at the Bristol Area Library and as a CLC YMCA Board member. She has been a member of Saint Patrick’s Catholic Church in Newcastle for over 40 years.
In her spare time she enjoyed traveling to new places and in recent years traveling to Scottsdale, Ariz. Mary was an animal lover who provided a home for several rescued cats and a family dog over the years. She was a close follower of the Philadelphia Phillies and a trivia savant. Mary was an easy conversational with friends.
Mary is predeceased by her parents. She is survived by her husband of 46 years, Roy J. Gauntt (Pemaquid Point); daughter, Tara Gauntt-Glick and husband, William Glick; grandson, Elliot Glick (Gales Ferry, Conn.); sister, Cathy Vallance and husband, William (Brewer); brother, Terry Milan (North Conway, N.H.); nieces, Christy Vallance, Emily Vallance, Katie Vallance, Amy Vallance; and nephew, Brian Vallance.
There will be a memorial service at the Learning Center at Pemaquid Point Lighthouse Park on October 30, 2026 at 11 a.m. There will also be a celebration of her life in Bangor at Saint Mary’s Catholic Church at a time to be announced.
Should friends so desire, donations may be made in Mary’s memory to Pancreatic Cancer Action Network (PANCAN) at pancan.org.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for her family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: ‘He’s a monster’: Convicted Tennessee murderer still on the run as authorities investigate Wisconsin bank robbery
text:
LAKE COUNTY, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) - The manhunt for escaped Tennessee inmate Jacob Allen Morley continues and authorities are investigating a possible link in Wisconsin after a man robbed a bank at gunpoint there on Tuesday.
Dane County authorities said the Bank of Deerfield was robbed just before it closed. A gunman walked in, demanded money, restrained two employees and left with cash. Nobody was hurt during the robbery.
The gunman stole a Lincoln MKZ from the parking lot to get away. The car was later found unoccupied.
The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said it is aware of the robbery in Wisconsin, but has not confirmed it is linked to Morley.
Morley escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex Monday. He stole a white 2008 Ford F-150 marked with Lindamood Planting Company. The truck was found abandoned early Tuesday in Marion, Illinois. Police said there is no evidence Morley is still in that area.
Morley was serving a life sentence for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield.
Tyreece Miller, the U.S. marshal for the Western District of Tennessee, is asking for help in the search for Morley. The reward for information leading to his arrest is now at $15,000.
“He’s a monster. He will do it again,” Birchfield’s friend Daniel Russell said.
Morley is on the Tennessee Most Wanted List and should be considered dangerous.
Anyone with information about Morley is asked to call 1-800-TBI-FIND immediately. If you see him, do not approach him and call 911.

title: Obituary: Sheila Donaldson
text:
FALMOUTH – Sheila Donaldson, 90, of Falmouth, Maine, died on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. She was the wife of the late Henry Thompson “Tom” Donaldson.
Born June 23, 1936, and raised in Washington, D.C., Sheila attended Holton-Arms and Hood College and worked at Woodward & Lothrop, Lord & Taylor, and Juniors. She met Tom over cocktails, and after five dates they married on Sept. 10, 1960, at The Little Chapel at St. Alban School. They shared a love of cats and dogs and a talent for finding houses and making them beautiful. They lived in several Washington homes before moving to Maine in 1984, where they settled at 58 Applegate Lane for 18 years, the longest they lived anywhere. In her final weeks, she made her home at Falmouth House.
Sheila was independent, stylish, and quick-witted, with a sly smile and a perfect comeback. She enjoyed conversation, reading, knitting, watching golf and tennis, and keeping up with friends and family by phone, where her timing and choice of emoji were unmatched. She had a kind word for everyone, including the nurses and caregivers who looked after her.
She is survived by her children, Suzanne Donaldson and her husband Steve Laird, Douglas Donaldson and his wife Kathryn Templeton; her grandchildren, Sophie Freehling, Jack Donaldson, Olivia Bouten; and great-grandchildren, Margot and Nora Freehling.

title: Rep. Golden urges negotiators to keep American shipbuilding measure in final defense bill

WASHINGTON (WABI) - Representative Jared Golden is pushing congressional leaders to keep American shipbuilding jobs at home.
Golden sent a letter to both the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, urging them to keep his amendment in the final defense authorization bill.
While the House approved a version barring overseas production in July, a Senate proposal would allow the Pentagon to build certain naval vessels abroad.
Golden is asking negotiators from both chambers to preserve his amendment before the final bill goes to a vote.

title: 3 Maine football storylines to follow against Rhode Island
text:
The University of Maine football team was unable to turn things around during a three-game homestand. The Black Bears’ losing streak continued, including a 35-6 defeat to Campbell last Saturday.
Now, the Black Bears (1-7, 1-4 Coastal Athletic Association) go on the road for the first time in a month to face Rhode Island (4-4, 1-3 CAA) at noon Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines to follow.
Where do they go from here?
Nothing really went right for Maine last week. The Black Bears’ offensive woes continued. They rushed for just 63 yards on 30 carries and went 2 for 17 on third down. Defensively, Maine had no answer for Campbell quarterback Kamden Sixkiller, who passed for 450 yards.
Yes, this was more of the same from the Black Bears. Firing offensive coordinator Mikahael Waters has not improved things offensively for Maine, which remains 121st of 124 FCS teams in scoring offense at 13.4 points per game. While the defense has had its moments, it is nowhere near good enough to make up for the offense’s struggles.
Maine has three games left, and after seven straight losses, time is running out to salvage something from this season. But could things get worse?
Maybe (or so the numbers say)
A 4-4 Rhode Island team is surely an easier foe for Maine than 7-1 Campbell, right? Not so fast. ESPN’s SP+, a metric that measures team efficiency on a down-to-down basis, sees the Rams as the 36th-best team in the Football Championship Subdivision — one spot ahead of the Fighting Camels. The model has Rhode Island as a 22-point favorite.
Albany next week is much of the same. The Great Danes (38th in SP+) are in the same tier as Campbell and Rhode Island. Even rival New Hampshire, which Maine faces in the finale, has a better ranking (97th) than the Black Bears (111th). A 1-10 season is not off the table.
The old guard goes at it
Speaking of the next three opponents, Maine fans might welcome contests against familiar faces. The CAA has changed a lot in recent years, with founding members Delaware, James Madison, Richmond, Villanova and William & Mary all departing, but Maine, UNH and Rhode Island are three of the four that remain.
Rhode Island has won four in a row over Maine after losing 14 straight to the Black Bears from 2007-21. UNH will meet Maine for the 116th time. Coach Jordan Stevens said Monday he is also happy to face Albany after the Black Bears and Great Danes, who met every year from 2009-24, did not play last season.

title: Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes in deadly firebomb attack on Colorado demonstrators
text:
Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes in deadly firebomb attack on Colorado demonstrators
An Egyptian man pleaded guilty to federal hate crime and other charges Thursday for a deadly firebombing attack on demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, last year.
Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison after pleading guilty to state charges last spring.
Yelling “Free Palestine,” Soliman lit and threw two Molotov cocktails at the demonstrators who were marching in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking in June 2025 because the demonstrators were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others.
Diamond died three weeks later. Her family says she suffered “indescribable pain.”
The charges Soliman pleaded guilty to in federal court in Denver included nine counts of hate crimes, two of using fire or an explosive to commit a felony and one of carrying an explosive while committing a felony.
The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty. Soliman is already serving a life sentence after pleading guilty to the state charges.
Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, described being unnerved by the attack in their city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado.
The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown. Soliman got near the demonstration on Pearl Street, a pedestrian mall lined with shops and restaurants, by posing as a gardener.
Federal authorities alleged Soliman planned the attack for a year. After his arrest, Soliman told police he sought “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel, according to an FBI affidavit.
Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum.
He was granted work authorization, but it too expired, federal officials said
Soliman was living with his wife and their five children in an apartment in Colorado Springs at the time of the attack. He worked a series of low-paying jobs.
The couple divorced in April. Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.
Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned for more harm than he carried out. He tried twice to buy a gun and was denied, they said.
He brought 18 Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — to the demonstration in a box, but only two were thrown.
Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt.
An injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.
While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.
“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.

title: 10 things to know about open enrollment for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Stacker) - This guide is for anyone who doesn’t have access to affordable health coverage through an employer. So, if you’re a 1099 worker (including self-employed or a gig worker) or if you’re between jobs, this guide from Intuit TurboTax is for you.
1. What is Open Enrollment?
The Open Enrollment Period, more commonly known as OEP, is the one time of year that you can buy or change your health insurance unless you experience a qualifying life event.
2. Who does Open Enrollment on marketplaces apply to?
OEP on federal or state-run marketplaces are mainly for people who aren’t covered by Medicaid, Medicare, or a parent’s health plan. You can still enroll if you have access to job-based coverage, but you likely won’t qualify for savings if the plan is considered affordable. So, for most people with a solid employer plan, sticking with that plan is the better deal.
3. When is Open Enrollment?
For the federal marketplace and many state-run marketplaces, OEP starts Nov. 1, 2026 and ends Dec. 15, 2026 for plans that start as early as Jan. 1, 2027, giving you six weeks to choose a health plan and get signed up. For plans with a later coverage start date, OEP does run through Jan. 15, 2027.
4. What can I expect for Open Enrollment 2027?
The original ACA premium tax credits (which help eligible households lower their payments towards premiums) are still in place. Many people still qualify for real savings, especially those without access to employer coverage.
Additionally, plans will continue to cover all the essential health benefits you’d look for in a health plan, such as emergency services, preventative care, prescription drugs, and more.
That said, premiums are higher this year for most marketplace shoppers. And the enhanced premium tax credits (which allowed more households to be eligible for the premium tax credit and provided larger subsidies to eligible households) expired in January 2026.
KFF, an independent source for health policy news, estimates that the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit combined with an increase in premiums charged by insurers means that ACA marketplace enrollees will pay about $780 more than last year (a 58% increase).
5. Where can I buy my health insurance?
You can buy health insurance directly through HealthCare.gov or your state’s own exchange, depending on where you live.
Most states use the federal marketplace at HealthCare.gov, but about 20 states (plus Washington, D.C.) run their own exchange instead. Use the links above to choose your state of residence and find the marketplace in your state.
6. Which states have extended enrollment windows?
Some states have different windows of dates available to buy health insurance. If you live in California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, or Washington, use this link to take note of the enrollment window.
7. Do I have to sign up for all types of insurance during Open Enrollment?
No. Open Enrollment only applies to health insurance.
However, many people choose to enroll in dental, vision, disability, life, and accident insurance during OEP in order to protect their entire physical and financial wellbeing all at once.
8. How am I going to afford health insurance?
Subsidies (financial assistance) are offered to help people afford health insurance. These come in the form of an advance premium tax credit when you enroll in Marketplace insurance if you are eligible. Eligibility depends on your household income at the time you apply for Marketplace insurance. If your actual income reported on your taxes is higher than when you applied for insurance you may have to pay back some of the advance premium tax credit at tax time. If your income is lower you may be eligible for more premium tax credit at tax time.
Because the enhanced subsidies have lapsed, it’s more important than ever to run your specific numbers rather than assume you’ll qualify for the same discount as in past years. Also, if you have access to affordable employer coverage, you generally won’t qualify for a subsidy at all.
9. What if I already have a plan from last year?
If you purchased health insurance during last year’s OEP, you will be automatically re-enrolled for next year.
You should be aware that insurers often change their plans a bit from year to year. This is especially true in 2027. Several insurers have left the marketplaces, so your old plan may not exist.
If you don’t review your coverage during Open Enrollment, you may see your monthly health payments increase, your doctor may stop accepting your plan, or your prescriptions may no longer be covered. You should also make sure you update your income and household information since that information impacts how much subsidy you could receive.
Make it a habit to review your plan each year to make sure it still meets your needs. Also, check to see whether other plans have been added to your area. You could find an even better deal than your current plan offers, but you won’t know unless you look.
10. Why does Open Enrollment exist?
OEP restricts when you can buy health insurance in order to maintain a needed balance for health insurance companies. By constraining the time period in which you can purchase health insurance, the amount of money going into and coming out of insurance companies’ pockets remains relatively balanced. This allows insurance companies to maintain a balanced pool of sick and healthy people, keeping the marketplaces stable.
The amount individuals pay in premiums works to counteract the money insurance companies are paying out towards claims. If people could sign up for insurance at any point, this balance wouldn’t exist and would cause an unhealthy disruption within the health insurance industry.
This story was produced by Intuit TurboTax and reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

title: ‘What does success look like?’
text:
Wiscasset School Committee Chair Tracey Whitney said Oct. 27, it's frustrating when people cite below state average test scores to "justify or not justify our school's existence" and reject school budgets. (Voters narrowly rejected the first two tries at this year's.) She said the narrative is, students are not achieving. But they are, including going onto good colleges, she said.
"What does success look like here in Wiscasset for our kids, (and) how do we produce the data that shows the importance of those things," Whitney asked in the workshop. The committee is working on how it will review academic achievement three times a year.
Member Doug Merrill suggested getting what the group grade point average (GPA) is for each grade, quarterly at Wiscasset Middle High School and three times a year at Wiscasset Elementary School. "At least (with that), we know we're (assessing) things they've been taught, instead of the state coming in with a pie in the sky task that we might not be teaching in the curriculum for another year.
"I want to know in-house, is the staff progressing forward with the curriculum in a way that we can measure it." Merrill said he doesn't care what the state says on achievement, because "they have no idea what (our) student body is, or how the teachers work together."
Whitney liked the class GPA idea. "But the sell is going to be with the general public. That, OK our test scores are 'here,' but this is the growth."
Vice Chair John Merry said a lot of the focus on growth needs to be at the elementary level, including getting students caught up to their grade level in reading. "Are we doing a good job as far as getting them back up to speed before they come to the high school?"
"It's a work in progress," Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson said.
An hour before the session, Andersson got an email from the state saying this is the last year it's using Northwest Evaluation Association's tests as the state assessment. She said state assessments are how districts get federal dollars — about a quarter million a year for Wiscasset schools.
The 3:57 p.m. Oct. 27 email from Maine Department of Education says the new vendor for the statewide reading and math assessment, starting with next fall's, is New Meridian. The assessment will offer "increased transparency and educator involvement," an adaptive design and "instructionally useful data," the email reads.
The committee plans more workshop time to arrive at how to gauge achievement. Andersson will have some employees join the discussion as subject matter experts at different grade levels.
Merry told Andersson, "Just forewarn them we're going to be thinking outside the box for a while."
"Yeah, this is going to be brainstorming it ...," Whitney said. "I don't want to be reinventing the wheel for teachers. That's not our job or our place. But I want us to work within the system that they have and see how they're doing what they're doing."
"(And) not just cramming another chore down their throat that they don't have time for," Merrill said.
The committee's next workshop is at 6 p.m. Nov. 17 at Wiscasset Middle High School.

title: Mild with a few late night showers before a Halloween cooldown
text:
Mild with a few late night showers before a Halloween cooldown
Near 70 degrees for some today but the weekend cools down in time for Halloween
Mild with a few late night showers before a Halloween cooldown
Near 70 degrees for some today but the weekend cools down in time for Halloween
Maine will stay mostly dry into next week, but a brief chance of showers arrives late Thursday night into the predawn hours Friday, mainly across northern areas. I do not expect significant weather impacts as high pressure remains in place.
Southwest winds will strengthen Thursday afternoon, making it breezy and helping temperatures climb well into the 60s. A few communities could reach 70. The night will be unusually mild for late October, with some locations holding in the 50s and coming within a few degrees of record-warm overnight lows.
A cold front will cross the state Friday, followed by dry conditions and temperatures closer to normal. For Halloween on Saturday, Highs will be in the 40s and 50s during the early evening, then falling into the 30s overnight. Hunting firearm season begins Saturday for Maine residents only and the weather looks perfect.
We could see more rain in early November, but it may take longer to get here than earlier forecasts suggested. There’s still plenty of time for that outlook to change.

title: Throwback Thursday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Maine has long been a setting for strange stories, supernatural tales, and things that go bump in the night. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
From dark forests and small towns to long stretches of coastline, Maine has provided plenty of inspiration for stories about the strange and unexplained. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1986, when WAGM Reporter Sara Coddington took a look at Strange Maine, a collection of weird and supernatural stories set here in the Pine Tree State.
Halloween literally means the eve before All Hallows Day, November 1st. It’s a time set aside in the Christian calendar for honoring departed souls. It’s said that people help disembodied spirits in their ascent from their earthly haunts or purgatory to heavenly spheres. America’s earliest settlers didn’t much like this practice. They thought it smacked of the devil in his works. But eventually, celebrating Halloween in less supernatural ways became general practice. Even book publishers are getting in the act. Just out is strange Maine.
“It’s a collection of Weird Tales, short stories, all of them set in Maine. There are 14 of them in the book. Stephen King is in there and a bunch of other famous and some not so famous, some national, some regional.”
King’s contribution to the book is one for the road. His creepy tale of vampires takes place in Jerusalem’s lot. Apparently, an illustration of the little girl in the story has changed from the original proof.
“Oh, this is a very strange event. We have the original art, which doesn’t have any fangs in it. If you look at the finished copy here in Strange Maine, you will see, without a doubt, real fangs. So this is a very weird Halloween happening.”
Why is Maine the location of so many horror tales?
“I think it probably has something to do with the isolation and remoteness that Maine has in comparison to many other places. They see the forest, they see the sparse population, the vast sea that we have really right out in front of us here. And this this is too many city folk. This is an odd situation.”
And Halloween itself can be full of odd situations. But Mainers don’t really believe the day has any mystic significance, do we?
Sara Coddington, Channel 8 News.

title: No script will bring me around to Susan Collins
text:
A young man stopped by, campaigning for Sen. Collins, New Jersey license plates.
His clipboard of talking points led with “Appropriations Committee.” I interjected, “Bath Iron Works will get their money without Collins.” Undeterred, he continued, point by point. Sensing I wasn’t buying what he was selling, he turned to attacking Troy Jackson.
I told him I read the voting records, in the paper and online. I said I’ve seen her vote more and more for corporations and the wealthy, less and less for women and the environment. I don’t know anyone who is better off today than two years ago.
And, I can never forgive her for increasing funding for a cruel, inhumane and racist ICE, killing with impunity and imprisoning people with no criminal record.
I believe in the promises of the Constitution. I don’t believe Republicans, including Collins, are defending it. Billionaires call the shots.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: More Showers Possible Friday Before Sunshine Returns for Halloween Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. We’ve had a pretty nice day across the region today, with temperatures climbing well above average for this time of year. Unfortunately, the warmer weather isn’t going to stick around for too much longer, as a cold front is expected to move through the region during the overnight hours tonight. This will bring a couple of opportunities for rain showers through the day Friday, before sunshine returns heading into the upcoming Halloween weekend. The other unfortunate part of this forecast is that we’re still not looking at the sort of substantial rainfall we desperately need to help improve our ongoing drought conditions.
Temperatures aren’t expected to cool off nearly as much as what we’ve experienced over the last couple of nights. With southwesterly winds continuing to bring warmer air into the region, low temperatures tonight will only fall back into the lower to upper 40s for most locations. That’s a pretty big difference compared to the teens and 20s we experienced earlier this week. Cloud coverage is expected to increase through the evening hours tonight, with scattered rain showers possible as we work our way into the overnight hours. The first round of showers will be associated with a cold front moving across the region early tomorrow morning. While I don’t expect everyone to see rainfall overnight, there’s certainly a chance for a few showers before we get into the morning hours Friday.
Heading into tomorrow, we’re looking at another relatively mild day across the region, although temperatures won’t be quite as warm as what we experienced today. High temperatures Friday are expected to climb into the lower to upper 50s, with some of our warmer locations in southern Aroostook County potentially reaching 60 degrees. We’ll see a mixture of sunshine and clouds during the morning hours, before additional cloud coverage develops during the afternoon. Another round of showers is possible during the afternoon and early evening hours, especially across northern portions of Aroostook County. This second round of showers will be associated with another cold front moving through the region, helping to bring cooler air back into the area heading into the weekend.
The good news is that the unsettled weather doesn’t look like it’ll stick around for too long. Once we get through the shower chances Friday, high pressure will begin to build back into the region, bringing the return of sunshine for Saturday. This is certainly good news for anyone with outdoor plans for Halloween. High temperatures Saturday will be noticeably cooler though, with most towns only reaching the lower to mid 40s during the afternoon hours. Northwesterly winds around 10 to 15 MPH, with some gusts approaching 25 MPH, will also make it feel a bit cooler outside. If you’re planning on heading out trick-or-treating Saturday evening, you may want to consider an extra layer underneath those costumes. Temperatures will have no problem falling through the 30s during the evening, before bottoming out in the lower to mid 20s overnight.
Sunday is shaping up to be another pretty nice day across the region, with plenty of sunshine expected once again. Temperatures will also begin to rebound, with highs climbing back into the upper 40s to lower 50s. Overall, I think we’re looking at a pretty decent Halloween weekend, especially considering we’re heading into November.
Looking at the latest rainfall potential map from the Weather Prediction Center, you’ll notice that there really isn’t a whole lot of rainfall expected across Aroostook County over the next several days. Despite having two opportunities for rain showers between tonight and Friday evening, the latest forecast guidance continues to suggest that most locations will likely see less than a tenth of an inch of rainfall. Some locations may see a little more depending on where the showers develop, but I don’t expect any of this rainfall to make a meaningful difference in our ongoing drought conditions.
According to the National Weather Service in Caribou, the entire forecast area remains in at least moderate drought, with 58 percent of the region (northern and eastern Maine) now experiencing severe drought conditions. Streamflow levels also remain exceptionally low, with 26 of the 38 monitored USGS stream gauges reporting flows much below normal. Unfortunately, the longer-range forecast isn’t looking particularly promising for substantial rainfall either. Our next opportunity for showers may arrive during the middle of next week, but even that system is currently expected to struggle with limited moisture. For more details on what to expect heading into the Halloween weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
text:
(Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep.
Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.”
The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening.
Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.”
The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

title: How Brunswick schools’ performing arts programs prepare students for life
text:
Every fall, the Brunswick schools fill with the sounds of students making music. And while families will eventually hear the finished pieces at a concert, the value of an arts education happens long before the final performance. As Ashley Albert, our choral director at Brunswick High School, says, “One of the things we focus on a lot in the performing arts is not the end product, but the process.”
That process deserves our attention. Through our performing arts programs, students learn to work with others, accept feedback, make lasting connections with like-minded students, and build resilience and confidence through practice. These are lessons our students learn in music programs and take with them into all areas of their education and life.
At Kate Furbish Elementary School, music teacher Danielle Murphy introduces children in kindergarten through second grade to music through singing, movement, and instruments. Some are hesitant to make a sound at first. Singing can feel especially vulnerable, she explains, and a group performance gives a shy child a chance to contribute alongside classmates. “When you have a performance of a group and a shy child is in the middle of the performance, just the fact they are working with all the other kids to create something beautiful, they end up having more confidence,” Murphy said.
Students also discover that they have something to teach others. When Murphy introduced songs in Spanish, she asked Spanish-speaking students to help check her pronunciation. “And I let them give examples to the other kids,” she said. “It was quite amazing how they all worked together for it.”
Those early experiences prepare students for the work ahead. Albert credits her elementary and junior high colleagues with developing the musicians who arrive in her high school classroom. Teachers coordinate their approaches to skills such as sight-reading music so students can build on what they have learned.
Middle school brings changes that require patience. For singers, even their own voices can begin to feel unfamiliar. “Your voice, which is the body’s instrument, is always changing,” Albert said. Young singers have to adjust to those changes while learning how their sound fits with the group.
Through music programs, students are also discovering their interests and finding other students who share those same interests. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that students who feel connected to school are more likely to have better attendance and less likely to experience substance use or violence. Our performing arts programs give students opportunities to develop those connections through shared work.
At the high school, students take on increasingly demanding music. Brandon Duras, our director of instrumental music, wants them to develop habits they can use wherever their interests lead. “Music gets them to think about how to practice and dedicate time and energy to something that they really enjoy and believe in doing,” Duras said.
That preparation becomes visible when students rehearse together. Everyone has a part to learn, and each musician has to listen to the people around them. Albert says students hear how they are doing as soon as they sing or play. “It’s something where you get immediate feedback all of the time,” she said.
Learning to use that feedback means listening to a correction and making another attempt. Albert also hears from graduates who say their performing arts experiences helped prepare them for job interviews and presentations. Those are useful skills for students who may never pursue music professionally.
When all the work, practice, and rehearsals have been completed, our wonderful community gives students an audience to validate their hard work. It is gratifying to see a full house at performances and concerts, including friends, families, and folks from the community who may not have a personal connection to a student performing, but are interested in supporting the arts, supporting the school, or simply enjoying an evening of entertainment.
I am grateful that Brunswick is that kind of community. I hope you will continue to support our programs and attend a performance this school year. Our teachers and students are preparing right now to show you the value of performing arts can have in a concert — and in life!
Phillip Potenziano is superintendent of Brunswick schools.

title: South Korean prosecutor seeks death penalty for ex-President Yoon over martial law debacle
text:
South Korean prosecutor seeks death penalty for ex-President Yoon over martial law debacle
A South Korean special prosecutor on Thursday demanded the death penalty for ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol, ahead of an appeals court verdict on rebellion charges over his brief imposition of martial law in December 2024.
The Seoul High Court has yet to set a date for a verdict on Yoon's appeal of a life sentence handed down in February by the Seoul Central District Court. The court found that he illegally mobilized troops and police to seize the legislature, arrest political opponents and establish unchecked rule for a “considerable time.”
Investigators led by Special Prosecutor Cho Eun-suk also appealed the ruling, arguing Yoon deserves the death penalty because his actions posed a grave threat to the country’s democracy. An execution would be unlikely. South Korea has not executed anyone since 1997, effectively maintaining a moratorium on capital punishment following calls for its abolition.
Related video: Pro and anti-Yoon rallies in Seoul as impeached president argues against his arrest, Jan. 2025
During the hearing at the high court, Cho’s team said only the death penalty could fully hold Yoon accountable for a crime as serious as orchestrating a rebellion and that the country’s long-standing pause on executions should not prevent courts from imposing death sentences.
Yoon’s legal team told reporters that prosecutors were repeating an argument “devoid of evidence and legal logic” and claimed that Yoon’s martial law was intended to raise public awareness about what he called attempts by the opposition-led legislature to paralyze state affairs. It said Yoon had no intention of causing harm or establishing authoritarian rule.
Yoon’s martial law decree, announced late at night on Dec. 3, 2024, lasted only hours until a quorum of lawmakers broke through a blockade of heavily armed soldiers and police at the National Assembly and voted to overturn it, forcing his Cabinet to lift the measure.
Yoon was suspended from office on Dec. 14, 2024, after being impeached by the liberal-led legislature and was formally removed by the Constitutional Court in April 2025. He was re-arrested in July 2025 and has faced multiple criminal trials over the martial law debacle and other allegations, with the rebellion charge carrying the heaviest punishment.
In addition to appealing his life sentence for rebellion, Yoon has also appealed a 30-year prison term in a case accusing him of ordering drone flights in 2024 to deliberately heighten tensions with North Korea and create a pretext for martial law at home. Yoon’s lawyers said the drone flights were a response to North Korea flying thousands of trash-carrying balloons into the South.

title: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert.
Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International, said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago.
Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings.
“That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.”
For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending.
“It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor. Sometimes you can get a good deal, but just be mindful that it’s not a free lunch. Even if it’s that 6 weeks of interest free payments you’ve got to make a payment now and another one in two weeks and another one in two weeks, just need to be careful that you’re not overspending.”
Rossman also cautioned about the interest owed on those deals and on credit card debt, which can often be in the 20% range.
Rossman said people who feel in too deep can always ask for help.

title: Ballot stacking: What is it and is it legal?
text:
Ballot stacking: What is it and is it legal?
Ballot stacking: What is it and is it legal?
A legal and political battle is unfolding in Alaska's Senate race as two candidates named Dan Sullivan appear on the ballot. It has sparked accusations of voter confusion and election fraud.
One Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Republican senator and ally of President Donald Trump. The other Dan Sullivan is running without party affiliation.
Republicans, including Trump, have accused the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola of recruiting the undeclared Dan Sullivan to purposely confuse voters and siphon votes away from the Republican Dan Sullivan, following a New York Times report alleging such actions.
Peltola has called the report a "distraction" and a "diversion."
Attempts to siphon votes from one candidate are not illegal. The controversial method, known as ballot stacking, is common in U.S. politics.
Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation into the matter. Trump has called for criminal prosecution against Peltola and her campaign, and accused her of election fraud.
On Thursday, the Associated Press reported that the Justice Department (DOJ) escalated a criminal investigation over the matter, including issuing grand jury subpoenas.
Trump previously said he directed the DOJ to sue to block Alaska from certifying the election if the Republican Dan Sullivan loses.
The race results could help determine which party controls the Senate, highlighting the high stakes of the election.

title: In Oxford County, land trust deal will dovetail with existing nature area
text:
Western Foothills Land Trust has acquired 85 acres along the eastern side of Moose Pond in Otisfield, protecting more than 3,500 feet of undeveloped shoreline.
The acquisition connects to the town-owned Two Ponds Nature Area, creating a 180-acre conservation and recreation area.
The property includes mixed forest and more than 20 acres of wetlands that provide wildlife habitat and help protect water quality. The beaver pond supports fish, waterfowl, amphibians and other wildlife.
“This is a once-in-a-generation conservation opportunity for Otisfield,” said Korey Morgan, executive director of Western Foothills Land Trust. “Few places combine this much undeveloped shoreline, wildlife habitat and recreational potential in a single property. Conserving this land ensures that future generations will be able to experience Moose Pond much as it exists today.”
The trust is working with Otisfield town officials and community partners to explore potential uses, including low-impact hiking trails, fishing access, wildlife observation and outdoor education.
“The conservation on Moose Pond is an incredible win for the people of our town,” said Peter Tilkimeier, chair of the Otisfield Conservation Committee. “This project represents an investment in our community’s future, and protects forests and shoreline while creating new opportunities for recreation, outdoor education, and conservation.
The acquisition builds on years of work by the trust, town officials, volunteers and residents. Funding came from Land for Maine’s Future, the Davis Conservation Foundation, the William P. Wharton Trust, Maine Outdoor Heritage Fund, Maine Community Foundation, Ram Island Conservation and anonymous donors.

title: RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
text:
RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development.
The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments for two weeks before finalizing the measure.
The document, primarily written by officials at HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unsafe health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development.
The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under normal FDA rules, those chemicals would be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness.
According to the document posted online, Kennedy determined the change “advances patient choice and freedom” while protecting people in the United States from peptides sold online that are often made from ingredients of unknown origin and quality.
Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.
Lee Rosebush of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine said in an online post that HHS had taken “a huge step for patient and provider medical freedom.” The group, which is not a medical professional society, represents people who prescribe or sell peptides.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers, which recently announced plans to offer wellness peptides once the government changed its policy. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth more than $2 billion.
Wellness peptides are not FDA approved
Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss.
The chemicals subject to the new policy have not been approved as safe and effective by the FDA. Still, they are promoted online by influencers and celebrities for a range of medical uses, including insomnia, anxiety, inflammatory conditions and migraines.
Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official, noted that the FDA has already approved rigorously tested drugs for all of those conditions.
As people “are diverted from those drugs toward this stuff, there will be more unnecessary pain and suffering,” said Lurie, who now leads the nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest.
He also questioned the timing of the change, days before the midterm election.
“This is a wink and nod to the MAHA faithful in the hope that they'll show up at the polls,” said Lurie, referring to Kennedy's “Make America Healthy Again” movement.
RFK Jr. and his MAHA followers support peptides
A spokesperson for HHS said the agency is “confronting the risks of black-market peptides” by giving Americans “a more controlled alternative through licensed U.S. compounders.”
It is the latest example of Kennedy reshaping U.S. health policy in the MAHA mold. Some of the biggest figures in that movement sell peptide injections and supplements.
The decision is a stark break from past FDA efforts to limit the availability of unproven wellness products, including peptides, stem cell therapies and dietary supplements, that make unsupported medical claims. But that approach put the agency at odds with Kennedy, who has publicly endorsed the benefits of all of those products.
The policy published Wednesday is a step back from HHS' original plan, according to two of the people who discussed its development.
HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.
FDA officials warned that the agency's scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming the peptides safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.
FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories. Additionally, compounders are directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the purity of peptides they use.
Lurie pointed out that the FDA, under federal law, does not have the authority to enforce those pharmacy requirements.
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which represents specialty pharmacies, said several details need to be clarified — including when the policy takes effect and how it will intersect with state pharmacy boards, who traditionally regulate pharmacists.
Decisions over compounding have long rested with the FDA, not HHS
Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.
The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.
It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. But federal law technically gives HHS authority over drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.
FDA has warned Americans about safety risks of unproven peptides
Many in the U.S. who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals.
In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.
At a meeting in July, FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.
But a panel of outside experts voted to drop restrictions on the six peptides named in Wednesday's document. The panel — selected by Kennedy’s HHS — included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.

title: TSA confiscates Wolverine-style claws at airport checkpoint
text:
SEATTLE (Gray News) - Transportation Security Administration officers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport recently stopped a suspicious carry-on item that looked more like something out of a Marvel movie.
According to the TSA, officers Douglas Linn and Dennis Oishi teamed up to identify and stop a dangerous item in a carry-on bag.
Officials said while reviewing X-ray images, Linn spotted the item and immediately recognized it required additional attention.
“I saw three blades and distinct claw-like features,” Linn said. “I was amazed, and even more so when it came out of the bag. I have never seen anything like this during my two years at TSA.”
Officials said the item resembled a mix between Wolverine-style claws and Freddy Krueger blades, noting that some accessories are better suited for movie screens rather than airplane cabins.
As the property search officer, Oishi conducted a bag search, confirmed the prohibited item and was said to handle the situation with the professionalism expected during checkpoint operations.
The passenger immediately remembered the items after Oishi removed them from the bag and voluntarily abandoned them at the checkpoint.
“In my seven years with TSA, this is one of the most unusual items I have encountered,” responding supervisory TSA officer Ann Rhoades said. “When Dennis asked the passenger if there was anything sharp in the bag, he said he wasn’t sure. Obviously, there was.”

title: Milford father charged with manslaughter in death of 13-month-old daughter
text:
MILFORD, Maine (WABI) - A Milford father has been charged with manslaughter and three counts of child endangerment following the death of his 13-month-old daughter, Maine State Police said.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, was taken into custody Wednesday after a nearly 10-month investigation into the death of Eleanora Ray McLaughlin.
The child died on Dec. 28, 2025. An autopsy determined her death was caused by hypothermia. In Bangor that day, the high temperature was 28 with an overnight low of 13 degrees.
DHHS involvement and legislative scrutiny
According to a Maine Department of Health and Human Services report obtained by the child’s mother, Erika Dupuis, their other two children were present in the home when Eleanora died. Dupuis, who was living in West Virginia at the time, said DHHS closed an investigation centered around their twin girls just six days before Eleanora’s death.
State Sen. Jeffrey Timberlake, R-Androscoggin, is one of three lawmakers who wrote to DHHS in January urging them to provide information about what happened to the child and speak before the Government Oversight Committee. No hearings have been held on Eleanora’s death.
“Why are we even here? ... On December 22, DHHS was at the premises and signed off on this case. And how do you sign off on a case when there is no heat, no running water in the house? They’re living basically in the back bedroom with an electric heater ... and how does DHHS sign off on that?“ Timberlake said.
Mother reacts to arrest ahead of Friday court date
Shane McLaughlin is being held at the Penobscot County Jail and is expected to appear in court Friday. The case is being prosecuted by the Maine Attorney General’s Office.
Dupuis, McLaughlin’s ex-wife, issued a statement:
“He’s simply a father who is allowed to get depressed when he is going through a divorce, handling three kids, and taking care of his mother, who frequented the hospital. It simply was a terrible tragedy for our family, but let’s not keep dragging the man through the mud, especially when he’s grieving his mother who just passed away. He’s already had his karma when he lost everything in life. And that’s all I have to say.”
Maine State Police ask anyone with information to contact Det. Jennifer Fiske at 207-973-3700, ext. 9, or submit tips online to the Major Crimes Unit – North via the Maine State Police tip portal.

title: Susan Collins may finally have overstayed her welcome

text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
Something no one seems to have asked Susan Collins, this time around, was why she thought it necessary to run for a sixth term.
First elected in the 20th century, she has already served far into the 21st, longer than any other popularly elected U.S. senator from Maine. After 30 years, it would seem she has nothing to prove.
Running for reelection for as long as possible now seems to be the default. It wasn’t always that way. I was apparently alone among Maine journalists in not being surprised that Olympia Snowe, who served alongside Collins for 14 years, decided not to seek reelection in 2012 after 18 years in the Senate, following 14 in the House.
Snowe was then “only” 65 — retirement age for most people — but the more obvious reason was that the Republican Party had left behind her brand of consensus politics in a rightward lurch that has continued, unchecked, to this day.
Snowe helped engineer major compromises to support rural hospitals and expand Medicare benefits — and was ready to do the same in 2009 when the Affordable Care Act was introduced. She soon realized, however, that no Republican — including Collins — would join her. Retirement, then, was the right decision.
So it has been for most of Maine’s leading lights whose service made this small state a watchword for senatorial excellence.
Ed Muskie, elected to four terms, stepped down two years early to become U.S. secretary of state. Bill Cohen departed after three terms and became Bill Clinton’s defense secretary, a rare crossover Cabinet pick. George Mitchell served a little over two terms and retired as Senate majority leader, going on to negotiate peace in Northern Ireland.
Collins’ childhood idol, Margaret Chase Smith, was the first Mainer elected to four terms. Smith, then 74, hadn’t intended to run in 1972, but changed her mind after a young Republican challenged her in the primary. She lost in November to Congressman Bill Hathaway, 48, then a typical age for those seeking statewide office.
Having won five terms, what does Collins expect to do in a sixth that she hasn’t already accomplished? It’s a question she’s struggled to answer throughout this nasty, bitter and seemingly interminable campaign.
The gap between traditional Republican Party politics and current practice that convinced Olympia Snowe to step down has become a chasm in Donald Trump’s second term. Try as Collins might, she can’t disclaim responsibility for Trump’s most outrageous actions, especially his unilateral decision to make war on Iran and his whimsical imposition of tariffs without rhyme or reason.
Democrats’ decision in July to jettison their nominee, Graham Platner, put Collins back in the driver’s seat; replacement candidates rarely win. But just as Collins was making her final pitch, Trump imposed new punitive tariffs on Canada — as Collins points out, our closest ally — while providing sanctions relief to Vladimir Putin’s Russian war machine.
Collins claims credit for a last-minute exemption for agricultural products, but what about all the other, equally nonsensical tariffs? If you’re looking for relief from high gas, diesel and fuel oil prices, not to mention food, you won’t vote to endorse Trump’s policies.
The same goes for Collins’ other claims. The $1.5 billion in grants she claims to have steered toward Maine are dwarfed by cuts in healthcare and nutrition benefits imposed in the 2025 budget bill she voted to advance.
Fortunately for those seeking an alternative, Troy Jackson has become a more serious candidate than Kamala Harris was in 2024. Harris replaced Joe Biden but didn’t put forth a single idea anyone remembers.
Jackson is for national healthcare. Collins says it would be “too expensive,” even though the U.S. pays far more per person than any other nation, and its heavily privatized system leaves a growing number of millions uninsured.
Jackson thinks workers need union representation to turn around the deplorable gap between pay for an average service sector job and what it takes to support a family. Collins never mentions the subject.
Jackson says everyone should pay their fair share under a progressive income tax. Collins favored tax cuts over two decades that created the billionaire class.
Finally, Jackson has changed and evolved over the years: witness his positions on abortion rights and gun safety. Collins appears incapable of change.
Yet Trump may be the determining factor in Maine’s Senate race, and many other races, as he insists the election must be about him and nothing else. To paraphrase Ronald Reagan, are you better off now than you were when Trump took office? The answer to that pertinent question will soon be known.

title: Bowdoinham man builds AI tool to help residents ask questions about their town
text:
Benjamin Brewer created an artificial intelligence tool “for anyone who’s ever tried to look something up on the town website and ended up 47 PDFs deep at 11 p.m. wondering if you’re even in the right decade,” he wrote on Facebook.
The Ask Bowdoinham AI tool allows anyone to ask questions about Bowdoinham. It generates answers by searching town documents and summarizing relevant portions. Users can choose how many sources they want the tool to pull up and type in a prompt or question. The tool then pulls the information, provides citations, and links to the documents used to answer the question. The tool also directs the user to the information within the document — Brewer said it’s sometimes a little off, but usually links to the correct page.
Brewer said he has been using AI agents to analyze town documents for his Slow Down Bowdoinham campaign, which aims to address speeding in the town. He said using AI been a major time-saving measure, which is helpful to him as a self-employed single dad.
He said he thought this kind of tool could be helpful to other Bowdoinham residents.
“There’s a lot of unhappy town members … and people are doing a lot of digging, so I figured I’d assist with that,” Brewer said.
Brewer is currently a house painter, but said as a former “computer science guy,” creating the tool took two or three nights.
Ask Bowdoinham is powered by two free programs, Groq and Open Router. Brewer said if too many people try to use it at once, it will stop generating summaries and only pull documents. The tool is an unofficial community project, meaning it is not affiliated with the town government.
Brewer wrote code that allows him to easily scan the town website and import new documents into Ask Bowdoinham. He plans to do this about once a week. When he first took documents from the town website, his IP address was blocked — he said he believes he was flagged as a bot.
In response to the question “What was discussed at Bowdoinham’s first public meeting about the Open Space Plan?” the tool generated a summary drawn from the meeting’s agenda.
Small changes in spelling and wording can change the summaries, and asking the same question multiple times can yield different results. The tool provided an accurate answer to “Who are the current Select Board members?” In response to the search “Current Select Board members,” the summary provided incorrect information drawn from a 2026 sample ballot. A day later, the same search garnered a summary, including two of the five current board members’ full names, and the first name of a third member.
Bowdoinham resident Hope Libby said she is a fan of Ask Bowdoinham because it saves time. She hasn’t been looking at the summaries the tool generates, and is using it purely to find information in long and complex documents. She most recently asked it about the town’s housing density, and located her answer in the 2025 Annual Report.
Brewer said the Ask Bowdoinham site has had low to moderate traffic — anywhere between two and 49 queries in a day, though he said some of the higher numbers may have been inflated by his own tests of the tool. He hasn’t gotten much feedback yet, but said he would appreciate hearing from users about what works and what doesn’t. He said he’ll continue to improve the tool if he can.
“If it’s gonna say something, I wanted to make sure that it’s legit … we already have enough incorrect information in the world, as far as I’m concerned,” he said.
In a Facebook post, Brewer cautioned town residents to excercise discretion when using the tool. “It reads the town’s documents, not minds — always click through to the original before quoting it at a meeting,” he wrote.
He said he envisions the tool helping Bowdoinham residents get the information they need while saving time.
“I hope … that it lets them get to the point of what they’re trying to do without putting the superfluous man-hours in,” said Brewer.

title: Gov. Mills reveals election picks after casting ballot
text:
FARMINGTON, Maine (WABI) - Gov. Janet Mills cast her ballot in her hometown of Farmington Thursday.
The governor wrote on social media that she voted for Democrat Hannah Pingree to become the next Maine governor.
Mills announced that she also voted for Democrats Matt Dunlap for Maine’s 2nd Congressional district and Troy Jackson in the U.S. Senate race.
Mills was running to become the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate, but she suspended her campaign ahead of the primary election.
Before her vote on Thursday, Mills had not said publicly who she would support.

title: State funding is lagging behind the University of Maine System’s growing costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine is sending more money than ever to the University of Maine System, but it isn’t keeping up with the system’s rising costs.
The University of Maine System received more than $300 million from the state this fiscal year. Despite that being a 44% jump from what the system received a decade ago, the proportion of university expenses it covers is shrinking.
A combination of dropping tuition revenue, inflation and state funding lagging behind rising expenses has forced administrators on campuses across the system to enact budget cuts. The University of Maine’s $19 million budget shortfall, which administrators also attributed to federal funding uncertainties and more than $1 billion in deferred campus maintenance, is the most recent example.
In 1989, state-appropriated funds covered almost three-quarters of the system’s total expenses, an all-time high. Those funds are now projected to account for less than half of all expenses next fiscal year, according to system spokesperson and legislative liaison Samantha Warren.
The percentage of expenses covered by state funding has stayed “flat or slightly up” in the last decade, Warren said.
The funds also aren’t keeping up with inflation. This year’s funding is worth just $10 million more than what the system received in 2014 when adjusting for inflation, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The system received $75 million more this year than in 2014.
A lack of meaningful increases has required universities in the system to rely on student tuition and fees to fund themselves. Despite enrollment rising across the system over the last four years, tuition revenue has been “flat or even falling” due to demographic shifts and scholarships or aid awarded to students, Warren said.
With layoffs and retrenchment looming, UMaine faculty, staff and students have called on the state to increase funding to the institution. The system has been doing the same, Warren said.
Through advocacy, which is not labeled as lobbying because the system is a state agency, Maine awarded $2 million for a research opportunity this fiscal year and raised funding by 4%, Warren said. In total, the system received $303.5 million this fiscal year.
But that 4% jump doesn’t even cover how much compensation costs went up last year, Warren said.
Even if state funds continue to go up and tuition is raised, universities will still need to cut costs or find other ways to bring in revenue, Warren said.
“If we remain committed to maintaining the most affordable higher education in New England and our state funding consistently falls short of keeping pace with rising operating costs, we need to cut those costs, find reliable new ways to generate revenue or do both, which is what UMaine is thoughtfully undertaking now,” Warren said.
Other New England institutions receive funds that cover less of their expenses. The University System of New Hampshire and University of Massachusetts System receive funding that covers roughly 10% and 23% of their expenses, respectively.
Although it wouldn’t solve the upcoming cuts, Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono, said there’s more opportunities to increase funding to public universities in the state.
The Legislature has been “shooting ourselves in the foot” by not funding the state’s universities, Tipping said. Investing in higher education brings revenue to Maine through the workforce and research, he said.
Funding for the university system has had bipartisan support in previous years, which led to the 4% hike that Tipping spearheaded. Although the state is facing a projected $1.3 billion shortfall next year, it shouldn’t be difficult to find more money to support higher education, Tipping said.
“We have other options,” Tipping said. “We still have tax breaks on the books for wealthy folks that I think we should take another look at for wealthy corporations. It’s all about priorities.”
The university system has already sent its priorities to the state for the 2028-29 fiscal year, Warren said.
The request falls short of what the system expects operating costs will be and what the state could fund, but it conveys to Gov. Janet Mills and whoever is next elected to the Blaine House that the system has “urgent needs for greater operations, capital and research funding,” Warren said.
While it’s unknown how the request will be received by the next governor, Warren said the university will continue to push for more funding through the state legislature.
“The system will fight like hell in Augusta to make the case for these needed new dollars, and demonstrate each day across our state how public investments in our public universities directly strengthen Maine’s people, economy and communities,” Warren said.

title: Inflation heats up again, data shows, days before midterm elections where cost of living dominates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country’s economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue.
Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains.
The economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, the Commerce Department said Thursday, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter.
Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years.
How long can this economic growth continue?
Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans’ ability to keep up. Thursday’s data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier.
As Americans splurged, the savings rate fell to 3.8% in September, its lowest level in four years, data published Thursday showed.
“High energy prices are chipping away at purchasing power,” Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote. “Real income failed to grow for a second consecutive month, while the saving rate continued to decline. Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters.”
Inflation worsens
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of the energy sector. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched.
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $4.23 on Thursday, 39% more than it cost a year ago. Diesel prices have risen much faster. While most consumers don’t buy diesel, it has an outsized impact on inflation because it is used in industrial sectors and shipping.
“The inflation outlook has become more concerning,” Bushmeneva said. “Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening.”
Polls show that rising inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks for his handling of rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon.
Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. From August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month.
Will rising inflation raise borrowing costs?
The new economic growth and inflation numbers arrive a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combating inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is now much more likely to raise its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy.
Strong growth also suggests that the Fed’s key interest rate, currently 3.9%, isn’t high enough to cool borrowing, spending, or inflation.
“If the Federal Reserve is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending, historically low jobless claims, stratospheric private non-residential investment, and sizzling inflation data,” Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax advisory firm, wrote.
Thursday’s inflation data come from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers’ shopping habits.
