title: UMaine men’s hockey defenseman has already outscored last season’s goal total
text:
As a freshman defenseman at the University of Maine last season, Loic Usereau scored two goals and five assists in 29 games.
He already has three goals through UMaine’s first six games this season.
Usereau admitted that he had a tough start last season after coming from the Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League. But his improvement so far this season prompted UMaine men’s hockey head coach Ben Barr to call Usereau a different player this year who is a stronger, quicker and better skater.
“The pace was a lot different. The skills, too. The guys were bigger, older. You had to [play] quicker,” Usereau said. “But I kind of found my game at the end and started this year with a bit more confidence and trust in my game. That has helped a lot.”
He has been paired with Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh, beginning with the optional six-week workout sessions this summer in Orono. Parekh has two goals and three assists, which gives the tandem five goals and three assists between them for the 4-2 Black Bears so far.
“It has helped a lot playing with [Parekh]. That has been lights out from the start,” Usereau said.
The feeling is mutual.
“[Loic] is a real high character, high energy,” Parekh said. “He knows what plays to make at all times. He is really dialed in.”
They are two of the team’s leaders in minutes played per game. Parekh averages 18:49 per game and Usereau is at 17:29.
The 21-year-old Usereau has always been a point-producing defenseman.
He had 29 goals and 76 assists in 190 regular season games in the QMJHL and two goals and nine assists in 18 playoff games. In his last two seasons with the Chicoutimi Sagueneens, he had 26 goals and 67 assists in 130 regular season contests.
The 6-foot, 176-pound native of Saint-Michel, Quebec, will bring a two-game goal-scoring streak into this weekend’s Hockey East series at Boston University.
He scored an important insurance goal with 5:14 remaining in last Saturday’s 3-0 win over Colgate, skating down to the low slot and one-timing a pass out from behind the net by Judah Makway.
He also scored the second goal in the previous night’s 3-0 win over Colgate with a well-screened wrist shot from the high slot.
“He can really shoot it,” Barr said. “He’s very dependable. He is super competitive. He’s smart, he has courage. He’s a great fit for us because of his character and work ethic.”
Usereau focused on the defensive aspect of his game a year ago, saying “you have to start by building some confidence from the coaching staff. And the more you have confidence, the more you can go out there and make some better plays or more creative plays to create offense.”
That foundation was established last year, said Usereau, whose two goals came in his last 11 games of 2025-26. He also had an assist during that span and was a plus-four in plus-minus. Players receive a plus-one if they are on the ice when their team scores an even-strength or shorthanded goal and a negative-one if the opponent scores one.
“I’ve been practicing with Parekh all summer and building my game,” Usereau said. “I’m trying to be a good, reliable guy on the [penalty kill] and in every situation I can play in. I’m just trusting my game and loving it.”
Senior center and alternate captain Max Scott said Usereau’s game is evolving every day.
“He is a good, puck-moving defenseman. He makes plays, he is great with his feet and, hopefully, he can keep it going here,” Scott said.
Graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said Usereau has been “playing great and brings so much to this team on and off the ice.”
Usereau loves being at UMaine, saying he thoroughly enjoys his teammates, the coaching staff and the area. He also said playing in the lively atmosphere at Alfond Arena is unreal.
“It’s a lot better than any other spot I’ve been to in this league,” Usereau said.
The Black Bears, who have made their first appearance in the top 20 in one of the two national polls this week by being ranked 19th in the U.S. College Hockey Online poll, will have their hands full against a BU team that is ranked 14th in one poll and tied for 13th in the other.
BU is 4-2 overall and 2-2 in the league. The Terriers have 18 NHL draft picks, including 11 selected in the first and second rounds.
Puck drop is at 7 p.m. on Friday and 6 p.m. on Saturday at Agganis Arena.

title: Susan Collins’ super PAC chief lobbied for a mystery group named for her hearing
text:
Scott Reed, the Republican strategist leading a super PAC spending heavily to reelect U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, was paid last year to lobby Congress on her signature issue by a group that has never said who funded it.
The group, Keeping America’s Edge, took its name from an April 2025 hearing Collins chaired on biomedical research. It formed nine days later and paid Reed’s firm and two others a combined $850,000 to lobby on funding for the National Institutes of Health, according to federal lobbying reports. It dissolved in July, telling regulators it never “commenced business.”
Nothing indicates Collins knew of the group or had a role in it, and her office said it had never heard of it until the Bangor Daily News asked questions. But the group adds to a web of ties between Collins and Reed, a longtime friend and former colleague of her husband, that has drawn scrutiny in the final weeks of her race against Democrat Troy Jackson.
Reed chairs Pine Tree Results, the super PAC that has booked nearly $32 million in ads backing Collins, according to AdImpact data. His lobbying firm, Chesapeake Enterprises, paid her husband, Tom Daffron, a consulting fee in 2025, according to her financial disclosure. Neither Reed nor Collins’ office has said what Daffron did or how much he was paid.
“There is always the risk of an appearance of a conflict of interest when a lobbying firm pays a lawmaker’s spouse, especially if the firm lobbies that lawmaker,” said Brendan Fischer of the Campaign Legal Center, a left-leaning watchdog group.
Reed has drawn complaints from watchdogs before. About a decade ago, the Campaign Legal Center accused a Reed-linked group of violating campaign finance law. Around the same time, the liberal Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington said Chesapeake had failed to file required lobbying reports.
Last month, ProPublica reported that FBI agents had examined a now-imprisoned defense contractor’s claim that Reed promised Collins would know the source of an illegal $150,000 donation to his previous pro-Collins super PAC in 2019. Collins called the report a “smear job,” defended Reed’s integrity and denied wrongdoing.
Few issues are closer to Collins than NIH funding. She founded the Senate Diabetes Caucus and the Bipartisan Congressional Task Force on Alzheimer’s Disease. Her father died with the disease in 2018. She chairs the Appropriations Committee, which writes the NIH budget, and sits on the health committee, which oversees the agency.
She has used those posts to push back on the Trump administration’s cuts to NIH research grants. She opened the April 30 hearing, titled “Biomedical Research: Keeping America’s Edge in Innovation,” by warning of proposed funding cuts, the firing of federal scientists, and policy uncertainties in the subject area.
Keeping America’s Edge was incorporated May 9. Five days later it hired Chesapeake, which listed Reed as its only lobbyist on the account and reported $250,000 for work on “NIH Funding” before the House and Senate. In June, the group added Miller Strategies, which reported $460,000, and Venture Government Strategies, which reported $140,000 and whose lobbyist Hamilton Bloom is a former Senate Appropriations subcommittee staff director. The work ended by January 2026.
While Chesapeake was lobbying for the group, Reed gave Collins’ campaign $7,000. Bloom and a Venture colleague gave Collins committees a combined $9,000 in March 2026.
The lobbying reports name no bill provision or dollar figure. Collins’ office said nothing in the Senate’s ensuing health spending bill reflected the group’s requests.
The group’s paperwork reveals little more. Its incorporation filing used language common to 501(c)(4) nonprofit groups, which can lobby without disclosing donors. It listed no directors, and its incorporator was Elliot Berke, a Republican political lawyer. It does not appear in IRS records of tax-exempt groups. Reed and Berke did not respond to requests for comment.
Now that the group has dissolved, it may never file a return showing what it spent. Federal lobbying law requires firms to disclose any outside group that helps fund and direct their work. None of the three firms listed one.
“At worst, this use of an unknown [nonprofit] is intended to hide who is actually behind the lobbying effort,” Fischer said. “I have not seen anything particularly like this.”
Berke attested in July that the group “has not commenced business” and that “no debt of the corporation remains unpaid.” That is difficult to square with lobbying reports listing the same Pennsylvania Avenue suite as the client’s address and $850,000 in fees.
Asked whether the group’s lobbyists had contacted Collins, her office or her committee staff, Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said: “None of these people lobbied our office about increasing NIH funding.” The office has long said Daffron has not lobbied anyone, including Collins, during their 14-year marriage.
The group left behind little but a name borrowed from Collins’ hearing, where she argued that cutting research money would cost the country its lead in medicine.
“We must preserve and strengthen America’s leadership for the sake of families all across this country,” she concluded in her opening remarks.

title: Trump plans for golf course are in the works, DOJ announces. What to know about the park
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that President Donald Trump’s announcements that there are plans for renovating the East Potomac Golf Course and there are plans to close the park beginning Nov. 15 are accurate.
“On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events—such as the U.S. Open” and other events.
“Thereafter, on November 15, 2026, the National Park Service will close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the Golf Course, consistent with the President’s directive,” the filing said.
The planning commission will consider the plan at its Dec. 3 meeting.
The announcement is the latest move in a 10-day period that started with a social media posting by Trump Oct. 18 that the park would be closed Nov. 15 for the next 15 months while the park undergoes renovation into what the president has called a world-class facility.
Trump’s social media postings touched off a series of court hearings in the lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League and two golfers challenging the plans. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction Oct. 26, due in part to the discrepancy between the president’s public announcements and the testimony from various National Park Service, Interior Department and Justice Department officials who testified that they had no knowledge of the plans Trump was announcing.
The current preliminary injunction temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
Reyes was planning another hearing to bring officials back to court to explain why the president continued to announce plans that officials said they had no knowledge of.
Wednesday’s filing explained that the National Park Service entered into a new lease agreement with the National Links Trust — the company currently responsible for operating the East Potomac Golf Course — under which the National Links Trust will cease operating the East Potomac Golf Course as of the close of business on or before Nov. 15, but will continue to operate two other public golf courses.
Trump’s social media posts on the renovation of the historic golf course had put Justice Department lawyers in the uncomfortable position of explaining whether the president of the United States should be believed or not.
On Tuesday, Reyes said the department should clarify “whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026.” She ordered Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. to appear in court Friday or Monday for a status hearing. On Wednesday, she then issued an order for Woodward to appear on Friday, along with at least one person from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor “with pre-existing experience on this case.”
Tuesday’s order came in response to Trump’s social media post late Monday criticizing Reyes’ temporary injunction stopping work at East Potomac Park.
That injunction, issued Monday, was in large part due to previous Trump announcements — via social media — that plans had been completed for the golf course and construction would begin next month. Trump said the facility would be closed for 15 months. The following day he set the timetable to “immediately.”
Much of the activity in the court has accelerated this month, after the government gave the plaintiffs in the case short notice on plans to cut down hundreds of trees at the course.
The plaintiffs challenging the project claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. Critics say Trump’s plan will make playing there unaffordable for the general public and destroy the site’s other uses.
In a Wednesday night posting on Truth Social, Trump called the golf course “highly dangerous, dilapidated, and absolutely disgusting.” He added that Reyes would be held responsible for anyone injured or killed at the course.
“No one will be more thrilled by our plans to renovate the Course and Driving Range than the Local Golfers who have played there for years, and have begged to have their Home Course brought into pristine condition,” he wrote.
The course renovation project is part of Trump’s aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape.
Those plans include construction of a huge ballroom at the White House, a massive arch and the creation of a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. The DC Preservation League is part of a coalition of organizations, including the Cultural Landscape Foundation and one D.C. resident, who have filed lawsuits challenging those plans.
There are several cases where judges have taken actions and issued injunctions or restraining orders because of the Trump administration’s push to begin work despite the pending lawsuits.
The golf course is one of two major and controversial projects with imminent starting dates in court this week.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan will hold a hearing Friday on a motion from plaintiffs in a lawsuit asking she call a temporary halt to plans to begin construction as early as Friday on the arch in the Memorial Circle. The arch is opposed by a small group of veterans and an architectural historian who sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. Chutkan had already said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to or in preparation for construction of the arch. The administration has announced plans to begin construction as early as Nov. 5, pending the approval of the construction by the National Capital Planning Commission.
Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex.”
Although plans submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission did not include defensive structures, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin submitted court filings Wednesday supporting the president’s comments that the defense structures would help combat the threat of drones.
The lawsuit Chutkan is overseeing is one of two filed challenging the construction of the arch. Earlier this month, the Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit opposing the construction, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against Trump’s planned monument.
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process.

title: At his Auburn Mall event, Bobby Charles wanted to be challenged. Here’s how it went.
text:
AUBURN — Many of those who gathered at the Auburn Mall on Thursday evening wore red shirts with Bobby Charles’ name on the front.
But the campaign stop for the Republican governor nominee wasn’t a rally — it was an invitation for open debate with Charles.
Several attendees did, in face-to-face, one-on-one conversations.
It was an event clearly crafted in the style of Jubilee’s widely watched “Surrounded” series — a made-for-social media production, with audience members voting out fellow question-askers with raised red flags if, after a few minutes of debate, their arguments didn’t land quite well enough.
In practice, though, Charles went on minuteslong monologues, often taking detours from questions to draw applause from the friendly crowd with comments like “and we will not have boys in girls’ sports” in response to questions about community college funding. Many of the conversations were friendly to Charles’ politics — including the final conversation, between Charles and Maine Wire personality Jon Fetherston.
Some of the conversations, though, shed some interesting light. Here were three of the most telling chats from the event.
THE ONE-ISSUE VOTER
The third person to step up, Margaret Rinaldi, of Wales, told Charles she had a miscarriage the morning of the release of the 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson U.S. Supreme Court decision — the one that overturned Roe v. Wade and returned control of abortion restrictions to the states.
Rinaldi said she had a second miscarriage recently and told Charles she was a “one-issue voter,” and that reproductive rights were her one issue.
“This is what Maine needs,” Charles said. “This is an earnest, honest, heartfelt conversation about something that matters.”
Charles reiterated his position that late-term abortion — which he declined to define — was unacceptable. And he said he would support exceptions to that rule if the life of the mother was in danger, or in cases of rape or incest.
And then he continued on a several-minutes-long speech about lagging state reimbursements for hospitals, which he said have caused the closure of birthing centers across the state under Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat he’s often linked with his opponent, Hannah Pingree.
Eventually, he got to the topic of recruiting healthcare professionals to the state. In doing so, he said he wants to forgive the student loans of nurses as one way to attract them to stay in Maine. An interesting exchange followed.
“You’re going to do that even though (President Donald) Trump says they’re not professional degrees?” Rinaldi asked, referring to a provision of the president’s signature legislation last year that capped student loans for certain degrees, including nursing.
“I really don’t care what Trump says,” Charles responded.
“This is the first time I’ve heard you not glaze him, and I’m very, very appreciative of that,” Rinaldi said.
TACKLING RACISM
Emily Angela, 29, lives in Lewiston and works at Central Maine Medical Center. As a Black woman, she said she has been a victim of racism regularly in Maine — in personal relationships, in looks at the grocery store and in her workplace.
In a state that’s nearly all-white, she said, the R next to Charles’ name carries with it a reputation for being insensitive, or worse, openly racist.
“How can I know, when I go and vote, that you will stand up to racism and that Black people in the state, even though there aren’t many of us, we can look at Bobby Charles and say, ‘Hey, he has our back?'” Angela asked.
Charles decried race-based attacks in his lengthy response, and said there is “no basis, ever, ever, ever, for racism in the state of Maine.”
“I think we could do a lot better when it comes to this issue,” Charles said. “Here you are, a wonderful contributor to the community, just like probably all the people here. And you’re saying, ‘Treat me fairly. Treat me justly. Treat me kindly. Because I’m exactly like you.'”
The conversation, which Charles again dominated, ended with a hug on stage.
The very next debater up, a Charles supporter, asked Charles about fraud in Maine, which state Republicans have largely pinned on “New Mainers” or Somali immigrants — a group at the center of racial tensions in Lewiston, especially.
FLAGS UP
Stacy Dostie, a 60-year-old independent from Sabattus, was the only debater to be flagged off her perch by the crowd.
Dostie, perhaps not coincidentally, also pushed back hardest of anyone against Charles.
Dostie challenged something Charles had said earlier in the night — that he hoped to dismantle Maine’s departments of Education and Health and Human Services to find fraud and eliminate inefficiencies.
“Now, that is out of the Trump playbook,” Dostie said. “That’s what he’s trying to do. And, in my opinion, it isn’t working very well.”
Charles, who had previously said Dostie was “exactly the kind of person I want in that chair,” answered by recounting his time in the federal government, working under former Secretary of State Colin Powell, who had assigned him to find efficiencies in diplomatic work all over the world, Charles said. He said he would find experts to help better understand where those cuts could be made most efficiently.
Eventually, Dostie interrupted. And after further discussion on community college, she interrupted again.
“You’re talking about putting a lot of commissions together and a lot of committees to look at things,” she said. “What about action?”
“I will be measured by action,” Charles responded.
A few minutes later, Dostie was voted off the stage by the audience.

title: Maine to receive nearly $3M in multi-state data privacy settlement with General Motors
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to states following a lawsuit alleging the company mishandled customer data. Maine is set to receive nearly $3 million.
A coalition of 36 Attorneys General, including Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, claims General Motors sold data tracking the customer’s driving habits to third parties and data brokers who then sold the data to insurance companies using its Smart Driver product.
As part of the settlement, General Motors is required to get explicit consent from customers before sharing their data.
A spokesperson for General Motors said in a statement to WABI, “This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices. Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”

title: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
text:
AUDUBON, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck.
Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling.
Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene.
The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries.
Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

title: Inflation heats up again, data shows, days before midterm elections where cost of living dominates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country’s economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue.
Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains.
The economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, the Commerce Department said Thursday, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter.
Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years.
How long can this economic growth continue?
Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans’ ability to keep up. Thursday’s data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier.
As Americans splurged, the savings rate fell to 3.8% in September, its lowest level in four years, data published Thursday showed.
“High energy prices are chipping away at purchasing power,” Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote. “Real income failed to grow for a second consecutive month, while the saving rate continued to decline. Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters.”
Inflation worsens
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of the energy sector. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched.
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $4.23 on Thursday, 39% more than it cost a year ago. Diesel prices have risen much faster. While most consumers don’t buy diesel, it has an outsized impact on inflation because it is used in industrial sectors and shipping.
“The inflation outlook has become more concerning,” Bushmeneva said. “Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening.”
Polls show that rising inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks for his handling of rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon.
Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. From August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month.
Will rising inflation raise borrowing costs?
The new economic growth and inflation numbers arrive a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combating inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is now much more likely to raise its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy.
Strong growth also suggests that the Fed’s key interest rate, currently 3.9%, isn’t high enough to cool borrowing, spending, or inflation.
“If the Federal Reserve is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending, historically low jobless claims, stratospheric private non-residential investment, and sizzling inflation data,” Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax advisory firm, wrote.
Thursday’s inflation data come from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers’ shopping habits.

title: Colorado QB Julian Lewis taken to hospital after medical emergency, father says
text:
Colorado QB Julian Lewis taken to hospital after medical emergency at school's athletic facility, father says
Colorado backup quarterback Julian “JuJu” Lewis suffered a medical emergency at the school's athletic facility on Wednesday and was taken to the hospital, his father said on social media.
T. Carlton Lewis posted in a statement on the platform X on Thursday morning that Lewis was “recovering and thankful to his medical team, teammates, and Colorado fans for their prayers and support.”
He added: “Please respect Julian and the Lewis family’s privacy.” No other information was provided.
Colorado issued a statement saying the school “extends our full support to JuJu and his family through this medical emergency.
“He remains in the thoughts of every CU player, coach, and staff member and we will continue to assist in any way we can in his full recovery,” the statement said. “His health and well-being remain our top priority during this time.”
Julian Lewis' teammate, wide receiver Joseph Williams, also posted about Lewis on social media: “Praying for you 10 I love you man God has your back twin."
Williams said in another post: "Y’all are so quick to judge us but don’t know what we may go through, athletes mental health matters also!!! God bless everyone.”
A highly touted recruit, Lewis, who's in his second year at Colorado, opened the season as the starter before coach Deion Sanders turned the offense over to Isaac Wilson. Lewis has thrown for 733 yards and six touchdowns this season, along with two interceptions.
Lewis turned in a record-setting afternoon against Weber State last month when he threw four touchdown passes in the first half and ran for another.
Colorado plays Kansas State on Saturday.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17 billion acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump’s pressure
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.
As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.
Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.
Trump’s pressure campaign hasn’t worked
Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT.”
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”
An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year.”
The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump’s pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.
Previous laws have been repealed
In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.
An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year-round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.
“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”

title: Letter to the Editor: How Low can a Party go?
Op-ed: Turning Maine into a hub for advanced manufacturing
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When the federal government announced its $450 million investment in the Portland-based Elmet Group Co. (Nasdaq: ELMT), it signaled something bigger than one company’s success. Maine manufacturers possess capabilities essential to our economy and national security.
The investment supports domestic tungsten production and processing, helping reduce dependence on foreign sources for materials used in defense, aerospace and other critical industries. It also demonstrates what is possible when specialized manufacturing capabilities align with national priorities.
The Manufacturers Association of Maine recently named Elmet Technologies our 2026 Manufacturer of the Year. That recognition is well deserved. But Elmet’s success also raises an important question: How can we create more opportunities across Maine’s manufacturing community?
Many Maine manufacturers quietly produce precision components, advanced materials and specialized equipment for customers around the world. Small and midsize companies are especially important. They may never receive investments of Elmet’s magnitude, but they can benefit through new customers, supplier relationships and access to emerging markets.
We are already seeing what coordinated efforts can accomplish.
The University of Maine-led Forest Bioproducts Advanced Manufacturing Tech Hub received $20 million in federal funding to advance innovation, commercialization and workforce development. It builds on Maine’s forest products heritage while creating opportunities for higher-value manufacturing.
Meanwhile, the Maine Space Corporation is working to develop a space economy, with potential opportunities in aerospace manufacturing, satellite technologies and supporting infrastructure. Emerging autonomous systems operating in the air, on land and at sea could open additional markets for Maine suppliers.
These sectors may seem unrelated, but they rely on many of the same strengths: precision manufacturing, advanced materials, electronics, engineering, testing and skilled workers.
Building on Maine’s strengths
Maine already has a strong foundation in defense manufacturing, precision machining, advanced materials, shipbuilding and specialized technologies. From major defense contractors to small, highly specialized manufacturers supplying critical components, our state possesses capabilities that support some of the nation’s most demanding industries.
Combined with our research institutions, workforce development programs and infrastructure, these assets provide a foundation for something much larger.
A statewide advanced manufacturing hub does not have to mean a single building or industrial park. It can mean a network that makes it easier for manufacturers to find local suppliers, collaborate with researchers, access testing facilities and develop their workforce.
Imagine a small machine shop discovering that its capabilities fit an aerospace supply chain, or a manufacturer finding a Maine partner instead of sourcing a component out of state. Imagine approaching federal agencies and investors with a clear picture of Maine’s collective capabilities rather than a series of disconnected proposals.
This approach should complement, not compete with, the initiatives already underway. It should also strengthen relationships among Maine manufacturers, because business development within our own state matters just as much as attracting opportunities from elsewhere.
None of this happens automatically. Manufacturers need reliable and affordable energy, access to capital, modern infrastructure and workers with the right skills. Some companies are deploying sophisticated automation; others are just beginning to modernize. Our strategy must create pathways for both.
Expanding capabilities
At MAME, we see an opportunity to help connect manufacturers, educators, researchers and economic development partners around shared priorities. The goal is not to create another silo. It is to make existing efforts more effective by working together.
Elmet’s investment deserves celebration. So do the forest bioproducts and space economy initiatives taking shape across Maine. Their greater promise lies in what we can build by connecting them.
Maine does not need to start from scratch. We need to connect, support and expand the capabilities we already have. Put another way, Maine has the building blocks of an advanced manufacturing hub. It’s now time to connect them.

title: Two people injured after fire in Harpswell; home destroyed
text:
Two people injured after fire in Harpswell; home destroyed
Several town fire departments responded to the fire
Two people injured after fire in Harpswell; home destroyed
Several town fire departments responded to the fire
Two people were sent to the hospital with burn injuries after a fire at a home in Harpswell Thursday morning. 
Several town fire departments, including Harpswell, Brunswick and West Bath, responded to the fire at 22 Smokehouse Road. Officials say the call came in around 4 a.m.
According to responding fire crews, four people were at the home and two were taken to the hospital to be treated for burn injuries. One of the occupants had to jump out of a second-story window to escape the flames.
The fire destroyed the single-family home and also spread to the nearby woods. Crews were able to get the flames under control by around 6:30 a.m. but were still working to put out hot spots.
The state fire marshal's office is now heading to the scene to investigate. Officials say it's too early to determine a cause; the homeowner believes the fire started in a stairwell.
There are no road closures associated with the response, but due to the narrow nature of the roads in the area and the size of the response, drivers should use caution.

title: ‘I rape little girls like you’: Former councilman arrested after allegedly making terrorist threats at Hooters
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A former Alabama city councilman was charged after allegedly making terrorist threats at a Hooters, according to authorities.
Former Mobile City Council member William Carroll, 56, was arrested Wednesday night on two counts of second-degree making terrorist threats.
Mobile police said the incident stems from an encounter on Oct. 14.
Officers responded to Hooters after receiving reports of a man making inappropriate and threatening comments toward an employee.
According to a Mobile County District Court complaint, Carroll told an employee, “I rape little girls like you,” and “I dig ditches and kill people before.” The complaint said the employee feared for her safety.
Another complaint said Carroll told a second employee, “I kill people for a living and rape little girls like her.”
Police said officers arrived and issued a trespass warning to Carroll.
Carroll was booked into the Mobile County Metro Jail shortly before 8 p.m. Wednesday.
Each charge carries a $3,000 bond. He was released shortly after 9 p.m. and has a bond hearing scheduled for Friday.

title: NICU nurse creates handmade Halloween costumes for babies
text:
'Really heartwarming': NICU nurse creates handmade Halloween costumes for babies
Families at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, are celebrating Halloween with handmade costumes for their babies, thanks to the efforts of NICU nurse Riley Smolksy.
Baby Ezra, born Monday at just 33 weeks, wore his first Halloween costume inspired by his big sister.
"Ezra's older sister is obsessed with Elmo, and she got to meet him yesterday, and she kept saying, 'Baby Elmo, baby Elmo,' so we’re really excited for him to be dressed up as Elmo for Halloween here,” said Ezra’s parents, David and Megan Schmiech.
Elmo was one of around 80 costumes Smolksy created with help from her mother, friends and Duquesne University's women's club soccer team.
"This is the first time we have an individual costume for every single baby, so we’re going to go around and give some out and hang out with families and parents and get to give them a little bit of normalcy around the holiday while they’re spending time in the NICU,” Smolksy said.
The costumes included creative options like candy bars and ketchup and mustard for twins, catering to babies of all sizes.
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
Owen, born 11 weeks early, celebrated his first Halloween dressed as a hot dog.
"The fact that the team was able to do that here is really heartwarming. It makes us feel like they’re a part of our family, which is really nice,” said Owen’s mothers, Sarah and Zoe Kreinberg.
For Smolksy, the effort was about brightening the families’ days.
“I think doing stuff like this maybe makes their dark days a little bit brighter,” she said.
Smolksy, who has been a nurse for six years, also creates keepsakes to mark the babies’ milestones, giving families something to take home from their time in the NICU.

title: Grand opening of Atlas Structural Systems Manufacturing
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON, ME – U.S. Senator Susan Collins attended the grand opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony for Atlas Structural Systems’ new manufacturing facility in Lewiston. The company, a subsidiary of J.D. Irving, Limited, has transformed the former Steel Service Center property into its first U.S. manufacturing facility. The 44,000-square-foot plant employs approximately 45 people and produces prefabricated building components for construction projects throughout the region.
“This is an exciting new chapter for manufacturing in Lewiston. By bringing new life to a longtime industrial property, Atlas Structural Systems is creating jobs for Mainers and strengthening our state’s manufacturing economy,” said Senator Collins. “I was pleased to join company leaders and members of the Lewiston-Auburn community to celebrate this important investment in the region’s future.”
Atlas Structural Systems operates 11 production facilities in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Canada. The Lewiston facility designs and manufactures engineered trusses and prefabricated walls, floors, and stair panels.

title: Letter: Matt Dunlap is right choice to protect Maine’s environment
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
If you are an outdoor enthusiast, please join me in voting for Matt Dunlap. I believe he is an outstanding individual who has dedicated his career to doing what is right for the people of Maine and the country.
Matt co-chaired the Legislature’s Inland Fish and Wildlife Committee while I was commissioner of the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife. He is a skilled statesman, working
effectively between parties to achieve important goals. During that period, I watched him take the lead on a wide variety of initiatives, such as improved hunting and fishing opportunities for
Mainers of all ages, with special new programs for youth. He supported land conservation by the Land for Maine’s Future Program (LMF), ensuring public access and protecting wildlife
habitat. He helped to develop the lifetime hunting-and-fishing license program as well as the current moose lottery system.
Most important, he ensured that the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife was on a firm financial footing. These are just a few of his many achievements.
From an environmental perspective, the years under Gov. Paul LePage’s leadership were a disaster. He hobbled LMF, the most popular land conservation program in the state, and he emasculated the Department of Environmental Protection, the agency responsible for ensuring a clean, healthy environment.
Is LePage the person we want to send to Washington to stave off President Donald Trump’s multiple attacks on the nation’s environment? A resounding no from me!
Please join me in supporting Matt Dunlap, an honorable man who will fight for a healthy environment, as he represents us in the U.S. Congress.
Bucky Owen
Orono

title: Maine high school football playoffs begin this weekend
text:
The high school football playoffs begin in four classes this weekend while two other classes wind up their regular season schedules.
The quarterfinal round of the playoffs will take place in Class B and D and the semifinal games will be contested in Eight-Player Large and Small. Meanwhile, Class A and C play their final regular season games leading up to their playoff openers next weekend.
In Class A North, the 4-3 Bangor High School Rams, led by quarterback Alex Tennett and explosive slot back Gavin Hughes, will entertain 6-1 Oxford Hills/Buckfield at Cameron Stadium at 7 p.m. Friday.
This is likely to be a preview of the A North semifinals the following week in South Paris.
Oxford Hills/Buckfield — sparked by the Ridley twins, Keegan and Mason — is the top seed and Bangor is the No. 4 seed. That is unlikely to change, although a Bangor victory could move the Rams up to third, especially if No. 3 Windham, 5-3, gets upset by 1-7 Deering of Portland.
Bangor upset Oxford Hills/Buckfield in the semifinals a year ago, 35-6, a week after Oxford Hills/Buckfield dealt Bangor a 34-7 regular season loss.
Portland, 6-2, is the No. 2 seed and will travel to play a 4-4 South Portland team that needs a win to qualify for the A South playoffs.
In Class C, top seed and undefeated 8-0 Leavitt High of Turner, coming off its most competitive game of the season, a 14-10 win at Hermon, will entertain a Foxcroft Academy team that has won seven in a row following a season-opening 24-0 loss to Hermon.
Hermon, now 6-2 after back-to-back losses to defending state C champ Greely High of Cumberland Center (28-14) and Leavitt, will wrap up its regular season with a 6 p.m. kickoff at York on Friday. York is 3-5 and has won three of its last four, although two of them were against non-playoff teams Brewer and Hampden Academy.
In Class B North playoff games, fifth seed Messalonskee of Oakland will travel to take on No. 4 Fryeburg Academy in a battle of 4-4 teams with the winner traveling to play top seed Lawrence of Fairfield the following week. Messalonskee beat Fryeburg Academy during the regular season, 28-20.
In the other quarterfinal, 2-6 Brunswick will trek to 5-3 Skowhegan with the winner advancing to take on No. 2 Cony High of Augusta. Skowhegan edged Brunswick 19-17 during the regular season in Skowhegan.
In Class D North, 2-6 Madison, the fifth seed, will make the trip to Lincoln to take on fourth seed Mattanawcook Academy (3-5). The victor will take on top seed Winslow. Madison and Mattanawcook Academy didn’t play each other during the regular season.
In the other quarterfinal, 1-7 Oak Hill of Sabattus, the sixth seed, will visit the 4-4 John Bapst of Bangor/Bangor Christian/Central of Corinth with the winner meeting second seed Maine Central Institute of Pittsfield.
John Bapst won the regular season meeting with Oak Hill, 26-12.
In the Eight Player Large North division, the No. 4 Houlton co-op team, 1-7, will tangle with host and top seed Old Town, 7-1, and Hancock County rivals Ellsworth/Sumner (4-4) and Mount Desert Island (5-3) will square off in Bar Harbor. Old Town beat Houlton 72-18, and MDI owns a 50-20 win over Ellsworth/Sumner.
In Eight-Player Small North, defending state champ Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin, 8-0 and the No. 1 seed, will entertain 3-4 Bucksport, the fourth seed, and No. 2 Orono (3-4) will await No. 3 Washington Academy of East Machias (5-2).
Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin topped Bucksport 42-12, while Orono and Washington Academy did not play during the regular season.

title: Do wildlife crossings save money and reduce car-vs.-animal crashes?
text:
Yes.
Research shows wildlife overpasses and underpasses, typically paired with fencing, can sharply reduce crashes and save money over time.
Parks Canada reports that at Canada’s Banff National Park, highway fencing and 44 crossings have reduced wildlife-vehicle collisions by more than 80%, including more than 96% for deer and elk.
A Washington State University study of 13 crossings estimated $235,000 to $443,000 in annual benefits per structure from avoided collisions.
The Federal Highway Administration found that crossing systems can cost society less than allowing crashes to continue. Savings depend on location, construction costs and wildlife activity.
Nationwide, federal transportation officials estimate wildlife collisions cause about 200 human deaths and 26,000 injuries annually, costing more than $10 billion.
Maine is building a wildlife crossing beneath Route 1 in Caribou. Local police and game wardens estimate at least 12 wildlife collisions annually there. Work is scheduled to finish by spring 2027.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

- Federal Highway Administration: Wildlife-Vehicle Collision Reduction Study: Report To Congress

title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
text:
Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.
Researchers from the California Institute of Technology compared the chemical composition of smoke from the Eaton Fire with that of a wildfire and found that the urban plume had more lead, arsenic and halogens (which include chlorine and bromine) linked to burning vehicles, building materials and electronics.
Related content above: Satellites to provide faster wildfire detection by 2030
“The main, key finding is really that wildfire smoke is very different fundamentally from the urban smoke,” said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, an author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. With the new technology they used to measure what was in the smoke, they were able to “actually see the very detailed component of these particles that we are breathing.”
Co-author Haroula Baliaka said understanding the different chemical compositions of smoke from an urban versus a wildland fire helps bridge a missing gap in research. Wildfires are growing larger, more intense, faster-moving and more frequent largely because of drier and warmer weather associated with human-caused climate change. As urban growth and climate change push more fires into cities, researchers said monitoring and emergency response will have to adapt.
Ed Avol, professor emeritus in the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California who has researched the health effects of air pollution for decades, said significant exposure to heavy metals is consistent with what he'd expect, “but certainly surprising because we haven’t been able to document this sort of thing.”
“One of the real advantages of this study is that it had the opportunity to make measurements sort of hour-by-hour across the sampling network. And typically we make measurements of airborne particulates and so forth a couple of times a week, at best,” said Avol, who wasn’t involved in the study.
Thousands of structures burned, releasing toxic chemicals
The two wind-whipped infernos in Altadena and the Pacific Palisades that ignited on Jan. 7, 2025, killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 structures, mostly homes, and everything in them — cars, paint, furniture, chemicals under sinks and more. Millions of people were exposed to smoke, which across the entire United States has been linked to tens of thousands of deaths annually. A recent study found that metal mixtures in the leftover smoke, ash and debris from the deadly 2023 Maui wildfires were harmful to the lung health of people living nearby long after the burning ended.
During the fires, researchers measured trace elements of fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, reported by instruments every hour in the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork (ASCENT), a relatively new network of air quality monitors across the U.S. that measures the size and chemical composition of these particulates in real time. Ng said ASCENT is the U.S.'s first measurement network able to measure the chemical composition of airborne particles in real time.
Researchers were able to see what chemicals were in the smoke, track how its composition changed over the fire's course, and distinguish emissions coming from burning structures. From there, they estimated how many people across Los Angeles were exposed to the heavy metals, particularly lead, during the fire's first days.
They compared the typical value of lead before the fires and the chemical makeup of smoke from a 2024 fire in Riverside County that burned mostly vegetation with data from the Eaton Fire plume. Contrasted with the wildfire smoke, the plume from the LA fire contained 50 times more lead, three times more arsenic, and seven times more halogens. At the peak of burning, about 7 million people were exposed for 24 hours to lead levels more than 80 times what's typical.
Lead is a neurotoxin that can stunt children’s development, lower IQ scores and increase blood pressure in adults. Scientists still don’t know how short-term, high exposure to lead impacts human health. Arsenic exposure is associated with various cancers.
Yaguang Wei, assistant professor in the department of environmental medicine at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who researches the health impacts of air pollution, wildfire smoke and severe weather, said their findings reinforced some conclusions of a recent study he co-authored that found, in part, that PM2.5 from wildfire smoke was more toxic than particulates from other sources.
“I think their findings are not surprising,” said Wei, who was not involved in the study. When fires burn properties, they're also burning “a lot of lead on your wall paint and the plastics and electronics and those are very toxic” when they burn, he said.
Monitoring, policies and emergency response need to adapt, experts say
Wei said the study has “important policy implications.” He thinks governments should take stronger actions to protect public health during these fires by investing in more wildfire monitoring and public alerts, and having more prescribed fires.
For Avol, the study is a reminder of our “strange and increasingly dangerous new world” where urban and wildland intersect — and increasingly catch fire.
“It reminds us to be cautious and be concerned and, you know, think about what we can do to minimize this. We’re not going to stop using all these materials containing metals and halogens and so forth in our homes,” he said. “How do we protect people from being exposed to that?”

title: Midterms 2026: The Balance of Power
text:
Midterms 2026: The Balance of Power
In the final stretch before the 2026 midterms, the fight for control of Congress is coming down to the wire. Here's what's at stake if Republicans or Democrats take control.
Midterms 2026: The Balance of Power
In the final stretch before the 2026 midterms, the fight for control of Congress is coming down to the wire. Here's what's at stake if Republicans or Democrats take control.
The 2026 midterm elections will determine the balance of power in Congress, with Democrats seeking to flip both the House and Senate in a high-stakes battle that could reshape President Donald Trump's legislative agenda.
Where the balance of power currently stands
Currently, Republicans hold majorities in both chambers, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 seats in the House.
Several political experts say Democrats have a chance at flipping one, if not both, chambers, though the extent of their gains remains uncertain.
All 435 House seats, which are up for election every two years, are up for grabs. In the Senate, 35 seats with 6-year terms are on the ballot this year.
What history shows
An analysis from the Get the Facts Data Team shows that the president's party often loses political power in midterm elections, with the House flipping five out of the last nine midterms. Analysts predict this year will be no different.
"The real question isn't whether the Democrats are going to take the House of Representatives. The real question is: are we going to get that big blue wave where they sweep into both the House and the Senate?" political analyst Todd Belt said. "Projections now are looking like the Democrats are going to get 15 or even more seats in the House of Representatives, and the Senate is well within their reach."
While the Senate has only changed control three times in the last nine midterms, according to the Get the Facts Data Team, Democrats need to gain four seats and hold battleground states like Michigan, Georgia, and New Hampshire to secure a majority.
Where the midterms stand
Rising voter frustration over inflation and the ongoing war in Iran are also pushing Democrats to target traditionally Republican states such as Texas and Alaska. President Trump has been actively campaigning in Republican strongholds to bolster turnout among his base.
"Donald Trump is going to places he has no business going to," Belt said. "He shouldn't have to campaign in Alaska or Texas because those are pretty red states. The reason he's going there is because he wants to boost the turnout from the people that are naturally likely to support him, but just might not turn up this election because of how they're feeling about the economy."
What's at stake
The balance of power in Congress will determine what gets done on Capitol Hill and what President Trump can accomplish with his agenda.
If Democrats take the House, they will gain control over committee investigations and federal spending bills. In the Senate, they would oversee the approval of the president's nominations for cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and ambassadors.
However, analysts warn that a divided government could lead to increased political gridlock.
Even if Democrats take the Senate, Belt warns they're unlikely to secure the 60 votes needed to pass most bills and overcome a filibuster. They would also fall short of the two-thirds majority required to override a presidential veto.
"We only had one major piece of legislation in this past Congress. That was the One Big Beautiful Bill," Belt said. "I don't think we're going to get any major pieces of legislation. We'll be lucky to keep the government funded if we see the Democrats have one or two of those chambers, and Donald Trump on the other side."

title: Maine Hospice Council ceases operations
text:
AUGUSTA — After careful consideration and extensive evaluation of available resources, the Maine Hospice Council Board members have made the difficult decision to cease operations and close the organization effective Oct. 17.
Referring to her one-on-one work with people, public speaking and consulting, MHC Executive Director Kandyce Powell, RN, MSN said, “I will continue to be available to anyone searching for hospice and end-of-life care resources at either 207-882-4032 or KandycePowell65@gmail.com.”
Over the past 35 years, the MHC has worked to advance the mission of promoting universal access to quality end-of-life and palliative care through innovation, creativity, education, advocacy and collaboration. The organization has been a leader in advocating for, training and educating providers and communities about hospice and palliative care.
All of the Council’s work has been grounded in identified needs. Leadership and staff listened to community members-including healthcare providers-to identify needs and gaps in end-of-life and serious illness care, in order to develop meaningful programs.
This approach guided extensive outreach to underserved and disenfranchised populations, including financial support, development and education for the Maine State Prison’s comprehensive Hospice and Palliative Care Program.
Notable initiatives over 35 years including, but not limited to, policy development; program development such as the Hospice Veteran Partnership and the Maine Pain Initiative; community listening sessions; international human rights presentations and program collaborations; successful grant writing, including support through the Robert Wood Johnson Community/State Partnership; and serving as a host site for numerous academic interns, doctoral students and other learners.
Throughout its years of operation, the MHC has been honored to collaborate with donors, volunteers, staff, community partners and supporters who make this important work possible.
“I acknowledge the dedicated work of the Council for all of the years under the leadership of Executive Director Kandyce Powell. The Council has been able to provide services to Maine people because of Kandyce’s commitment and perseverance,” MHC Board President Alicia Murray, DNP, MSN, RN, CHPN said
“This decision was not made lightly,” Murray added. “We are incredibly proud of the impact our organization has made and deeply grateful to everyone who supported our mission. While closing our doors is difficult, we celebrate the lives touched, the relationships built and the lasting contributions made to our community.”
The Maine Hospice Council extends its heartfelt appreciation to its employees, volunteers, board members, donors, grant foundations, community partners and the individuals and families it has served. Their commitment and support enabled the organization to pursue its mission for more than 40 years.
Although the MHC is closing, the values and impact of its work will continue through the individuals, organizations and communities that carry the mission of quality end-of-life care forward.

title: ‘Dune 3’s Popcorn Bucket Is Even Crazier Than ‘Dune 2’s
text:
The ‘Dune 3’ Popcorn Bucket Is Even Crazier Than the ‘Dune 2’ One
The whole collectible (and/or outlandish) popcorn bucket trend in movie theaters all started with the sandworm bucket for Dune: Part Two. The mad scientists who create these things stuck a gaping sandworm maw on top of a popcorn bucket and created a viral sensation.
Just about every blockbuster in its wake for the last two years has tried to top it. So you knew that Dune: Part Three would have to go very hard to compete with franchise precedent. How do you outdo a giant tub of popcorn with a spiny alien orifice on top?
How about two spiny alien orifices?
As just revealed on the film’s official social media channels, there will be a Dune: Part Three popcorn bucket with two sandworms (his and hers!) on the lid. AMC Theatres also has an option that appears to be battery-powered, with only one sandworm plus a working copy of the gadget that pounds on the sands of Arrakis to summon the sandworms.
READ MORE: The Wildest Movie Theater Popcorn Buckets Ever
Not to be outdone, Regal Cinemas will have their own proprietary popcorn bucket for the film as well. Theirs is shaped like a Spacing Guild Navigator. If shoving your arm into a sandworm does not sound appealing, well, this is an alternate option.
Dune: Part Three opens in theaters on December 18, the same day as the fall’s other biggest blockbuster, Avengers: Doomsday. Which means the gauntlet has officially been thrown down here. The ball is now in your court, Marvel. You’ve got to give the people what they want, Kevin Feige. Can you make a popcorn bucket with three weird orifices on it???

title: St. Mary’s Steps for Hope raises $100K for behavioral healthcare
text:
LEWISTON, ME – St. Mary’s Health System raised more than $100,000 through its Steps for Hope Run/Walk 5K on Sunday, October 11, to support behavioral health services and improve access to care for people in the community.
Held at Bates College in Lewiston, the event brought together runners, walkers and community supporters to raise awareness and funds for behavioral healthcare at St. Mary’s.
“Steps for Hope is a powerful example of what can happen when a community comes together around a shared need,” said Win Brown, president of St. Mary’s Health System. “The support behind this event helps us continue expanding access to behavioral healthcare and building stronger connections across the care we provide.”
Behavioral health is part of a broader continuum of care at St. Mary’s that includes emergency care, medical and surgical services, primary and specialty care, and long-term and post-acute care. Over the past year, St. Mary’s has expanded its behavioral health services through the introduction of partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient programs, a Behavioral Health Home, increased treatment capacity and additional support for adolescents and adults who need care beyond traditional outpatient appointments.
Funds raised through Steps for Hope will support behavioral health programs and services for children, adolescents and adults at St. Mary’s.

title: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history.
With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms.
“It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University.
Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars.
Texas now holds the record for the most expensive nonpresidential race in U.S. history, with more than $560 million in political advertising spending and reservations, according to AdImpact.
Ohio’s Senate race has also surpassed $500 million, making it one of only three nonpresidential races to reach that milestone. The third was Ohio’s 2024 Senate contest.
Republicans have maintained an advantage in political advertising, spending approximately $5.18 billion this election cycle, compared with $4.77 billion for Democrats, according to AdImpact.
The Republican National Committee has also emphasized its intention to deploy its available resources before Election Day.
“There’s no saving money for a rainy day. Whatever we can get that can be deployed is going to be deployed,” RNC chief of staff Mike Ambrosini told The New York Times.
Democrats, meanwhile, have pointed to grassroots fundraising as evidence of enthusiasm among their supporters.
“When you have hundreds of thousands of contributors who are giving 5, 10, 15 dollars, they’re very excited. That is one indicator of enthusiasm,” Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said.
While both parties rely on smaller contributions, some of the largest financial commitments have come from billionaire donors.
Elon Musk has contributed nearly $450 million to Republican causes during the election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission.
By comparison, two of the largest Democratic megadonors, George Soros and Michael Bloomberg, have contributed approximately $102 million and $84 million, respectively.
Despite the Republican financial advantage, Belt told Gray Media’s Washington Bureau the election could offer a test of whether money or political messaging proves more influential.
“It’s almost a perfect natural experiment, where the Republicans have the money and the Democrats have the voice against the administration,” he said.
And while money alone may not determine the outcome, Belt said a lack of advertising could prove costly in close races.
“If you allow your side to go dark at the end of the campaign, you might miss out on a few of those voters and in a very close race, that could make all the difference,” he said.

title: Man convicted of shooting woman in the head after argument
text:
BEAUFORT, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A man is expected to spend two decades behind bars for shooting a woman in the head after a verbal argument in an apartment parking lot in 2023.
This week, Bernard “Berney” Garvin Jr., 35, was found guilty of attempted murder and possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime.
Deputies with the Beaufort County Sheriff’s Office responded to reports of a shooting at the Hilton Head Gardens apartment complex in June of that year.
Upon arrival, they reported finding a pool of blood, spent shell casings on the pavement and bullet damage on a parked minivan.
Further investigation revealed that a woman was grazed in the head by a bullet after she argued with Garvin before arriving at the complex.
Beaufort County authorities said a woman was driving her friend’s minivan and dropped her off at the complex, as she planned to ride home with a male friend who followed in his vehicle that day.
As both vehicles pulled into the parking lot, the occupants reported seeing Garvin and another woman tussling over a liquor bottle as several other people at an all-day party roamed around.
The female victim exited the vehicle and asked him why he was “beating that woman” before they started to exchange angry words.
As the man in the other vehicle tried to get the female victim to get in his car so they could leave, Garvin reportedly pulled out a gun and shot the woman in the head.
14th Circuit Solicitor’s Office spokesman Jeff Kidd said Garvin fired at least four shots.
The woman was taken to the hospital before being transferred to another hospital, where she was placed in intensive care for possible brain bleeding.
Multiple witnesses were able to identify Garvin as the shooter, and he was arrested three months later in Georgia, Beaufort County authorities said.
Garvin is said to have a criminal history dating back to 2011 that includes convictions for assault and battery, pointing and presenting a firearm, driving under suspension and parole violations.
The judge sentenced Garvin to 20 years in prison plus five years’ probation.
