title: Alaska's governor orders probe into Democratic candidate over Dan Sullivan ballot controversy
text:
US Senate candidate Mary Peltola denies role as DOJ issues subpoenas in Alaska election probe
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.
“I just want to clear the air," she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."
Peltola is running against Sen. Dan Sullivan. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part an alleged effort to confuse voters.
The race is considered key to control of the U.S. Senate. More subpoenas were expected, according to the person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.
The Justice Department for months has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The potential targets of the investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.
Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”
“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
Alaska's Republican governor has also ordered an investigation
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Later, as he rallied for Republican Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."
Peltola dismisses the claims as a ‘distraction’
Peltola alluded to the controversy in a fundraising post Thursday. “They can’t win on their record so they’re trying to intimidate me into backing down,” she said, adding later: “This is just another distraction as they avoid answering for the skyrocketing cost of living we’re facing because of their tariffs and forever wars. It won’t work.”
In Juneau, Alaska, independent Carter Bancroft said he voted Thursday for Peltola. “I’m very certain in the candidates I wanted to vote for and I wanted to vote for Mary Peltola,” he said.
But he said the latest claims have bothered him. He worries they give “ammunition” to Trump and others to attack Peltola or other Democratic candidates. “And I think I’m bothered by shenanigans on either side," Bancroft said, especially actions intended “to confuse things or try to trick people.”
John Delgado, an independent who leans Republican, said he has “warmed up” to Sen. Sullivan, especially in light of the recent claims. He agrees that Peltola should drop out of the race.
The situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.
In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.
“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”
State Supreme Court OK'd the other Sullivan on the ballot
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.
The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.
Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”

title: 2 men allegedly sexually assaulted 5 Maine girls
text:

Diego Ramirez, 29, of Rumford was indicted on four counts of gross sexual assault, one count of sexual abuse of a minor, two counts of unlawful sexual contact, one count of unlawful sexual contact, one count of aggravated unlawful furnishing of cannabis, one count of endangering the welfare of a child, one count of furnishing liquor to a minor, and one count of allowing a minor to possess or consume alcohol, according to the Rumford Police Department.
Nkialuzitu Mayingi, 31, of Gorham was indicted on five counts of gross sexual assault, four counts of unlawful sexual contact, one count of aggravated unlawful furnishing of cannabis, one count of endangering the welfare of a child and one count of furnishing liquor to a minor.
The investigation into Ramirez and Mayingi began on Aug. 3 after police learned about an alleged sexual assault at Swainbrook Apartments on Spruce Street. That investigation revealed at least five girls, ranging in age from 12 to 14, had been sexually assaulted, according to police.
The girls met a man whom they didn’t know in Rumford and followed him to a unit at Swainbrook Apartments, where they were joined by a second man, whom they also didn’t know, police said.
While there, the men allegedly plied the girls with alcohol and cannabis before sexually assaulting them.
Ramirez and Mayingi were arrested and taken to the Oxford County Jail in South Paris.
“Protecting children from sexual abuse and assault is among our highest responsibilities, and we take that responsibility very seriously,” Rumford Police Chief Tony Milligan said in a Thursday statement.

title: Owner of Lewiston, Bangor hospitals agrees to $2M settlement over data breach
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Covenant Health, which owns hospitals in Lewiston and Bangor, has agreed to pay $2 million to settle a class action lawsuit over a data breach that impacted at least 284,000 Maine residents last year.
The breach hit patients at St. Joseph Healthcare in Bangor, St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center in Lewiston and other Covenant Health facilities across New England. An unauthorized party gained access to the health system’s IT network in May 2025, compromising the private health information of more than 500,000 patients until it was discovered in July, according to the class action settlement agreement.
Compromised information may have included patients’ names, addresses, Social Security numbers, treatment details and health insurance information.
Claiming the health system did not protect their private information, nearly a dozen patients sued Covenant Health and joined a class action lawsuit that represents all patients impacted by the breach. Covenant Health agreed to pay $2 million to settle the lawsuit, without admitting any liability or wrongdoing.
Settlement class members can submit a claim to receive up to $5,000 in cash for documented losses, or get a cash payment of an estimated $75. All members will receive two years of complimentary credit monitoring services, according to the Covenant Health data settlement website. Mailed notices have gone out to members of the settlement class. Claims can be submitted online or mailed, so long as they are postmarked by Dec. 30.
A hearing will determine whether the court grants final approval to the settlement. It will take place at the Penobscot County Superior Court in 2027, according to the order.
There was a final hearing Wednesday regarding a similar settlement agreement between patients and Central Maine Healthcare. The health system, which owns Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston as well as hospitals in Rumford and Bridgton, agreed to pay more than $1.3 million to resolve claims that it did not protect patient information during a 2025 data breach.
The Maine Business and Consumer Court did not immediately respond to an inquiry about the result of the hearing.

title: Caretaker charged for recording 92-year-old man suffocating his wife with plastic bag in senior living center, police say
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A Kentucky woman’s designated caretaker was arrested after allegedly recording an incident in which her 92-year-old husband allegedly tried to suffocate her instead of helping the victim.
Bert Morris, 92, was charged Wednesday with attempted murder and first-degree strangulation.
According to Morris’ arrest citation, Louisville Metro Police officers responded to a senior living center after a report of a domestic violence incident.
Police said Morris was found pinching his wife’s nose after “placing a plastic bag over her face.” The citation said the bag could be seen sealing around her mouth and continued to tighten around her head while Morris held her nose.
According to the citation, Morris made a statement that his wife “needed to die.”
Terrence Gabie, 41, was also arrested Wednesday and is facing charges of knowingly abusing or neglecting an adult.
Court documents state Gabie recorded a 71-second video of the incident instead of helping the victim.
Another nurse had to intervene and separate the victim and Morris, court documents state.
Gabie was the victim’s designated caretaker during her time at the assisted living facility.
Morris’ wife was taken to a local hospital, where she was unconscious.
Morris pleaded not guilty in court Thursday. His bond was reduced from $250,000 to $150,000. He is scheduled to appear in court Nov. 6 for a preliminary hearing.
Gabie was also arraigned in court Thursday, where he pleaded not guilty and his bond was set at $10,000. He was released on a personal recognizance bond.
His preliminary hearing is scheduled for Nov. 6.

title: We Walk the Line: Turning loss into a lifeline
text:
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
LANSING, Mich. (Aging Untold) — Members of the military and first responders run toward crisis and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health.
A growing number of veterans and first responders are dying by suicide, struggling with the invisible wounds of service.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs estimates an average of 22 veterans take their own lives each day, and hundreds of first responders die by suicide annually.
For Tonya and Scott Shea, the mission is personal. Their son, Army Specialist Connor Shea, was a quiet, old soul with a passion for fishing and Johnny Cash.
“His peaceful part of him was fishing. And he would just go on the lakes with his buddies or by himself, put in some headphones, listen to some Johnny Cash, cast some reels, and he was just simple,” Tonya Shea said.
Connor served two years at the National Training Center in the Mojave Desert.
The isolation, dangerous exercises and COVID-19 lockdowns took a toll. Shortly after spending the holidays with his family, he died by suicide at 21.
“I think everything was a fog from that point,” Scott said.
Months later, the family’s bulldog inspired them to create their nonprofit, We Walk the Line, raising funds for Blue Star Service Dogs.
“This big lug of a bulldog would just curl up next to you and put his head in your lap, and just look at you like you’re going to be OK. And I got you. And so we were like service dogs, like service dogs are expensive,” Tonya Shea said.
Blue Star, based in Michigan, provides service dogs to veterans and first responders with PTSD or traumatic brain injuries.
“A lot of our veterans and first responders are broken. We’re almost their last hope. They find us, they come in, they’ve tried the medicine, they’ve tried the therapy, nothing’s worked,” said Executive Director Trish Barnes.
“The dog will watch the person’s back, will block somebody if they’re in their personal space, pick up dropped items, make them feel like they have a purpose again. They’re able to go to their kids’ sports events, the grocery store by themselves,” she said.
Blue Star adopts shelter dogs and trains them in prisons before pairing them with veterans and first responders.
Marine veteran Laszlo Szalay said his service dog saved him after a head injury triggered a mental health crisis.
“Once I got my dog, then I had a reason to get up in the morning. I had to take care of him. And it gave me purpose,” he said.
“We teach our dogs deep pressure therapy, waking up from night terrors, find my medication, so many different obstacles,” said trainer Glenn Dennard, who served more than 17 years in prison for second-degree murder.
The Sheas have sponsored several service dogs through their nonprofit.
“I think it comes down to, if we can prevent another family from going through what we have gone through. I think he’d be proud of that, for sure,” Scott Shea said.

title: How to choose the right health insurance plan for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How to choose the right health insurance plan for 2027
'Your premiums will change. Your out-of-pocket costs can change. Drug coverage can change.'
How to choose the right health insurance plan for 2027
'Your premiums will change. Your out-of-pocket costs can change. Drug coverage can change.'
Millions of Americans are choosing their health insurance for 2027 or will be soon. Whether your coverage comes through an employer, the ACA Marketplace or Medicare, what you pay next year will likely change.
"Your premiums will change. Your out-of-pocket costs can change. Drug coverage can change," said Louise Norris of healthinsurance.org.
To help you sort through your options, we spoke with health policy analyst Louise Norris.
Costs are rising
First up, employer-sponsored plans, which are the largest source of health coverage in the United States, serving over 60% of people under 65, are expected to get more expensive. The annual National Survey of Employer-Sponsored Health Plans projects the average cost of health benefits will rise more than 8% in 2027.
According to healthinsurance.org, 12 insurers are leaving the ACA marketplace at the end of 2026. Remaining insurers have proposed premium increases averaging 15%. Twenty-nine states and Washington, D.C., have finalized increases so far. However, Norris said, 87% of ACA insurees received some subsidy in 2026. “But it is probably still the vast majority of marketplace enrollees are getting a subsidy. And those subsidies do cover, for most people, the bulk of their premium. So average net premiums are much, much lower than average full-price premiums because of those subsidies,” said Norris.
Those with Medicare Part D plans may also experience a rise in the cost of prescription drugs. Not only is the deductible increasing from $615 to $700 in 2027, but so are the out-of-pocket limits. “The out-of-pocket limit was $2,100 this year for drugs covered by your Part D plan," said Norris. "That is increasing to $2,400 for 2027."
Even if you like your plan, shop around
“It will almost certainly change in some way and you don't know if there might be a better option available to you unless you actively comparison shop,” said Norris.
That is true for every kind of coverage. If your employer offers more than one plan, or you buy on the Marketplace, or you want to make changes to your Medicare coverage, the open enrollment period is your chance to switch.
Start by doing your research. You can visit healthinsurance.org for helpful information on employer-sponsored plans and ACA Marketplace plans. And for a full breakdown on changes coming to Medicare, visit medicareresources.org.
Start with how you used your coverage
Before you renew or pick a new plan, review how you used your insurance this year:
- How often did you go to the doctor?
- What prescriptions did you need?
- How much did you pay out of pocket?
The answers matter because plans differ in which doctors and drugs they cover. "Some plans cover some doctors and not others; some plans cover some drugs and not others," Norris said. "Even if a drug is covered, you want to know what the out-of-pocket costs will be."
Next, think about any major medical expenses you expect next year, such as a planned surgery.
Compare the total cost of each plan, not just the premium
Once you know your likely needs, compare the total cost of each plan, including the deductible, copays, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum.
- Monthly premium (x 12): what you pay each month to have coverage.
- Deductible: what you pay for covered services and drugs before the plan pays anything, except free preventive care.
- Copayments and coinsurance: what you pay each time you get care, such as $20 for a doctor visit or 30% of a hospital bill.
- Out-of-pocket maximum: the most you’ll spend on covered services in a year. After that, the plan pays 100%.
Your expected usage can change which plan comes out ahead.
Also check how each plan handles doctor visits. One plan may charge a flat $25 copay, while another counts visits toward your deductible, and then you could pay $120, $150 or $200 per visit, depending on the rate the plan negotiated with that doctor.
Finally, check each plan’s doctors, hospitals and drug coverage. Every plan sets its own network and drug rules, and a covered drug can still cost very different amounts from plan to plan.
A word of caution for folks transitioning from an employer-sponsored plan to the ACA marketplace: “You don't want to assume that the drug coverage or provider network is the same, even if you had that same company's coverage through an employer,” said Norris. “People should know that they have different provider networks. They have different coverage rules.”
Consider a Health Savings Account
If a high-deductible plan makes sense for you, a health savings account (HSA) can help cover out-of-pocket medical costs. For 2027, HSA contribution limits increase to $4,500 for individuals and $9,000 for families.
Norris said an HSA can also offer reassurance. "If you are able to fund an HSA and you're diligent about continuing to put money in there, it can certainly also bring peace of mind of knowing that if something happens and you need to meet your out-of-pocket max or hit your deductible, you have the money there."
Key Dates
- Oct. 15–Dec. 7, 2026: Medicare open enrollment
- Nov. 1, 2026: Marketplace open enrollment begins in most states (HealthCare.gov typically opens window shopping in the last week of October)
- Dec. 15, 2026: Deadline for Marketplace coverage starting Jan. 1
- January 15, 2027: Marketplace open enrollment ends in most states
- Employer-sponsored plan enrollment dates are set by the employer and usually take place between September and November.

Casco Bay Food & Beverage, a Lewiston-based provider of workplace food and beverage services, has named Chris Perry as its next president.
Perry will oversee the day-to-day operations and regional growth, while company founder Ted Morton, who was president, will step into the CEO role.
“Chris brings a unique combination of strategic vision, hands-on operational experience and a genuine passion for developing people,” Morton told Mainebiz. “His ability to build strong teams and create meaningful customer relationships aligns perfectly with our vision for the future of Casco Bay Food & Beverage. We believe his leadership will help strengthen our operations, enhance the customer experience, and position our company for continued growth.”
Perry brings more than 25 years of business leadership experience, including strategic planning, business development, operational improvement and team development.
Most recently, Perry served as chief lending officer at South Portland-based Atlantic Federal Credit Union. His other previous leadership roles include positions at Bangor Savings Bank, Bar Harbor Bank & Trust, Androscoggin Bank and TD Bank.
He earned a bachelor’s in business administration from the University of Southern Maine.
“What excites me most about joining Casco Bay Food & Beverage is the opportunity to lead a respected, family-founded and employee-owned Maine company with a strong foundation and tremendous potential for the future,” said Perry.
“Great organizations are built by developing people, empowering teams, and creating a culture where individuals can do their best work,” he added. “Together, we will continue delivering exceptional service to our customers, supporting Maine businesses and investing in the growth of our employees and communities.”
About the company
Casco Bay Food & Beverage, founded in 2007, provides workplace food and beverage services to businesses and organizations throughout Maine. Its offerings include vending, micro markets, office coffee services and fresh food options.

title: Man charged in connection with terrifying attempted kidnapping caught on video
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) — A 23-year-old man in Hawaii has been charged in connection with a terrifying attempted kidnapping that was caught on video.
Police identified the suspect as Diesel Makanikaiaulu Kawelo and arrested him. He was charged Wednesday with kidnapping.
His bail was set at $500,000.
The kidnapping attempt happened in the middle of the afternoon Monday in Honolulu.
Authorities said they were called to Kainalu condominiums about the reported kidnapping.
Surveillance video from the area showed a truck parked outside the condominium complex that afternoon. A man was then seen going inside the garage, appearing to confront two women and chase one of them.
A 77-year-old condo resident, who asked not to be identified, said the man picked up her 24-year-old friend.
Police said the suspect elbowed the 77-year-old woman in the face.
“He shoved me away from my friend and he picked her up,” she said. “He looked like a monster. He just had so much hatred and craziness in his eyes.”
The woman added, “I was yelling, ‘Help! Help!’ and she was yelling, too. She was saying, ‘You don’t want to do this. Don’t do this.’”
The 77-year-old said her friend was trying to fend off the kidnapper while she was hoping others would hear their screams for help.
Neighbor and witness Beverly Louis said she could see the man bear-hugging the woman and dragging her to the back of his truck.
“I just started screaming, ‘Drop her! Drop her! Drop her!’” Louis said. “She was screaming for her life. She was terrified.”
Neighbor and fellow witness Mike Finkelstein said he also yelled at the man to let the woman go.
“Let her go. I’ve called the police. I’m coming down there after you,” Finkelstein recalled yelling.
Several neighbors then intervened after seeing and hearing the commotion, helping the 24-year-old break free.
Witnesses said the suspect got into his truck and sped off. Police were able to take him into custody a few hours later after he was seen running naked in a nearby neighborhood, police said.
The 77-year-old woman thanked her fellow residents for their help but said she and her friend were continuing to have nightmares as the neighborhood remained on edge.

title: What’s the Most Snow Bangor Has Ever Received on Halloween?
text:
What’s the Most Snow Bangor Has Ever Received on Halloween?
Halloween in Maine can call for an extra layer, but Bangor’s snowfall record for the holiday might surprise you.
👇 KEEP READING: The Most Popular Halloween Costumes for Boys and Girls from 1980 - 2025 👇
According to the National Weather Service’s Halloween history, Bangor’s holiday snowfall record is only a trace, observed on Oct. 31st, 2010.
That means less than one-tenth of an inch, too little to count as measurable snowfall.
For comparison, Caribou recorded 7.6 inches of snow on Halloween in 1959.
Even there, measurable snowfall on the holiday is uncommon, with a 2024 Northeast Regional Climate Center review finding it occurred on approximately 6% of Halloweens in Caribou’s historical records.
While that may be the case for Bangor, the city has still had its share of snowy, wintry weather around Halloween.
For example, a nor’easter brought 6 inches of snow to Bangor on Oct. 30th, 2011, just one day before the holiday. Bangor’s weather station reported 1 inch of snow on the ground on Halloween morning that year, with no new snowfall during the day.
Halloween has also brought unusually warm weather to Bangor.
On Oct. 31st, 2024, the city reached 78 degrees, breaking the previous holiday record of 71 degrees set in 1956.
And there you have it! A snowy Halloween in Bangor could involve snow left on the ground from an earlier storm, which is measured separately from snowfall on the holiday itself.

title: Maine joins nationwide lawsuit challenging Trump's gutting of anti-corruption law
text:
Maine is joining nearly 20 states in suing to stop the Trump administration from gutting an anti-corruption law.
Congress passed the Corporate Transparency Act, which requires corporations, LLCs and other entities to report identifying information about their beneficial owners to the U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
That is meant to stop shell companies from hiding financial transactions from law enforcement, who can use the data to trace dirty money, track down stolen assets and uncover bribes and political corruption, according to the Maine attorney general’s office, which announced the lawsuit Thursday morning.
President Donald Trump vetoed the bill in the waning days of his first administration. The House and Senate overrode his veto.
On March 26, 2025, the Treasury Department issued a rule that exempted 99.9% of businesses from the law, according to the attorney general’s office. The financial crime office has said it will delete all data previously reported to it.
The lawsuit alleges the Trump administration is violating the Administrative Procedure Act and the separation of powers and take care clauses of the U.S. Constitution.
“It is inexplicable that the Trump Administration wants to change the rules to make it harder to catch and prosecute white collar crime,” Attorney General Frey said in a statement. “The bipartisan law the Administration is trying to dismantle is an effective mechanism for law enforcement to uncover illegal financial schemes and hold wrongdoers accountable. The American people deserve a system where people and corporations are accountable to the law.”
The coalition of states wants a judge to vacate the Treasury’s new rule and declare it unlawful and prevent the financial crime office from purging its database.
Frey joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia.

title: Humans accidentally canceled the next ice age
text:
Humans accidentally canceled the next ice age
Humans accidentally canceled the next ice age
Around 20,000 years ago, the once-vast Laurentide Ice Sheet sprawled from the Arctic Circle as far south as Illinois and was up to two miles thick in parts. All that remains of it now is the Delaware-sized Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in Canada's Nunavut territory.
Roughly 2,000 years ago, this ice cap started to slowly and steadily re-expand. Its growth marked the start of a new period of glaciation, commonly called an ice age, according to the new study published in the journal Science.
But around 1960, as human-driven climate change pushed up summer temperatures, the ice cap abruptly began to shrink.
"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen — and yet it stopped," said Nicolás Young, a study author and a geochemist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, part of the Columbia Climate School. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system."
For millions of years, the planet has moved in and out of ice ages, driven by shifts in Earth's orbit, and the Laurentide Ice Sheet often serves as a starting point.
Young and a group of scientists wanted to understand whether the ice sheet had ever been smaller than it currently is and then regrown. It's a tough task, as geological clues are often erased as ice regrows.
The Barnes Ice Cap, however, is frozen to its bedrock and doesn't slide, meaning it has preserved the plants it entombed as it grew. The scientists gathered long-dead mosses near the ice cap's edge and analyzed them to figure out when they were last alive. "We can actually track the expansion of the ice margin as it's progressively covering mosses and killing (them)," Young said.
They also examined nearby rocks to find out how long they had been ice-free by testing for a rare, radioactive isotope that accumulates once a rock is exposed to air.
The techniques helped them reconstruct a picture of the ice's past. They found the ice sheet reached its minimum size about 3,000 years ago, then started to regrow roughly 2,000 years ago in response to cooler temperatures.
This regrowth should be considered the start of a new ice age, but it never got past its infancy before it reversed course in the 1960s, the study authors argue. "We think that it's no coincidence that that's at the same time as we've pumped an extraordinary amount of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere," Young said. Climate pollution has "essentially overpowered" the other mechanisms that "want to make that region cool," he added.
Meredith Kelly, an earth sciences professor at Dartmouth College who was not involved with the study, said the research applies techniques including "novel radiocarbon dating of plants" to set out a good picture of the ice cap's advance and retreat.
The conclusions that the advance of the Barnes Ice Cap suggests the start of an ice age could be right, she added, but a comparison with glaciers in other regions that were also advancing at a similar time would help to understand more about the mechanisms at play.
Andrey Ganopolski, a physicist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said there has been plenty of research into whether carbon pollution may significantly delay the onset of the next ice age.
But, he added, other modeling studies, including his own, conclude the next ice age wouldn't be expected for another 50,000 years or so — even without global warming. The growth of the Barnes Ice Cap "is insufficient to support the conclusion that a new glacial cycle had already begun and was subsequently aborted," he said.
Young and co-authors, however, argue the first regrowth of the Laurentide Ice Sheet counts as the start of an ice age and we don't need to wait for the formation of enormous ice sheets to declare one has begun.
The findings also throw new light on a controversial period in the 1970s, when some scientists suggested the world might be entering a new ice age, Young said. This idea was picked up by the media, including a now-infamous article in Newsweek with the headline "The Cooling World," which warned of a food crisis as the world chilled.
It's a period climate change skeptics and deniers often reference to discredit scientists as alarmist and incorrect. But Young believes the new research suggests they were right, that "a new glaciation actually had started; it was just getting going, and now it's stopped."
Young cautioned that the study should not be interpreted as suggesting global warming has "saved humanity from an ice age."
Periods of glaciation happen over very long time frames. It would have taken thousands of years before the ice cap would have approached a size where it would have affected people's everyday lives, he said.
Instead, the findings reveal just how profoundly humans have pushed Earth's systems out of whack. Not only have we avoided this ice age, Young said, but "we've probably put off any chance of any other future glaciation for a very, very long time."

title: 11 Central In Bangor Is Looking For A New Owner: Turnkey Restaurant Includes Recipes, Bar Setup, And Established Clientele
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Longtime Bangor Entrepreneurs Look To Sell Popular Downtown Restaurant
Since opening its doors in 2012, the downtown Bangor restaurant 11 Central has become a popular spot for folks to meet up, grab a bite or a drink, and celebrate important milestones in the Queen City.
Read More: New Burger Restaurant Coming to Downtown Bangor This November
While the business has changed hands before, most recently in 2020 when local Bangor business owners Mike and Melissa Towle took the helm, its reputation for being a downtown destination has remained the same.
The Towles, who have connections with other businesses throughout Bangor in the past, including the Penobscot Pour House and Happy Endings. They cite their growing kids as the inspiration behind their desire to downsize their portfolio so they have more time to spend with family. They recently put the restaurant on the market.
They listed it as a turnkey business, according to a post by Caldwell Banker.
"The thoughtfully designed restaurant offers approximately 49 seats throughout the dining and lounge areas, plus an additional 12 seats at the bar. The space is well suited for dinner service, cocktails, private gatherings, and special events, with an established identity and customer base already in place. This is a complete business sale-not simply a restaurant space or equipment package. The 11 Central name and brand, recipes, website and social media presence, business phone numbers, owned POS system, furniture, fixtures, restaurant and bar equipment, food and liquor inventory, and other operating assets are included in the sale. The goal is a seamless transition, giving a new owner the opportunity to step into an established restaurant operation without building one from the ground up. "
It should be noted that the business is what's for sale, not the building, as the space is leased and the building is owned by someone else.
Read More: New Brewer, Maine, Restaurant and Pub Opening in November
Mike Towle said in a post online this week that the decision was a bittersweet one, but that it was time for the couple to slow down a bit.
The 11 Central Facebook page said the establishment was closed Wednesday due to an "unforeseen mechanical issue" but that it would reopen Thursday the 29th, at 4 pm.
In case you were interested in the business, they have the price listed at $500,000.

title: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University.
Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century.
This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
“We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. That’s also true when we look at gubernatorial contests,” Dittmar said.
Dittmar said the trend gives the upcoming 120th Congress a chance to be more than just 28% female, the current makeup on Capitol Hill.
With women across all ethnic and racial groups heading out in droves to vote, politicians hoping to go to Washington must keep that voting base in mind.
Previous midterms were dominated by traditionally female issues, including the #MeToo movement in 2018 and the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Dittmar said this year is different.
“At the end of the day across the board, that affordability piece seems to be paramount,” Dittmar said.
Affordability is critical to women, but equally as important to men. While recent headlines about sexual assault and violence, issues traditionally seen as female-coded, are prompting reaction from candidates, Dittmar says the impact of those controversies in November may be slim.
“In terms of where we see women this year: high energy in terms of their concerns, but those concerns are something that’s more universal,” Dittmar said.
Something else to consider: the gender gap is different between the two parties. Women make up 42% of congressional Democrats, which brings the party closer to parity. However, women make up only 15% of congressional Republicans.

title: ‘Amazed that she’s alive’: 18-year-old driver in ICU after hitting moose on icy road
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A mother in Alaska said her 18-year-old daughter is lucky to be alive after hitting a moose Monday night while driving down an icy Anchorage road.
“That’s what we’ve been hearing this entire ordeal, from the EMTs to the doctors; they are amazed that she’s alive,” Megan Stone said about her daughter’s crash.
According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway.
Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake.
When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools.
Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds.
“Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. In this case, it landed on the hood and kind of the windshield and roof area. We see forces of 30,000 to 40,000 pounds being put onto that car.”
Fish and Game Biologist Cory Stantorf said there are usually about 100 moose-vehicle collisions in the Anchorage area every year, but this is the time when they start to increase.
“Not only do we have moose moving because of the rut, following cows, we are also doing that morning commute in the pitch-black, but kids are also going to school in the pitch-black, and there’s not a lot of contrast without snow to illuminate these moose,” Stantorf said. “So drivers really need to slow down because there’s just not the reaction time that we have in the summer.”
As for Autumn, her mother said Wednesday that she was still in the ICU, where she was expected to remain for several days.
Stone said her daughter has some brain bruising, lacerations and a broken hand, but didn’t appear to have any catastrophic injuries.
Stone said she’s seen pictures of the wreck and was relieved her daughter survived.
“It’s horrifying to see those photos as her mom, but I’m also grateful, because I can put into context just how close we were to losing her,” she said.

title: Ukraine war continues despite Trump’s promise to end it
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The war in Ukraine has lasted more than four-and-a-half years, and fighting continues despite repeated efforts by President Donald Trump to end the conflict.
Trump made a pledge on the campaign trail dozens of times during the last presidential campaign.
“Before I even arrive at the Oval Office shortly after I win the presidency, I will have the horrible war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump said at a July 7, 2023, rally in Council Bluffs, Iowa. “Somebody said, are you on Russia’s side? Are you on Ukraine’s side? You know what? The side — I want people to stop dying. That’s the side I’m on.”
That campaign promise has not been fulfilled.
Trump has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice at the White House. He met once with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in August 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
“I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting,” Trump said. “There were many, many points that we agreed on. Most of them, I would say. A couple of big ones that we haven’t quite got there, but we’ve made some headway. So, there’s no deal until there’s a deal.”
On Sept. 18, Trump signed bipartisan legislation named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) that imposes sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia. On Oct. 16 Trump signed an executive order waiving those sanctions.

title: UN reports a sharp rise in Afghanistan poppy cultivation despite a Taliban ban
text:
UN reports a sharp rise in Afghanistan poppy cultivation despite a Taliban ban
Poppy cultivation and opium production in Afghanistan rose sharply over the past year, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said on Thursday, describing it as the first significant increase since the country’s Taliban rulers imposed a narcotics ban in 2022.
The agency attributed the rise to deepening poverty, which it said has driven some farmers to cultivate opium clandestinely. It called on the international community to provide support to farmers to help curb reliance on illicit crops.
Afghanistan was the world’s biggest opium producer and a major source of heroin in Europe and Asia when the Taliban seized power in August 2021. They pledged to wipe out the country’s drug cultivation industry and imposed a formal ban in April 2022, dealing a heavy blow to hundreds of thousands of farmers and day laborers who relied on proceeds from the crop to survive.
Related video above: Get the Facts: What's the process of declaring war?
The U.N. agency said cultivation was up 330% and production rose by 400% compared to last year. Cultivation rose to more than 106,000 acres in 2026 from 24,700 acres a year earlier, it said.
Farmers were concealing small poppy plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds to evade detection, the report said.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” a statement quoted the agency’s executive director, Monica Juma, as saying.
“The [Taliban authorities] and the international community need to work together to support farming communities by investing in livelihoods, farming infrastructure and access to markets,” she added.
The Taliban rejected the agency’s findings, insisting that the UNODC’s report had “not accurately reflected the actual situation and has overlooked the practical achievements of the fight against narcotics.”
It argued that the U.N. agency had relied on “satellite images, estimates and incorrect information from biased groups.”
“In 2026, more than 26,000 hectares of land in the provinces where cultivation had taken place were cleared of narcotic-producing crops,” a statement from the Interior Ministry said.
“These operations were carried out at considerable financial and human cost and under difficult field conditions," it said. "Therefore, any assessment that fails to take these measures and their results into account in its calculations is incomplete and unfair.”
The U.N. agency said that while cultivation and production remained below levels prior to the 2022 narcotics ban, the increase was the highest since the ban came into effect. The agency said that continued monitoring was required as it was too early to determine whether the increase was temporary or an indication of a resurgence in opium cultivation and production.
Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi on Tuesday described the fight against narcotics as one of the Taliban administration’s greatest achievements. However, he also said the international community has a role to play to keep the drugs issue under control.
“An effective fight against this phenomenon is a shared responsibility of both Afghanistan and the international community,” Muttaqi said. “It is essential alongside security measures to support alternative livelihoods for farmers, provide treatment for those struggling with addiction, and enhance regional and international cooperation against drug-trafficking networks.”

title: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
text:
(Aging Untold) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant.
Start with a conversation with your provider
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone.
“Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said.
Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation.
Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said.
“When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said.
Antidepressants are not “happy pills”
Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness.
“They’re not happy pills. They don’t take away the sadness, but they will be a way for you to work on how you got there or what else is going on,” Rogers said.
She listed chronic stress, a thyroid imbalance and nutritional deficiencies as examples of what could be going on.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said medication doesn’t change the circumstance.
“What they’ll do is they’ll change the chemical imbalance in the brain to help you get to a place to be better,” Cradduck said. “But you can’t just take a pill and be done.”
She said talk therapy is part of the process. The conversation does not have to be with a therapist, she said, but it needs to address the issues that led to the low mood.
“You need to be willing to face that, or it’s just going to continue in a cycle,” Cradduck said.
Ask about the drug, the dose and the withdrawal symptoms
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommended a good psychiatrist and a thorough assessment.
Those who decide to take an antidepressant should get help deciding which one as well as the dose, then track how it’s affecting you, she said.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommended finding a good psychiatrist and getting a thorough assessment to help you decide whether to take an antidepressant, which one and at what dose. She also recommended tracking how it’s affecting you.
She described a client who was prescribed an antidepressant and felt like she was having a panic attack, with a racing heartbeat and sweating. The client called her psychiatrist, who took her off the medication and prescribed a different one.
O’Rourke said she’d want to know the withdrawal symptoms before someone starts taking an antidepressant.
Rogers said there are a lot of withdrawal symptoms.
“You cannot just stop it all of a sudden,” she said.
Rogers said people do not all respond to the same drugs. She said if you can afford it, finding out your genetic variations is one investment worth making, because it can help you respond better to your situation.
Look for support beyond medication
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose mentioned talk therapy, journaling and filling your mind with as much positivity as possible along with seeking support from medical professionals.
“Don’t forget about things like your thyroid, or your hormones or your nutrients,” Rogers added.
“Talk to your doctors, seek answers, get your rebound and come back,” Ambrose said. “Try everything you can because it’s worth bringing yourself back.”
Rogers said it does not have to be one isolated thing that brought you to this point.

title: Control of the Maine Legislature hinges on these battleground races
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine State Legislature won’t get the same attention as the high-stakes battles for Senate and governor.
But Republicans and Democrats are locked in a struggle that will decide the state’s direction for the next two years.
In electoral battlegrounds from Wells to Bowdoinham to Deer Isle, voters will choose their state lawmaker — and in more than two dozen House districts, the result really could go either way.
In 2024, just 60 votes across three House districts determined the fate of the final two years of Gov. Janet Mills’ tenure in the Blaine House. Democrats won all three, and with them, a slim majority.
If Republicans manage to win either chamber on Tuesday, the first two years of a likely Hannah Pingree administration would be almost certainly muted by partisan blockades: Lawmakers would have to find compromise on key issues like property taxes and hospital funding and housing costs — or risk no progress at all.
Republicans winning control of Maine’s upper chamber, the Senate, is a long shot, and the party’s money-holders seem to know it.
In that body, Democrats hold a five-seat majority, and while competition is still hot in about a half-dozen districts, conditions would need to ripen immediately for the GOP to win a majority for the first time since 2016. Senate President Mattie Daughtry, D-Cumberland, said in a statement that she is “confident in the campaigns (Democrats) have run and looking forward to a great day next Tuesday.”
But in Maine’s 151-seat House, Republicans appear to have a real chance of wrestling back control for the first time since 2012.
Since new maps were adopted in 2021, more than two dozen House districts have been decided by just a few percentage points. In this cycle, the Press Herald picked out the 28 districts expected to be the most competitive, based on the results of the two most recent elections and whether the sitting member is running for reelection.
There are more than a dozen of these battleground districts held by Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents. If Republicans can pick up just three seats, they’ll have a majority — giving them control over committees and leverage over the state Senate and governor.
“(Maine is) a blue state to be sure, but that doesn’t mean it’s not very competitive throughout large regions of the state,” Colby College professor of government Dan Shea said. “So it’s refreshing that we would have balanced, competitive, state legislative seats. I think it’s good for democracy.”
Nationally, Republicans face political headwinds. A historically unpopular Republican president and Republican-controlled Congress have presided during a rise in fuel and trade costs, and a solid majority of voters plan to pick a Democrat for U.S. House, polls show. Red states like Iowa and Kansas have turned suddenly into battlegrounds. Democrats continue to dominate early voting in Maine, too.
But Maine Republicans do have the advantage of having their most popular figure, Sen. Susan Collins, at the top of the ballot. Maine Republican Party Chair Jim Deyermond said he is optimistic about his party’s chances, despite national headwinds, partly because of Collins’ popularity, and partly because of what he sees as strong candidate recruitment across the state.
House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, D-Biddeford, who himself is running unopposed, said in a statement that “an incredible group of candidates” that has knocked on thousands of doors across the state “will work every day to build a stronger, more prosperous Maine.”
In state legislative races, tiny districts and candidate-dependent dynamics could easily buck national trends, Mark Brewer, a political science professor at the University of Maine in Orono, said.
“The district specifics in these kinds of races always matter, and the candidate specifics always matter,” Brewer said. “Just because you’re seeing one dynamic play out in, say, state legislative District 70 doesn’t mean that the same thing is going to be playing out in state legislative District 10.”
Let’s run through the Maine House districts that are in play, starting with the three most competitive from last cycle.
THE 60-VOTE DISTRICTS
These three districts will be among the most closely watched of the lot, having been decided by a total of 60 votes in 2024. If Republicans had won two of these seats then, they would’ve had a majority in the State House.
House District 52: Incumbent Rep. Sally Cluchey-D vs. David Guilmette-R
- 2022 margin: D+12.8
- 2024 margin: D+0.3
- Covers Bowdoinham, Richmond and part of Bowdoin
Cluchey, D-Bowdoinham, is running for her third term on her constituent services — she often touts on social media when she registers residents in her district for Maine’s Medicare Savings Program. Guilmette, a former Kennebec County Sheriff’s deputy, is running a much more nationalized campaign, with focuses on gun rights, immigration and school choice.
House District 96: Luke Jensen-D vs. Kerryl Lee Clement-R
- 2022 margin: D+2.9
- 2024 margin: D+0.8
- Covers part of Lewiston
Rep. Mike Lajoie, D-Lewiston, isn’t running for a seventh term, and Lewiston school board member Jensen is hoping to keep his tightly contested seat by focusing on rising cost of living. Clement, the Republican, is emphasizing his background in law enforcement and on the Lewiston City Council, pitching himself as a “public servant, not a politician.”
House District 75: Scott Landry-D vs. Randall Gauvin-R
- 2022 margin: D+30.6
- 2024 margin: D+0.2
- Covers Chesterville and Farmington
This is a race between two men who serve together on the Farmington Select Board. Landry is running to return to the Maine House. In 2024, he chose not to run, nearly causing this once-safe blue district to flip red. He’s running on lowering cost of living. Gauvin, the Republican who nearly flipped this seat two years ago, is focusing on “traditional Maine values,” fiscal responsibility and parental rights.
REPUBLICAN FLIPS
Republicans need to hold most, if not all, of the House districts they flipped two years ago to win a majority. Here are those districts.
House District 13: Incumbent Rep. Russell White-R vs. Michael Cunningham II-D
- 2022 margin: D+15.8
- 2024 margin: R+8.9
- Covers Ellsworth, Waltham, Fletchers Landing Township and Central Hancock
White, R-Ellsworth, like many other Maine Republicans this cycle, is focusing his campaign on energy costs and high taxes. But he’s also using national issues, notably emphasizing immigration enforcement and gun rights. Cunningham, the Democrat, is running a relatively less political campaign; his top focus, his website says, is “bringing people together.”
House District 17: Incumbent Rep. Steven Bishop-R vs. Ronald Russell-D
- 2022 margin: D+3.4
- 2024 margin: R+2.8
- Covers Bucksport, Orland, Penobscot and Verona Island
Bishop, R-Bucksport, is highlighting his record as a Maine State Chamber of Commerce-endorsed small business owner in his bid for a second term. His Democratic opponent, Russell, is also a business owner, having previously chaired Main Street Bucksport and represented this district for a term before Bishop defeated him two years ago. This could be a telling rematch.
House District 45: Rebecca Stephens-R vs. Clint Collamore-D
- 2022 margin: D+6.5
- 2023 special election margin: R+4.6
- 2024 margin: R+12.9
- Covers Bremen, Friendship, Waldoboro and Washington
With the Republican incumbent not running, this is an open seat. Collamore is vying to regain the seat his party lost after he resigned and was briefly jailed in 2023 amid a signature-forging scandal. Stephens, a Republican former school board and select board member, is running on fiscal responsibility and cutting taxes.
House District 83: Incumbent Rep. Marygrace Cimino-R vs. Timothy Becker-D
- 2022 margin: I+4.0
- 2024 margin: R+1.2
- Covers Bridgton, Denmark and Harrison
Cimino, R-Bridgton, is campaigning against the budget increases during Mills’ tenure as governor and for tax cuts. Becker, a tax attorney, is also hoping to tackle rising property taxes, along with access to affordable healthcare.
House District 86: Incumbent Rep. Rolf Olsen-R vs. Abigail Geer-D
- 2022 margin: D+3.2
- 2024 margin: R+4.1
- Covers Casco, Frye Island, Raymond and part of Poland
Olsen, R-Raymond, is basing his first reelection campaign on eliminating fraud and waste and cutting state spending — both common Maine Republican refrains this year. Geer, the Democrat, is hoping to increase state funding for childcare and public education and to improve rural healthcare access.
House District 88: Incumbent Rep. Quentin Chapman-R vs. Dana Staples-D
- 2022 margin: D+1.7
- 2024 margin: R+9.8
- Covers part of Auburn
Chapman, R-Auburn, has taken to filming homeless encampments and blasting needle exchanges on social media, saying his city is exacerbating drug addiction issues. That appears to be his top focus. Staples, a former Auburn City Council member, is running on lowering the cost of living and his willingness to compromise.
House District 107: Incumbent Rep. Mark Cooper-R vs. Joseph Campbell-D
- 2022 margin: D+3.0
- 2024 margin: R+2.5
- Covers part of Windham
Cooper, R-Windham, a farmer and contractor, wants to make Augusta more efficient — eliminating MaineCare fraud and streamlining education funding. Full-time substitute teacher Campbell, who, at 27, is among the youngest candidates for the Maine Legislature this cycle, is running on securing the social safety net and shifting tax burden to richer Mainers.
House District 145: Caleb Chase-R vs. Kristin Davis-D
- 2022 margin: D+3.4
- 2024 margin: R+4.0
- Covers part of Wells
Another 27-year-old, Chase, is focusing his campaign on his small business ownership and his willingness to listen to subject-matter experts. He and his Democratic opponent, Davis, have mutually agreed to run purely positive campaigns and have each condemned the use of outside money in the race. Davis has largely focused her campaign on childcare affordability and tax relief.
OPEN SEATS
While these House seats haven’t flipped party control since 2022, the incumbent isn’t running again, and the past two elections have been tight. Since many of these districts are Democrat-held, there are key opportunities here for Republicans.
House District 44: Shawn Saindon-I vs. Ray Thombs Jr.-R
- 2022 margin: I+8.1
- 2024 margin: I+7.1
- Covers Hope, Union and Warren
This Midcoast district is currently represented by a Democratic-leaning independent: Rep. Bill Pleucker of Warren, who is term-limited. Fellow Warren independent Saindon is running to maintain that streak and, his website says, to work “toward solutions instead of political talking points.” Thombs, the Republican, is campaigning against paid family medical leave and a 2023 reproductive privacy bill. On his website, he says Maine needs “heaven’s help now more than ever.”
House District 55: Maureen AuCoin-D vs. Charles Hippler IV-R
- 2022 margin: D+9.8
- 2024 margin: D+2.2
- Covers Hallowell, Manchester and West Gardiner
With incumbent Rep. Dan Shagoury, D-Hallowell, not running for reelection, AuCoin, a former city council member and code enforcement officer for Hallowell, is campaigning on affordability and pushing for universal healthcare access. A Manchester Select Board member, Hippler wants to raise the homestead exemption for property taxes, cut regulations and slash the state budget.
House District 59: Katrina Couch Ray-Saulis-D vs. John Reny-R
- 2022 margin: D+21.0
- 2024 margin: D+6.8
- Covers part of Augusta
The district that covers the Maine State House complex and the west side of Augusta has historically tilted toward Democrats — but with incumbent Rep. David Rollins retiring, Ray-Saulis is pitching an anti-billionaire, pro-union candidacy not unlike the Democrat at the top of Maine’s ballot, Troy Jackson. Meanwhile, Republican groups have supported Reny, a local business owner, with the most outside spending of any House candidate this cycle. This race could be a big bellwether.
House District 67: Shawn Dixon-R vs. Matthew Townsend-D
- 2022 margin: R+11.6
- 2024 margin: R+4.1
- Covers Benton and Fairfield
In the seat currently held by term-limited firebrand Rep. Shelley Rudnicki, R-Fairfield, Benton Select Board member Dixon is running on eliminating fraud and lowering energy bills. His Democratic opponent, Townsend, is focusing on healthcare access — a topic especially salient in the wake of Waterville’s Inland Hospital closing last year.
House District 90: James Sorcek-R vs. Pamela Hart-D
- 2022 margin: uncontested
- 2024 margin: R+2.8
- Covers Minot and part of Auburn
Rep. Laurel Libby, R-Auburn, left big shoes to fill when she announced last year that she would not run for another term. Sorcek, the Republican running to replace her, wants to eliminate property taxes altogether. Hart, the Democrat, is focusing on affordable housing and healthcare.
House District 141: Marc Boisse-R vs. Rebecca Flood Andrews-D vs. David Mongeau-I
- 2022 margin: R+11.4
- 2024 margin: R+0.02
- Covers Newfield, Shapleigh, part of Springvale and part of Sanford
After winning in 2024 by just one vote, Rep. Lucas Lanigan, R-Sanford, left his seat open this year — and three candidates are vying to replace him. Boisse, the Republican wants to rein in electricity costs and “protect girls’ sports.” Flood Andrews says she is focused on finding common ground. And the independent, Mongeau, says he wants to buck the two-party system.
House District 142: Ayn Hanselmann-D vs. Domingo Torres-R
- 2022 margin: D+7.1
- 2024 margin: D+1.7
- Covers part of Springvale and part of Sanford
Hanselmann hopes to keep this seat blue by emphasizing her eight years of experience on the Sanford City Council, where she says she has seen firsthand the local impact of state policy. Torres, the Republican, is running on lowering taxes and energy costs.
THE OTHER BATTLEGROUNDS
Eight other House districts have been decided by single digits in the past two elections and are likely to remain competitive this year. Here’s the lay of the land in those races.
House District 15: Incumbent Rep. Holly Eaton-D vs. Clifford Noyes-I
- 2022 margin: D+8.5
- 2024 margin: D+4.89
- Covers Brooklin, Stonington, Tremont and seven other towns in Hancock and Knox counties
Eaton, D-Deer Isle, is running for a third term by focusing on the working waterfront she grew up on. She’s being challenged by an independent, Noyes, a school board member on Mount Desert Island who’s running to lower taxes.
House District 20: Incumbent Rep. Dani O’Halloran-D vs. Patrick Jude-R
- 2022 margin: D+1.3
- 2024 margin: D+2.37
- Covers part of Brewer
O’Halloran, D-Brewer, is hoping to win a second term in this tightly contested district. Her campaign has focused largely on affordability concerns, from heating oil to electricity to groceries. Jude is running on reducing welfare spending, expanding addiction treatment and removing business regulations.
House District 37: Incumbent Rep. Reagan Paul-R vs. Alan Orcutt-D
- 2022 margin: R+4.4
- 2024 margin: R+9.3
- Covers Searsport, Stockton Springs, Prospect, Winterport and part of Frankfort
Paul, R-Winterport, is one of the rising stars of the Maine GOP, especially online. She has emphasized her Christian faith as a core tenet of her legislative ethos. She’s challenged by Orcutt, who is running on improving healthcare access and limiting wasteful state spending.
House District 47: Incumbent Rep. Wayne Farrin-D vs. Chester Grover III-R
- 2022 margin: R+5.6
- 2024 margin: D+3.4
- Covers Alna, Jefferson, Whitefield and Wiscasset
Farrin, D-Jefferson, who owns and operates the local general store, is running his first re-election campaign on housing affordability and maintaining local roads and infrastructure. His Republican challenger, Grover, is running on his six-generation Wiscasset roots and small-business ownership.
House District 54: Incumbent Rep. Karen Montell-D vs. Michelle Tucker-R
- 2022 margin: D+3.6
- 2024 margin: D+8.5
- Covers Farmingdale and Gardiner
Tucker got her start in Gardiner politics challenging a local high school’s new student health facility, which she claimed would lead to students receiving gender-transition care without parental consent. Now on the school board, Tucker is challenging Montell, D-Gardiner, who is running for a third term advocating for state employees — a big constituency just downriver from Augusta.
House District 56: Incumbent Rep. Randall Greenwood-R vs. Robin Upton-Sukeforth-D
- 2022 margin: R+1.8
- 2024 margin: R+9.9
- Covers Litchfield, Monmouth and Wales
Greenwood, R-Wales, is running for his fourth consecutive term in the House. Greenwood, also a Wales Select Board member, is being challenged by Upton-Sukeforth, a Democrat running on workers’ rights and healthcare access.
House District 58: Incumbent Rep. Sharon Frost-I vs. Dexter ‘Buzz’ Bridges-R
- 2022 margin: R+5.4
- 2024 margin: I+0.7
- Covers New Sharon, Belgrade, Mount Vernon, Fayette, Rome and Vienna
Frost, I-Belgrade, a former educator, is running her first reelection campaign with a focus on education and the environment. She touts her partisan independence, but usually votes with Democrats. Bridges, a veteran and former animal control officer, is running on lowering the tax burden and energy costs.
House District 81: Incumbent Rep. Peter Wood-R vs. Christopher Easton-D
- 2022 margin: R+8.6
- 2024 margin: R+0.4
- Covers Norway, Sweden and eight other Oxford County towns
Wood, R-Norway, is hoping to hold his closely contested seat against a Democratic challenger, Easton. Wood is running on his small business ownership and local ties, and Easton is emphasizing his decade of teaching experience.
House District 98: Incumbent Rep. Kilton Webb-D vs. William St. Michel-R
- 2022 margin: R+4.3
- 2024 margin: D+0.9
- Covers Durham, Pownal, part of Topsham, part of Bowdoin and part of Lisbon
Webb, D-Durham, is running his first reelection campaign on improving job opportunities and lowering energy costs. St. Michel, his Republican challenger, is the retired longtime Durham fire chief, and says he wants to “rescue hard-working Mainers” from taxes and regulations.
House District 106: Incumbent Rep. Barbara Bagshaw-R vs. Bradley Youngs-D
- 2022 margin: R+0.5
- 2024 margin: R+6.7
- Covers part of Windham
Running for her third term, Bagshaw, R-Windham, says she wants to cap property taxes as a primary fix for rising cost of living. Youngs is hoping to tackle childcare affordability and deteriorating road infrastructure.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 29 to correct the vote margin across the three closest State House races in 2024, and the number of seats Republicans need to gain a Maine House majority in 2026.

title: Heating oil prices continue to climb to record highs in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The winter season just got more expensive for Mainers.
Heating oil prices have once again hit a state record.
The current average for a gallon of oil is now $6.05, up a penny from last week, according to the Department of Energy Resources.
That means filling a 275-gallon tank would cost $750 more compared to 2025.
For those relying on kerosene, the average price sits at $7.06 per gallon.

title: We Walk the Line: Turning loss into a lifeline
text:
(Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.)
LANSING, Mich. (Aging Untold) — Members of the military and first responders run toward crisis and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health.
A growing number of veterans and first responders are dying by suicide, struggling with the invisible wounds of service.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs estimates an average of 22 veterans take their own lives each day, and hundreds of first responders die by suicide annually.
For Tonya and Scott Shea, the mission is personal. Their son, Army Specialist Connor Shea, was a quiet, old soul with a passion for fishing and Johnny Cash.
“His peaceful part of him was fishing. And he would just go on the lakes with his buddies or by himself, put in some headphones, listen to some Johnny Cash, cast some reels, and he was just simple,” Tonya Shea said.
Connor served two years at the National Training Center in the Mojave Desert.
The isolation, dangerous exercises and COVID-19 lockdowns took a toll. Shortly after spending the holidays with his family, he died by suicide at 21.
“I think everything was a fog from that point,” Scott said.
Months later, the family’s bulldog inspired them to create their nonprofit, We Walk the Line, raising funds for Blue Star Service Dogs.
“This big lug of a bulldog would just curl up next to you and put his head in your lap, and just look at you like you’re going to be OK. And I got you. And so we were like service dogs, like service dogs are expensive,” Tonya Shea said.
Blue Star, based in Michigan, provides service dogs to veterans and first responders with PTSD or traumatic brain injuries.
“A lot of our veterans and first responders are broken. We’re almost their last hope. They find us, they come in, they’ve tried the medicine, they’ve tried the therapy, nothing’s worked,” said Executive Director Trish Barnes.
“The dog will watch the person’s back, will block somebody if they’re in their personal space, pick up dropped items, make them feel like they have a purpose again. They’re able to go to their kids’ sports events, the grocery store by themselves,” she said.
Blue Star adopts shelter dogs and trains them in prisons before pairing them with veterans and first responders.
Marine veteran Laszlo Szalay said his service dog saved him after a head injury triggered a mental health crisis.
“Once I got my dog, then I had a reason to get up in the morning. I had to take care of him. And it gave me purpose,” he said.
“We teach our dogs deep pressure therapy, waking up from night terrors, find my medication, so many different obstacles,” said trainer Glenn Dennard, who served more than 17 years in prison for second-degree murder.
The Sheas have sponsored several service dogs through their nonprofit.
“I think it comes down to, if we can prevent another family from going through what we have gone through. I think he’d be proud of that, for sure,” Scott Shea said.
