title: Here’s how much the Iran war has cost American taxpayers so far
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities.
The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.
The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week’s midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump’s last two years in office.
The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House is also asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.
Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.
“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. ”Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”
In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war’s costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.
The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force’s costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army’s are more than $2 billion. The Navy’s costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.
When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.
The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or the disposal of Iranian drones.
While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or “finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration has also reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: See which Maine towns have the most toxic firefighting foam
text:
Fire stations across Maine are sitting on thousands of gallons of toxic firefighting foam in back rooms, storage closets and truck tanks, creating environmental hazards in dozens of communities.
Survey results from the Office of the State Fire Marshal show at least 9,100 gallons of the substance, called aqueous film-forming foam, owned by 120 fire and emergency management departments, from rural areas of Aroostook County to coastal towns near Portland.
“We currently have approximately 16 or 17 plastic 55-gallon drums containing an estimated 700 gallons,” said David Lloyd, town manager of Howland, a small, rural town at the confluence of the Penobscot and Piscataquis rivers.
It’s the state’s biggest publicly owned stockpile of the foam, which contains forever chemicals known as PFAS.
A former fire chief who served in the Maine National Guard accepted it as a donation before anybody knew it was dangerous, Lloyd said. Now he’s trying to get rid of it but can’t afford the $17,000 disposal fee. Meanwhile, he stores it in a heated building to avoid leaks.
First responders must work around the foam stockpiles, which are often stored in aging plastic pails without specialized safety equipment. Residents who live nearby face the risk of poisoned well water if a container ruptures or leaks into the soil.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, are called forever chemicals because they don’t break down in nature and build up in the body. Long-term exposure is linked to high cholesterol, liver damage, developmental delays and cancer.
Over the last decade, Maine has spent more than $100 million as it became a national leader in the fight against PFAS, but dwindling funds have forced state officials to make difficult choices about whom to help and whom to turn away.
Industrial sludge spread on farm fields has ruined dozens of agricultural operations that state regulators are trying to help bounce back. A 1,450-gallon foam spill at the former Brunswick Naval Air Station in 2024 poisoned local waterways, clam beds and private drinking wells.
Most Maine fire departments built up the stockpiles decades ago, long before scientists understood its health risks. Federal surplus programs, airport safety rules and local paper mill operations funneled barrels of foam into small municipal stations.
In Presque Isle, Federal Aviation Administration rules required local rescue trucks to hold 220 gallons of foam and an equal amount in reserve. In Van Buren, firefighters inherited a supply from the former Loring Air Force base that has sat untouched for over 20 years.
“We took foam in as a donation, a surplus thing from the Coast Guard, because of the airport,” said Owls Head Fire Chief Steven “Skip” Hallett. “Nobody would say yes to it today knowing it is dangerous, but now we are stuck with it because we do not have the money to get rid of it.”
Disposal quotes gathered by local fire chiefs range from $10,000 in Owls Head to $17,000 in Howland and $80,000 in Presque Isle. That doesn’t include the cost of buying replacement foam without forever chemicals.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection estimated that burning the foam costs approximately $240 per 5-gallon container, while hazardous waste transport adds a fee of $400per fire station.
However, the survey brings an unexpected financial silver lining for taxpayers. Over 90% of departments statewide responded to the survey, and 219 — about two-thirds of that group — reported no foam at all.
Based on the DEP’s estimates, cleanup of all known municipal stockpiles would cost under $500,000. That’s much lower than the $5 million state officials originally estimated.
The survey does not include foam stored at private facilities, such as fuel depots, mills and private airports. South Portland fuel tank farms, which fire officials estimate hold an additional 10,000 gallons, would increase the cost of eliminating all AFFF in Maine.
Maine lawmakers authorized a voluntary collection program, but they failed to provide funding to execute the cleanup. State Rep. Dan Ankeles, D-Brunswick, is drafting a bill that would earmark a share of any state PFAS settlement money for AFFF collection and disposal.
“We have a manageable amount of public foam, and we need to get a contractor in to take this stuff away before another spill happens,” said Ankeles, who introduced the bill that led to the AFFF survey after the airport spill in his home district.

title: A group has spent $15K to influence the Bangor City Council election
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Money is flooding into races up and down the ballot during a highly-watched election year in Maine, and Bangor is no exception.
Two groups are supporting competing slates of endorsed candidates in a crowded Bangor City Council race, including one political action committee backing conservative candidates that has collected double the donations of all of last year’s candidates combined, representing a significant influx of cash to the council race.
The vast majority of the PAC money in the race comes from real estate investors and companies, a community that’s become more vocal at City Council meetings this year in its criticisms of Bangor’s government. Tuesday’s council election will be a test of whether those critics represent a majority of Bangor voters.
Concerned Citizens of Bangor, which is backing three of the more conservative candidates in the race, has raised nearly $30,000 and spent more than $15,000, according to campaign finance reports filed with the City Clerk’s office and obtained by the Bangor Daily News through a public records request.
“We’re in a crisis,” said Philip Henry, a local real estate investor who is spearheading the Concerned Citizens project, in reference to persistent issues in Bangor around public drug use and homelessness. “I think that’s pretty much, I think, why people were willing to contribute.”
On the flip side, Food and Medicine, a progressive Brewer-based organization that runs anti-poverty programs in the Bangor area, often endorses candidates in the Bangor City Council election and has spent money on mailers and canvassing, although it’s only spent about $300 on municipal candidates this year.
Food and Medicine has taken money from a national PAC working to get Democrats elected and is also advocating for candidates in state and federal races.
Bangor’s local government is officially nonpartisan, which means that city councilors are bound by the city charter to maintain a nonpartisan structure, and that candidates’ party affiliations do not appear beside their names on the ballot. That doesn’t preclude political groups from supporting candidates or otherwise influencing local elections.
Concerned Citizens, which identifies itself as nonpartisan but is closely aligned with policies and talking points being used by Republicans across the state, has spent more than $15,000, mostly on social media and online advertising.
“We need a more balanced approach,” Henry said of partisan influences on the council, adding that he doesn’t think any one party should get too much power. “For the time that we’re in right now, I think we need to vote Republican, or in this case, we need to vote common sense.”
The PAC endorsed candidates Anthony Cote, Terry Dinkins and Joseph Pratt and has run seven ads on Facebook and Instagram, mostly advocating for its preferred candidates. Some also include attacks on Food and Medicine’s chosen candidates Adam Baker, Andrei Yermakov and incumbent Joe Leonard. One ad includes footage of people slumped over in the streets of a city that does not resemble Bangor.
Oftentimes, PACs operate independently from the people they support, meaning the candidates don’t necessarily have any say in the ads run by the groups or the money that flows through them. Neither of the two PACs that are active in Bangor’s council election this year have donated directly to a candidate.
The ads highlight issues like needle distribution and responsible spending and say its chosen candidates will “save Bangor.” Henry named drugs as a top issue for the campaign, saying he’d like to see additional drug enforcement and no more syringe distribution in the city.
Concerned Citizens paid Florida-based Harris Media $13,000 for online ads. The conservative political marketing agency is owned by Vincent Harris, is also a strategist for Republican Bobby Charles’s gubernatorial campaign and has worked for Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and a pro-Trump SuperPAC.
More than $23,000 — about 80% of donations to the PAC — came from realtors or real estate-related companies, including $10,000 that came from several LLCs linked to Maine Real Estate Management, a major property manager in the city.
Henry attributed that trend in part to the relationships he and others in his group have with other business leaders in the city.
About a third of contributions to the PAC came from three LLCs that are all tied to Maine Real Estate Management, a major property management company in the city that’s owned by Jesse McCue. The property management company oversees about 3,000 units across the state, according to McCue’s LinkedIn profile.
Those three LLCs all donated on the same day and listed post office boxes as their addresses, according to the PAC’s campaign finance filings. Two of the LLCs — JM Investment Group LLC and C&M Investment Group LLC — listed the same post office box. McCue is named as a part owner of both companies on filings with the Maine Secretary of State’s office.
The other company, Apartment Living LLC, lists Tristan Thomas as an owner in its Secretary of State filings. Those files list 21 Main St., Suite 101 as Thomas’s address, the same suite as Maine Real Estate Management’s downtown Bangor office. The BDN could not find contact information for Thomas.
The three LLCs own at least six properties each in the city, property records show, ranging from smaller residential buildings to commercial properties to the Tower 99 luxury apartment complex downtown.
McCue did not respond to phone calls, emails and text messages requesting comment.
The PAC’s funding is separate from Maine for Keeps, the nonprofit headed by the wealthy tech entrepreneur and Cape Elizabeth resident Jonathan Bush that is pouring tens of thousands of dollars into local elections in Maine, although the two groups are aligned in some shared complaints about the city and have both hired the same social media agency.
While Concerned Citizens of Bangor is focusing on three candidates, Bush’s group is not endorsing or contributing to any in particular. His nonprofit, Maine for Keeps, had spent about $60,000 on what the entrepreneur called an “issue-based campaign” as of Oct. 21, he told the BDN. He did not respond to a follow-up question asking how that money was split between the campaign’s three target cities of Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville.
Maine for Keeps does not need to report any campaign finance filings because its ads don’t support or oppose any named candidates. Analysis of public information on the Meta Ad Library shows the group has spent at least $3,800 on Facebook and Instagram ads targeting Bangor.
Food and Medicine is also spending money on the council election, although its expenditures are far smaller.
The group is an anti-poverty organization that runs various programs in the area, such as community gardens and food distribution to those in need. It’s closely affiliated with the Eastern Maine Labor Council, which also participated in its candidate endorsement deliberations, according to Jack McKay, the executive director of Food and Medicine.
Food and Medicine’s PAC spent about $890 in the latest campaign finance reporting period, which ran from Oct. 1 to Oct. 20, on mailers, door cards and canvassing staff that included support for city-level Bangor candidates as well as those running for state and federal races, according to filings on the state ethics commission website. The BDN excluded expenditures that only related to state and federal candidates from its analysis of municipal election spending.
Split between the eight candidates the group endorsed up and down the ballot, that means it spent just over $110 on each City Council candidate, or about $330 on the three endorsed municipal candidates.
Mailers advertising the progressive slate say that the group’s chosen candidates “will work hardest for everyday Mainers, not special interests.” They list Movement Voter PAC and Food and Medicine as the PAC’s top donors. The former is a nationwide group working to fund a “blue wave” in Senate, House and downballot races across the country, according to its website. The group’s “Maine 2026 plan” posted online focuses on the federal races in the state.
The Food and Medicine PAC has not taken in any new contributions in this election cycle, although it has tens of thousands in the bank leftover from previous cycles, according to state filings, and Federal Election Commission records show that Movement Voter PAC has given $40,000 to the Food and Medicine nonprofit this year.
As a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, which the federal government defines as a social welfare organization that may engage in political activity as long as social welfare remains its primary purpose, Food and Medicine is allowed to accept political donations and create a PAC.
McKay, the executive director and a Bangor resident, emphasized that his organization runs many different programs, and electoral work is one piece of that.
“We believe it’s a better country when people directly affected have a voice in public policy matters,” he said.
Concerned Citizens of Bangor has repeatedly criticized Food and Medicine for its political organizing since it’s also received city money for social programs in the past.
Last year, the nonprofit spent just over $1,000 combined on the three City Council candidates it endorsed, according to BDN analysis of that year’s state filings.

High pressure moves offshore tonight ahead of a cold front crossing late tonight into early Friday. Expect a dry, mild evening, with clouds increasing overnight. title: FDA plans to update infant formula nutrition requirements
text:
FDA plans to update infant formula nutrition requirements for first time in nearly 30 years
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is proposing changes to nutrient requirements for infant formula. The update marks the first nutrition review for formula in nearly 30 years, the agency’s acting director, Kyle Diamantas, said Thursday.
The review is part of the Trump administration’s Operation Stork Speed initiative, which was announced in March 2025.
The first phase of the review focuses on four of 30 required nutrients in formula: iodine, manganese, vitamin A and vitamin D.
- Iodine is important for the production of thyroid hormone and brain development in infants. The proposed rule triples the amount of iodine required in infant formula, from 5 micrograms to 15, and sets a new upper limit of 50 micrograms.
- Manganese is a trace mineral that supports enzyme function and bone development. The proposal reduces the minimum required amount from 5 micrograms to 1 microgram per 100 calories, and it establishes a new limit of 50 micrograms.
- Vitamin A supports vision, immune function and cell growth. The proposal decreases the amount of vitamin A required in formula, from 250 international units per 100 calories to 233 IU. It would also change the units of measure for vitamin A from IU to retinol activity equivalents, or RAE.
- Vitamin D helps with development of bones and teeth and helps prevent rickets, or soft bones. The proposed rule doubles the minimum required amount of vitamin D from 1 to 2 micrograms and increases the maximum amount allowed to 3 micrograms.
- The proposed rule also reaffirms requirements for chloride, potassium, selenium and sodium.
The nutrition review was conducted by the FDA’s staff scientists and will be submitted for peer review, as required by law.
“Parents deserve confidence in every bottle they feed their baby,” U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a news release.
“Under President Trump’s Operation Stork Speed and Make America Healthy Again agenda, we are proposing stronger nutrient requirements, testing formula for contaminants, and putting the results directly in parents’ hands. We will hold infant formula manufacturers to rigorous scientific standards and put babies’ health first.”
The FDA looked at several lines of evidence supporting the changes, including nutrient reference values, or what the minimum amount would be to support health growth and development, as well as what would be considered toxic for an infant. It also looked at the nutrient composition of human milk, nutrient standards used by other countries and new studies published since 1998.
Diamantas said the agency is seeking public input on nutrients that are not currently required to be added to infant formula but are commonly added by manufacturers, including long-chain fatty acids like ARA and DHA, as well as L-carnitine, which helps the body break down fats and use them in tissues.
“There’s evidence that these nutrients contribute to neurodevelopment and health in infancy. And we want to hear from the scientific community, from clinicians, from industry, and the public as we consider whether or not to make these nutrients mandatory in the U.S. infant formula supply,” Diamantas said.
The FDA said its nutrient review for infant formula is ongoing. Subsequent phases of this review will assess all of the remaining required nutrients, potential new nutrient requirements and carbohydrate sources, Diamantas said.
On Thursday, health officials also provided an update on ongoing testing for chemical contaminants in infant formula; the latest batch of results “continue to be reassuring,” Diamantas said.

title: Man convicted of shooting woman in the head after argument
text:
BEAUFORT, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A man is expected to spend two decades behind bars for shooting a woman in the head after a verbal argument in an apartment parking lot in 2023.
This week, Bernard “Berney” Garvin Jr., 35, was found guilty of attempted murder and possession of a weapon during the commission of a violent crime.
Deputies with the Beaufort County Sheriff’s Office responded to reports of a shooting at the Hilton Head Gardens apartment complex in June of that year.
Upon arrival, they reported finding a pool of blood, spent shell casings on the pavement and bullet damage on a parked minivan.
Further investigation revealed that a woman was grazed in the head by a bullet after she argued with Garvin before arriving at the complex.
Beaufort County authorities said a woman was driving her friend’s minivan and dropped her off at the complex, as she planned to ride home with a male friend who followed in his vehicle that day.
As both vehicles pulled into the parking lot, the occupants reported seeing Garvin and another woman tussling over a liquor bottle as several other people at an all-day party roamed around.
The female victim exited the vehicle and asked him why he was “beating that woman” before they started to exchange angry words.
As the man in the other vehicle tried to get the female victim to get in his car so they could leave, Garvin reportedly pulled out a gun and shot the woman in the head.
14th Circuit Solicitor’s Office spokesman Jeff Kidd said Garvin fired at least four shots.
The woman was taken to the hospital before being transferred to another hospital, where she was placed in intensive care for possible brain bleeding.
Multiple witnesses were able to identify Garvin as the shooter, and he was arrested three months later in Georgia, Beaufort County authorities said.
Garvin is said to have a criminal history dating back to 2011 that includes convictions for assault and battery, pointing and presenting a firearm, driving under suspension and parole violations.
The judge sentenced Garvin to 20 years in prison plus five years’ probation.

title: Maine’s Hunters for the Hungry Program Accepting Donations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry’s Hunters for the Hungry program is working to tackle food insecurity with the help of generous hunters across the state.
The program transforms game meat donations into thousands of nutritious meals for Maine’s most vulnerable populations.
Hunters for the Hungry is a collaboration between the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, state biologists, Maine State Troopers, and hunters. It supplies wild game meat, which is lean and high in protein, to food pantries, soup kitchens, and homeless shelters.

title: Another Aroostook town weighs closing its police department
text:
A town at the edge of the North Maine Woods is considering shutting down one of Aroostook County’s few remaining police departments.
Ashland will hold a public hearing and special town meeting vote next week to decide whether to close its police department at the end of the year.
It’s becoming a familiar scenario as Maine towns weigh budget constraints and struggle to staff local departments. Should Ashland’s department close, it would leave The County with just six municipal police departments and shift policing duties for yet another town to the Maine State Police and Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office.
In the last six years, five small Maine towns have dissolved their municipal departments, largely because of recruiting difficulties. Millinocket closed in 2020, followed by Van Buren in 2021, Limestone in 2023, Washburn in 2024 and Mexico last year.
For Ashland, a town of 1,200, the challenge boils down to two choices: fund a police department with a $503,000 budget, according to the March town meeting warrant, or slash the next year’s budget and potentially cut property taxes.
The choice came up at the Oct. 19 Town Council meeting, when the group referred to residents’ property tax concerns.
Ashland’s 2026 mill rate is 20.93, with a state valuation of $115.1 million, according to state records. That valuation is up from $104.9 million in 2025, which means property taxes can rise.
“How do we go about finding out if the police department is a viable department to fund in the future based on what the tax rates have gone up to be?” Councilor Kevin Robinson asked. “And is that something that needs to be looked at?”
The key is knowing whether or not residents want to pay for the department, Council Chairperson Sherri Calhoun said.
“The middle ground is, is there a way to have a police department that’s half the price of the police department we have now,” she said. “But they told us last year it wasn’t possible.”
Councilor Tyler Michaud suggested a public hearing, which the group approved.
The special town meeting warrant, posted Wednesday on the Facebook page The Ashland, Maine Bulletin, states that residents will be asked “to see if the town will vote to continue operating a municipal police department effective January 1, 2027.”
If the article doesn’t pass, the department will be dissolved on Dec. 31.
Police Chief Michael Montpetit has written several posts on the same page highlighting statistics and tasks of the department. From Jan. 1 to Oct. 20, the department logged 2,562 service calls and made 211 traffic stops, he wrote Tuesday.
“I am fighting this fight because I know how badly the people of Ashland need us here,” he stated. “The future of an essential service is far too important to be taken lightly.”
Service calls such as animal control, assisting older residents and being present at school would go way if the department closes, which is no fault of the sheriff’s deputies and state troopers, who simply don’t have time to cover community needs, he wrote.
Earlier this year, Montpetit told the Bangor Daily News he worried Ashland could be the next town to close its department, which employs three full-time officers, himself included, and six reserve staff.
Neither Montpetit nor Town Manager Alicia Burby immediately responded to requests for comment.
The hearing is slated at 7 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 4, at the Ashland Recreation Center. The special town meeting will follow on Thursday, Nov. 5, at the same time and place.

title: Longtime Bangor law firm merges with Rudman Winchell
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A decades-old Bangor law firm has merged with Rudman Winchell, one of the state’s most prominent legal groups.
Gross, Minsky & Mogul, which operated for four decades in Bangor, closed its doors and merged with Rudman Winchell on Oct. 1. Clients transferred to the new firm, according to a news release.
The merger is the most recent shift in the area’s law firms. Eaton Peabody closed its doors in May 2025 after 85 years in business. A group of eight lawyers from the firm started Viridian Law in Ellsworth and other lawyers joined Verrill, a Portland-based law firm, which opened an office in Bangor.
The transition has gone remarkably well in the weeks since the merger, Rudman Winchell partner Michael Hockenbury said, describing it as a seamless unification of the two groups.
Steve Mogul and Ed Gould, lawyers who formerly worked at Gross, Minsky & Mogul, started practicing law together in the 1980s after they graduated law school, Gould said. Hockenbury approached him about joining the firms, which allowed the focus to remain in the Bangor area, Gould said.
Combining the firms creates more capacity for clients, Hockenbury said. Bringing in experienced lawyers allows the firm to invest more in mentorship for younger lawyers as it works to retain staff. The goal is to continue serving the community for decades, as it has for the last 100 years, Hockenbury said.
“We’re very happy with the way things have gone and excited to see where it takes us,” he said.

title: Brewers beat Rays in Game 5 to win first World Series title in franchise history
text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers playing in the smallest market in the majors are World Series champions for the first time.
Hey, Milwaukee: grab a brat, raise a beer and prepare for that parade.
To borrow a line from Bob Uecker, your title drought is up, outta here, gone.
Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings, rookie Cooper Pratt had two more hits and two RBIs, and Milwaukee beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on Wednesday night to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.
“It’s the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city’s waited a long, long time for this,” said captain Christian Yelich, who got hugs from franchise icon Robin Yount on the field when it was over. “We’re so happy to bring it home to them.”
World Series MVP William Contreras hit an RBI double and Misiorowski allowed just two hits before leaving the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee’s dugout for the last three games.
They filled the entire infield section of the ballpark for the trophy presentation and were still chanting “Let’s go Brewers!” almost two hours after the final pitch.
The 22-year-old Pratt set a Series rookie record with six straight hits before his sacrifice fly in the sixth. Jackson Chourio set a five-game Series record with 11 hits.
“This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real,” said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June. “This is surreal. It only took four months!”
The championship comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers’ only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.
But this team displayed the toughness and resilience of 67-year-old manager Pat Murphy, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.
“This group of guys right here, the 2026 team, will be remembered forever — and they deserve that because they were a team,” Murphy said. “They’re not worried about their own stats. No one cares about that. They care about coming together and winning tonight.”
With their flame-throwing, 24-year-old two-time All-Star on the mound, the Brewers rebounded from a heartbreaking, 4-3 extra-inning loss in Game 4 when they were three outs from a sweep in the 12th before a stellar bullpen finally faltered.
Pitching on four days’ rest for only the fifth time in 34 starts this year, The Miz had his longest outing since throwing 6 1/3 innings against the Cubs on Sept. 8. Leg cramps also forced him out of two outings earlier in the season.
“I don’t even have words,” Misiorowski said. “It’s amazing, just watching my guys celebrate. And the city — I know they’re going crazy in Milwaukee. It’s awesome.”
Misiorowski, who broke the World Series velocity record with a 103.5 mph fastball on the first pitch last Friday, opened with 12 straight four-seamers between 100.9-103 mph. He topped out at 103 twice among his 86 pitches, 58 strikes.
The 6-foot-7 right-hander didn’t record a strikeout in the first three innings for the first time in his two-year career and finished with two, matching his career low. But he was fired up after Yandy Díaz missed a cutter to end the fifth: The Miz pumped his fist twice and punched the air walking off the mound.
The NL Cy Young Award favorite allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter in a 3-2 victory in the opener. He was 2-0 with a 0.84 ERA in the best-of-seven Series.
JoJo Romero got two outs, Abner Uribe recorded two more and closer Trevor Megill pitched the last two innings, allowing an RBI double to Chandler Simpson with two outs in the ninth.
Megill retired Richie Palacios on a grounder to end it, threw his arms in the air and was mobbed by teammates near the mound while Brewers fans celebrated in the stands.
First baseman Jake Bauers tucked the ball in his back pocket before piling on and later gave the souvenir to Murphy, saying the skipper “deserved it.”
“Milwaukee has waited 44 years, and Milwaukee, you have your world championship!” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said from the postgame stage on the field.
Pratt, who was 4 for 5 with a tiebreaking solo homer in the 12th inning of Game 4, gave the Brewers a 1-0 lead with an RBI single against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in the second. Pratt singled for his sixth straight hit in the fifth and scored on David Hamilton’s single off Kevin Kelly.
Contreras hit an RBI double off Garrett Cleavinger in the sixth and Pratt added a sac fly to make it 4-0.
The teams combined for just four home runs in the Series, three by Milwaukee. The Brewers scored a major league-low 32.1% of their runs on homers this season and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Brewers led the majors with 103 wins in the regular season and went 11-2 in the postseason, including seven comeback wins and a sweep of the mighty Dodgers in the National League Championship Series.
“That’s the best team I’ve ever played against,” Rasmussen said.
Making history
Milwaukee’s only other MLB championship was won in 1957 by the Braves, who moved to Atlanta for the 1966 season.
Murphy’s team finished what Harvey Kuenn’s star-studded crew couldn’t accomplish 44 years ago as the American League champions. Harvey’s Wallbangers had five Hall of Famers: Yount, Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers, who missed the postseason with a forearm injury.
They also had a Hall of Fame broadcaster in the booth. The beloved Uecker died in January 2025 at age 90 after announcing Brewers games for 54 years.
“Cooperstown will remember the 2026 Brewers,” Murphy said.
Still seeking a title
The Rays, an expansion team that debuted in 1998, dropped to 0-3 in the World Series after defeats in 2008 and 2020. They’re one of four MLB franchises that have never won one. Colorado, San Diego and Seattle are the others.
“They’re banged-up and hurting right now, but just grateful for the way they carried themselves all season long, winning a bunch of games. It’s as close-knit of a group as I’ve ever been around,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said.
Lockout looming
This might have been the last Major League Baseball game for an extended period.
The Brewers won the World Series at a time when owners are pushing the players’ association for a salary cap because they maintain small-market teams can’t regularly succeed. A management lockout is likely to start Dec. 2 and could threaten the 2027 season.
This was the first Series since 1991 between teams in the bottom half of payrolls. The Brewers ranked 19th as of Aug. 31, and the Rays were 25th.

title: Rural Prosperity Summit Addresses County Issues
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Six federal agencies were in the county to hear about Aroostook’s biggest challenges. The Aroostook Partnership and the Northern Maine Development Commission hosted a Rural Prosperity Summit at Northern Maine Community College where officials discussed how they can help the county prosper.
Nearly seventy people attended the county’s Rural Prosperity Summit at NMCC. Officials from six federal agencies attended including the Environmental Protection Agency, the USDA Rural Development, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Small Business Administration, and the Department of Labor.
Kiersten Purington, President and CEO of the Aroostook Partnership said: “It’s incredibly rare to have not just one but six federal agencies represented in Maine at the same time. Let alone in a rural place like Aroostook County. They’ve done a tremendous job of presenting the programs that their agencies can offer and we’re now in the middle of listening sessions which is allowing individuals from the community to come out here to talk to connect to raise issues to gain more awareness and meet the people who can help affect change.”
During the summit community members brought up issues the county has being seeing recently. “We’ve had members of our community raise issues around affordable housing, cost of inflation, tariffs, issues with regard to access to healthcare, aging in place, food sources. These are all such important issues that members of the community here feel deeply about and most importantly our voices are being heard,” continued Purington.
John Butera, State Director for Maine Rural Development added: “They’re problems that are not just particularly here in the county. They’re national problems: affordable housing, a trained workforce, things of that nature. They’re hard challenges. They’re not easy but it starts somewhere and it has to start with a conversation. We want to be a partner, and we want to try to help put all the pieces together to help the economy grow and for people to be prosperous. That’s really what it’s all about at the end of the day.”
Purington says she hopes that the people who attended the summit left with a greater understanding of what these federal agencies offer. Butera says the agencies will take the conversations back to Washington, D.C. where they will discuss the county’s issues and work to address them.

title: Pres. Trump to campaign for midterms in Daytona Beach Friday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is scheduled to campaign at another midterm rally in Daytona Beach, Fla. on Friday, in one of his final bids to boost Republican voter turnout for the upcoming elections.
The rally is part of the president’s homestretch of midterm events, after the Republican National Committee announced on Thursday that rallies in Kansas and Iowa would be canceled and replaced with a series of “tele-rallies.”
“With Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled,” party officials said in a press release.
Republican Gubernatorial candidate and Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) is also expected to attend the rally. He has been leading in recent polls against Democrat David Jolly, but the race is considered close enough to be competitive.
Trump also is expected to stump for Republicans who are running for Congress including Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) and Rep. Randy Fine’s (R-Fla.), who represents the Daytona Beach area.
Republicans hold 20 out of the 28 House seats in the state. That number may increase after the elections because of recent redistricting efforts.

title: Shaw’s sued after truck driver fatally crushed by rock salt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine family is suing Shaw’s Supermarkets after a man died months after he was crushed by 50-pound bags of salt.
Randall “Randy” Rackliffe, of Saco, died Sept. 12, eight months after an unstable pallet of water bottles and rock salt shifted in a semi-trailer, crushing him on Jan. 18, according to a lawsuit filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court of Maine in Portland.
Rackliffe, 62, spent those intervening months hospitalized, the lawsuit said. It seeks unspecified damages for Rackliffe’s medical expenses, mental anguish, pain, suffering and premature death.
His sister, Joya Kim Maynard, is suing Shaw’s as a representative of Rackliffe’s estate. The lawsuit alleges Shaw’s failed to meet the standard of care, causing the wrongful death of Rackliffe.
Shaw’s parent company, Albertsons Companies, did not respond to a request for comment.
“[Rackliffe] took immense pride in his work,” Maynard’s attorney, Taylor Asen, said. “His injuries were among the most horrific I’ve seen in my career. I wouldn’t wish the months of pain and suffering he endured on anyone. His suffering and death were entirely preventable. His family is determined to hold Shaw’s accountable for the devastating harm it caused and to ensure that Shaw’s makes safety a priority.”
Rackliffe was a truck driver for Brown Dog Carries and Logistics, which moves freight for Shaw’s, the lawsuit said. He picked up a trailer loaded by Shaw’s employees in Wells on Jan. 18.
He drove the trailer to a Raynham, Massachusetts, store where Shaw’s employees started unloading the pallets, which had 50-pound bags of Morton’s SafeT-Salt stacked on top of shrink-wrapped cases of bottled water, according to the lawsuit.
Rackliffe was standing in the trailer, holding a pallet of paper products steady so employees could remove the rock salt and water. As Shaw’s employees moved the pallets, the 50-pound rock salt bags tipped over and crushed Rackliffe, the lawsuit said.
Shaw’s failed to have procedures in place to ensure goods were stacked and unloaded in a safe manner, and failed to appropriately secure goods to pallets, the lawsuit said.
Rackliffe was fatally injured because of Shaw’s negligence, the lawsuit said.
Rackliffe had two daughters and four grandchildren, his obituary said. It thanked the staff at Maine Medical Center for giving him a fighting chance.
“Given Dad’s resilience and strong will, this is not the outcome we ever anticipated,” the obituary said. “He showed tremendous strength and fought incredibly hard every single day. Anyone who knew Dad knows that he was bullheaded, self-sufficient, and not one to give up easily. He fought this battle with the same determination that carried him through life.”

title: Patrick Stewart’s cause of death revealed: ‘Brief and poignant journey’
text:
Patrick Stewart died after battling Alzheimer’s, Lewy body dementia: What to know
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed English actor known for his roles in "Star Trek" and "X-Men," has died.
Stewart died Wednesday following what his publicist called a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. He was 86.
Stewart, whose career spanned more than six decades in theater, television and film, had not publicly disclosed his diagnoses prior to his death.
Related: Remembering acting icon Patrick Stewart.
The two conditions can overlap
Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are different conditions, but both can affect memory, thinking and everyday life.
Lewy body dementia can also cause changes in alertness, visual hallucinations, sleep problems and movement difficulties, according to the National Institute on Aging.
The conditions can occur together. When a person has brain changes linked to more than one type of dementia, it is called mixed dementia, according to the Alzheimer's Association. Alzheimer’s-related changes are often found alongside Lewy bodies, though having one condition does not necessarily mean a person has the other.
What is Lewy body dementia?
Lewy body dementia is linked to abnormal protein deposits in the brain, called Lewy bodies. Named after the scientist that discovered them, Lewy bodies can disrupt brain functions that affect thinking, movement, behavior, mood and sleep.
Common signs include changes in attention, seeing things that are not there, and stiffness or difficulty walking.
The condition drew wide public attention after CNN founder Ted Turner revealed his diagnosis in 2018. Robin Williams’s autopsy later found Lewy body disease, although his condition was not publicly diagnosed while he was alive.
Lewy body dementia is the second most common type of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, according to Mayo Clinic.
What is Alzheimer’s disease?
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia. It gradually damages parts of the brain involved in memory and thinking.
Memory problems are often an early sign, but the disease can also affect language, judgment and reasoning, according to the Alzheimer's Association.
Over time, these changes can make everyday tasks harder.
Both Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer's are devastating conditions.
A statement posted to Stewart's Instagram page reads in part, “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

title: Who might be Cinderella, and other Week 9 high school football storylines
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
For teams in four Maine high school football classes, the regular season is done; for two other classes, this is the final weekend. With so much football behind us, we mostly know which teams are contenders and which are not.
Yet every once in a while, a team that has flown under the radar makes a deep run in November. Could that happen this year? Let’s examine that and more in this week’s look at the state’s biggest storylines.
Who might make an unexpected playoff run?
In Class B North, Fryeburg Academy (4-4) nearly beat Cony to start the season before giving Lawrence a fight in Week 2. Fresh off an impressive win over Skowhegan, the fourth-seeded Raiders, who host No. 5 Messalonskee (4-4) in the quarterfinals, could have a run in them.
Class B South looks wide open, so don’t count any out, including the bottom three seeds: No. 4 Falmouth, No. 5 Westbrook and No. 6 Cheverus. Falmouth, which host Westbrook, nearly knocked off Class C contender Greely, but don’t forget that Westbrook is the reigning state champ. Cheverus, meanwhile, travels back to No. 3 Biddeford (5-3), one week after trouncing the Tigers, 44-8.
Class C looks top-heavy between Leavitt, Greely and Hermon. But Nokomis has been on the cusp of a breakthrough all season, and after the Warriors (3-5) outgained Wells 333-136 in a victory Saturday, Class C foes should not overlook them. Nokomis closes the regular season at Oceanside (5-3) on Friday.
In Class D, don’t sleep on John Bapst (4-4). The third-seeded Crusaders, who were competitive against Winthrop last week, host No. 6 Oak Hill (1-7) in the North quarterfinals and would face No. 2 Maine Central Institute (6-2) in the semifinals. The North title game is at Cameron Stadium, where Bapst plays its home games.
Winslow, Winthrop and Class D déjà vu
The road to the Class D North title, though, goes through Winslow. The Black Raiders (7-1) went 5-0 in the regular season against D North opponents, winning by an average of 33.6 points, to easily claim the No. 1 seed.
One has to wonder, then: Might we see a Winslow-Winthrop Class D title game for a second straight year? Others will have a say, but there are plenty of similarities between the Black Raiders and Ramblers — both with one another and in comparison to last year.
Since a 14-13 Week 1 loss at Wells that coach Wes Littlefield said “really bothered” the Black Raiders, Winslow has rolled, holding its next six opponents to six points or fewer. That streak ended in a 50-18 win over Madison on Saturday. Among the Black Raiders’ other wins are victories over John Bapst, Freeport, MCI and Morse.
“I think they really took it to heart losing that game down at Wells,” Littlefield said. “Really, they’ve been pretty focused (ever since) losing states last year. … Guys like Michael Loubier and Isaac Bulger got a taste of it, and they were not happy with how they finished the end of the year. They’d like to get back there.”
Like Winslow, Winthrop (7-1) suffered an early one-point loss, 29-28 at Freeport in Week 2. The Ramblers, also like the Black Raiders did, then held six straight opponents to one score or fewer.
To win D South, the No. 2 Ramblers might have to avenge the loss to No. 1 Freeport (6-2). Therein lies another similarity to Winslow, which lost to John Bapst in Week 4 last year before beating the Crusaders in the North final.
On the outside looking in
It seems as if more teams than ever make the playoffs in the modern era. Still, there are some teams that feel as if they should still be playing — or will have that feeling after this weekend.
Either Noble (3-5) or South Portland (4-4) will miss out in A South. If the Red Riots beat Portland (6-2) or if Noble falls to Scarborough (0-8), South Portland qualifies as the No. 4 seed. A Knights win and a Red Riots loss, though? That changes things, and the final spot comes down to how two games in New Hampshire unfold.
There’s always plenty on the line when Edward Little and Lewiston meet. Yet while the Red Eddies (3-4) have had their moments this year, they cannot mathematically catch Windham or Bangor in A North. Thus, their season will conclude Saturday, win or lose.
In B North, Mt. Blue must feel unlucky despite a 2-6 finish. The Cougars nearly beat Fryeburg in Week 7 and came close against Skowhegan in Week 1. The team that beat out Mt. Blue for the final playoff spot? Brunswick, which lost 39-6 to the Cougars in Week 5.
Eight-man Large South was a gauntlet, and one of the odd teams out is Lake Region (2-6). The Lakers’ losses this year were to Yarmouth, Spruce Mountain, Stearns, Gray-New Gloucester, Old Town and Cape Elizabeth — teams that were a combined 40-7.

title: Sen. Collins and Jackson hit campaign trail days until the midterms

Sen. Collins and Jackson hit campaign trail days until the midterms
Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson hit the campaign trail Wednesday with less than a week away from Election Day.
Jackson spent the day campaigning with Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly in Brunswick. Kelly is the latest senator joining Jackson ahead of the midterms, following Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
"What I have is a deep desire to help people in this country get quality affordable healthcare, get prescription drugs, childcare, and I'm not going to be catering to billionaires like Susan does," Jackson said.
Collins greeted employees at Bath Iron Works during their shift change in the afternoon. She continues to point voters to her experience over Jackson in Washington.
"They should consider who can do more for the people of Maine," Collins said. "Someone who is the chair of the appropriations committee that's been the first opportunity that a Maine senator has had in nearly a century, or someone who is at the bottom for seniority?"
The high-stakes race could help determine which party holds the majority in the Senate.
Vacationland is at the front and center of this midterm cycle. Collins is on the ballot again, seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Jackson, the state's former Senate president, is trying to take down a senator who has held the seat for nearly 30 years.
Come Nov. 3, Mainers must choose one candidate to represent them in Washington.

title: Actress Elke Sommer, known for roles in 1960s comedies and espionage films, dies at 85
text:
Actress Elke Sommer, known for roles in 1960s comedies and espionage films, dies at 85
Elke Sommer, the striking blonde bombshell of German descent who was a mainstay of 1960s Hollywood comedies and espionage movies including “The Prize” and “A Shot in the Dark,” has died. She was 85.
Video above: Remembering those we've lost in 2026
Sommer died at home in Bel Air, in Los Angeles, on Wednesday, her stepson Sebastian Walther told the German outlet Bild. The Los Angeles Police Department told The Associated Press that it responded to the death of an 85-year-old woman on Sommer’s block Wednesday night.
With big almond eyes and golden locks, often styled high in a beehive, Sommer worked with some of the biggest stars of the time, including Paul Newman in “The Prize,” Peter Sellers in the Pink Panther film “A Shot in the Dark,” James Garner and Dick Van Dyke in “The Art of Love,” Bob Hope in “Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number!” and Dean Martin and Sharon Tate in “The Wrecking Crew.”
Sommer was born Elke Schletz in Berlin in the midst of the World War II, on Nov. 5, 1940, though the family had to evacuate to the south in 1942. Her father, who died when she was 14, was a Protestant pastor.
She’d intended to study languages, but during a trip to Italy with her mother, Renata, in 1958, she caught the eye of someone in the Italian film industry who invited her to appear in her first film: “The Friend of the Jaguar.” Actor and filmmaker Vittorio De Sica noticed her too, and soon she was working nonstop throughout Europe, in Italy, Spain and England, with the newly adopted surname Sommer.
Her big Hollywood break came from producer Pandro S. Berman, who had seen her in a German drama that screened for the Golden Globes, and offered her a role in “The Prize” where she played chaperone and love interest to Newman’s Nobel Prize-winning character. In the trade publication Variety’s review, they wrote that Sommer, “hasn’t a very scintillating role, but has the looks to make that a secondary issue.” And it would win her the Golden Globe for most promising newcomer.
In Blake Edwards’ Pink Panther sequel “A Shot in the Dark,” she played Maria Gambrelli, a maid framed for murder, who also sparks the romantic interest of Sellers’ Inspector Clouseau. She also posed for Playboy Magazine around that time, in photographs shot by her first husband Joe Hyams. They married in November 1964 and divorced in 1981.
In 1993 she married German hotelier Wolf Walther, who died in July at age 77.
Sommer didn’t take the sex symbol designation too seriously, saying that it was essentially meaningless. She told Film Talk in a 2014 interview that some of her favorite actors, like Rita Hayworth and Ava Gardner, were also considered sex symbols. Besides, she said, she was always just acting the part.
“My whole life, I have been directed, I have been produced, I spoke the lines written for the character,” she said in the interview. “I was always playing, and the only thing I could bring was my energy. So what is it, this sex appeal? Why was I voted in this list of most sexy women? It’s not because of my looks or anything; it’s because of the energy.”

title: Severe drought expands across central Maine
text:
Severe drought expands across central Maine
Lack of rain keeps portions of Maine in extreme drought
Severe drought expands across central Maine
Lack of rain keeps portions of Maine in extreme drought
Severe drought expanded across central Maine this week as little precipitation fell across the Northeast, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor update released Thursday, Oct. 29.
All of Maine remained in drought, with conditions ranging from moderate to extreme. Severe drought covered much of northern Maine and portions of central and southern Maine, while extreme drought persisted along parts of the southern and midcoast coastline.
The report reflects conditions as of 8 a.m. Tuesday, Oct. 27. Its map shows moderate drought across much of western and eastern Maine, with more intense conditions concentrated in northern areas and portions of the central and coastal regions.
The monitor's regional summary said very little precipitation fell across the Northeast during the past week, leading to deterioration in a few areas. However, heavier precipitation before the past one to two weeks helped prevent more widespread worsening.
Most of the region's drought designations remained unchanged. Central Maine was an exception, with an expansion of severe drought.
Maine remained the only state in the Northeast with severe or extreme drought, according to the regional summary. Elsewhere in the region, moderate drought was confined to a few small areas in its northern and southern portions.

title: Hugh Jackman, William Shatner and George Takei among those paying tribute to Patrick Stewart
text:
Hugh Jackman, William Shatner and George Takei among those paying tribute to Patrick Stewart
Following the death of Patrick Stewart at 86, a slew of tributes from acting colleagues and even Marvel Studios poured in. Known for his roles as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" films, Stewart died in Los Angeles on Wednesday after what his spokesperson described as a “brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
Related video above: Patrick Stewart makes his mark in Hollywood
William Shatner
“What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.” — the actor and Stewart's fellow “Star Trek” alum, in a statement.
Hugh Jackman
“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.” — the actor and Stewart's “X-Men” co-star, on Instagram.
Minnie Driver
“Is this year some kind of portal to a much, much better place that all the greatest people know about and so have gently made their exits ? Dearest Patrick. Who always had the best advice, the funniest story, the patience to listen. I’m just bereft. All love to your family, and you, in my heart forever.” — the actor and Stewart's “The Wilde Wedding” co-star, on social media.
Cary Elwes
“My heart is seriously heavy today. We have lost the marvelous #PatrickStewart. I first met Patrick on the set of Lady Jane back in 1984 and fell in love with him immediately. Not only was amiable and kind with a great sense of humor, he was incredible to work with. His command of the screen with his sheer presence and that unmistakable voice was a sight to behold. Almost a decade later when Mel and I were discussing who should play King Richard in Men in Tights, I told him it has to be Patrick. Fortunately for us he accepted and once again shared his joy and talent with us all. My now shattered heart goes out to Sunny, his children, friends and fans, of which I will always be one. Good night, sweet Prince.” — the actor and Stewart's “Lady Jane” and “Robin Hood: Men in Tights” co-star, on Instagram.
Rebecca Romijn
“I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years, and to have been in his orbit … both as a fellow mutant and as a fellow member of Starfleet. He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humor, and that booming voice of his that always spoke to the very back of the room, as every classically trained Shakespearean great needs to master, has always been an inspiration. I send my condolences to his family, and I’ll miss my friend dearly. Rest in peace, Patrick.” — the actor and Stewart's co-star in “X-Men” and “Star Trek” universe movies, in a video on social media.
Kevin Feige
"I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the firstX-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.
"It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed." — the producer and president at Marvel Studios, in a statement.
George Takei
“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.” — the actor and Stewart’s fellow “Star Trek” alum, on social media.
Seth MacFarlane
"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us. I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on ‘American Dad!,’ ‘Family Guy,’ and ‘Ted.' He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come. I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film. He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, ‘Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.’ We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet." — the actor and producer, on Instagram.
Ricky Gervais
RIP Patrick Stewart. What an actor. I still can’t believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn’t even mind when I ruined every take. Legend." — the actor, on Instagram alongside a video of an outtake while filming a scene from the BBC/HBO comedy series “Extras.”
Marvel Studios
“All of us at Marvel Studios are deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday. He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.” — in a social media post.
SAG-AFTRA
“Sir Patrick Stewart will live on in our hearts and memories through his remarkable career spanning the British stage, television and film. Our condolences to his family, friends, colleagues and a galaxy of fans. #SagAftraMember since 1987.” — in a social media post.
Kumail Nanjiani
“Sir Patrick Stewart was the best. I don’t know what else I can say.” — the actor, on social media.

title: Time’s long past up for twice-yearly clock-changing
text:
On Halloween this year, the sun will set in Portland at 5:33 p.m. One day later, for no good reason, sunset on Sunday will occur 61 minutes earlier after a return to “standard time.”
Here in Maine, there is clear and robust support for a return to a single, year-round time — a move that would end confusion, keep our daily routines on schedule and remove one little irritant from our busy lives.
In Washington, D.C., they just can’t get on the same page. The U.S. House agreed by a wide margin over the summer that the nation should stop changing its clocks twice a year. Both U.S. Reps. Jared Golden and Chellie Pingree joined the majority in favor of the proposal.
But despite their support for the bill, it remains stalled in the Senate, which specializes in making sure nothing much happens on Capitol Hill.
Both of Maine’s senators, Republican Susan Collins and independent Angus King, favor leaving daylight saving time permanently in place.
Collins once said changing the clocks twice annually “has been linked to higher rates of accidents, depression and other health issues.”
“Like many Maine people, I’m tired of 4 p.m. sunsets and time-change whiplash that throws our collective routines out of whack,” King said.
Even President Donald Trump, a man who is wrong about almost everything, recognized that “a vast majority of the country want it” and called this week for passage of the measure.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson said during a July debate that he wants to leave daylight saving time in place year-round because he knows some Maine children have long bus rides to school. They’ll be safer, he said, if there is more light for early-morning winter bus runs.
State Sen. Rick Bennett, the independent gubernatorial candidate from Oxford, convinced his colleagues in the Legislature last year to unanimously endorse a bill to end the clock-changing shuffle we experience twice a year.
Bennett told lawmakers at the time, “I am overwhelmed by the increasing numbers of people I hear from who ask, ‘Why do we bother to change our clocks for four months of the year?’ Like these folks, I find this practice is anachronistic and lacking in common sense.”
Of course, getting rid of something just because it is “anachronistic and lacking in common sense” has never worked out smoothly in the nation’s capital, especially when a smattering of senators don’t want to see common sense prevail.
Sen. Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, one of the naysayers, said that “if permanent daylight saving time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans.”
We in Maine know something about dark and dismal winters.
We also know that whatever time our clocks say will have no impact at all on the nature of our winters. They will remain, as always, too cold, with too little daylight.
There aren’t many issues where I think we ought to give Trump a win. This is one of them.
It’s past time to have my microwave’s clock be reasonably accurate all year long.

title: US Navy sailor killed in WWII identified after 82 years
text:
US Navy sailor killed in WWII identified after 82 years
The remains of a U.S. Navy sailor from northwest Iowa, who died as a prisoner of war during World War II, have been identified after more than 82 years.
The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency said the remains belong to Robert Glenn Shove of Cherokee.
Shove died in a Japanese prison camp in the Philippines in October 1943.
He enlisted in Des Moines in 1940 and served aboard the USS Canopus.
Shove's remains were recovered after the war but were not identified at the time.
He will be laid to rest on Nov. 7 at Memorial Park Cemetery off Morningside Avenue in Sioux City.

title: Wiscasset Students Study Ocean and Climate First-Hand
text:
Wiscasset Middle High School students in Wyatt Ray’s ocean and climate class got hands-on experience with a salt marsh estuarine ecosystem at Midcoast Conservancy’s Marsh River Preserve, in Newcastle.
Ocean and climate is a physical science elective course offered in the first semester. In the second semester, students can choose to continue with marine life, which covers the life science side of the subject.
At the preserve, students collected water samples to examine back at school. They recorded the date, time, and weather conditions, along with anything they could see, hear, feel, or smell. They documented data collection methods and sketched pictures of the collection sites.

text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Federal officials have appointed two prosecutors to oversee voting rights and election security in Maine during the upcoming general election.
The U.S. Department of Justice announced Assistant U.S. Attorneys John Osborn and Andrew McCormack will lead election-day monitoring efforts for the District of Maine.
Osborn and McCormack are tasked with overseeing the handling of election-day complaints, including allegations of voter intimidation, discrimination, ballot fraud, voter impersonation and bribery.
Officials will be on duty in Bangor and Portland to take reports of any issues.

title: Cornell faculty to move forward with no-confidence vote over handling of sexual assault allegations
text:
Cornell faculty to move forward with no-confidence vote over handling of sexual assault allegations
Cornell University faculty debated Wednesday over whether they had enough information to pass judgment on the school’s leadership following its handling of a woman’s report that she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024, with some professors urging patience and others arguing that years of institutional failures demanded action.
The discussion unfolded during a Faculty Senate meeting closed to the media, according to a recording obtained by The Associated Press. Faculty members are now moving forward with an electronic vote on a proposed no-confidence resolution against the university’s administration, with voting set to conclude Nov. 6.
A no-confidence vote would be largely symbolic but it could send a message to the university’s trustees, who ultimately decide who leads it.
Related video above: Wes Moore orders sexual assault policy review
The debate was at times personal, with faculty members describing fears of retaliation, sharing experiences of harassment and acknowledging their nervousness about speaking publicly.
Beth Frances Milles, an associate professor of performing arts who is also a Cornell graduate and parent, made an emotional plea for civility, describing messages from women who had experienced sexual assault, including former college classmates.
“There are so many things to talk about,” she said. “Please, let’s talk about it together and not sneer at each other when we disagree.”
After at least an hour of debate, members voted down an attempt to delay voting on the resolution until an independent investigation into Cornell's handling of the sexual assault allegations is completed.
Faculty members speak
Anne Marie Brady, a Faculty Senate member who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said she left Wednesday’s meeting encouraged and particularly struck by the breadth of faculty who spoke.
Several expressed fear of retaliation for criticizing the administration, she said. Brady, who is not on the tenure track, said she and other contingent faculty members also risked professional consequences by speaking publicly.
“The more people who speak out, the more we protect each other,” Brady said in a phone interview after the meeting.
During the meeting, economics professor Seth Sanders, speaking in favor of postponing the vote, acknowledged that sexual assault was a serious problem on campus but argued that faculty needed more information before judging the administration’s response. He said about 80% of faculty in his department opposed the no-confidence resolution for now, with many wanting to await the independent investigation.
“I don’t think setting it up as having confidence in the administration or supporting the administration is right,” Sanders said. “I think it’s legitimate to think that you don’t know whether to have confidence because you don’t know what happened or why in the Jane Doe case.”
Inna Zakharevich, an associate professor of mathematics, also supported postponing the vote, arguing that a declaration of no confidence “needs to be more than just an expression of displeasure.”
“It needs to be airtight to read as an indictment, with clear points about what the administration did wrong and what we would have liked them to do right,” she said. "But we don’t have that information right now."
Jennifer Colt, a Faculty Senator for the university library, argued that those advocating to postpone the vote were asking “the Senate to become bystanders."
“It asks us to stand by and do nothing,” she said.
The resolution was introduced at an Oct. 14 meeting when angry members confronted Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff about the university’s handling of the allegations.
Several female faculty members call for president's resignation
Wednesday’s meeting came a day after 20 female science and engineering faculty members called on Kotlikoff to resign in a letter to Cornell’s trustees obtained by AP.
“What our community needed was clear leadership; instead, it faced a leadership vacuum,” the professors wrote.
The proposed resolution expresses no confidence in Cornell’s administration over its response to sexual assault on campus but does not explicitly call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Faculty Sen. Noah Tamarkin, an anthropology professor and co-sponsor of the resolution, said it was intended to pressure university leaders to change how sexual assault is addressed and to give faculty and students a greater role in decision-making, not necessarily force anyone from office.
Materials science and engineering Professor Lara Estroff, one of the signatories of the letter, said she opposed delaying the vote. But she also criticized the resolution itself, saying its reference to the university’s administration was too vague and that she preferred the letter’s explicit call for Kotlikoff to resign.
“I wouldn’t vote for the resolution as it is worded,” said Estroff, who is not a Faculty Senate member.
Cornell president defends his leadership
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven men have denied her allegations.
The criminal investigation by Cornell’s police department stalled after the district attorney declined to pursue charges. In a New York Times interview, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the investigation.
At an Oct. 14 Faculty Senate meeting, Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps but defended his leadership and asked for more time to reform student social life, according to a recording obtained by the AP.
