title: A Lewiston-based fund that supports families grieving a child is running dry
text:
Without the support of a Lewiston nonprofit, Traci Alden says she would not have been able to bury her children.
Alden gave birth to two stillborn babies between 2008 and 2012. When she lost her daughter, she couldn’t bring herself to bury the ashes. When she lost her son four years later, an organization called the Colby Fund paid for the cremation, memorial services and urn.
It gave her the space to grieve.
“You don’t expect it,” said Alden, 44, of Auburn. “You don’t have money set aside. We weren’t financially in a place where we could do that. So, because of the Colby Fund, I was actually able to bury both of my children together, which is absolutely amazing.”
Over the past year, the volunteer-run nonprofit paid $18,000 to support two dozen grieving families and cover the costs associated with losing their children. But fundraising challenges have jeopardized the future of those services. The organization fell $4,000 short of its fundraising goal at the annual Walk to Remember in Rumford earlier this month, said Tammy Fournier, who co-founded the Colby Fund in 2003.
That annual fundraiser has sustained decades of services, including hospital bereavement trainings and advocacy. Now, Fournier said she is setting aside all remaining funds for the financial assistance program.
“Parents are buying cribs and diapers,” Fournier said. “They’re not buying caskets and grave sites. The Colby Fund helps defer those costs for those families, and we are at risk of not being able to provide for those services in our community shortly.”
She said declining attendance at Colby Fund events, from the annual walk to a monthly support group in Lewiston, seems to correspond with the closure of birthing units in the area and across Maine in recent years. A trained birth and bereavement doula, Fournier has found herself traveling more and more to hospitals outside of Lewiston-Auburn to be with families as they navigate postpartum bereavement, including to Portland, Norway and even Portsmouth.
Many families say they can’t make the drive to Lewiston.
But the need has not changed. Roughly one in four pregnancies end in miscarriage and there are about 2 million stillbirths each year, according to the World Health Organization. The Colby Fund provides support to families that lose a child from any stage of pregnancy to 3 years old.
Fournier did not have that kind of support after losing her son, Gunner, at 26 weeks. She remembers leaving the hospital in 1991 with nothing but a prescription and a recommendation to see a counselor. There weren’t support groups. Her friends were all having babies.
She didn’t know how to talk about her son, who she never got to see or hold.
“A person that has a stillborn feels awkward having a funeral for a baby that no one’s met or loved, except them,” Fournier said. “And when you’re a young couple, you go: Do I spend that kind of money? Nobody loved them like I did. They weren’t born yet. Who’s going to come for my dead baby?”
When someone else offers to pay for the funeral, those questions fade into the background.
Fournier is hoping to find sponsors who will help sustain the Colby Fund. Consistent funding would help, but grant applications take time that she and the other volunteers don’t have. Right now, she just wants to get the word out.
At the memorial gardens at St. Mary’s Regional Medical Center and Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston, dozens of memorial plaques dot the wall with loving inscriptions. Alden has one for her daughter, paid for by the Colby Fund. She still hasn’t found the right words for her son.
Fournier tells her they will come.
On the day of the Walk to Remember, Alden was cheering on her 13-year-old daughter at a softball tournament. Life has gotten busy, in a good way. It’s been years since she attended the support group.
She still sees the Colby Fund as a necessity, for herself and other Maine families who have yet to suffer the most unthinkable loss.
“I needed somebody that could truly understand my pain, my heartache, and basically someone there to teach me how to get through life,” Alden said. “That has always been the Colby Fund.”

title: ‘Amazed that she’s alive’: 18-year-old driver in ICU after hitting moose on icy road
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - A mother in Alaska said her 18-year-old daughter is lucky to be alive after hitting a moose Monday night while driving down an icy Anchorage road.
“That’s what we’ve been hearing this entire ordeal, from the EMTs to the doctors; they are amazed that she’s alive,” Megan Stone said about her daughter’s crash.
According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway.
Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake.
When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools.
Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds.
“Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. In this case, it landed on the hood and kind of the windshield and roof area. We see forces of 30,000 to 40,000 pounds being put onto that car.”
Fish and Game Biologist Cory Stantorf said there are usually about 100 moose-vehicle collisions in the Anchorage area every year, but this is the time when they start to increase.
“Not only do we have moose moving because of the rut, following cows, we are also doing that morning commute in the pitch-black, but kids are also going to school in the pitch-black, and there’s not a lot of contrast without snow to illuminate these moose,” Stantorf said. “So drivers really need to slow down because there’s just not the reaction time that we have in the summer.”
As for Autumn, her mother said Wednesday that she was still in the ICU, where she was expected to remain for several days.
Stone said her daughter has some brain bruising, lacerations and a broken hand, but didn’t appear to have any catastrophic injuries.
Stone said she’s seen pictures of the wreck and was relieved her daughter survived.
“It’s horrifying to see those photos as her mom, but I’m also grateful, because I can put into context just how close we were to losing her,” she said.

title: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
text:
(AP) - Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen.
He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.” The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and The New York Times said it was “a must-see.”
“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”
Starship commander grew up without a toilet
Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
In his memoir, “Making It So,” Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. “Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”
The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard
“The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time,” he would write.
Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. “People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?‘” he told the AP. “Telly?”
Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film “Excalibur.” He had just done a production of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. “I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail.”
It didn’t, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the “Star Trek” franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”
His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in ‘Henry IV,’ which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.
Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series “Star Trek: Picard.”)
Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another “Star Trek” icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
The show gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films “Conspiracy Theory,” “L.A. Story” and on Broadway, where he starred in “The Tempest,” “The Caretaker” and David Mamet’s “A Life in the Theater.” He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.
A brave and commanding persona. But sexy?
In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide’s “Top Turn-Ons,” based on a readers’ poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: “Absurd.”
Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned in four more movies before Professor X’s death in 2017’s “Logan.” He reappeared in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” in 2022 and is reprising the role in the upcoming “Avengers: Doomsday.”
He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane’s Starz show “Blunt Talk” for two series and voiced Poop in “The Emoji Movie.” He made appearances on “Robot Chicken,” “Futurama” and “The Simpsons” (in one episode, Homer loses his hair, and Stewart tells him it’s great to be bald.)
Later in life, he proved internet-savvy and found new fans with his humor, posing in a bath in a lobster suit and triggering memes when he posted a photo of him picking apples. When he was mistakenly outed as gay by a British newspaper, he said it was a nice change. “At least I didn’t wake up to the internet telling me I was dead again,” he tweeted.
He married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, with the actor’s “X-Men” co-star McKellen officiating. Stewart later tweeted a photo of the newlyweds in a ball pit.
He also is survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.

title: Indictment: 6 accused of filing 9,000 fraudulent tax returns seeking $177 million in refunds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — A tax preparation service used a variety of bogus deductions to file thousands of returns seeking $177 million in fraudulent refunds, according to a federal indictment unsealed Wednesday.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Mobile said the investigation is part of an ongoing operation led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Internal Revenue Service and the FBI.
Defendants named in the indictment
The lead defendant is Jennifer Beverly, 47, who owned JB Accounting Tax Service LLC on Broad Street. She is charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud.
The indictment also names one of her employees, former University of Alabama basketball player Kennedy Lawrence Stovall Winston, 42. Winston, who attended Blount High School, also faces an unrelated federal fraud charge related to stolen Treasury checks.
Four other employees of the tax preparation service face conspiracy and wire fraud charges:
- Jadasha Bowman, 28
- Solida Lucille Green, 36
- Paris Lovett, also known as Paris Johnson, 30
- Shermeka Benjamin, 38
Allegations in the indictment
The indictment alleges that, from about 2021 through 2024, the defendants filed more than 9,000 fraudulent returns.
Of the $177 million in claimed refunds, the IRS issued $81 million, according to the indictment.
The indictment details a variety of tax deductions and credits that prosecutors allege the defendants improperly claimed. Those include COVID-19 credits, fuel tax credits, credit repayments, estimated tax payments and education credits.
Statements from federal agencies
Maisha Horton, acting special agent in charge of the Atlanta Field Office of the IRS Criminal Investigation Division, called the alleged abuse “staggering” in a prepared statement.
“Tax return preparers are entrusted with sensitive financial information and have a responsibility to uphold the integrity of our nation’s tax system, not exploit it for personal financial gain,” she said in the statement. “Those who seek to enrich themselves by manipulating tax credits and defrauding the American taxpayer should understand that IRS Criminal Investigation, along with the FBI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office, is committed to uncovering these schemes, following the money, and holding those responsible accountable.”
Christopher Flowers, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Mobile Field Office, said in a statement that the charges demonstrated a strong partnership among federal law enforcement agencies.
“These allegations involve a serious breach of trust, and our agencies worked closely to identify the extent of the fraudulent activity and ensure accountability,” he said in the statement. “Rebuilding public trust is one of the FBI’s core priorities, and we will continue to pursue anyone who exploits our financial and tax systems for personal gain.”
Court information
A court date has not been set for the defendants. If convicted, each faces a maximum of 20 years in prison.

title: Here are 3 Maine high school football games to watch in Week 9
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
For some football teams in Maine, playoff time has arrived. For others, this is the final week to either clinch a berth or settle their postseason paths.
However you slice it, it’s crunch time on the gridiron.
In Classes A and C, teams head into their regular-season finales. In Classes B and D and in the eight-man divisions, it’s elimination time, and title hopes are at stake from here on out.
Here are three games that should be among the weekend’s best:
Messalonskee (4-4) at Fryeburg Academy (4-4), 6 p.m. Friday
The first matchup between these teams was a tight battle, with Messalonskee holding on for a 28-20 victory in Oakland. The Raiders, seeded fourth in Class B North, will have home-field advantage this time in a quarterfinal matchup against the fifth-seeded Eagles.
Messalonskee’s ability to move the ball through the air made the difference last time, as Fin Minkel threw three touchdown passes, all to Malachi Cusano. Minkel also added a 37-yard touchdown run.
Fryeburg has a dual-threat quarterback of its own in Marcus Sutton, who had a 56-yard touchdown run last week against Skowhegan. Lars Bruhn (two) and Buk Awe had rushing touchdowns in the first matchup.
Portland (6-2) at South Portland (4-4), 7 p.m. Friday
For South Portland, the mission is simple: Win, and the Red Riots, currently fifth in A South and one spot out of the four-team playoff field, would earn the No. 4 seed. The Bulldogs, meanwhile, are looking to secure a home playoff matchup with Windham in Class A North.
Portland, led by the powerful rushing duo of Alex Martin and David Gomes, has gone 2-2 after a 4-0 start and has been outscored by 37 points in that stretch. South Portland, which earlier in the season battled Thornton Academy and Bonny Eagle in close losses, has dropped two straight to put its playoff hopes in jeopardy.
Christopher Salamone has been the top offensive threat and playmaker for the Red Riots.
Westbrook (3-5) at Falmouth (3-5), 6:30 p.m. Friday
The last two Class B champions will meet in the first round of the B South playoffs. The first matchup between the teams was a memorable one, as the Navigators edged the defending champs 22-18 in September. Andre Hicks III had a 90-yard kick return to put the Blue Blazes ahead with 7:23 to play, only for Micah Derrig to find Alex Hau for a 10-yard touchdown pass with 1:59 left.
Fourth-seeded Falmouth has scuffled lately, dropping two straight and three of its last four, while fifth-seeded Westbrook has seen success with wins over Deering and Gorham sandwiched around a six-point loss to second-seeded Kennebunk. The Blue Blazes have allowed only 14.7 points per game over that stretch but will be tested by a Navigators offense that has reached 20 points in all but one game.

title: What to know about Scarborough and Old Orchard Beach’s radio system referendum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Election Day, Scarborough and Old Orchard Beach residents will see a referendum question on their ballots asking whether they want to upgrade to the radio communications system used by both towns’ public safety, public service and school departments.
Scarborough public safety officials held a meeting Monday to answer residents’ questions about the referendum. Here’s what they shared.
WHAT’S WRONG WITH THE OLD SYSTEM?
Public safety officials have reported communication problems during emergency situations. The current radio system — a 150 megahertz analog VHF (very high frequency) system — uses technology from the 1950s and infrastructure from the 1990s. Most of the equipment needs to be replaced, but it’s becoming increasingly difficult to find replacement parts. Coverage is unreliable in schools, commercial buildings, residential neighborhoods, beaches and north Scarborough.
“Every day, our police officers, firefighters and paramedics rely on radio communications to respond to emergencies, coordinate critical operations and protect our town,” Scarborough Police Chief Mark Holmquist said. “However, the radio system we rely upon today is built on aging technology with components that are decades old and well past their end of life.”
WHAT IS THE PROPOSED UPGRADE?
The proposed upgrade is an 800 megahertz digital system that would provide more flexibility and scalability. It would add new 180 foot towers in both towns, like the one near the public safety building in Scarborough.
The new system would offer 99.8% coverage for portable radios on the street, and 99.9% vehicle radio coverage. The plan would support 868 radios for police, fire, public works, schools and other essential municipal services in both towns.
HOW MUCH DOES IT COST?
The project will cost an estimated $12.4 million, with Scarborough contributing $9.2 million and Old Orchard Beach $3.2 million. However, other funding sources could reduce those municipal shares.
The towns are pursuing federal grants, which would bring the total project cost down to $7.4 million — $5.6 million for Scarborough and $1.8 million for Old Orchard Beach.
In anticipation of receiving that $5 million in federal funding, the Scarborough referendum question asks residents to approve the issuance of up to $6 million in bonds. Old Orchard Beach’s referendum question asks residents to approve $3.3 million, which would cover the total project cost for the town if no other funding is secured.
If the proposal is approved, there would be $250,000 to $350,000 of radio maintenance costs in fiscal year 2029, according to Joe Thornton, communications director at Scarborough Public Safety.
“$250,000 is a lot of money, but I want to protect what we buy,” Thornton said. “And I don’t want to be here again in 10 years because we didn’t keep up with maintaining the system.”
If voters approve the referendums and the towns receive the federal funding, the new system will be in place by the end of 2028 and last 15 to 20 years.
WAS THERE A CHEAPER OPTION?
In 2024, the towns hired an independent consultant to analyze the state of the municipal radio system. The two options proposed were to upgrade to a digital system or repair the current VHF system. Upgrading to a digital system costs $12.4 million and would allow the towns to expand their communication system and better communicate with each other and neighboring communities, most of which use a digital system.
Repairing the current system would cost about 25% less, Thornton said, but wouldn’t allow them to expand in the future or communicate directly with neighboring communities.
“We think the money is better spent on a solution that fixes the three major area concerns and allows us to not be back in the same position in five years,” Thornton said.
With a growing population, Scarborough needs a communications system that can expand, Scarborough Fire Chief Rich Kindelan said.
WHAT IF THE TOWNS DON’T GET THE FEDERAL GRANT?
Passing the referendum will help the towns’ case to get congressional funding and make it easier to convince Maine’s congressional delegation to support the project, Thornton said.
A successful referendum also would open up alternative grant opportunities that require a local funding commitment.
Town officials want to bring in as much grant support as possible to reduce the amount of taxpayer money used in the project.
WHAT IF ONLY ONE TOWN APPROVES THE REFERENDUM?
If only Scarborough approves the referendum, the project can move forward without Old Orchard Beach.
If only Old Orchard Beach passes the measure, it will be authorized to spend $3.2 million, but would have to start the project over and get its own bids, Thornton said.
There is no plan B if Scarborough doesn’t pass the referendum. What Scarborough public officials have been doing so far is living with the risk that if something goes wrong, they just have to hope they have the money in the current operations budget to fix it, Kindelan said.
“There’s a huge liability,” he said. “Your public safety department has always made due with what they had, but it’s not a smart way to do business.”

title: Two people injured after fire in Harpswell; home destroyed
text:
HARPSWELL, Maine (WMTW) - Two people were sent to the hospital with burn injuries after a fire at a home in Harpswell Thursday morning.
Several town fire departments, including Harpswell, Brunswick and West Bath responded to the fire on 22 Smokehouse Road. Officials say the call came in around 4:00 a.m.
According to responding fire crews, 4 people were at the home and 2 were taken to the hospital to be treated for burn injuries. One of the occupants had to jump out of a second-story window to escape the flames.
The fire destroyed the single-family home and also spread to the nearby woods. Crews were able to get the flames under control by around 6:30 a.m. but were still working to put out hot spots.
The State Fire Marshall’s office is now heading to the scene to investigate. Officials say it’s too early to determine a cause; the homeowner believes the fire started in a stairwell.
There are no road closures associated with the response but due to the narrow nature of the roads in the area and the size of the response, drivers should take caution.

title: Lindsay Clancy may testify in Patrick Clancy's wrongful death lawsuit, attorney says
text:
Lindsay Clancy may testify in Patrick Clancy's wrongful death lawsuit, attorney says
Attorneys for Patrick Clancy, the husband of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, appeared in court for a hearing Wednesday to decide if his wrongful death lawsuit can proceed.
Patrick Clancy is suing his wife's medical providers, claiming they overmedicated her while she was suffering from postpartum depression.
His attorneys said Lindsay Clancy could take the stand to say she told the health providers she had homicidal ideation.
"We believe that Lindsay Clancy, once her Fifth Amendment issues are resolved one way or the other, will testify that she told these defendants explicitly that she had homicidal ideation," attorney Howard Cooper said.
However, Lindsay Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said his client "never indicated that she intended to testify in Mr. Clancy's lawsuit. Mr. Clancy's counsel does not speak for Lindsay Clancy."
On Wednesday, the healthcare professionals being sued asked the judge to dismiss the case.
Lawyers for those professionals said Lindsay never communicated an explicit threat to kill or injure her children, so it's unfair to hold those doctors accountable.
No immediate decision on the motion was made on Wednesday. Patrick Clancy did not appear in court.
Lindsay Clancy was indicted on three counts each of murder and strangulation in the 2023 deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 7-month-old son Callan.
Clancy, 36, admitted to killing her three children at their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.
A mistrial was declared Sept. 4 after jurors told the judge they were hopelessly deadlocked, with an 11-1 split in favor of acquittal after seven days of deliberations. Patrick Clancy was the first witness to testify in her trial.
Patrick Clancy's lawsuit against Dr. Jennifer A. Tufts, nurse Rebecca H. Jollotta, Aster Mental Health Inc. and South Shore Health System, Inc. alleges their negligent treatment of Lindsay Clancy "resulted in tragedy, namely, allegations that Lindsay took the lives of her children."
The lawsuit alleges that the defendants failed to properly monitor and treat Lindsay Clancy's mental health condition and said they failed to coordinate care between multiple treating clinicians, regularly meeting with Lindsay Clancy over video conference rather than in person and having some appointments that were only 17 minutes long.
Plymouth County prosecutors filed a 30-page motion Wednesday asking a judge to throw out Lindsay Clancy attorney's request to dismiss the charges. Attorney Kevin Reddington argued a retrial would amount to double jeopardy, due to a lone holdout juror.
Lindsay Clancy's lawsuit
In a separate lawsuit, Lindsay Clancy's attorneys have continued to pursue a civil case against her doctors and the hospitals that treated her.
Her lawsuit, which was filed in January, alleges a "catastrophic failure" of multiple medical providers in diagnosing and treating her psychiatric condition.
Two of the defendants named in Clancy's lawsuit, Dr. Jennifer Tufts and Nurse Practitioner Rebecca Jollotta, both testified during the criminal trial.
According to Lindsay Clancy's lawsuit, the medical professionals failed to diagnose her properly with bipolar disorder and instead prescribed treatments that "exacerbated her condition and precipitated a severe psychotic break."
The lawsuit alleges that the medications contributed to a state of psychosis in which Lindsay Clancy hallucinated that she was hearing commands from a man's voice and could only observe her body's actions.

title: Trump calls for prosecution of Democratic Alaska Senate candidate over spoiler candidate controversy
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — President Donald Trump called for the criminal prosecution of the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Alaska on Wednesday after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
“I think they should be prosecuted,” the Republican president said about Peltola and the other Sullivan, responding to questions about a report in The New York Times. He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”
Sen. Sullivan, appearing Wednesday night on Fox News, pressed Peltola to “come clean.”
He said he would tell Alaskans to “look Mary Peltola in the eye and ask her, ‘Did you cheat?’ She won’t even answer that question.”
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Peltola’s campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state’s August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday’s general election.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
He did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.
Peltola calls report a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement, said: “Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.”
During a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction, it’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run.
Murkowski says Alaskans ‘deserve the honest truth’
Alaska Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has endorsed Sullivan and is a longtime friend of Peltola, said in a statement that Alaskans “deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials.”
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan’s candidacy.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.
“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.
Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s a good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”
Candidates in Alaska have raised questions, challenges before
It’s not the first time a candidate’s appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.
The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.
Through Tuesday, more than 61,000 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: Easton, state officials prepare for Election Day
text:
EASTON, Maine (WAGM) - Town and state officials are preparing for Election Day, with polls opening Tuesday, Nov. 3.
In Easton, the work leading up to Election Day starts weeks in advance, said Cheryl Clark, the town manager and a former election clerk of 32 years.
Weeks of preparation in Easton
Clark said staff test equipment, check state requirements, and set up for Election Day.
“It’s quite a bit of work, but you have to have it ready for election day. So we keep up on it,” Clark said.
Polling place requirements
The state sets requirements for each polling place based on its size and layout. In Easton, the polls have been at the community center on Station Road since 2020.
Clark said the decision comes down to a layout that works for voters and clerks.
“We do review it every year and make sure, depending on the election, just in case we have poll watchers or petitioners. But it’s a really good space for that. We can keep everybody on the inside of the guardrail when they’re voting and they can see the voting booth. We do read through the requirements and make sure we’re fulfilling them,” Clark said.
State planning for disruptions
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said her office has trained clerks, law enforcement and election wardens. She said they also have planned for potential disruptions.
“We’ve done scenario planning for any possibility, whether that is weather-related or swatting like we saw in some polling places in 2024, or whether the federal government were to send law enforcement to the polls, which would be illegal,” Bellows said.
Bellows said these are all precautionary measures. She said she expects a successful Election Day and hopes Maine will again lead the nation in voter turnout, as it did in 2022.
“We’re ready for anything, but what we expect is that it will be a yet another exciting day where every eligible Maine citizen has that right to register to vote, cast their ballot, and know their ballot will be counted,” Bellows said.
Same-day registration
Eligible voters can register and vote on the same day.
Clark said there is one main goal with all the work leading up to Election Day.
“Just come and vote would be great,” Clark said.

title: ‘Smile’ Is Getting a Third Film
text:
Say Cheese, ‘Smile’ Is Getting a Third Film
Here’s news that will bring smiles to horror fans’ faces: Smile is getting a third film.
The hit horror franchise will become a trilogy in the very near future. According to Variety, “Paramount has hired David Bruckner to direct and Nick Antosca to write the screenplay. They’re taking over for Parker Finn, who created the series and will remain involved as a producer alongside Temple Hill. (Finn pitched the framework for the third installment.)”
Finn’s Smile films, which are inspired by his own short “Laurie Hasn’t Slept,” follow people with terrifying hallucinations of extremely smiley people. In the first film, a therapist witnesses one of their patients’ death, sparking the visions which may in fact be a curse. In the second, a pop star undergoes a similar nightmarish experience. How (or if) the third film will connect to the prior two isn’t known at this time.
READ MORE: The 10 Worst Horror Movies of the Last 10 Years
If you’re surprised by this news, don’t be. Take a look at the box office chart for the year; it’s all horror movies this year. Almost all the biggest hits of 2026 are horror films, from Obsession to Backrooms to Resident Evil to Scream 7 to Scary Movie. (I mean, yeah it’s a comedy, but look at the title.)
The only thing Hollywood loves more than a hit is copying a hit over and over again until people are so sick of it they can’t stand it anymore. Then Hollywood makes a parody of it (like Scary Movie!) and starts over again. That means any whiff of IP in the horror space is gonna get a sequel or a remake in the next few years. Mark my words.

title: Vehicle ends up vertical after crashing through camper in Sidney
text:
Vehicle ends up vertical after crashing through camper in Sidney, Maine
A Subaru Outback ended up standing vertically on its nose after a crash in Sidney on Wednesday morning.
The Kennebec County Sheriff's Office says a Ford F-150, driven by an 18-year-old woman from Augusta, tried to pass the Subaru at about 6:42 a.m. going around a corner on West River Road near Ferry Road when there was an oncoming car.
The truck and Subaru came into contact, sending the Subaru, driven by a 48-year-old man from Sidney, off the road and into a culvert. The Subaru then hit a camper on a lawn and came to rest standing up and down.
Firefighters had to extricate the driver from the Subaru. He was taken to the hospital but police said his injuries were minor. The driver of the truck was not hurt. The Subaru was destroyed, as well as the camper.
As of Wednesday afternoon, no charges had been filed in the crash.

title: The deadline to request a Maine absentee ballot is today
text:
The deadline to request an absentee ballot is Thursday.
Thanks to Maine’s no-excuse early voting law, anyone can vote via an absentee ballot for any reason.
Absentee ballots have been available since earlier this month, but the deadline to request a ballot or vote early in person at your town office or city hall is 5 p.m. Thursday, the third business day before the election.
You can request an absentee ballot online here and track its status here.
If you already have an absentee ballot, you must return it to your local clerk’s office no later than 8 p.m. on Election Day.
The U.S. Postal Service recommends mailing your ballot at least seven days ahead of the election. Given the election is less than a week away, the secretary of state’s office suggests returning your completed ballot in person to your town office or city hall, or using a designated absentee ballot drop box in your community.

title: Who’s right about access and the nuances of hunting etiquette
text:
This story was originally published in October 2023.
Who’s right is not an argument I want to pursue when people have rifles loaded to hunt deer, but there is such a thing as hunting etiquette.
When a landowner allows public access for hunting, there is still just one person who owns the land and has final say on who uses it and who doesn’t.
Maine law allows public access to private land if the landowner does not post the property.
But hunters who care that public access to private land is shrinking make extra efforts to keep landowners happy. One unwritten rule among ethical hunters is to find out who the owner is, knock on the person’s door and ask for permission to hunt on the land.
It gives the landowner a chance to make special requests, including where or what not to hunt on the property, where to park and what equipment such as tree stands are acceptable. It keeps the landowner in control.
Some people ask landowners for written permission to hunt on their property. Others are happy with a verbal agreement. The bottom line is that most landowners really appreciate the courtesy, and the hunter has a better experience because there is less chance of an unpleasant confrontation.
Well, usually anyway.
When a hunter who hasn’t done any homework makes inaccurate assumptions about ownership and his own rights, and also is belligerent and confrontational, it can ruin your day if you let it.
I am bringing it up because I ran into such a person while hunting on opening day. We were on opposite sides of a power line from each other, with a hillock between us, and watching the open spaces in opposite directions.
I had a right to be where I was. I was legal and hunting with someone who had written permission for him and guests of his choosing to use the land for that purpose.
But the other hunter, who had rudely pitched his popup blind practically on top of someone else’s ground blind, felt I was too near and came out yelling.
When told that we had written permission to be there, he insisted it was power company land and permission wasn’t needed and he was going to call the warden if I didn’t move. In other words, he had no idea who owned the land and had made no attempt at a courtesy request to be there.
And he obviously did not know the law or have a clue about hunting etiquette.
People with his attitude about public access are part of the reason we are losing hunting grounds.
But I also think he reacted angrily because he knew he had unethically pitched his popup so near someone else’s established blind, and he was trying to convince himself that because he had arrived there before the other person that morning, he was in the right.
There was so much foul language and belligerence when he could have just nicely asked if I would give him more space. We both arrived in the dark, afterall, and sometimes that sort of thing happens. I am a reasonable person.
There are state laws about not interfering with lawful hunters and how far away you need to be from buildings, but there is nothing specifying how far apart hunters should be. In terms of common sense, hunters should be safe distances from each other. Many people use 100 yards as a minimum.
As an ethical hunter, I was really disgusted by the man’s rudeness and childish behavior. And even though I didn’t legally have to move, I relocated anyway because I have a personal rule against arguing with idiots.
I left the powerline and walked a ways into the woods along an old tote road until I found a fresh travel path that deer had made. I set up there and enjoyed the peace and stillness of the woods, broken only by the sounds of falling leaves — which are really loud by the way — and the occasional birds, including a woodcock that zinged past my head.
And there was Divine Justice. I had heard only one shot in the distance all morning, but close to noon there was kind of a thump noise in the woods to my left. I was suddenly staring into the beautiful eyes of a fleeing doe. Upon recognizing me as human, she pivoted and bounded away.
I never had a shot. No angle. Too many trees between us. But about 10 minutes later, I heard a couple of shots. One of my friends and his 14-year-old son had shot at the doe. The teen succeeded and filled his antlerless deer tag.
Turns out that another acquaintance who had been walking in the woods and hunting probably spooked her in the first place. I didn’t get my deer on opening day, but I am going to take credit for an assist — sort of.
So although my day started out a little rocky, I think it ended perfectly.

title: Does early snow mean we’re in for a rough winter? Keith Carson explains
text:
Parts of Maine accumulated snow on Oct. 13 and 14, and even by our standards, it was a bit on the early side. So does that mean we are in for a long, cold and snowy winter?
It’s not quite that simple. (It’s always been a sick dream of mine to write a setup like this and then end the article and not follow up.)
Let’s start with analyzing other
The average date when Caribou’s first inch of snow arrives is Nov. 7, with the earliest ever recorded coming on Sept. 29 (that’s messed up) and the latest on Dec. 12. Of the top 10 earliest snowfall years, not a single one of those years ended up in the top 10 for total snow by the end of the season (which I define as Oct. 1 through May 15, because I’m a realist). And those winters were, on average, below normal snowfall seasons.
Meanwhile in Portland, the average arrival of the first inch of snow is much more sane — Nov. 29 — with the earliest ever being Oct. 10 and the latest coming all the way on Jan. 16. Two of the 10 earliest snowfall years there reached into the top 10 for total snow by the end of the season. But the signal here is still very weak.
In fact, the earliest inch on record in Portland was 1980, and that year finished dead last (like me for 15 years in the “Best Weathercast” category at the Emmys) for total snow in Portland’s recorded history.
So, long story short, an early first snow in no way means that you’re in for a snowy winter overall.
But let’s zoom out further and talk about what we expect for Maine’s winter based on atmospheric teleconnections. As you’ve probably heard, we’re in the middle of a record-breaking El Nino right now.
See that line that looks like it doesn’t even belong on the same chart? Yeah, that’s this year.
“Godzilla,” “mega,” “unprecedented” — whatever you want to call it, it’s about as strong a teleconnection signal as you can get.
What does an El Nino winter in the Northeast typically look like? If I had to use just a few words I’d say, “wet and mild.” Here’s the official NOAA winter weather outlook, which strongly mirrors that description and is heavily leaning on the El Nino connection.
Note that the “mild” signal is a bit stronger than the “wet” signal. That’s because storm tracks are harder to predict at the seasonal level than temperature signals.
If I were a betting man, I’d say it’s very unlikely we have a colder-than-average winter. (We don’t have many of those anymore, in general, because of climate change, but we did squeak one out last winter, which happens sometimes based on regional patterns and teleconnections.)
So taken at face value, we’re looking at a winter that runs above average temperature-wise and has a good amount of mixed precipitation events and a fair share of straight rain events, especially along the coast.
The split between the coast, inland Maine and the mountains could be a pretty big deal this winter, because temperatures being above average during a storm in a place like Portland very often lead to a changeover to rain. Inland, that could mean more mixing with sleet. The mountains, though, might be able to hang on to snow, even when the rest of the state gets rain. (This portion of the forecast was brought to you by Boyne Resorts and the Ski Maine Association.)
Historically speaking, even in the mountains, El Nino winters are not “big” for us when it comes to seasonal snow totals. But no teleconnection can dictate or predict wobbles in individual low pressure systems, and if we lock into a juicy pattern for a week or two, it will still be very wintry indeed for that time period.
But all things considered: I’ll take the under.
Keith Carson, an award-winning Maine meteorologist previously of News Center Maine and The Weather Channel, is the director of environment & science communications for the Maine Conservation Voters nonprofit.

title: More than sweet treats: Hampden Halloween tradition raises funds for Children’s Miracle Network
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - Halloween is filled with creepy decorations and scary movies, but one neighborhood takes the opportunity to give back to the community.
“I mean, it’s just so much fun. I remember being a kid and doing trick-or-treating, you just run around, you get a bunch of candy, you eat a bunch of candy, you have a great time,” Dave Barrett said.
Children will be filling baskets with chocolate bars and other sweets, while donations are also collected on Constitution Avenue in Hampden.
The donations are collected for Children’s Miracle Network during Halloween trick-or-treating, and Barrett, an advocate for the organization, said this is the 10th year of the effort.
Children’s Miracle Network supports children’s hospitals across the country, including Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center.
Barrett said he started the effort because Halloween is a children’s holiday and Children’s Miracle Network is a children’s charity.
“This is the 10th year since we started, so we thought, you know, if it’s a children’s charity, it’s a children’s holiday, this is the perfect event to raise a little bit of money,” Barrett said. “So, I stand out on the corner, I got a little Jack-o’-lantern bucket, and I say, give me some money, help sick kids.”
Angela Ellingwood, whose son is a cancer survivor, said her family has a connection to the cause. She said her son, Adrian, was diagnosed with cancer and received treatment in Brewer.
“My son was diagnosed with cancer and we ended up having to go through cancer treatment here in Brewer, and it was the money that is donated to the Children’s Miracle Network goes directly to local hospitals,” Ellingwood said.
Ellingwood said being able to stay at home during treatment made the process easier for Adrian.
“But in this area, in this hospital, you’re with your family. You’re, my son was with his dog. Every night we went home and he was able to be in familiar surroundings. And we wouldn’t have that if there wasn’t the support,” Ellingwood said.
Barrett said after seeing childhood cancer touch his neighborhood, the effort became more personal.
“It’s the right thing to do to help these families who have these, and having had them in our neighborhood and experiencing going through some of that, vicariously through the neighborhood is, it really really creates urgency, in a way that you don’t otherwise see if you don’t know the people who are experiencing these things,” Barrett said.
Adrian has beaten his cancer. Ellingwood said giving a check back to the hospital that treated him is a high honor.
“Dave asked if Adrian would like to bring the check to the Children’s Miracle Network, and it was just such an honor for us to give back to the organizations and the hospital that had given us so much,” Ellingwood said.

title: Letter: Billionaires have outsize influence on elections, war and media
text:

With billionaires gaining more and more wealth and power, one person, one vote looks dead. Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX received nearly $7 billion in federal contracts this year, has committed roughly $366 million to affect who wins and loses on Nov. 3. That buys many thousands of votes.
Sen. Susan Collins, whose reelection campaign is the beneficiary of the second largest donation from Musk’s super PAC, America PAC, is also backed by a total of $126 million from a large network of Republican super PACs. Chris Murphy, D-Connecticut, asked how could they not have anticipated that spike given it was the fourth nationwide “day of action” in 20 months.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Elon Musk used his undo influence on the Ukraine war by capping the speed of SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink that Ukraine uses to protect Kyiv from Russian drones and missiles. text:
Popular Maine Haunted House Has Closed for Good
With Halloween happening THIS SATURDAY, spooky season is almost here! But unfortunately, there's some sad news for Maine's haunted house fans.
After several seasons of screams, scares, and unforgettable nights in the dark, Farmington Fright Fest is closing its doors for good. That means its three haunted attractions will not be returning this year,or in the years to come.
The event was voted one of the scariest Halloween attractions in the state of Maine, earning a reputation for delivering plenty of frights and unforgettable nights for Halloween fans.
Since 2021, Farmington Fright Fest has brought three spine-tingling weekends of terror to western Maine, giving local thrill-seekers something to look forward to every fall. For many, it became a Halloween tradition and a must-visit destination for anyone looking to get their scare on.
Read More: Bucksport, Maine Is Home To A Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
Kind of a bummer, right? Especially with Halloween just days away!
Thankfully, there are still plenty of spooky spots throughout New England where you can get your fright fix, including some great options right here in the Bangor area.
Maineiac Manor is located in the former Hollister location in the Bangor Mall, directly across from Spencer's. The 6,500-square-foot attraction has become a destination for anyone looking for a good scare.
Its spooky fun doesn't stop when Halloween is over, either. Maineiac Manor has offered a Krampus-themed Christmas haunted house in December and plans to bring visitors a regular schedule of creepy events and seasonal fun throughout the year.
When you visit, you'll encounter mesmerizing sets, handmade props, and actors in killer costumes hiding in the shadows — and sometimes right out in plain sight, ready to make you jump out of your skin!
And don't sleep on New Hampshire!
Haunted Overload, located in Lee, is one of the most distinctive haunted attractions in New England. It's an enormous outdoor experience built directly into the landscape, featuring gigantic homemade monsters, elaborate structures, eerie lighting, and larger-than-life Halloween scenery.
It's a whole different experience from a traditional haunted house. Instead of walking from room to room, you'll make your way through an outdoor world filled with enormous creatures and elaborate sets. The sheer scale is part of what makes Haunted Overload so memorable, and worth the drive for serious Halloween fans.
So, while we're sad to see Farmington Fright Fest go, Halloween isn't over just yet. With the big night arriving this Saturday, there's still time to squeeze in one more spooky adventure!

title: 2 college students found dead after going missing during Colorado hike
text:
(AP) - Two Colorado college students have been found dead after going missing during a hiking trip in the Rocky Mountains last weekend when a heavy snowstorm hit, authorities said.
The bodies of Kaden Matsuda, 19, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, of New York, were found Wednesday afternoon in a basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles southeast of Aspen, the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement posted on social media.
They left Colorado Mountain College Leadville’s campus on Friday, telling family and friends they planned to hike up Ice Mountain, a nearly 14,000-foot peak near West Apostle Mountain that requires technical climbing, the sheriff’s office said. They were expected back by Sunday, but college staff reported them missing on Monday morning.
The sheriff’s office said the causes of their deaths were under investigation, but foul play was not suspected. Authorities said they would not offer theories on what may have happened until autopsies are completed.
“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson’s family and friends,” Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the statement Wednesday night. “We are very proud of our team’s efforts to find them before this weekend’s coming storm. Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family.”
About 60 search and rescue volunteers, aided by helicopters, drones and dogs, searched for the two men.
The helicopter crew on Tuesday discovered a tent collapsed under the snow with their sleeping bags, a stove and clothing near a lake northwest of Ice Mountain — but the students were nowhere to be found.
Based on the tent’s location, officials said they were aiming for the 13,597-foot West Apostle Mountain.
Friends and family described both as experienced hikers and climbers.
The sheriff’s office said their climbing equipment was not in their dorms, tent or vehicle, suggesting they left their tent prepared for a technical climb. Trash inside the tent indicated they had eaten before starting their hike, officials said.
Matsuda was studying to become a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was studying to become a mountain guide, Rohrich said.
Authorities had been concerned that aerial searches could be limited in upcoming days because of poor weather that was expected to begin Friday.

title: The vote is sacred, as is every voter in Maine and beyond
text:
Some prayers are spoken. Some are sung. And some take the form of a pen filling in an oval on a paper ballot, in a school gym or a church basement, on a Tuesday in November.
On a recent Wednesday afternoon, I stood in Lewiston beside a bus with four words painted on its side: “The Vote Is Sacred.” The nonpartisan tour, organized nationally by Interfaith Alliance, is crossing 15 states this fall. Here in Maine, Multifaith Justice Maine and the Maine Council of Churches hosted it. I stood with colleagues from Christian, Jewish, Muslim, and other spiritual traditions, united around two convictions: The vote must be protected, and every voter carries inherent dignity. It moved me more than I expected.
It also sobered me. My friend and colleague, the Rev. Jodi Cohen Hayashida, shared that as organizers prepared for the press conference, they learned that the far-right propaganda publication, The Maine Wire, had stationed itself at Lewiston City Hall, where immigrant voters were casting their ballots. I want to amplify her words because she named it better than I can:
“This home-grown harassment reflects a larger national effort to intimidate vulnerable voters in our communities — our neighbors, our loved ones — and keep them from using their voices and the power of their own vote. Every one of our faith traditions refutes this harassment and intimidation. Every one of our faith traditions calls us into solidarity, not just today, but in the days to come.”
Solidarity, not just today. That is the heart of it.
The tour takes its name from the late congressman John Lewis, a Civil Rights leader and Baptist minister, who called the vote “precious, almost sacred.” He knew the cost. He bled for it on a bridge in Selma.
Why would people of faith call a civic act sacred? Not because any party or candidate is holy. I won’t tell you whom to vote for. I will ask you to vote, and to make sure your neighbors can, too.
Nearly every tradition teaches that each person carries something precious: the image of God, the spark of the divine, or, as my Unitarian Universalist faith puts it, inherent worth and dignity. At its best, democracy puts that belief into public practice. One person, one vote. The newly naturalized citizen and the eighth-generation Mainer count exactly the same. No one gets to stand at the door and decide otherwise.
So check on your neighbors. Offer a ride. Help someone find their polling place. And if you see a voter being watched or hassled, stand beside them. A quiet, calm presence is its own kind of prayer.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, and early voting is already underway. Make a plan. Bring someone with you. And when you step into that little booth, know that you are doing something holy. You are saying with your whole self that you belong to this community, and that it belongs to you.
The Rev. Dr. Kharma R. Amos is minister of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick, uubrunswick.org.

title: Mild end to the week, chilly for Halloween
text:
Mild end to the week, chilly for Halloween
Mild end to the week, chilly for Halloween
Milder days to end the week, with temperatures climbing into the 60s for most on Thursday and Friday. A cold front crosses Thursday night and may bring a brief, passing shower or sprinkle.
Mostly sunny skies are expected on Friday, except in northern Maine where clouds and a few spotty showers will linger. Breezy northwest winds gust to 25 to 30 mph in the afternoon and evening.
Turning chilly for Halloween, with temperatures maxing out in the 40s and low 50s Saturday afternoon. Trick-or-treaters will see temperatures in the 40s this year and a light northwest breeze under clear skies Saturday evening. Sunset is at 5:33 PM.
Temperatures fall below freezing overnight, making for a frigid Sunday morning. Daylight Saving Time ends Saturday night, so it will be a brighter morning, but the sun will set at 4:31 p.m.
The long dry stretch looks to continue next week, with temperatures running warmer than average for early November. By Friday or Saturday (Nov. 6/7), some much-needed widespread rain could finally make its way to Maine.

title: Man charged in connection with terrifying attempted kidnapping caught on video
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) — A 23-year-old man in Hawaii has been charged in connection with a terrifying attempted kidnapping that was caught on video.
Police identified the suspect as Diesel Makanikaiaulu Kawelo and arrested him. He was charged Wednesday with kidnapping.
His bail was set at $500,000.
The kidnapping attempt happened in the middle of the afternoon Monday in Honolulu.
Authorities said they were called to Kainalu condominiums about the reported kidnapping.
Surveillance video from the area showed a truck parked outside the condominium complex that afternoon. A man was then seen going inside the garage, appearing to confront two women and chase one of them.
A 77-year-old condo resident, who asked not to be identified, said the man picked up her 24-year-old friend.
Police said the suspect elbowed the 77-year-old woman in the face.
“He shoved me away from my friend and he picked her up,” she said. “He looked like a monster. He just had so much hatred and craziness in his eyes.”
The woman added, “I was yelling, ‘Help! Help!’ and she was yelling, too. She was saying, ‘You don’t want to do this. Don’t do this.’”
The 77-year-old said her friend was trying to fend off the kidnapper while she was hoping others would hear their screams for help.
Neighbor and witness Beverly Louis said she could see the man bear-hugging the woman and dragging her to the back of his truck.
“I just started screaming, ‘Drop her! Drop her! Drop her!’” Louis said. “She was screaming for her life. She was terrified.”
Neighbor and fellow witness Mike Finkelstein said he also yelled at the man to let the woman go.
“Let her go. I’ve called the police. I’m coming down there after you,” Finkelstein recalled yelling.
Several neighbors then intervened after seeing and hearing the commotion, helping the 24-year-old break free.
Witnesses said the suspect got into his truck and sped off. Police were able to take him into custody a few hours later after he was seen running naked in a nearby neighborhood, police said.
The 77-year-old woman thanked her fellow residents for their help but said she and her friend were continuing to have nightmares as the neighborhood remained on edge.

title: Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86
text:
Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen.
He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.” The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and The New York Times said it was “a must-see.”
“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”
Starship commander grew up without a toilet
Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
In his memoir, “Making It So,” Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. “Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”
The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard
“The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time,” he would write.
Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. “People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?‘” he told the AP. “Telly?”
Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film “Excalibur.” He had just done a production of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. “I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail.”
It didn’t, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the “Star Trek” franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”
His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in ‘Henry IV,’ which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.
Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series “Star Trek: Picard.”)
Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another “Star Trek” icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
The show gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films “Conspiracy Theory,” “L.A. Story” and on Broadway, where he starred in “The Tempest,” “The Caretaker” and David Mamet’s “A Life in the Theater.” He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.
A brave and commanding persona. But sexy?
In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide’s “Top Turn-Ons,” based on a readers’ poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: “Absurd.”
Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned in four more movies before Professor X’s death in 2017’s “Logan.” He reappeared in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” in 2022 and is reprising the role in the upcoming “Avengers: Doomsday.”
He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane’s Starz show “Blunt Talk” for two series and voiced Poop in “The Emoji Movie.” He made appearances on “Robot Chicken,” “Futurama” and “The Simpsons” (in one episode, Homer loses his hair, and Stewart tells him it’s great to be bald.)
Later in life, he proved internet-savvy and found new fans with his humor, posing in a bath in a lobster suit and triggering memes when he posted a photo of him picking apples. When he was mistakenly outed as gay by a British newspaper, he said it was a nice change. “At least I didn’t wake up to the internet telling me I was dead again,” he tweeted.
He married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, with the actor’s “X-Men” co-star McKellen officiating. Stewart later tweeted a photo of the newlyweds in a ball pit.
He also is survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.
__
AP Film Writer Lindsey Bahr contributed reporting.

title: Tennessee governor suspects Christa Pike’s sentence will stay the same after failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said he suspects Christa Pike’s sentence will remain the same following her failed execution last month, unless the courts determine otherwise.
Lee’s comments on Pike
Lee was asked Wednesday whether the state will try to execute Pike again or if he will commute her sentence to life in prison.
“As it related to a particular individual like Christa Pike and her crime, she’s still incarcerated under the laws of the state of Tennessee,” Lee said. “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Pike’s condition
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
In September, Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug. The execution attempt failed.
Pike is back in prison after spending days in the hospital. She is now able to speak in full sentences and walk on her own.
Executions paused, commissioner resigns
Lee has paused executions through the end of the year to determine what went wrong in Pike’s attempt.
Frank Strada resigned from his role as commissioner of the Department of Correction following the botched execution, which was the second in Tennessee this year. Lee said Strada will leave by the end of the month and that he expects to announce a replacement within the next few days.

title: Shaw’s sued over death of Saco trucker crushed by rock salt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The estate of a truck driver who lived in Saco has filed a wrongful death claim against Shaw’s Supermarket Inc. after a pallet stacked with 50-pound bags of rock salt tipped over and fell on him, causing injuries that ultimately killed him, court papers state.
Randall “Randy” Rackliffe was a driver for Brown Dog Carriers of Biddeford when he picked up a loaded trailer on Jan. 18 at the Shaw’s Distribution Center in Wells, according to a federal lawsuit filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Portland.
The trailer had been packed by Shaw’s employees and included pallets carrying bags of Morton’s Safe-T-Salt stacked on top of shrink-wrapped cases of bottled water, according to the claim filed by Joya Kim Maynard of Mars Hill, Rackliffe’s sister and personal representative of his estate.
Rackliffe drove the trailer to a Shaw’s in Raynham, Massachusetts, where store employees began moving pallets out of the trailer, the lawsuit states.
“Randy was standing to the side of the Shaw’s employees in the trailer, holding steady a pallet containing paper products in order to make it easier for the Shaw’s employees to extract the pallets of water and rock salt,” according to the suit.
“The pallets were unstable and improperly secured,” the lawsuit states. “As the Shaw’s employees moved the pallets of water and rock salt, the bags of rock salt tipped over, striking and crushing Randy.”
Rackliffe was hospitalized for his injuries at Maine Medical Center in Portland and died there eight months later on Sept. 12. He was 62 and left behind two daughters and four grandchildren, according to his obituary.
The lawsuit seeks damages from Shaw’s, claiming that the company’s negligence in ensuring the safe loading and unloading of goods caused Rackliffe to suffer “catastrophic, multisystem trauma from his crush injury.”
Shaw’s did not immediately respond to requests for an interview. The Massachusetts-based company, which was founded in Portland, operates 150 stores across New England.

Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.

Tristan Miniutti rushed for three touchdowns as Noble kept its playoff hopes alive with a 51-8 win over Scarborough in a Class A South regular-season finale Thursday night in Scarborough.
