title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran’s response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
It’s unclear how soon the US military would be ready
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It’s unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that’s driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
“Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said.
___
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Konstantin Toropin and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

title: State high school girls volleyball titles up for grabs this weekend in Bangor, South Portland
text:
Gorham, Washington Academy of East Machias, and Mount Desert Island will be looking to defend their state volleyball championships in Class A, B and C, respectively, this weekend while George Stevens Academy of Blue Hill will look to claim the D title after losing to Narraguagus High of Harrington in the final a year ago.
There will be one match on Friday night beginning at 7 when top seed George Stevens Academy will square off with third seed Woodland at Husson University in Bangor.
Both teams are 14-2, and GSA won the regular season match between the two, 3-0, in Blue Hill on Oct. 6.
On Saturday, the Class A final between second seed Gorham and No. 4 Scarborough will take place beginning at 10 a.m. at Southern Maine Community College in South Portland. Gorham is 13-3, including a pair of 3-2 regular season victories over Scarborough, which is 12-4.
Gorham is seeking its fourth straight Class A crown.
Top seed Gardiner, 13-3, and third seed Mount Desert Island, 9-7, will meet at Husson at 1 p.m. Gardiner won the regular season matchup, 3-2, in Gardiner earlier this month.

title: Ramaswamy campaign ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother will no longer air
text:
Ramaswamy campaign ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother will no longer air
An ad in the Ohio governor’s race that drew nationwide attention will no longer air on the state's airwaves.
The ad from Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign featured the estranged mother of his opponent, Democrat Amy Acton.
The ad, created by Ramaswamy's campaign, shows Acton's mother calling her a liar and telling people they shouldn’t vote for her daughter.
Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed that the ad is off the air and that the campaign has six other ads that are currently running, saying the ad with Acton’s mother has run through its cycle.
Acton’s campaign released a statement after learning that the ad won’t be airing any longer, saying it shouldn’t have been run in the first place.
Acton explained that she has not seen her mother since the late 1970s because her mother stayed married to a man whom Acton accuses of sexually abusing her when she was 12 years old.
Last week, a statement from Ramaswamy's spokesperson Connie Luck said, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor."

title: Letter: Democrats can deliver clean energy
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Thanks to the present administration, unaffordable costs for heat and electricity are going to make the winter ahead a challenge. The decrease in oil supply caused by the unauthorized war with Iran has allowed prices on everything transported or made with oil to skyrocket. Energy from oil and gas, fossil fuels, is now more expensive than energy from solar and wind.
Currently, wind farms can deliver energy at half the cost of fossil fuels. Widespread rooftop solar would achieve the kind of energy independence needed to protect against private or foreign control.
Almost 50 years ago, Exxon research scientists accurately predicted that fossil fuel emissions would lead to global warming. Exxon from 1977 to 2003 issued propaganda that denied their own research in order to mislead the public and undermine the development of renewable energy. Continued fossil fuel use resulting in environmental damage and pollution has cost U.S. taxpayers $700 billion every year, according to the International Monetary Fund.
There was bipartisan support for climate protection bills until 2010 when Citizens United was passed and allowed fossil fuel corporations to spend unlimited amounts of money on political campaigns and climate legislation was blocked. As Republican Sen. John McCain warned Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse as they worked on a bipartisan climate package: “The fossil fuel industry has basically locked up my party on this.”
People need low cost clean energy. When you vote in November, think about this future within our reach and those who I believe will make it possible — Matt Dunlap, Troy Jackson, and Hannah Pingree.
Elizabeth Hill
Brooksville

title: We need a stronger senator to protect the culture, economies, and traditions of Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Ken Elowe of Bristol is a retired director of the Bureau of Fish and Wildlife Resource Management at the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife.
As a registered independent with a long history in Maine government, I had many chances to work with Maine’s delegation, including Sen. Susan Collins. I voted for her over several election cycles. But things have changed, and the challenges faced by people and businesses in Maine have changed. I believe Collins has changed also.
Maine’s economy, culture, traditions, and recreation has its foundation in natural resources. From commercial fishing, farming, timber management, sawmills, paper mills, recreational fishing, hunting and guiding, and historic sporting lodges, our coastal, inland, and rural businesses statewide are rooted in the amazing natural resources that we have and share.
These natural resource businesses are solid ways to make a living, but at times, operate on narrow economic margins. Changes to markets or operating costs can quickly shrink those margins and cause different business decisions. We saw this when changes happened to Maine’s paper industries, with mills separating from their traditional timberlands. I believe we are on the threshold of major challenges again for our foundational industries.
The high cost of diesel fuel is a major challenge for those heating their homes with oil. It is likewise a major economic challenge for the timber industries, which rely on diesel fuel for logging operations, trucking, and sawmills. Likewise, farm equipment runs on diesel, and most lobster and other fishing vessels also depend on diesel fuel. High fuel costs are reducing operating margins. With tariffs impacting equipment, parts, and product markets, operating margins are reduced even more.
These industries provide jobs all across the rural landscapes of the state. Hard economic decisions made necessary by high fuel costs and tariffs will likely cause loss of jobs in areas that have few alternatives. But the present challenges of high diesel fuel costs and tariffs are not due soley to global shifts in manufacturing or competitive economics. They are worsened by national policies that created antagonistic tariff and trade relations with long-time allies and a war with Iran that created the present high oil prices and does not seem to have an easy or smooth way out.
All across the country, people that hunt, fish, camp, and recreate on private lands commonly do so while paying large lease sums for the privilege. Maine, and much of New England, has a culture and tradition of respectful use of private lands. Our forests are the foundation of our wood economies and also our recreational economies, culture and traditions. These privileges are not guaranteed, and a large-scale change to landowners that do not have a history of Maine’s traditions may greatly shift available jobs in logging, sawmills and the recreational sectors.
Sen. Collins may be successful in bringing some project dollars to Maine. But we are breaking new ground with the current administration. Collins has enabled and I believe is complicit in the one-sided decisions impacting our foundational economies and traditions.
Her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee should afford her the ability to leverage other Republicans to stand up against unilateral decisions being made by this administration. She is, as a senior senator and chair of a powerful committee, more than only one vote. If she truly is as effective as she claims, I believe Collins should be able to leverage pressure to rein in this administration. She has not, and continually falls back on the excuse of being only one vote, as she seemingly will not help take back the role of Congress as a co-equal branch of government.
Our citizens, economy, jobs, culture and traditions are being stressed. We need someone that will help shift the balance and give Congress back to us as a functional and equal branch of government. I believe it is time to elect Troy Jackson, for the sake of Maine and the nation.

title: Maine Gov. Janet Mills casts her vote, shares who she supported
text:
Maine Gov. Janet Mills casts her vote, shares who she supported
More than 275,000 Maine voters have already cast their ballots, as in-person absentee voting comes to an end on Thursday.
That total includes Gov. Janet Mills, D-Maine, who voted on Thursday in her hometown of Farmington. She shared on social media that she voted a straight Democratic ballot, including Hannah Pingree for governor, Matt Dunlap for Maine's Second Congressional District, Troy Jackson for Senate, Scott Landry for Maine House, and Bob Sullebarger for Maine Senate.
"I encourage Maine people to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot who will stand up for our values and stand up to Trump," Mills wrote on X.
Mills was once a candidate for the Democratic nomination for Senate before suspending her campaign prior to primary day. After Jackson became the nominee, she did not endorse him and had not publicly said who she was supporting in the race.
In July, after Jackson became the nominee, Mills said she had not, to that point, spoken with Jackson, "but clearly Susan Collins is vulnerable, and she should be — she should be defeated,” Mills said in an interview with Maine's Total Coverage in Dresden.

2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history.
With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms.
“It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University.
Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars.
Texas now holds the record for the most expensive nonpresidential race in U.S. history, with more than $560 million in political advertising spending and reservations, according to AdImpact.
Ohio’s Senate race has also surpassed $500 million, making it one of only three nonpresidential races to reach that milestone. The third was Ohio’s 2024 Senate contest.
Republicans have maintained an advantage in political advertising, spending approximately $5.18 billion this election cycle, compared with $4.77 billion for Democrats, according to AdImpact.
The Republican National Committee has also emphasized its intention to deploy its available resources before Election Day.
“There’s no saving money for a rainy day. Whatever we can get that can be deployed is going to be deployed,” RNC chief of staff Mike Ambrosini told The New York Times.
Democrats, meanwhile, have pointed to grassroots fundraising as evidence of enthusiasm among their supporters.
“When you have hundreds of thousands of contributors who are giving 5, 10, 15 dollars, they’re very excited. That is one indicator of enthusiasm,” Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said.
While both parties rely on smaller contributions, some of the largest financial commitments have come from billionaire donors.
Elon Musk has contributed nearly $450 million to Republican causes during the election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission.
By comparison, two of the largest Democratic megadonors, George Soros and Michael Bloomberg, have contributed approximately $102 million and $84 million, respectively.
Despite the Republican financial advantage, Belt told Gray Media’s Washington Bureau the election could offer a test of whether money or political messaging proves more influential.
“It’s almost a perfect natural experiment, where the Republicans have the money and the Democrats have the voice against the administration,” he said.
And while money alone may not determine the outcome, Belt said a lack of advertising could prove costly in close races.
“If you allow your side to go dark at the end of the campaign, you might miss out on a few of those voters and in a very close race, that could make all the difference,” he said.

title: Your Choice Your Voice: How changes to health care are impacting Mainers
text:
Your Choice Your Voice: How changes to health care are impacting Mainers
In the quiet town of Round Pond, you’ll find Leah Hurwitz and her husband raising their two children. The family of four settled in Midcoast Maine for the slow pace and quiet lifestyle.
“You want to soak up every minute with them,” Hurwitz said about her daughters.
Hurwitz wanted to welcome a fifth member into her family but says her second baby will most likely be her last. The closest place for her to deliver a baby safely is set to close at the end of this year.
Maine Health’s Board of Trustees voted this past August to end labor and delivery services at their Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta.
“Someone is taking this opportunity not just for me, but from a lot of women in this community,” Hurwitz said.
By next year, the nearest unit for Hurwitz would be roughly a 45-minute drive, and even longer if there’s traffic.
It’s a risk not worth taking, Hurwitz said, because of her last delivery. A planned C-section for her second baby in Portland turned into an early delivery at Lincoln Hospital in an instant. Her daughter lost oxygen for several minutes during delivery and had to be resuscitated after birth.
“The idea of going through that again and having a different result, I don't think we could survive it,” Hurwitz said. "We would not have an alive baby if we didn't live this close to a labor and delivery department."
Other moms statewide are facing the same dilemma. Roughly a dozen labor and delivery units in Maine have closed in the last decade. Other rural hospitals and medical services are falling off the map statewide too.
Hospital closures coupled with concerns over access to Medicaid and affording healthcare leave voters wondering how the candidates asking for their votes will take on this issue.
Recent polling of Maine’s Total Coverage viewers shows access to healthcare and other services is one of the issues top of mind heading into the election cycle.

title: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
text:
North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters Thursday, South Korea’s military said, days after the North threatened to resume front-line propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy new weapons along the rivals’ tense border.
The launches also followed leader Kim Jong Un’s surprise weekend visit to China, the North's main ally and economic pipeline, to push for greater cooperation.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected about 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the North's eastern costal town of Wonsan and that they each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles). It said South Korea's military maintained its readiness to repel any provocations by North Korea under a solid alliance with the United States.
Related video: The ongoing conflict in Iran is impacting U.S. borrowing rates, financial experts say
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected ballistic missile launch by North Korea.
Animosity between the Koreas have deepened since last month’s land mine blasts at the border that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of planting mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded it apologize. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea said it would restart propaganda broadcasts and place new weapons systems on alert along the border in protest of what it called repeated warning shots by South Korean troops at border areas. South Korea later proposed talks on clarifying the border to prevent accidental clashes, but North Korea hasn't responded.
During a visit to a South Korean border town earlier this week, Associated Press journalists saw North Korean artillery guns located on the other side of the border, which weren't previously visible.
In recent years, North Korea has been placing more mines, barbed-wire fences and other defense structures along the border in line with Kim's policy of severing ties with South Korea. Seoul has said North Korean troops have repeatedly violated the border during the work and that South Korea's military has responded with firing warning shots. North Korea has denied the alleged border breaches.
Thursday's launches were the latest in a series of weapons tests by North Korea in recent weeks, which included submarine-launched cruise missiles and hypersonic missiles. Experts say North Korea likely aimed to pressure the U.S. into making bigger concessions as President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim.
On Saturday, Kim visited the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly inaugurated bridge to pay respect at a memorial marking China’s support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War. It was his sixth visit to China since succeeding his father as North Korean leader in late 2011.
At the memorial, Kim said North Korea will firmly carry forward “the invincible" friendship with China. Later he met top Chinese Communist Party official Wang Huning and reaffirmed his resolve to develop bilateral cooperation.
Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China after years of prioritizing ties with Russia by sending troops and ammunitions to support its war against Ukraine.
___
Associated Press writer Mari Yamaguchi in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Man accused of Colorado demonstration attack to change plea to federal hate crime charges
text:
DENVER (AP) — An Egyptian man is scheduled to change his not guilty plea to federal hate crime and other charges Thursday for a deadly firebombing attack on demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, last year.
Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison after pleading guilty to state charges last spring.
Yelling “Free Palestine,” Soliman lit and threw two Molotov cocktails at the demonstrators who were marching in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking in June 2025 because the demonstrators were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others.
Diamond died three weeks later. Her family says she suffered “indescribable pain.”
The charges Soliman previously pleaded not guilty to in federal court in Denver include nine counts of hate crimes, two of using fire or an explosive to commit a felony and one of carrying an explosive while committing a felony.
The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty. Soliman is already serving a life sentence after pleading guilty to the state charges.
Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, described being unnerved by the attack in their city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado.
The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown. Soliman got near the demonstration on Pearl Street, a pedestrian mall lined with shops and restaurants, by posing as a gardener.
Federal authorities alleged Soliman planned the attack for a year. After his arrest, Soliman told police he sought “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel, according to an FBI affidavit.
Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum.
He was granted work authorization, but it too expired, federal officials said
Soliman was living with his wife and their five children in an apartment in Colorado Springs at the time of the attack. He worked a series of low-paying jobs.
The couple divorced in April. Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.
Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned for more harm than he carried out. He tried twice to buy a gun and was denied, they said.
He brought 18 Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — to the demonstration in a box, but only two were thrown.
Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt.
An injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.
While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.
“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.
___
Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.

title: Make no bones about it, the giant skeleton has become an American Halloween fixture
text:
It reared its bony head in 2020, during that first, chaotic pandemic year that was rife with grief and fear but also toilet paper hoarding and questionable lockdown-inspired purchases. Behold Skelly, the 12-foot, 90-pound skeleton, on sale for $299 from Home Depot, just in time for Halloween — at least, if you can get your hands on one.
Many did, because this is America. And when we get sad, stressed or bored, we shop, drowning our collective anxieties in things that we definitely don’t need but most certainly want.
So, beginning in 2020, Skelly showed up on suburban lawns from California to New Jersey and on brownstone stoops in Brooklyn, naked or dressed in a costume, towering over jack-o’-lanterns and plastic gravestones with spooky puns like “Rest In Pieces.” It didn’t take long for people to realize that keeping Skelly out year-round meant new opportunities to dress him for every season: Christmas, Fourth of July, or even just a bikini for summer.
In 2024, Skelly got glowing LCD eyeballs. And in 2026, a Bluetooth connection lets you record sounds or speak into it live, entertaining (or unsettling) your whole block. He also has a dog, a cat, and a smaller, 6½-foot version for those who can’t quite commit to a giant. It has sold out before Halloween every year.
“It is the ultimate American decoration,” says Aubrey Horowitz, merchant of Decorative Holiday at Home Depot. “We really love this sense of nostalgia and having some form of connection with our communities and the people that live around us. And frankly, you know, a lot of times bigger is better.”
I did not celebrate Halloween until I arrived in the U.S. from Eastern Europe at age 13. I was shocked by the sheer size of everything: giant cars, highways with all those lanes, enormous gallons of milk instead of our polite liters, skyscrapers so tall they were licking the clouds.
We also weren’t used to whimsy. Gaudy yard decor, whether for Halloween or Christmas, was as foreign a concept as warehouse shopping or smiling at strangers.
Skelly would have certainly stopped us in our tracks. It still does. The uniquely American delight it brings to me, an immigrant still often in awe of Americans’ seasonal joy and over-the-top ornamentations, is contagious.
The U.S. did not invent Halloween. But Halloween excess, with its pillowcases full of candy, elaborate costumes for everyone from babies to adults to dogs (and a few unlucky cats), could not be more American.
And why have a 5′8″ skeleton when you can have a 12-foot one?
___
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

title: Senate races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
text:
Senate races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
Senate races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
Control of the U.S. Senate is up for grabs. And Republicans increasingly find themselves on defense as they try to hold on to their majority in the chamber.
The political winds are swirling against President Donald Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.
Senate Republicans were optimistic going into the election thanks in large part to the map.
Currently, the GOP holds a 53-47 majority.
Related video above | More than 12 million Americans have already voted. Here's what the early data reveals
Thirty-five seats are up for reelection: Republicans hold 22, while Democrats hold 13. With Republican Vice President JD Vance’s ability to break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control of the chamber.
Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.
The most straightforward path for Democrats to win the majority involves holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
The challenge for Democrats is that besides Maine, Trump won all of those pickup targets in 2016, 2020 and 2024. To win back the upper chamber, Democrats will have to persuade a significant number of voters who cast ballots for Trump over the last decade to vote for the opposing party this time.
THE KEY RACES
Here are the races that will decide which party controls the Senate next year, from the battlegrounds Democrats need to hold to the Republican-held states they need to flip.
DEMOCRATS TARGETING REPUBLICAN SEATS
- ALASKA | Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is up for reelection against Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola -- and an outsider who shares Sullivan's name. The controversy over the second Sullivan has added a volatile twist to the ranked-choice contest.
- KANSAS | Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is defending a seat in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, but Democrat Adam Hamilton has made the race unexpectedly competitive. Kansas has a typically Republican-leaning voter base, and Democrats haven't won the Kansas Senate seat since 1932.
- MAINE | Republican Sen. Susan Collins is in a close race with Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president, in a state that backed Kamala Harris in 2024. Collins is pitching her seniority and ability to deliver for Maine, while Jackson is tying her to President Donald Trump and the cost of living.
- NORTH CAROLINA | Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor, faces Republican Michael Whatley in an open-seat race that Republicans once viewed as central to their Senate strategy. The race has become a major test of whether Democrats can compete in a state that has leaned Republican in recent federal elections.
- OHIO | Republican Sen. Jon Husted is defending his seat against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in a race that could help decide control of the chamber. Brown’s comeback bid has made the contest highly competitive, drawing major spending and visits from national figures.
- TEXAS | Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico are locked in a close contest that has put a Texas Senate seat in play for Democrats. A Talarico win in Texas would be historic -- as no Democrat has won a Texas Senate race since 1988.
REPUBLICANS TARGETING DEMOCRATIC SEATS
- GEORGIA | Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff faces Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a pivotal race as Republicans defend their Senate majority. Ossoff is seeking another term in a state Trump carried in 2024, and Democrats are campaigning with former President Barack Obama.
- MICHIGAN | Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are competing for an open seat after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection. El-Sayed, a physician and former public health director, and Rogers, a former congressman who led the House Intelligence Committee, are vying for a seat that could shape the Senate majority.
- NEW HAMPSHIRE | Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John Sununu are competing for the open seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. Sununu’s return to politics gives Republicans a well-known nominee, while Pappas is seeking to keep the seat in Democratic hands.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: 2 college students found dead after going missing during Colorado hike
text:
(AP) - Two Colorado college students have been found dead after going missing during a hiking trip in the Rocky Mountains last weekend when a heavy snowstorm hit, authorities said.
The bodies of Kaden Matsuda, 19, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, of New York, were found Wednesday afternoon in a basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles southeast of Aspen, the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement posted on social media.
They left Colorado Mountain College Leadville’s campus on Friday, telling family and friends they planned to hike up Ice Mountain, a nearly 14,000-foot peak near West Apostle Mountain that requires technical climbing, the sheriff’s office said. They were expected back by Sunday, but college staff reported them missing on Monday morning.
The sheriff’s office said the causes of their deaths were under investigation, but foul play was not suspected. Authorities said they would not offer theories on what may have happened until autopsies are completed.
“Our heart aches for Kaden and Jackson’s family and friends,” Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the statement Wednesday night. “We are very proud of our team’s efforts to find them before this weekend’s coming storm. Although this is a gut punch, our prayers were answered that we would find Kaden and Jackson, allowing some closure for the family.”
About 60 search and rescue volunteers, aided by helicopters, drones and dogs, searched for the two men.
The helicopter crew on Tuesday discovered a tent collapsed under the snow with their sleeping bags, a stove and clothing near a lake northwest of Ice Mountain — but the students were nowhere to be found.
Based on the tent’s location, officials said they were aiming for the 13,597-foot West Apostle Mountain.
Friends and family described both as experienced hikers and climbers.
The sheriff’s office said their climbing equipment was not in their dorms, tent or vehicle, suggesting they left their tent prepared for a technical climb. Trash inside the tent indicated they had eaten before starting their hike, officials said.
Matsuda was studying to become a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was studying to become a mountain guide, Rohrich said.
Authorities had been concerned that aerial searches could be limited in upcoming days because of poor weather that was expected to begin Friday.
___
Yu reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Milford man arrested 10 months after daughter froze to death
text:
A Milford man was arrested Wednesday night, 10 months after his 1-year-old daughter froze to death at the family’s home.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, is charged with manslaughter in the death of his daughter, Eleanora Ray McLaughlin, Maine State Police said Thursday morning.
The toddler died at Shane McLaughlin’s house on Dec. 28. In April, the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner said Eleanora died of hypothermia and ruled her cause of death as accidental. There are five categories for manner of death: natural, accident, suicide, homicide and undetermined.
McLaughlin is also charged with three counts of child endangerment. Eleanora was living with her twin sister and an older brother at their father’s house at the time of her death.
McLaughlin is in the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor and is expected to make a court appearance Friday.

title: What the latest CNN poll found about Maine’s races before Election Day
text:
The latest poll of Maine’s top-of-the-ticket races found that Democrat Troy Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, remain essentially neck-and-neck in their U.S. Senate race, while Democrat Hannah Pingree continues to comfortably lead the gubernatorial field.
In other words, not much is changing in the polls ahead of next Tuesday’s election, as Maine’s candidates and their allies make their final pushes to win over a small share of undecided voters.
The newest survey, conducted for CNN by public opinion research firm SSRS, came out Thursday morning and had Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, receiving 49% support among likely voters to 45% for Collins, the five-term Republican incumbent from Caribou. The poll had 4% of respondents list neither candidate and 2% put down “other.”
Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven, led Republican Bobby Charles, a Leeds lawyer who worked under several former Republican presidents, by 53% to 39% in the survey of likely voters that notably did not ask respondents about independent Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator from Oxford. Bennett has struggled to climb out of the single digits in polling of the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills.
The survey follows a Marist Poll released Tuesday that was an outlier by being the only one to find Charles tied with Pingree in the gubernatorial race. Most have shown Pingree up double digits.
The CNN poll reached 783 registered Maine voters surveyed online or by telephone from Oct. 20-25. It had a margin of error of +/- 4.5 percentage points, with 32% of respondents describing themselves as Democrats, 29% identifying as Republicans and 38% identifying as independents or members of another party.
The results were nearly identical to a CNN poll of the Maine races between late August and early September.
The electorate in rural Maine is notoriously difficult to survey, and Jackson is well aware that Collins was down in the polls before the 2020 election that she ended up winning over Democrat Sara Gideon by roughly nine points.
While other polls have suggested Collins may once again outperform other Republicans in a midterm election year that looks favorable for Democrats amid President Donald Trump’s low approval ratings, the new CNN poll hinted at warning signs for the incumbent.
Trump’s approval rating among the likely Maine voters was 32%. Asked about what they think Collins would “do more to support” if elected, 54% of respondents said she would do more to support “the interests of Donald Trump and the Republican Party” versus 46% who said she would support “the interests of people in Maine.”
Still, the same percentage said Jackson would do more to support the interests of people in Maine, and 52% said he would do more to support “the interests of the Democratic Party.”
The economy and cost of living have been top of mind for American voters in national polls amid soaring gas prices and an unpopular war in Iran, and that held for Maine voters in the CNN poll. Some 44% of respondents listed the economy as their top issue followed by 27% putting the “state of U.S. democracy.”

title: AI can do great things but nobody knows where it is going. That’s scary.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Stephen Gilbert is co-founder and CEO of Anchour, a branding and marketing agency headquartered in New Gloucester that works with consumer brands, credit unions, and service businesses across the country.
I’ve worked with artificial intelligence every day since 2022, even before ChatGPT came out and made it dinner-table conversation. It comes with my job. I run a branding and marketing agency in Maine, and AI now touches almost everything we do.
People in my line of work usually sound very sure of themselves about AI. I’m not. How fast it’s moving scares me.
When I started, AI was a light assistant. You typed a question, it typed back, and sometimes it sped things up. It was handy, a little clumsy, and easy to keep at arm’s length.
Four years later, it takes on deep, multi-step work by itself. It makes a plan, does the job inside the software we already use, checks its own work, and reports back.
Take a brand photo shoot. Before anyone picks up a camera, someone has to dream up the concept and show the client every shot. That used to take our team days. Now we can go from a rough idea to life-like previews of the whole shoot in an afternoon. That gives us more time to get the idea right.
I’ve built more tools with AI than I can count, including ones our team uses every day for brand writing, media planning and client reports. It helps me do my job, and it makes my work better. It teaches me something almost every day. What it can do is amazing.
And it still freaks me out.
Nobody knows where this is going, including the companies building it. The governor’s office has said nearly one in five American workers is highly exposed to AI. It might wipe out a lot of jobs. It might create work none of us can picture yet. Unless someone has figured out time travel, anyone who tells you they know how this ends is guessing.
What I do know is what it’s done for us. Used properly, it’s done far more good than bad.
It’s leveled the playing field for a small agency in New Gloucester. A few years ago, only the big national agencies could afford a full research department and engineers building their own proprietary software. Now, with AI, we can do both. That’s how we’ve beaten much bigger firms for major projects with national brands, the kind we wouldn’t have had a shot at before.
AI is only as good as the people using it. It can hand you a pile of ideas in seconds. It takes someone with lots of talent and judgment to know which one is right, make it great, and catch what the machine got wrong. That’s why we keep hiring. Our team has grown from about 25 people in 2024 to 45 today. I can’t promise that lasts, and I won’t pretend to.
My ask, whether you run a business, work for one, or are still in school: Learn it now. Use it, and get a feel for what it can do and where it fails. The people who understand this technology will have a say in how it’s used at work, in our towns and in our government. The people who wait will have those decisions made for them.
Maine’s AI task force has recommended a public AI literacy campaign. I agree. You can be uneasy about AI and still learn how it works. I’m both.
I’ve spent four years inside this shift, and I still don’t know where it ends. I’d rather face it with my eyes open, and I hope more Mainers will too.

text:
Maine’s nonprofit arts and cultural organizations support more than 7,300 jobs, a new study has found.
University of Maine economist Todd Gabe identified more than 1,400 nonprofit organizations — including libraries, museums, theaters, musical groups and historical societies — using Internal Revenue Service data. Gabe’s study, released this week, estimates that those organizations directly employ more than 5,600 people, paying them more than $125 million.
The groups support more than 7,300 jobs statewide when factoring in suppliers and household spending, the study found. The organizations contributed an estimated $226 million to labor income and $660 million in economic output across the state, according to the study.
“Most of these organizations are quite small, but collectively, they are sizable in terms of their employment and their economic impact,” Gabe said.
Some of the groups in the study include the Portland Museum of Art, the Bowdoin International Music Festival, the Penobscot Theatre Company in Bangor, as well as small libraries and art galleries. The study was funded by a federal grant and conducted with input from the Cultural Alliance of Maine.
The study also found that Maine has the third-highest concentration of nonprofit arts and cultural groups per capita in the country, behind Washington, D.C., and Vermont, at 103 per 100,000 residents. Maine also has the third-highest number of nonprofit museums, theaters and historical preservation societies per capita in the U.S., and the second-highest number of libraries per capita, Gabe said.
The study is part of Gabe’s ongoing research into the economic value of arts and culture. He has studied Maine’s creative economy since the early 2000s.

title: Space heaters under recall after units reportedly catch fire
text:
(Gray News) - Almost 340,000 space heaters are under recall throughout the United States due to the risk of fire and burns.
DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported.
About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026.
According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. DREO said they received 17 reports of ignition, three resulting in property damage and one burning a person’s hand.
Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one.
Consumers will be instructed to cut the electrical cord of the old space heater after it’s been unplugged and to send in a photo of it.

title: Houlton Pulls Off Stunning Overtime Upset as County Teams Advance
text:
The County Scoreboard: Houlton Stuns Top Seed in Overtime as County Soccer Teams Keep Moving Through the Playoffs
If Wednesday's tournament soccer games proved anything, it's that a higher seed doesn't guarantee much once the ball starts rolling.
Houlton's boys delivered one of the biggest upsets of the postseason, knocking off top-seeded Mattanawcook with just four seconds remaining in overtime. Presque Isle's girls took care of business at home, Central Aroostook's boys survived a penalty-kick finish, and Hodgdon won a back-and-forth battle against Easton.
On the girls' side, Central Aroostook and Madawaska also earned their places in the Class D North semifinals.
It was another afternoon when several County teams saw their seasons come to an end, while others moved one step closer to playing for a regional championship.
Here's how Wednesday, October 28, played out.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Presque Isle Moves On, Will Host Cony Saturday
(3) Presque Isle 3, (6) Skowhegan 1
Presque Isle's girls are moving on to the Class B North semifinals after a 3-1 victory over Skowhegan on Wednesday.
Peyton Boinske led the Lady Wildcats with two goals, while Carrlyn Buck added another to complete the scoring.
The victory sends third-seeded Presque Isle into Saturday's semifinal round, where they'll host seventh-seeded Cony at 1 p.m.
Cony earned its place in the semifinals with a 2-1 upset of second-seeded Gardiner.
That sets up an interesting matchup in Presque Isle. The Wildcats will have home-field advantage, but they'll be facing a Cony team that has already knocked off one of the highest seeds in the bracket.
Next game: (7) Cony at (3) Presque Isle, Saturday at 1 p.m.
Class D North: Central Aroostook Holds Off Van Buren
(3) Central Aroostook 3, (6) Van Buren 2
Central Aroostook's girls are headed to the Class D North semifinals after holding off Van Buren in a 3-2 quarterfinal victory.
Lilly Burtt scored twice for the Lady Panthers, while Stevi Pierce added the third goal.
Van Buren made a game of it, with Emily Lapierre scoring early for the Lady Crusaders and Madelyn Marquis finding the back of the net late.
The Crusaders kept the pressure on, but Central Aroostook held on to secure the win.
The third-seeded Panthers now move into the regional semifinals, where they'll face second-seeded Fort Fairfield in another all-County matchup.
Fort Fairfield advanced Tuesday with a 4-0 victory over Washburn.
Class D North: Madawaska Wins Overtime Thriller at Ashland
(5) Madawaska 2, (4) Ashland 1 (OT)
Madawaska is also moving on after pulling out a 2-1 overtime victory over Ashland.
The fifth-seeded Owls went on the road against fourth-seeded Ashland and came away with the win, extending their tournament run into the Class D North semifinals.
It was another close matchup between two County programs, with Madawaska finding a way to get the job done in extra time.
The Owls will face the winner of the quarterfinal between top-seeded Penobscot Valley and eighth-seeded Schenck.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Hodgdon Wins Back-and-Forth Battle Against Easton
(4) Hodgdon 3, (5) Easton 2
Hodgdon and Easton gave fans one of Wednesday's most entertaining quarterfinal matchups.
Fourth-seeded Hodgdon jumped out to a two-goal lead, but fifth-seeded Easton wasn't going away.
The Bears responded with two goals of their own to even the score before Hodgdon found the goal it needed to move on.
Wyatt Oliver scored twice for the Hawks, while Finn Gardiner added the other goal.
Jacob Tuttle and Noah Arbab each contributed an assist.
Mason Pelletier scored both goals for Easton.
Hodgdon goalkeeper Aiden Ciarleglio made several important saves to help preserve the victory, finishing with nine saves on 14 shots.
At the other end, Easton goalkeeper Gavyn Kilcollins was busy throughout the game, recording 14 saves on 28 shots.
The 3-2 victory sends Hodgdon into the Class D North semifinals, ending Easton's tournament run.
Class D North: Central Aroostook Survives Penalty Kicks
(2) Central Aroostook 3, (7) Penobscot Valley 2 (PKs)
Central Aroostook's boys are moving on, but they certainly had to work for it.
The second-seeded Panthers survived a tough quarterfinal matchup against seventh-seeded Penobscot Valley, advancing after penalty kicks following a 2-2 tie.
Mitchell Burtt with both Panthers goals in regulation, himself, Jensen Bell and Ben Woodworth had successful PK's, Henry Brochu and Cayden Shute had the regulation goals for the Howlers.
The 2-1 result sends Central Aroostook into the Class D North semifinals, where the Panthers will meet third-seeded Fort Fairfield.
Fort Fairfield earned its semifinal berth Tuesday with a 3-0 shutout of Washburn.
That sets up another all-County matchup with a trip to the regional championship on the line.
Eight-Person Boys: Baillargeon Brothers Deliver Stunning Houlton Upset
(9) Houlton 2, (1) Mattanawcook 1 (OT)
This one might be remembered for quite a while in Houlton.
The ninth-seeded Shires pulled off a stunning 2-1 overtime victory over top-seeded Mattanawcook, with the winning goal coming in the final seconds of extra time.
Will Baillargeon scored Houlton's first goal to help keep the Shires in the game.
Then, with just four seconds remaining in overtime, his brother James Baillargeon delivered the game-winner.
Four seconds.
That's how close Houlton came to needing more soccer to decide the outcome, but James made sure the Shires wouldn't have to wait any longer.
The victory sends ninth-seeded Houlton into the eight-person boys regional semifinals, where they'll face fourth-seeded and undefeated Penobscot Christian.
It's a remarkable postseason run for a Houlton team that entered the tournament as the ninth seed and has now knocked off the number-one team in the bracket.
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: High school student accused of trying to make bombs for ISIS, deputies say
text:
GAINESVILLE, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - A Florida high school student was arrested after an investigation into his contact with a terrorist organization revealed he was attempting to make bombs, authorities said.
Alachua County sheriff’s deputies said the 15-year-old is a student at Buchholz High School.
The sheriff’s office and FBI conducted a joint investigation on Friday at the teen’s home after investigators learned he was having online conversations with members and supporters of the Islamic State group, also known as ISIS.
Investigators say the teen asked for help to build drones and explosives to attack people at an unknown location.
Authorities spoke with the 15-year-old’s parents, who allowed them to search the boy’s phone. They reportedly found files containing instructions for making explosive devices and chemical compounds, as well as ISIS propaganda.
On Monday, investigators searched the teen’s home with his parents’ consent after they revealed the information found on the phone.
Inside, they found two jars in his bedroom. The 15-year-old reportedly told investigators the jars contained chemicals used to make “TATP,” or triacetone triperoxide, a dangerous explosive.
The Alachua County Bomb Squad unit responded to the home and secured the materials. Detectives then searched the home.
The 15-year-old was charged with making or attempting to make a destructive device. Additional charges could be added as the investigation continues.
Family members said off camera that they still had many questions about the investigation and declined to comment further.

title: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail.
“Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.”
The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners.
“To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said.
In recent months on the campaign trail, President Donald Trump has said that the U.S. economy is doing well, often conflicting with what recent consumer surveys have found on voters’ economic opinions.
“The economy is the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far,” said Trump, at an Aug. 5 rally in Las Vegas.
The trend is not unusual. Each election cycle, the party in power in Washington typically proclaims that the U.S. economy is strong.
Despite the stark differences that voters appear to be thinking about this election season, Rebucci said Americans have long lived with inequality in the economy.
“This is an economy that is comfortable with inequality,” he said. “The issue is not about eliminating the inequality, but to adjust the system in such a way that we can live better with that inequality. And in particular, the most important thing that people need to be perceiving is that they’ve got a shot at being in that top 10%, top 1%.”

title: Lewiston-Auburn Boys & Girls Club chapter hit by more cuts in grant funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The week before the Boys & Girls Club of Southern Maine’s annual fall fundraiser last week, officials received news the program lost 50% of one of its important federal grants. It was more bad financial news for the club.
The Boys & Girls Club of Southern Maine serves over 400 children and teens in Lewiston, Auburn, Portland and South Portland.
Colleen Cooper, the chief executive officer for the Boys & Girls Club of Southern Maine, said the loss of the grant is a significant hit to the organization.
Officials in the program will have to adjust, but they remain committed to keeping the clubs open, specifically in Lewiston and Auburn, Cooper said.
“When you think about it more broadly, not just through our organization, but families and other organizations that had their resources cut short, or in half, the kids are the ones who suffer the most,” she said.
The funding cut was in the club’s Temporary Assistance for Needy Families grant through the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Cooper said. The $115,000 grant was reduced by 50%, to $57,500. The funds are used for youth development programs, out-of-school activities and after-school care programs, as well as general family assistance.
The national nonprofit Boys & Girls Club has over 5,000 chapters across the country, with five in Maine. The clubs are funded with a mix of donations, state and federal assistance programs and grants.
According to the southern Maine club’s most recent tax filing in 2025, $7.8 million of the program’s $9.5 million budget is from contributions and grants, which is about 83.4% of overall revenue.
The cut in the federal grant adds to the chapter’s financial challenges. In 2024, the club received $8.9 million in grants, about $1 million more than in 2025.
Cooper, who has served as the chief executive officer for the Southern Maine club for almost a year, said the program has seen “lots” of federal funding cuts over the years. Cooper worked for a Massachusetts chapter before.
The goal, eventually, is to shift the club’s overall funding model, but leaders had already budgeted the grant money for the year, Cooper said.
“My broader concern is that the needs of young people are going to grow significantly and outpace what organizations are going to be able to provide. From a macro perspective, we need to really look at that and how to invest in young people,” Cooper said.
Cooper spoke of the importance of investing in young people, especially with the youth violence Lewiston is experiencing.
The goal of the club is to help young people realize their potential through after-school, vacation and summer programs. Based on data collected by the organization, 93% of students who go through club programs have a career path in mind to explore at the time of their high school graduation. The students also have better outcomes in managing emotions because of the trauma-informed approach staff takes with students. And, 81% of club members earn mostly As and Bs, according to the data.
Cooper said young people want a sense and place of belonging where they can be supported by adults who care about them. Staff connect with the students through listening, helping with homework and playing sports and other activities, she said.
“I think we have to get back to that village mentality of helping young people, and our team is part of that help,” Cooper said.

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure
text:
Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure
WASHINGTON —
The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.
As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.
Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.
Video below: Here's what happens to your body when clocks 'fall back' an hour
Trump’s pressure campaign hasn’t worked
Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT."
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”
An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year."
The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump's pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.
Previous laws have been repealed
In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.
An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.
“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”

title: Fed up with all the attack ads
text:
As yet another tedious campaign season draws to a close, it would be a relief if the TV ads would simply tell us what the candidates are for and hoping to accomplish. It is very tiresome to hear or watch the constantly repeated character attacks. We have begun muting them.
In the future I would love to see these regulated or done away with in our state. Perhaps Maine could serve as a model for local, regional and national elections. We deserve better than this.
Mary Anderson
Peaks Island

title: Watts Hall Community Arts bean supper raises $1,430 for local food pantry
text:
THOMASTON – Watts Hall Community Arts is proud to share that the Dot Jameson & Lucy Mayo Memorial Bean Supper, held on Oct. 10, raised $1,430 for the Thomaston Inter-Church Fellowship Food Pantry.
Watts Hall Community Arts Board members Daryl Hahn and Cathy Harn and Managing Director Kendray Rodriguez presented the donation to Food Pantry manager Roberta Carmichael and volunteer Judy Hastings on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The total came from a combination of admission fees and additional donations from attendees.
The supper honored the legacies of Dot Jameson and Lucy Mayo, two longtime members of the community who shared a love of cooking and a tradition of making baked beans.
Watts Hall Community Arts extends its thanks to everyone who attended and contributed to the supper. Community members who would like to support the Thomaston Inter-Church Fellowship Food Pantry are encouraged to drop off donations of peanut butter or breakfast cereal, which are the pantry’s current biggest needs, to the Thomaston Municipal Building, 13 Valley St.
To learn more about the Thomaston Inter-Church Fellowship Food Pantry, please visit thomastonfoodpantry.org. For more information about Watts Hall Community Arts, visit wattshallthomaston.com.
Watts Hall Community Arts is committed to ensuring that Watts Hall continues the proud tradition of enriching community life in Thomaston and Midcoast Maine. Our mission is to ensure that this historic building continues to serve as a center for community engagement while promoting the Hall as a premier arts and entertainment venue that contributes to the heart and soul of a vibrant Main Street.

title: Hampden Academy seniors put the ‘fun’ in fundraiser by painting parking spaces
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - Before saying goodbye at graduation, Hampden Academy seniors are leaving their mark.
Every year, each grade on the student council is tasked with creating an impactful project to benefit the school.
“Our faculty council was super impressed, not just with our juniors, this year’s seniors, but just every grade level came with a lot of thought they had behind a certain project,” said Ryan Crane, Hampden Academy assistant principal and student council co-advisor. “This one certainly was met with a ton of support from our teachers and staff.”
The now-seniors decided to beautify the parking lot over the summer by painting their designated spots.
Senior and student council member Kenzie Merrill said they got the idea from looking online and at other schools: “We wanted a new idea and just something that was cool and hadn’t been done before [at Hampden Academy].”
About 15 gallons of paint were supplied at a discount by Erickson’s Hardware, and students brought their own supplies to share.
Most students spent a day in August painting their parking spots together, saying it truly put the “fun” in fundraiser.
“Every parking spot is just like a little picture of the person who painted them,” commented Zoelle Raymond, a senior and student council member. “Everyone has their own personality in their spot, and it’s just nice to see all of those.”
Serving as a fundraiser for parent-organized Project Graduation, the painted parking spaces raised $600 toward the $22,000 goal to put on the safe post-commencement celebration.
“The parents work really hard to make it a good experience for us,” senior and student council member Annabelle Levesque explained. “And so, if we could kind of take it into our own hands and give back a little bit of money too, that’s important, too.”
Not only do the painted spaces benefit seniors through fundraising, but students added that the artwork brightens the day for parents, visitors, and passersby.
For students, the greatest impact comes from spending time together as a class before graduation day.
“For Project Graduation, it’s just like one last night together. And so, all these efforts go toward that and it makes it really special for us,” Merrill said.
Project Graduation hosts students overnight at a venue with games, prizes, and activities to eliminate the risk of drinking and driving. Other year-round fundraising efforts include selling concessions at athletic games and school events.

title: InvestigateTV+: Tracking the trackers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As the number of cameras capturing vehicle information multiplies, so do concerns of privacy for everyday people. InvestigateTV+ explores what can happen when the tool is misused and meet one man on a mission to track every police camera in the country.
Plus, four-legged companions jump into action to help heal our heroes. We share the recent gift bringing military members support in the form of service animals.
Tracking the trackers
Flock Safety says its cameras don’t track people.
But the company’s own training videos show police using the system to track suspects “from location to location to location.”
And some of its cameras are designed to follow people as they walk.
“And they quite literally use AI to zoom in and follow you around whether you’re a person of interest or not,” said Benn Jordan, a security researcher who found dozens of Flock cameras streaming openly online.
Service dogs helping vets
Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation.
To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog.
Undiagnosed diabetes
Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide.
Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina.
A barbershop quartet
The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship.
“The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen.
Four men with four different careers create one sound.
