title: Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid rule forcing sick recipients to prove frailty
text:
Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid rule forcing sick recipients to prove frailty
Chronically ill people on Medicaid won't be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for "medically frail" exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill."
The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to comply with the law's work requirements.
The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well.
"The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems," Stearns said in his 16-page ruling.
Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns' decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful.
It is likely to mean some people will be able to obtain or keep coverage, said Morgan Henderson, an economist who studies Medicaid at The Hilltop Institute at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. "Those individuals who would have lost coverage because they're sick but they're not quite sick enough," he said, "they might have their coverage preserved now."
North Carolina Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai said it would also help patients avoid some stressful situations.
"One of our top priorities is to make sure people can get the critical health care they need without facing confusing paperwork or the fear of losing coverage during treatment," he said in a statement. "This decision allows us to focus on what matters most: delivering reliable health care to our state's most vulnerable residents when they need it most."
Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty, including the requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment.
Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said "the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States' concerns of disenrollment compelling."
CMS declined to comment.
The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump's big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government's safety net healthcare program.
Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others.
___
Associated Press reporter Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this article from Haddonfield, New Jersey.

title: Aging Untold: How to spot the early signs of Parkinson’s and when to talk to a doctor
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine the subtle, easily overlooked early warning signs of Parkinson’s disease and discuss when to talk with a physician.
Plus, we explore what to consider when starting antidepressants, emphasizing the importance of setting realistic expectations and building a comprehensive support plan.
Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs.
Parkinson’s disease can start long before a tremor and the subtle changes are easy to miss.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the loss of smell, constipation or changes in handwriting can be early signs.
By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done.
Resources are available for people living with Parkinson’s. Read the full article here.
When feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself lasts for weeks or months and it starts affecting sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options.
For some people, that might include a discussion about whether an antidepressant should be part of the treatment.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone, so talk with your provider. Chronic stress, a thyroid imbalance and nutritional deficiencies could be contributing.
Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness and there are withdrawal symptoms.
“They’re not happy pills. They don’t take away the sadness, but they will be a way for you to work on how you got there or what else is going on,” Rogers said.
Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
Remote work opportunities continue years after the COVID-19 pandemic, and some communities are offering cash incentives to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere.
Cumberland, Maryland, launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city.
Tulsa, Oklahoma, launched Tulsa Remote before the pandemic. It pays remote workers $10,000 to move to Tulsa and rent or buy a home.
When there is a crisis, first responders and members of the military run toward it, and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health.
Two nonprofits in Michigan are working together to help, providing free therapy and service dogs to veterans and first responders.
Tonya and Scott Shea created their nonprofit, We Walk the Line, raising funds for Blue Star Service Dogs.
The Sheas’ 21-year-old son, Army Spc. Connor Shea, served two years at the National Training Center in the Mojave Desert. The isolation, dangerous exercises and COVID-19 lockdowns took a toll. Shortly after spending the holidays with his family, he died by suicide.
Months later, the family’s bulldog inspired them to create their nonprofit.

title: Man accused in Cornell rape lawsuit wants Letitia James removed from investigation over her posts
text:
Should social media posts disqualify New York’s attorney general from leading a criminal investigation into gang rape allegations at Cornell University?
That’s the question before a state judge on Thursday as one of the accused men seeks to remove Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor overseeing the renewed criminal probe.
One of at least two cases against James contends she is biased because she posted messages expressing support for the accuser just days before she was appointed to the case.
The former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024. The former student said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent.
“What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James posted to X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order taking the case away from the local prosecutor, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024, and naming James as special prosecutor.
Within days, lawyers for two of the men named as defendants in Jane Doe‘s lawsuit filed challenges to James’ appointment — one that Judge James R. Farrell is hearing on Thursday, and the other in Tompkins County, where Cornell is located.
James, a Democrat, is not expected to attend the hearing in Monticello, about 72 miles (116 kilometers) northwest of Manhattan.
A lawyer for the man whose case is being heard Thursday wrote that James’ social media post “has unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants” named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit.
The lawyer, Andrew Miltenberg, asked that Farrell order Hochul to appoint a special prosecutor “who is free from actual or perceived conflicts of interest or bias.”
James’ office argued in a court filing that the challenge is “procedurally defective and substantively meritless,” noting that courts have previously ruled that the governor is free to exercise her executive power as she chooses, such as in appointing a special prosecutor.
“While Petitioner relies on the AG’s remarks in a single social media post as proof that the various ills he fears will come to pass, such speculative and conclusory claims of harm — premised entirely on his own mischaracterization of the AG’s statements — are insufficient for hardship,” Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars wrote.
At a news conference to announce her appointment, James declined to comment when asked about the social media posts. But Hochul said she had no qualms about naming her as special prosecutor.
“I have every confidence in our attorney general to do what she has always done: Look at the facts, examine the record, draw the proper conclusions,” Hochul said. “That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case.”
James has been involved in a number of high-profile cases, most notably against the National Rifle Association and President Donald Trump. She labeled him a “con man” and “carnival barker” and pledged to shine a “bright light into every dark corner of his real estate dealings.” She also led a civil investigation that led to Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s resignation over sexual harassment allegations.

title: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
text:
(Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep.
Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.”
The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening.
Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.”
The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

title: Business owner, strangers clean out struggling widower’s home for free: ‘I wanted to help’
text:
SOUTH KINGSTOWN, R.I. (WJAR) — A 22-year-old Rhode Island man helped a widower in a tough spot with a free whole-house cleanout and a fundraiser.
Henry Milder, owner of HM Home Improvement, and his crew started a whole-house cleanout early Sunday morning along Juniper Lane in Wakefield.
Milder is doing the job for free.
Milder said his business offers several services, including house and garage cleanouts and landscaping work.
“I have a lot of services I offer, so if people have a house they need cleaned out, or garage or any landscaping work, they can give me a call,” Milder said.
The homeowner
David Garasole, 62, lives in the home with his pet parrot, Roxy.
“This is the house I grew up in. It was my parents’ house in 1974,” Garasole said.
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
Garasole said his wife Tracy, the love of his life, lived in the home. She died by suicide 10 years ago after battling depression.
“I’m not over it. She died and all my bills doubled and everything. I’ve been trying to keep the house afloat,” Garasole said.
Garasole’s work as a painter slowed down. Items piled up in the home.
“It’s just depressing to be in here and I had to get out,” Garasole said.
The job
A search online led Garasole to Milder.
Milder said Garasole called him and said he needed his house cleaned out.
So, Milder came to look at the job.
Garasole said he became emotional while talking with Milder because he was embarrassed about the mess and the amount of clutter.
“He doesn’t even have heat in the house right now,” Milder said. “It’s no way a man should live, so I wanted to help him out, and he’s in a tough spot.”
Instead of giving Garasole a price, Milder told him he would do the job for free.
“He didn’t believe me. He really didn’t believe me. He was like, ‘Are you actually going to come back?’ I was like, ‘Yeah, I’m going to come back, David,’” Milder said.
Volunteers
Milder reached out to his local community for additional help. Employees, friends and strangers volunteered their time.
“I was so surprised because no one ever does that,” Garasole said.
Garasole said that, item by item, he can breathe a little better.
“All these kids, they’re all just nice wanting to help me. Look at the stuff,” Garasole said.
Milder said he spent about two hours talking with Garasole at the home, and Garasole became emotional and thanked him.
“That response alone kind of made it worth it, just seeing how thankful and how much this is going to help him out,” Milder said.
Additional help
Garasole said Milder offered to help him move into an apartment.
“He even said he would help me move into my apartment,” Garasole said.
A GoFundMe was added to provide funds to help Garasole get back on his feet.
“We just met once. That’s it, and now we’re friends for life, and I can’t believe what he did for me,” Garasole said.

title: More than 41 million voters have already cast early ballots; here's where
text:
More than 41 million voters have cast early ballots ahead of Election Day. See turnout by state
With Election Day less than a week away, voters in several states have cast millions of early ballots.
More than 41 million voters have cast ballots early, either in person or by mail, according to the latest data from the University of Florida Election Lab. The University of Florida Election Lab gathers data directly from state and regional sources and has tracked early voting since 2008.
The data does not show election results, so it's not yet known which candidates will win their races. Some states do report voters' party affiliation, which the data includes.
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early voting and analyzing trends in the data. All figures are as of Thursday morning. Here's what to know.
States with high early voting turnout
With the election five days away, more than 41 million voters have cast early ballots; that's more than a third of all votes cast in the 2022 election.
In Texas, early ballots cast in person or by mail already make up more than 70% of the state’s 2022 turnout. Texas has a close, competitive Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.
Texas is one of 10 states that require voters to provide an excuse to vote by mail. About 5.6 million ballots have been cast in person.
Mississippi, Alabama and New Hampshire do not offer universal early voting and require voters to provide an excuse to vote by mail.
Georgia is another state seeing high early voting turnout, with more than two million ballots already cast. That's about 58% of the total turnout the state saw in the 2022 midterm elections. Georgia has competitive races for the Senate and governor.
Incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican challenger Mike Collins. The governor's race is between former Atlanta Democratic Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee Rick Jackson.
Tennessee and North Carolina also have high turnout, with early voting accounting for 58% and 56% of the 2022 midterm turnout, respectively.
How is early voting turnout in competitive states?
Republican nominee and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democratic nominee and former state health director Amy Acton are competing for Ohio's open governor seat.
In Ohio, more than a million voters have cast ballots, making up nearly 31% of the votes cast in the 2022 midterm election.
The Cook Political Report has called both the race for governor and the U.S. Senate seat in the state as competitive.
About 1.5 million voters in Michigan have voted ahead of Election Day. The state allows voters to vote early in person or by mail. More than 80% of those early votes were cast by mail.
Democrat nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are competing for the state's open Senate seat.

title: 10-year-old girl found ‘tied up in a closet’ after being taken from apartment; suspect arrested, US Marshals say
text:
CANBY, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — A 10-year-old girl who was taken from her apartment early Wednesday was found that afternoon and a suspect was arrested, according to the U.S. Marshals Service.
The U.S. Marshals Service said tactical teams rescued the girl from a home in Oregon City, Oregon. She was found “tied up in a closet” and taken to the hospital.
Vince Edgar Chavez tried to run away out of the back of the house, but was arrested, according to the U.S. Marshals.
Investigators said a man went into an apartment at 1:39 a.m., hurt a 12-year-old child and took the 10-year-old. The 12-year-old was rushed to the hospital and was still being treated as of Wednesday afternoon.
Police said the parents are cooperating with the investigation.
The community asked why an Amber Alert was not issued when the girl was taken from her apartment, and the Canby Police Department said it had not gathered the information required for an alert.
Carus Elementary, where the girl is a student, had increased police presence during Wednesday’s afternoon dismissal “out of an abundance of caution.”
“Our hearts are with this child and her family,” the school district said. “Please know that we are here to support our students, staff and families in whatever ways we can.”

title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men Star, Dies at 86
text:
Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ Star, Dies at 86
In news that will be felt in many corners of the pop culture universe, Patrick Stewart’s family has announced that the great actor of stage, film, and television has died.
In a post to Stewart’s Instagram account they wrote: “We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lew Body Dementia.”
Stewart was 86 years old.
READ MORE: Every X-Men Movie Ranked From Worst to Best
Born in England in 1940, Stewart was an acclaimed Shakespearean actor long before he found the roles for which he became internationally famous. He joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and was knighted for his outstanding work as an actor in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth. At that time, he said he owed “literally everything” to an English teacher named Cecil Dormand who had encouraged him to become a performer. ("Although many people in my life have had great influence on me, without this man none of it would have happened,” he added.)
Over the years, he appeared on stage in England in America in productions ranging from The Tempest to A Christmas Carol, from Antony and Cleopatra to Macbeth. But his career was shifted forever when he took the roles of Captain Jean-Luc Picard on the Star Trek sequel series, Star Trek: The Next Generation. A strikingly different captain from William Shatner’s Captain Kirk, Stewart brought strength, wisdom, and subtlety to the role of Picard.
Stewart played Picard on seven seasons of The Next Generation, then in four big-screen movies, and finally in the recent Paramount+ streaming series Star Trek: Picard.
Shortly after The Next Generation ended its run in syndication, Stewart took on another iconic pop-culture role: Professor Charles Xavier, leader of the Marvel superhero team the X-Men. Stewart played “Professor X” numerous times, from 2000’s X-Men up until shortly before his death; he will appear in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday as Xavier later this fall.
In addition to those two signature roles, Stewart also appeared in films like David Lynch’s Dune, L.A. Story, The Pagemaster, Conspiracy Theory, and in television series like American Dad! and I, Claudius. He could bring great gravity to a role with his distinctive, distinguished voice, but he also had a sense of humor about himself and his regal persona; he also played the Poop Emoji in 2017’s The Emoji Movie.
Stewart’s family concluded their online tribute to him this way:
His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties. He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for his dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role - in art and life.”

title: DOJ subpoenas California election officials as special master takes up disputed voter claims
text:
DOJ subpoenas California officials in escalation of its scrutiny of local elections
The U.S. Justice Department has issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration.
Related video above: Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know
The Associated Press obtained copies of three subpoenas sent Oct. 21 and Oct. 24 to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder, ordering them to appear in court on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The documents request any records, documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls. The subpoenas also seek information relating to the office's “methods for screening for unlawful voting by aliens” and anything about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted.
All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar, said, “threats and intimidated have no place in elections.”
A letter accompanying a subpoena sent to the county registrar's Custodian of Records says it was issued “in connection with an official criminal investigation being conducted by the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations.” It doesn't detail the specifics of the investigation.
The issuance of a subpoena does not necessarily mean the person who receives it is the target of a criminal investigation.
But First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli recently warned that “any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”
Subpoenas come amid ongoing court battle
The Trump administration has sued to force California to set aside up to 20,000 ballots it suspects went to noncitizens and not count them until citizenship can be verified. A district court judge on Tuesday rejected that request, then on Thursday appointed a special master to evaluate the administration's claims.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter did not specify the exact scope of special master Daniel B. Garrie's responsibilities, but said he would be tasked with “developing the factual record” for the court.
In a Tuesday court hearing, Carter said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list of over 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters since there has been extensive debate over its reliability and both sides have agreed that it includes an unspecified number of citizens.
Carter also said at the hearing that a special master could investigate California’s claims that it cannot logistically separate the ballots in time for the county election certification deadline on Dec. 3. The federal government has contested that assertion.
It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters.
Trump administration appeals to higher court
Meanwhile, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to quickly weigh in.
The Justice Department said in a late Wednesday filing that it's essential the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals issue a ruling as soon as possible due to “irreversible ballot processing occurring on an ongoing basis.”
Carter’s decision was the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections in the midterms that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term. The Justice Department has made similar demands in other states, including Washington. Noncitizen voting has been a central focus of Trump’s political messaging for years, although available data indicates it is exceedingly rare.
Trump blasted Carter's ruling against the federal government on Thursday morning before heading to a campaign rally in South Carolina.
“California is very corrupt. The elections are extremely corrupt. The judge should not have done that but we’ll appeal that, of course," he told reporters. Trump added without evidence that there are “hundreds of thousands” and then amended it to “millions, in my opinion” of “bad ballots” in California.
Carter, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, argued that the Justice Department's demands were a clear violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls or election procedure within 90 days of an election.
A number of US citizens were included in the Justice Department's list of names
Both sides agree that an unspecified number of citizens were inadvertently included. Carter argued that separating the ballots at this point would risk disenfranchising citizens and “wreak havoc” on the election certification process.
Over 500,000 votes have already been processed in Los Angeles County alone, according to court filings. The system also protects voter privacy: Once a vote is processed, it cannot be traced back to the person who cast it.
Carter is to rule on the government’s renewed request for a preliminary injunction, which would bar the state from counting the ballots until the litigation is resolved. He said he will do so after a Nov. 13 evidentiary hearing with input from the special master.
He said that if the federal government suspected noncitizens were voting, it could continue to prosecute those cases criminally. Federal authorities have charged over two dozen foreign nationals in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people officials allege have illegally registered or voted in U.S. elections.
Appeals panel judges have said they wouldn't support setting aside ballots this close to midterms
The appeal will be the second time that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider the case.
The first time was just last week when the Justice Department argued before an appeals court panel that a fast ruling on its request was needed to stop any counting of the ballots.
Although the panel ruled it was premature for an appeals court to get involved before a lower-court ruling, two of the three judges wrote separate concurrences making it clear they wouldn’t support setting aside ballots at this late date. They questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s list of alleged noncitizen voters and argued that to set aside votes risks disenfranchising citizens.
One judge dissented, arguing that federal law bars noncitizens from voting and requires California to vet the potentially illegal ballots before counting them. The failure to do so, he wrote, would cause irreparable harm to the election.
__
This story has been updated to correct that the subpoenas viewed by AP were sent Oct. 21 and Oct. 24, not Oct. 29.

title: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide.
Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina.
It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations.
But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes.
“Every day, almost every hour” battle
Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight.
Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35.
“Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said.
Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor.
Tucker said at the time of his diagnosis, he weighed about 250 pounds, while juggling graduate school and long hours — along with what he now calls a diet full of junk food.
He said he followed medical advice, changed how he ate, and started exercising. He lost more than 30 pounds — but the diabetes remained.
“What I learned, it was also hereditary,” Tucker said. “My father had it, grandfather had diabetes.”
And even with better habits, the grind can be exhausting.
The “diabetes belt”
Novant Health endocrinologist Dr. Adam Spitz said North Carolina is part of what’s often called the “diabetes belt,” a region where rates tend to be higher.
Spitz said diagnoses have continued to climb, even as medications improve.
“We’ve got about a million people in NC with diabetes,” Spitz said. “But we have another quarter million people who have undiagnosed diabetes. And that is very scary because they can start to develop all the complications without even knowing it.”
Those complications can include heart disease, advanced kidney disease, and eye disease. The American Diabetes Association said Type 2 diabetes is the leading cause of amputation in the United States.
Spitz said newer medications — including GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy — have helped many patients, but other challenges remain.
“We’ve got more people, especially in rural or under-served communities who don’t have access to health care,” Spitz said. “And don’t have good education on healthy lifestyle.”
Millions more have prediabetes
Spitz said the stakes are even bigger because an estimated 3 million people in North Carolina have prediabetes.
“They are at a fork in the road where they can either go on to get diabetes, or they can prevent it,” Spitz said.
Doctors say prevention often requires major, sustained changes — improving diet and adding regular exercise — and many people struggle to keep those changes long-term.
Tucker said he’s committed to those changes. He bikes, stays active, and uses technology to help manage his condition, including a continuous glucose monitor that shows his blood sugar in real time.
He even recorded a recent doctor’s visit in which he was told his numbers are improving.
“Your average sugar is 129, which is also improved from our last time,” the doctor said in Tucker’s video.
For Tucker, the motivation is simple: stay healthy long enough to enjoy life — and avoid the worst outcomes he’s seen in others.
What to look for
The most common signs associated with undiagnosed diabetes include excessive thirst, extreme fatigue, and frequent urination.
You should consult your doctor for further testing.

title: What to know about the impacts of Flávio Bolsonaro’s move from Brazil to the US
text:
What to know about the impacts of Flávio Bolsonaro’s move from Brazil to the US
Flávio Bolsonaro is now in Miami after fleeing to the U.S. following his stunning defeat to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential elections.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede and has positioned himself as the “leader of Brazil” while declaring that there was electoral fraud, without providing evidence. In a letter on Wednesday, the senator for Rio de Janeiro said he relocated to the U.S. because he is the victim of political and judicial persecution.
Related video: Incumbent Lula wins Brazil presidential election
The departure of the 45-year-old ally of U.S. President Donald Trump from Brazil days after losing the runoff vote is sending shock waves across Brazil’s right and reverberating across the region, and it may spell more trouble for relations between Washington and Brasilia.
Here’s what to know about the possible impacts of Bolsonaro’s exodus from Brazil.
The shake-up of Brazil’s right
Bolsonaro has promised to lead the opposition to Lula from abroad. “I will say what you cannot say, and I will assume the risks you cannot take,” he said in a letter on Wednesday, addressing himself to political representatives of his party.
But Bolsonaro’s move to Miami complicates that vow, analysts say, leaving a power vacuum on the Brazilian right, which had united around Flávio’s presidential bid. His father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, appointed him as his political heir last December. The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.
“Flávio’s departure, along with the difficulty of directing the process from a distance and all the criticism he is likely to face for saying he wouldn’t flee and then fleeing, is likely to weaken him,” said Carlos Melo, a political-science professor at Insper university.
But as a political force, the right may lose neither influence nor impact following his departure due to its gains in Congress, said Luciana Santana, a political scientist at the Federal University of Alagoas.
“The group in Congress retains instruments to block proposals, negotiate with government and dispute the public agenda,” Santana said.
Impact on the global far right
A Bolsonaro win would have aligned Brazil with many of its regional neighbors, where conservatives have swept to power in seven presidential elections in 18 months.
Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with rising crime have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of mass arrests and suspended civil liberties.
Bolsonaro’s defeat is a setback for the far-right in the region and beyond, as it stops its ascension to the presidency of an economic powerhouse in the region that has significant diplomatic weight, said Santana.
But Lula’s win will not necessarily translate into the overall weakening of the movement, she said. As well as the gains in Congress, Flávio received nearly 60 million votes, indicating the competitiveness of the movement in Brazil.
Beyond Brazil’s borders, the international repercussions of Flávio’s flight depend on how the episode will be interpreted.
“Bolsonaro’s escape can be used by international networks as a symbol of alleged persecution. This could mobilize those who most strongly identify with the movement,” said Santana.
Tense relations between Washington and Brasilia
As congratulations poured in from Brazil’s allies and rivals around the world, Trump suggested Monday, without providing evidence, that Lula’s reelection was “rigged.”
But when asked about Bolsonaro’s assertion on Wednesday that he was the “rightful president-elect of Brazil” — a term the defeated candidate later softened to “leader of Brazil” — the U.S. president said he would not comment. Instead, Trump said he has given Bolsonaro a “pass” to come into the country.
“I won’t get involved,” Trump said, before repeating his claim that the election was “very strange.”
Lula’s win cements Latin America’s most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington and limits Trump’s drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere.
Lula has championed Brazil’s long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies.
While Bolsonaro’s presence in the U.S. adds “a new layer of problems to the already complicated bilateral relationship,” it is unlikely to be decisive, said Oliver Stuenkel, a political scientist and researcher at the Carnegie Endowment think-tank.
While there will now be two Bolsonaro brothers potentially lobbying the U.S. government on behalf of specific policies vis-a-vis Brazil, whether Washington heeds any such calls remains to be seen, Stuenkel said.
“Either Trump will pursue a pragmatic stance and basically recognize that U.S. pressure to elect Flávio failed (…) or there will continue to be continued friction,” he said.

title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say
text:
US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say
U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Related video above: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
It's unclear how soon the U.S. military would be ready
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It's unclear how soon after Election Day the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard — roughly 9,000 troops in all — from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete — a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump may be looking at a post-election timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then — especially if they feel U.S. action is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
“Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said.

title: US bans imports from 3 Chinese biotech companies over forced labor allegations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
US bans imports from 3 Chinese biotech companies over forced labor allegations
The Trump administration said Wednesday that it is blocking shipments by the Chinese biotech company BGI Group and its affiliates, alleging ties to forced labor in China's far-west ethnic region of Xinjiang.
Starting Thursday, U.S. Customs and Border Protection will bar goods by BGI Group, a major biotech company known for its genetic sequencing technologies, as well as BGI Genomics and MGI Tech. The Department of Homeland Security said the companies are either sourcing materials from Xinjiang or working with the regional government to “recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor” of members of persecuted ethnic groups in Xinjiang, including Uyghurs.
Adding the companies to a trade blacklist comes as biotechnology is emerging as another front in the economic and tech competition between the U.S. and China. The Treasury Department last week proposed new restrictions on U.S. investments in biotechnology, artificial intelligence and supercomputing from flowing into countries such as China.
Related video: How are President Trump's tariff policies affecting businesses?
China said it rejected any accusation of forced labor and called the ban an act of “political manipulation” and “bullying under the guise of ‘protecting human rights.’”
“These listings run counter to the consensus reached by the two countries’ heads of state, seriously undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and violate the spirit of humanitarianism,” said China's Ministry of Commerce in a Thursday morning statement. “China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its interests.”
The latest trade actions precede an expected meeting next month between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where BGI Group is based. Xi could then travel to Florida in December for the Group of 20 leaders summit and meet Trump for the fourth time this year as the two try to keep ties stable during a trade truce.
BGI Group rejected the allegations, saying in a statement Wednesday that it "has not engaged in any form of forced labor.” It added that “we firmly oppose all forms of forced labor.”
The company has controlling stakes in BGI Genomics and MGI Tech, DHS said.
BGI Group has for several years been a concern to U.S. lawmakers and policymakers, who are worried that its alleged ties to the Chinese government and access to massive genetic data could hurt U.S. national security and commercial interests. The company has long stressed its private ownership and said it does not serve patients in the U.S. and has no access to Americans' genetic data.
While Congress failed to pass legislation banning BGI from doing business with federally funded medical providers, it passed a similar provision at the end of last year without naming specific companies. It asked for a list of “biotechnology companies of concerns” to be compiled.
The Pentagon has labeled BGI Group, BGI Genomics and MGI Tech as Chinese military companies, a designation that carries reputational damage.
In its announcement Wednesday, DHS pointed to “credible information, including corporate and government reporting” showing that BGI Group, BGI Genomics and MGI Tech have supported genetic testing in Xinjiang.
“The collection and analysis of genetic material facilitate the monitoring, surveillance, and repression of ethnic minorities by the government of the People’s Republic of China, including the abhorrent practice of forced labor,” the department said.
The new restrictions are part of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which then-President Joe Biden signed into law at the end of 2021 following allegations of human rights abuses by Beijing against members of the ethnic Uyghur group and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang.
The Chinese government has refuted the claims as lies and defended its practice and policy in Xinjiang as fighting terror and ensuring stability.
In August, the Trump administration drastically expanded the blacklist under that law to include 43 Chinese companies, for a total of 187 entities. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has vowed to protect American workers from getting undercut or cheated by foreign companies using "slave labor."
—
AP writer Huizhong Wu contributed to this report from Bangkok.

title: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert.
Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International, said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago.
Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings.
“That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.”
For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending.
“It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor. Sometimes you can get a good deal, but just be mindful that it’s not a free lunch. Even if it’s that 6 weeks of interest free payments you’ve got to make a payment now and another one in two weeks and another one in two weeks, just need to be careful that you’re not overspending.”
Rossman also cautioned about the interest owed on those deals and on credit card debt, which can often be in the 20% range.
Rossman said people who feel in too deep can always ask for help.

title: Discarded smoking materials likely cause in Pittston fire that displaced 6
text:
Discarded smoking materials likely cause in Pittston fire that displaced 6
Six people were displaced after a fire spread from an exterior deck and caused extensive damage to a home Wednesday afternoon
Discarded smoking materials likely cause in Pittston fire that displaced 6
Six people were displaced after a fire spread from an exterior deck and caused extensive damage to a home Wednesday afternoon
Six people were displaced after a fire heavily damaged a home in Pittston Wednesday afternoon, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
Firefighters from the Pittston Fire Department responded to a home at 7 Stage Road around 4:08 p.m. Investigators determined the fire started on an exterior deck and was most likely caused by improperly discarded smoking materials.
The fire spread from the deck to a small mudroom attached to the home before extending throughout the house, causing extensive damage. Officials said most of the residents were home when the fire was discovered and quickly escaped.
An elderly resident was transported to MaineGeneral Medical Center for evaluation of preexisting medical conditions.
A man who contacted Maine's Total Coverage on Wednesday said he and a coworker were driving past the home when they noticed part of the porch was on fire. The man said they stopped and helped residents get to safety.
The Fire Marshal's Office reminds residents to fully extinguish cigarettes and other smoking materials before disposing of them in a sturdy, noncombustible container.

title: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday.
June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014.
Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007.
His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors.
Jones’ teams captured two WAC titles, in 1999 and 2007, and his run-and-shoot offense produced record-breaking quarterbacks, most notably Heisman Trophy finalist Colt Brennan.
Jones coached five All-Americans, 52 all-conference performers and 16 NFL draft picks. He also started his coaching career at Hawaii as a graduate assistant in 1983 and played quarterback for the university from 1973-74.
Jones agreed to become the next offensive coordinator at Kapolei High School in 2016. He was most recently the offensive coordinator of the Seattle Sea Dragons.
Additionally, Jones coached for three years in the NFL.

title: Former reality TV contestant from Gray pleads guilty to theft of SNAP benefits
text:
A former reality TV contestant from Gray has pleaded guilty to one count of Class B theft by unauthorized taking, after prosecutors say she received more than $129,000 in public benefits that she wasn’t entitled to have.
Jodi Lawless Theriault had been scheduled for a jury trial this week, more than four years after she was indicted and pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors have alleged that she received funds through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and MaineCare from 2009 to 2016.
Theriault allegedly misrepresented her income and assets during six-month review assessments for the benefits, according to an investigative report that is in her court file. State officials launched an investigation in 2016, three years after receiving a “citizen’s complaint” from a former friend in California who told the state that Theriault had admitted to defrauding its public benefits system.
She never reported that the father of her three children was another member of her household, the state said. Theriault was also accused of failing to disclose several of the family’s luxury items, her income from several jobs, including as a fitness trainer, and other assets.
Theriault’s defense attorney, Verne Paradie said Thursday that the defense disputes the roughly $129,000 amount. He said Theriault pleaded guilty to the theft count only as it related to some of the alleged SNAP benefits. According to court records, the state believes Theriault was overpaid roughly $54,000 in SNAP benefits.
Theriault will be sentenced at a later date. She faces up to 10 years in prison.
Paradie said the defense hopes Theriault will avoid prison, and that he anticipates she’ll be ordered to pay restitution.
“She’s working hard to support her kids,” Paradie said. “She just wanted to put this behind her.”
The trial was expected to involve numerous witnesses, including her children’s father, who is serving a five-year manslaughter sentence related to a fight and shooting on Forest Avenue in 2024. Attorneys had selected a jury Monday and a judge had just denied Paradie’s pretrial motions arguing that it was unfair for the state to prosecute Theriault for alleged conduct that occurred more than six years before she was indicted.
Theriault has appeared on at least two reality TV shows since 2016.
As a contestant on Steve Austin’s “Broke Skull Challenge” in February of that year, she ran in 100-degree heat with a 45-pound log on her back, but ultimately was sent home after losing a brawl involving seven other women.
In 2017, she was on the History network show “The Selection: Special Operations Experiment,” which challenged 30 people with no military experience to endure the same physical and mental challenges that Navy SEAL and Army Ranger recruits sign up for.

title: Troy Jackson sought Janet Mills’ backing after telling Susan Collins ‘shut up,’ source says
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson didn’t reach out to Gov. Janet Mills to ask for her support until after a debate earlier this month that sparked backlash for the Democrat when he told Republican Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up,” a source familiar with Mills’ side of the interaction said.
Mills announced on social media Thursday that she voted for Jackson and other Democrats down the ballot, saying they would “stand up for our values and stand up to Trump.”
But the reachout from Jackson to Mills, with whom he’s had a frosty relationship and who vetoed several of his priority bills when he was Maine Senate president, came after the governor had said consistently “for months” that she “was open to a conversation with Troy,” the source said.
The interactions between the campaign and Mills’ team, as described by the source, suggested flashes of lingering tension between the prominent Democrats just five days before Jackson faces Collins in a heated, tight race that could decide control of the Senate.
Jackson left a voicemail with the governor acknowledging he’d like to discuss an endorsement on Oct. 16. Mills was leaving Boston for Ireland that evening, but the pair’s teams discussed getting them together to talk about how she could help Jackson flip a seat that Collins has held for five terms, the source said.
“Earlier this week, Troy’s team indicated that a meeting would not fit into the campaign’s final stretch schedule,” the person said.
The Jackson campaign did not comment directly on the interactions with Mills and her team. David Farmer, a senior adviser to the Jackson campaign, said the candidate was grateful for Mills’ vote and appreciated her service to the state.
“Together, they passed some of the strongest abortion protections in the country, and the governor showed the country that Maine is ready and able to stand up to Donald Trump when it matters,” he said. “That’s the kind of fight he’ll bring to the [U.S.] Senate.”
Collins and her allies criticized Jackson, including in an ad, after he told her to shut up when she suggested a heckler during a debate was a supporter of the Democrat. Republicans have sought to paint Jackson as abrasive with women and tied the incident to previous dust ups while he was in Augusta and Bangor Daily News reporting on an assault charge when he was 19.
Jackson and several women lawmakers backing him have strongly disputed the claims. Some supporters of the former Allagash logger argued it was Collins who was rude by needling Jackson during a chaotic moment in the only debate featuring a live audience.
When she was still in the U.S. Senate primary against Graham Platner, whom Jackson later replaced, Mills targeted Platner’s disparaging social media remarks about women and sexual assault survivors. Many of Mills’ longtime supporters were reluctant to vote for Platner, who won the June primary after the governor’s campaign ran out of cash but later dropped out when an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape.
A coalition of labor organizers, progressives and many Maine local and state Democrats then rallied behind Jackson, who had placed third in the party’s gubernatorial primary, and nominated him to face Collins.
Jackson’s approach to Mills also came after he and other Democrats seeking to replace the governor tried to distance themselves from her earlier this year. Mills had backed Pingree, the former Maine House speaker and eventual nominee, in that five-way primary.
Out of the contenders at the time, Jackson had the most adversarial history with the governor. In the primary’s first debate, he pointed to prescription drugs as a failure and argued Maine could have had a drug price cap on the books for three years, while Colorado had just passed a similar bill.
Progressives who had hoped he would challenge Mills in 2022 were also frustrated by Mills’ prior vetoes of bills requiring the hiring of unions for public construction, and employment and arbitration laws.

title: Houlton Pulls Off Stunning Overtime Upset as County Teams Advance
text:
The County Scoreboard: Houlton Stuns Top Seed in Overtime as County Soccer Teams Keep Moving Through the Playoffs
If Wednesday's tournament soccer games proved anything, it's that a higher seed doesn't guarantee much once the ball starts rolling.
Houlton's boys delivered one of the biggest upsets of the postseason, knocking off top-seeded Mattanawcook with just four seconds remaining in overtime. Presque Isle's girls took care of business at home, Central Aroostook's boys survived a penalty-kick finish, and Hodgdon won a back-and-forth battle against Easton.
On the girls' side, Central Aroostook and Madawaska also earned their places in the Class D North semifinals.
It was another afternoon when several County teams saw their seasons come to an end, while others moved one step closer to playing for a regional championship.
Here's how Wednesday, October 28, played out.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Presque Isle Moves On, Will Host Cony Saturday
(3) Presque Isle 3, (6) Skowhegan 1
Presque Isle's girls are moving on to the Class B North semifinals after a 3-1 victory over Skowhegan on Wednesday.
Peyton Boinske led the Lady Wildcats with two goals, while Carrlyn Buck added another to complete the scoring.
The victory sends third-seeded Presque Isle into Saturday's semifinal round, where they'll host seventh-seeded Cony at 1 p.m.
Cony earned its place in the semifinals with a 2-1 upset of second-seeded Gardiner.
That sets up an interesting matchup in Presque Isle. The Wildcats will have home-field advantage, but they'll be facing a Cony team that has already knocked off one of the highest seeds in the bracket.
Next game: (7) Cony at (3) Presque Isle, Saturday at 1 p.m.
Class D North: Central Aroostook Holds Off Van Buren
(3) Central Aroostook 3, (6) Van Buren 2
Central Aroostook's girls are headed to the Class D North semifinals after holding off Van Buren in a 3-2 quarterfinal victory.
Lilly Burtt scored twice for the Lady Panthers, while Stevi Pierce added the third goal.
Van Buren made a game of it, with Emily Lapierre scoring early for the Lady Crusaders and Madelyn Marquis finding the back of the net late.
The Crusaders kept the pressure on, but Central Aroostook held on to secure the win.
The third-seeded Panthers now move into the regional semifinals, where they'll face second-seeded Fort Fairfield in another all-County matchup.
Fort Fairfield advanced Tuesday with a 4-0 victory over Washburn.
Class D North: Madawaska Wins Overtime Thriller at Ashland
(5) Madawaska 2, (4) Ashland 1 (OT)
Madawaska is also moving on after pulling out a 2-1 overtime victory over Ashland.
The fifth-seeded Owls went on the road against fourth-seeded Ashland and came away with the win, extending their tournament run into the Class D North semifinals.
It was another close matchup between two County programs, with Madawaska finding a way to get the job done in extra time.
The Owls will face the winner of the quarterfinal between top-seeded Penobscot Valley and eighth-seeded Schenck.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Hodgdon Wins Back-and-Forth Battle Against Easton
(4) Hodgdon 3, (5) Easton 2
Hodgdon and Easton gave fans one of Wednesday's most entertaining quarterfinal matchups.
Fourth-seeded Hodgdon jumped out to a two-goal lead, but fifth-seeded Easton wasn't going away.
The Bears responded with two goals of their own to even the score before Hodgdon found the goal it needed to move on.
Wyatt Oliver scored twice for the Hawks, while Finn Gardiner added the other goal.
Jacob Tuttle and Noah Arbab each contributed an assist.
Mason Pelletier scored both goals for Easton.
Hodgdon goalkeeper Aiden Ciarleglio made several important saves to help preserve the victory, finishing with nine saves on 14 shots.
At the other end, Easton goalkeeper Gavyn Kilcollins was busy throughout the game, recording 14 saves on 28 shots.
The 3-2 victory sends Hodgdon into the Class D North semifinals, ending Easton's tournament run.
Class D North: Central Aroostook Survives Penalty Kicks
(2) Central Aroostook 3, (7) Penobscot Valley 2 (PKs)
Central Aroostook's boys are moving on, but they certainly had to work for it.
The second-seeded Panthers survived a tough quarterfinal matchup against seventh-seeded Penobscot Valley, advancing after penalty kicks following a 2-2 tie.
Mitchell Burtt with both Panthers goals in regulation, himself, Jensen Bell and Ben Woodworth had successful PK's, Henry Brochu and Cayden Shute had the regulation goals for the Howlers.
The 2-1 result sends Central Aroostook into the Class D North semifinals, where the Panthers will meet third-seeded Fort Fairfield.
Fort Fairfield earned its semifinal berth Tuesday with a 3-0 shutout of Washburn.
That sets up another all-County matchup with a trip to the regional championship on the line.
Eight-Person Boys: Baillargeon Brothers Deliver Stunning Houlton Upset
(9) Houlton 2, (1) Mattanawcook 1 (OT)
This one might be remembered for quite a while in Houlton.
The ninth-seeded Shires pulled off a stunning 2-1 overtime victory over top-seeded Mattanawcook, with the winning goal coming in the final seconds of extra time.
Will Baillargeon scored Houlton's first goal to help keep the Shires in the game.
Then, with just four seconds remaining in overtime, his brother James Baillargeon delivered the game-winner.
Four seconds.
That's how close Houlton came to needing more soccer to decide the outcome, but James made sure the Shires wouldn't have to wait any longer.
The victory sends ninth-seeded Houlton into the eight-person boys regional semifinals, where they'll face fourth-seeded and undefeated Penobscot Christian.
It's a remarkable postseason run for a Houlton team that entered the tournament as the ninth seed and has now knocked off the number-one team in the bracket.

title: President Trump touts economic gains, but not all Americans feel the benefits
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Trump touts economic gains, but not all Americans feel the benefits
President Donald Trump celebrates tax cuts and income growth ahead of the midterms, but rising inflation and voter dissatisfaction with the economy remain significant issues.
President Trump touts economic gains, but not all Americans feel the benefits
President Donald Trump celebrates tax cuts and income growth ahead of the midterms, but rising inflation and voter dissatisfaction with the economy remain significant issues.
The U.S. economy grew at its fastest pace in a year last quarter, giving President Donald Trump something to celebrate just five days before the midterm elections.
"The U.S. economy is booming at 3.4%, which is a historic economic level," Trump told supporters at a rally in South Carolina Thursday.
"Wait until you hear your income numbers just came out, record-setting income, individual income at a record-setting level," Trump added.
But new government figures released Thursday tell a more complicated story.
The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Meanwhile, annual inflation accelerated to 3.6% in September, and inflation-adjusted disposable personal income fell 0.3% for the month.
In a statement Thursday, the White House credited Trump's policies with tax cuts, lower prescription drug prices, job creation and rising wages.
But how much are Americans actually benefiting?
Tax cuts and prescription drugs
The president's 2025 tax law expanded benefits for families with children, seniors and certain workers. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimates the legislation will reduce federal income taxes for most households compared with prior law.
The Tax Policy Center estimates that taxpayers benefiting from new deductions for qualifying tips and overtime will save an average of $1,480 and $1,200, respectively.
But the benefits are uneven. CBO projects that middle- and upper-income households will gain resources overall, primarily through lower taxes, while lower-income households will lose resources when reductions to Medicaid and food assistance are included.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said higher costs have also eaten into some of the financial relief.
"But basically what ended up happening is that extra tax refund money covered the cost of higher gas prices," Long said.
On prescription drugs, the administration has expanded TrumpRx, offering discounts on hundreds of medications. Long called it an area of progress, particularly for uninsured patients. But KFF found that insured patients may already pay less through other options.
Why Americans are experiencing two different economies
The White House also claims wages are outpacing inflation. But government figures show average hourly earnings increased 3% over the past year, while consumer prices rose 3.7%. Inflation-adjusted hourly earnings fell 0.7%.
Long said the trend contrasts with much of Trump's first term, when wages generally grew faster than prices.
She described today's economy as "very much a K-shaped economy," where higher-income Americans are benefiting from stock market gains while those earning less struggle with rising expenses.
Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, said Americans' financial circumstances can produce dramatically different experiences of the same economy.
"So much of how you view the economy depends on where you're viewing it from," Schulz said. He added that for someone with substantial stock investments or a growing 401(k), rising markets can translate into greater wealth and financial security.
But for someone trying to purchase a first home, replace a car or pay off student loans, those same economic conditions can feel far less encouraging. Higher borrowing costs and everyday expenses make it harder to get ahead.
That divide is increasingly visible in how some consumers pay for necessities. A LendingTree survey found that 29% of buy now, pay later users had used installment loans to purchase groceries, more than double the share two years earlier. Fifty-four percent said they needed the loans to make ends meet.
Schulz acknowledged that the loans have become more widely available, but said their growing use also reflects financial pressure.
"Some of it is also unmistakably a sign of struggle," he said.
That financial pressure is showing up in public opinion. An October AP-NORC poll found 74% of registered voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy.

title: Obama doubles down on ‘Cheesecake Factory’ joke after criticism from Trump
text:
(AP) — Former President Barack Obama is pushing back on Republicans’ reactions to a recent quip he made about President Donald Trump’s White House renovations and decor.
Obama said Trump’s gold accents looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
“These are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems,” Obama said in Georgia, pushing back on criticism he received for his comments. He said Republicans would rather have “phony outrage” and “talk about the Cheesecake Factory.”
Republicans painted Obama’s comment as insulting to middle-class Americans who enjoy the restaurant.
But Obama name-checked middle-class establishments he’s patronized with his daughters, including the California Pizza Kitchen, Cheesecake Factory and Chuck E. Cheese.
He said it’s telling that the White House did not dispute his main argument that Trump cares about trivialities, not helping Americans.
“The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” Obama said. “That part didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory.”

title: Isolated Showers Overnight. Above Average Highs Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A cold front moving from northwest to southeast will bring increased cloud cover with the chance of isolated rain showers. Rainfall will be light, with many communities that will be lucky to pick up a few hundredths of an inch. Overnight lows settle into the mid 40s to low 50s.
Friday: Coastal Clearing, Inland Showers
The cold front clears the coast by daybreak Friday. Skies will clear from the Foothills toward the Coast, where the warmest temperatures will reach the low to mid 60s. Inland areas will see more stubborn cloud cover and occasional showers, keeping highs in the 50s. Northwest winds pick up everywhere Friday, gusting between 20 to 30 mph.
Halloween: Mostly Sunny, Dry, and Chilly
Halloween stays completely dry with highs in the 40s. A northwest breeze will gust to 25 mph before weakening by early afternoon. If you have trick-or-treaters heading out, plan on an extra layer or two as evening temperatures dip quickly into the 30s after sunset.
Daylight Saving Time Reminder: Don’t forget to turn clocks back one hour before bed Saturday night. Daylight Saving Time ends Sunday morning, granting an extra hour of sleep, with sunrise and sunset times occurring an hour earlier. Make sure to check the batteries on your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.
Sunday & Beyond
Sunday brings mostly sunny skies with highs ranging from the upper 40s to mid-50s. Dry conditions continue into early next week with seasonable temperatures.
