title: Joey Brunelle will answer the call for Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This fall I’ll vote for Joey Brunelle to become Portland city councilor at-large. Of all the candidates running, he will best represent Portlanders. He has used the extensive knowledge and understanding of Portland to work on issues to improve the quality of life for Portlanders. Those include making housing more affordable, making Portland’s energy greener and making city government more responsive to the needs of its people while helping us better understand how city government works.
And, because Brunelle is the only Clean Elections candidate running for this office, he will listen to us.
I was surprised to discover that the other candidates running against him are not participating in Portland’s Clean Elections program. As we step into the voting booth this fall, we need to ask ourselves: Whose email will the candidate answer first, ours or that of a large donor?
Scott Vonnegut
Portland

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent
text:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent
Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press "pool."
CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president.
Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in "the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press," Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets' attorney, said in a statement.
The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent.
At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is "viewpoint discrimination" forbidden by the First Amendment's free-speech protections.
Trump insists that he doesn't have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning.
"Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable," the outlets wrote in their filing, "and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government."
The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him.
In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets' Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump's ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.
Kelly rejected Trump's reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump's stated belief that the outlets' reporting was inaccurate and biased.
"Simply put," Kelly wrote in the opinion, "That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination" — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.

title: The Latest: Trump and Obama make closing stretch appeals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Georgia Democrats rallied with former President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump tried to energize his base in Ohio as both parties offered closing messages ahead of Tuesday’s Election Day.
Trump called for the criminal prosecution of the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Alaska on Wednesday after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy posted early Thursday on social media, ordering a probe over whether the Peltola campaign should face charges.
A federal judge rejected a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations that they are likely noncitizens, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections. The ruling comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state.
The Latest:
US unemployment claims slide to 194,000, the lowest since mid-July
The Labor Department report Thursday suggests layoffs remain low and most Americans enjoy job security.
Applications for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have remained at historically low levels, never topping 230,000 in a single week.
But hiring has been lackluster: So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have been adding an average of 68,000 jobs a month, including a disappointing 29,000 last month. It’s better than in 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring.
Consumer spending has remained resilient and a surge in investment in artificial intelligence has lifted the GDP.
Inflation accelerated last month, highlighting affordability issues for voters
An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated as Americans go to vote with affordability concerns a central issue.
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September compared with a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Annual inflation has worsened since the Iran war spiked oil and gas prices. U.S. oil prices still top $100 a barrel, up from less than $70 before the war. Polls show the inflation has soured most voters on the president’s handling of the economy. Trump’s campaign promise was gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25.
Alaska governor orders state probe over whether Peltola campaign should face charges
Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s directive, posted early Thursday on social media, comes a day after Trump called for the criminal prosecution of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola.
It all comes following revelations that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
During a campaign stop on Wednesday, Peltola suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
Sununu says he would follow Collins’ example
New Hampshire Republican John E. Sununu says his former Senate colleague Susan Collins has been a “great model” for standing up to Trump.
Sununu, who is trying to regain the seat he lost in 2008, was asked during a debate Wednesday night to name a Republican member of Congress who has done what he promises to do: Oppose Trump on a key issue and remain effective.
“Susan Collins is a great example, a great model,” said Sununu, who is facing Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas in the race for an open seat. “She stands up for what she believes in, I’ll stand up for what I believe in.”
Collins, who is being challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson, has broken with Trump over the years but Democrats argue she is still too close to him.
Pappas repeatedly linked Sununu to Trump during the debate, including after Sununu criticized him for campaigning with former Vice President Kamala Harris last weekend.
Judge says Trump effort to segregate California ballots would ‘wreak havoc’
A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred,” Carter wrote. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process.”
Prosecutors for the Justice Department said they would immediately appeal the decision.
The decision is the latest legal setback for Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.
Trump wants Democratic Alaska Senate candidate prosecuted over spoiler controversy
Trump called for the criminal prosecution of the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Alaska on Wednesday after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
“I think they should be prosecuted,” the Republican president said about Peltola and the other Sullivan, responding to questions about a report in The New York Times.
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Peltola’s campaign discussing recruiting people with the same name as the two-term Republican before landing on a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan, now one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot in the general election.
Trump and Obama appeal to voters in pivotal states
Georgia Democrats rallied with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, at the same time President Donald Trump was in Ohio attempting to energize his base, as both parties began crystallizing their closing messages ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Trump has been on a weekslong sprint around the country, doing 20-plus rallies this month alone while packing upcoming days with more travel. But as Americans confront record fuel prices, rising costs and an unpopular war in Iran, the president has been keeping his focus on states that he won handily two years ago.
“If you can get out to vote,” Trump told a raucous crowd in Chillicothe, south of Columbus, Ohio’s capital, “we’re going to have a tremendous victory.”
The last Democratic president to serve two terms, Obama is increasingly campaigning for his party and gleefully acting as a foil to Trump — including criticizing the Republican for spending too much time leading White House renovations and for becoming wealthier while in office.

title: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University.
Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century.
This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
“We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. That’s also true when we look at gubernatorial contests,” Dittmar said.
Dittmar said the trend gives the upcoming 120th Congress a chance to be more than just 28% female, the current makeup on Capitol Hill.
With women across all ethnic and racial groups heading out in droves to vote, politicians hoping to go to Washington must keep that voting base in mind.
Previous midterms were dominated by traditionally female issues, including the #MeToo movement in 2018 and the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022.
Dittmar said this year is different.
“At the end of the day across the board, that affordability piece seems to be paramount,” Dittmar said.
Affordability is critical to women, but equally as important to men. While recent headlines about sexual assault and violence, issues traditionally seen as female-coded, are prompting reaction from candidates, Dittmar says the impact of those controversies in November may be slim.
“In terms of where we see women this year: high energy in terms of their concerns, but those concerns are something that’s more universal,” Dittmar said.
Something else to consider: the gender gap is different between the two parties. Women make up 42% of congressional Democrats, which brings the party closer to parity. However, women make up only 15% of congressional Republicans.

title: UMaine men’s hockey looking for its 1st win in 8 years at Boston University
text:
It has been a while since the University of Maine men’s hockey team beat Boston University at Agganis Arena. Eight years, to be exact.
The last win was on Nov. 17, 2018, when UMaine received 40 saves from now-Boston Bruins goalie Jeremy Swayman and a game-winning goal from Chase Pearson to notch a 3-1 victory.
Since then, BU has won the last eight meetings at Agganis Arena, including three consecutive one-goal victories. BU edged UMaine 3-2 in overtime a year ago on Ryder Ritchie’s goal 1:42 into the three-on-three OT session.
Both teams will come into this weekend’s series with overall records of 4-2. BU is 2-2 in Hockey East play while UMaine will be playing its first two league contests. BU is ranked 14th in one national poll and tied for 13th in the other, while UMaine is ranked 19th in the U.S. College Hockey Online poll.
“We haven’t won down there since I’ve been coaching here,” sixth-year UMaine head coach Ben Barr said. “That’s a place where we haven’t been very good.”
The Terriers have 18 National Hockey League draft choices, including 11 who were selected in the first or second round.
The series will feature a clash of styles as BU will look to play an up-tempo, run-and-gun type of game while UMaine will look to slow the Terriers down and keep them pinned in their own end with their aggressive forecheck.
“We have to hold onto the puck and make good decisions with it,” Barr said. “We have to shrink the game and play in the offensive zone. We have to play in the trenches as much as we can. If we get in an up-and-down-the-ice game with them, that won’t be successful for us.”
UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler agreed the team has to play its own game.
“We’re a hard-nosed team that thrives below the [faceoff] dots. They like to run-and-gun. They have a lot of skill,” Fowler said.
Fowler noted that the Black Bears need to put pucks behind the BU defensemen so they can establish the forecheck.
UMaine has been led in scoring by right wing Lee Parks, who has five goals and an assist and a five-game goal-scoring streak. Left wing Tanner Klimpke (3 goals, 3 assists) and center Max Scott (0 & 6) share the scoring lead with Parks. Defensemen Isa Parekh (2 & 3) and Lukas Peterson (0 & 5) are next.
Goalie Albin Boija is 3-1 with a 1.52 goals-against average and a .926 save percentage. Petter Wickstrom Stumer is 1-1 with a 1.48 GAA and a .940 save percentage.
BU has been paced by center Tynan Lawrence (4 & 3), right wing Ritchie (3 & 2) and left wing Jack Murtagh (1 & 4). They are linemates. Center Kamil Bednarik (2 & 3) will miss Friday’s game after being suspended by the league for a spearing major and game disqualification obtained in a 6-3 win over UConn on Saturday night.
Mikhail Yegorov has been between the pipes for all six games and is 4-2 with a 1.99 GAA and a .924 save percentage.
Friday’s game will have a 7 p.m. puck drop. Saturday’s game will begin at 6 p.m.

title: Camden-Rockport Beats Medomak Girls in Busline League Final
text:
The Medomak Middle School girls soccer team lost to Camden Rockport 2-0 in the Busline League championship game on Wednesday, Oct. 21 at Wasgatt Field in Rockland. It was the 15th straight Busline League title for the Schooners.
The upset-minded Riverhawks (8 3) kept undefeated Camden-Rockport (10-0) at bay in the first half, which ended in a scoreless tie in front of hundreds of fans that had gathered for the championship game on a beautiful autumn evening.
Camden-Rockport held a large advantage in ball possession and shots on goal, but Riverhawks goalie Jessalynn Peaslee made some nice saves to keep the typically dangerous Schooners off the scoreboard.

title: Pentagon accuses newly fired general of leaking sensitive information to the media
text:
Pentagon accuses newly fired general of leaking sensitive information to the media
The Pentagon has accused a newly ousted three-star general of leaking sensitive information to the media just hours after officials confirmed his removal from a top military planning post.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, a defense official said late Wednesday. Typically, the general in the position and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans for both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president.
No reason was given for the firing, the latest in a series of ousters or departures of military leaders under Hegseth. However, a Pentagon official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, later said in a statement that Sylvia was under investigation over allegations of sharing classified information about the Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other topics with journalists.
The statement claims that Sylvia failed three polygraph tests about leaking classified information.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a social media post that the department “took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information” without mentioning Sylvia by name. He said the matter has been sent to the Justice Department for "potential further legal action."
It is not clear why the Pentagon would appear to be pursuing charges in civilian courts instead of trying the general in the military justice system.
Sylvia did not immediately respond to a voicemail, text messages, emails and a LinkedIn message on accounts and numbers that appear to belong to him.
When asked about Sylvia’s firing by reporters Thursday, President Donald Trump said, "She’s gonna have big problems,” incorrectly identifying the male general as a woman.
“We’re very much looking for leakers,” Trump said.
In a confusing twist, the Joint Staff on Thursday also withdrew a statement from a day earlier that wished Sylvia well because “upon further review, we determined that the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances.”
A spokesperson late Wednesday had said the Joint Staff extended its “deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation.”
The firing of Sylvia from the Pentagon's top military planning post comes as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war following next week's midterm elections. The Pentagon official, however, insisted Sylvia was not a “central planner” on the Iran conflict and said that was the purview of U.S. Central Command.
Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led.
His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valor, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat.
Sylvia's case is Hegseth's latest accusation against top Pentagon officials of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests.
In a joint statement shared by senior aide Dan Caldwell, the trio protested the firing and said they were “incredibly disappointed by the manner in which our service at the Department of Defense ended. Unnamed Pentagon officials have slandered our character with baseless attacks on our way out the door.”
Hegseth never provided more information on what the three were accused of, and Caldwell would go on to be hired by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
Under Hegseth, the Pentagon also has carried out a series of moves restricting media access, including requiring that journalists be escorted while on Pentagon grounds and declaring that its press office was a classified space inaccessible to journalists.
Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

title: Justice Department subpoenas California officials in escalation of its scrutiny of local elections
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Justice Department on Thursday issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration.
The subpoenas were being issued by all four U.S. attorneys in California, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar, said, “threats and intimidated have no place in elections.”
The Associated Press obtained copies of two subpoenas sent to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder to appear in court on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
This follows a federal judge’s appointment of a special master earlier Thursday to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has about 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, less than 24 hours after he rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter did not specify the exact scope of special master Daniel B. Garrie’s responsibilities, but said he would be tasked with “developing the factual record” for the court.
In a Tuesday court hearing, Carter had said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list of over 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters since there has been extensive debate over its reliability and both sides have agreed that it includes an unspecified number of citizens.
Carter also said at the hearing that a special master could investigate California’s claims that it cannot logistically separate the ballots in time for the county election certification deadline on Dec. 3. The federal government has contested that assertion.
It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters.
Special master appointed amidst Trump administration appeal to higher court
Meanwhile, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to quickly weigh in on whether it can temporarily prevent California from counting the disputed ballots. It wants the state to set them aside and only count them if a voter’s citizenship can be verified.
The Justice Department said in a late Wednesday filing that it’s essential the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals issue a ruling as soon as possible due to “irreversible ballot processing occurring on an ongoing basis.”
The appeal came just hours after Carter issued a blistering order against the department’s last-minute effort to compel California to segregate the ballots from its vote count.
The department says it believes those ballots were sent to people who are registered to vote even though they are not U.S. citizens. Early voting has been underway in the state for weeks and millions of people have already cast ballots.
Trump blasts judge’s decision and says California’s elections are ‘extremely corrupt’
Carter’s decision was the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections in the midterms that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term. The Justice Department has made similar demands in other states including Washington. Noncitizen voting has been a central focus of Trump’s political messaging for years, although available data indicates it is exceedingly rare.
Trump blasted Carter’s ruling against the federal government on Thursday morning before heading to a campaign rally in South Carolina.
“California is very corrupt. The elections are extremely corrupt. The judge should not have done that but we’ll appeal that, of course,” he told reporters. Trump added without evidence that there are “hundreds of thousands” and then amended it to “millions, in my opinion” of “bad ballots” in California.
Carter, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, argued that the Justice Department’s demands were a clear violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls or election procedure within 90 days of an election.
A number of US citizens were included in the Justice Department’s list of names
Carter also questioned the reliability of the department’s list of names, since both sides agree that an unspecified number of citizens were inadvertently included. He argued that separating the ballots at this point would risk disenfranchising citizens and “wreak havoc” on the election certification process.
Over 500,000 votes have already been processed in Los Angeles County alone, according to court filings. The system also protects voter privacy: Once a vote is processed, it cannot be traced back to the person who cast it.
Carter is to rule on the government’s renewed request for a preliminary injunction, which would bar the state from counting the ballots until the litigation is resolved. He said he will do so after a Nov. 13 evidentiary hearing with input from the special master.
He said that if the federal government suspected noncitizens were voting, it could continue to prosecute those cases criminally. Federal authorities have charged over two dozen foreign nationals in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people officials allege have illegally registered or voted in U.S. elections.
Appeals panel judges have said they wouldn’t support setting aside ballots this close to midterms
The Justice Department has argued that it is in the government’s interest to prevent fraudulent voting before it happens. Federal prosecutors also have said voters won’t be disenfranchised by delaying the tabulation of their ballots while their citizenship is checked — an assertion disputed by county election officials.
The appeal will be the second time that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider the case.
The first time was just last week when the Justice Department argued before an appeals court panel that a fast ruling on its request was needed to stop any counting of the ballots.
Although the panel ruled it was premature for an appeals court to get involved before a lower-court ruling, two of the three judges wrote separate concurrences making it clear they wouldn’t support setting aside ballots at this late date. They questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s list of alleged noncitizen voters and argued that to set aside votes risks disenfranchising citizens.
One judge dissented, arguing that federal law bars noncitizens from voting and compels California to vet the potentially illegal ballots before they are counted. The failure to do so, he wrote, would cause irreparable harm to the election.
It’s not clear whether the case will appear before a new panel of judges or the same three that reviewed the case last time.

title: Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting
text:
Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting
A federal judge has rejected a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people, warning it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections.
Wednesday's ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state.
Related video above: Homestretch: Will President Trump's trips to ruby red states and swing districts sway voters?
The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term.
The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 names it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The federal government also had asked the appeals court for a quick ruling — before a district judge’s scheduled Oct. 27 hearing in the case — but that effort was rejected by the higher court.

title: Business owner, strangers clean out struggling widower’s home for free: ‘I wanted to help’
text:
SOUTH KINGSTOWN, R.I. (WJAR) — A 22-year-old Rhode Island man helped a widower in a tough spot with a free whole-house cleanout and a fundraiser.
Henry Milder, owner of HM Home Improvement, and his crew started a whole-house cleanout early Sunday morning along Juniper Lane in Wakefield.
Milder is doing the job for free.
Milder said his business offers several services, including house and garage cleanouts and landscaping work.
“I have a lot of services I offer, so if people have a house they need cleaned out, or garage or any landscaping work, they can give me a call,” Milder said.
The homeowner
David Garasole, 62, lives in the home with his pet parrot, Roxy.
“This is the house I grew up in. It was my parents’ house in 1974,” Garasole said.
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
Garasole said his wife Tracy, the love of his life, lived in the home. She died by suicide 10 years ago after battling depression.
“I’m not over it. She died and all my bills doubled and everything. I’ve been trying to keep the house afloat,” Garasole said.
Garasole’s work as a painter slowed down. Items piled up in the home.
“It’s just depressing to be in here and I had to get out,” Garasole said.
The job
A search online led Garasole to Milder.
Milder said Garasole called him and said he needed his house cleaned out.
So, Milder came to look at the job.
Garasole said he became emotional while talking with Milder because he was embarrassed about the mess and the amount of clutter.
“He doesn’t even have heat in the house right now,” Milder said. “It’s no way a man should live, so I wanted to help him out, and he’s in a tough spot.”
Instead of giving Garasole a price, Milder told him he would do the job for free.
“He didn’t believe me. He really didn’t believe me. He was like, ‘Are you actually going to come back?’ I was like, ‘Yeah, I’m going to come back, David,’” Milder said.
Volunteers
Milder reached out to his local community for additional help. Employees, friends and strangers volunteered their time.
“I was so surprised because no one ever does that,” Garasole said.
Garasole said that, item by item, he can breathe a little better.
“All these kids, they’re all just nice wanting to help me. Look at the stuff,” Garasole said.
Milder said he spent about two hours talking with Garasole at the home, and Garasole became emotional and thanked him.
“That response alone kind of made it worth it, just seeing how thankful and how much this is going to help him out,” Milder said.
Additional help
Garasole said Milder offered to help him move into an apartment.
“He even said he would help me move into my apartment,” Garasole said.
A GoFundMe was added to provide funds to help Garasole get back on his feet.
“We just met once. That’s it, and now we’re friends for life, and I can’t believe what he did for me,” Garasole said.

title: Aging Untold: How to spot the early signs of Parkinson’s and when to talk to a doctor
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine the subtle, easily overlooked early warning signs of Parkinson’s disease and discuss when to talk with a physician.
Plus, we explore what to consider when starting antidepressants, emphasizing the importance of setting realistic expectations and building a comprehensive support plan.
Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs.
Parkinson’s disease can start long before a tremor and the subtle changes are easy to miss.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the loss of smell, constipation or changes in handwriting can be early signs.
By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done.
Resources are available for people living with Parkinson’s. Read the full article here.
When feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself lasts for weeks or months and it starts affecting sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options.
For some people, that might include a discussion about whether an antidepressant should be part of the treatment.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone, so talk with your provider. Chronic stress, a thyroid imbalance and nutritional deficiencies could be contributing.
Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness and there are withdrawal symptoms.
“They’re not happy pills. They don’t take away the sadness, but they will be a way for you to work on how you got there or what else is going on,” Rogers said.
Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
Remote work opportunities continue years after the COVID-19 pandemic, and some communities are offering cash incentives to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere.
Cumberland, Maryland, launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city.
Tulsa, Oklahoma, launched Tulsa Remote before the pandemic. It pays remote workers $10,000 to move to Tulsa and rent or buy a home.
When there is a crisis, first responders and members of the military run toward it, and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health.
Two nonprofits in Michigan are working together to help, providing free therapy and service dogs to veterans and first responders.
Tonya and Scott Shea created their nonprofit, We Walk the Line, raising funds for Blue Star Service Dogs.
The Sheas’ 21-year-old son, Army Spc. Connor Shea, served two years at the National Training Center in the Mojave Desert. The isolation, dangerous exercises and COVID-19 lockdowns took a toll. Shortly after spending the holidays with his family, he died by suicide.
Months later, the family’s bulldog inspired them to create their nonprofit.

The information provided should not be used for diagnosing or treating a health problem or disease, and those seeking personal medical advice should consult with a licensed physician. Always seek the advice of your doctor or other qualified health provider regarding a medical condition. title: InvestigateTV+: Tracking the trackers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As the number of cameras capturing vehicle information multiplies, so do concerns of privacy for everyday people. InvestigateTV+ explores what can happen when the tool is misused and meet one man on a mission to track every police camera in the country.
Plus, four-legged companions jump into action to help heal our heroes. We share the recent gift bringing military members support in the form of service animals.
Tracking the trackers
Flock Safety says its cameras don’t track people.
But the company’s own training videos show police using the system to track suspects “from location to location to location.”
And some of its cameras are designed to follow people as they walk.
“And they quite literally use AI to zoom in and follow you around whether you’re a person of interest or not,” said Benn Jordan, a security researcher who found dozens of Flock cameras streaming openly online.
Service dogs helping vets
Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation.
To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog.
Undiagnosed diabetes
Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide.
Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina.
A barbershop quartet
The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship.
“The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen.
Four men with four different careers create one sound.

title: Emergency heating oil ought to have been better targeted
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is regarding the Oct. 22 report about the release of 315,000 barrels of heating oil into the Northeast market (“Feds release emergency heating oil to lower Maine prices; Collins, King claim win”).
With 42 gallons of oil in each barrel of heating oil, and approximately 3.9 million heating oil users in the Northeast, this will result in a little less than 3.5 gallons per user. I suspect that this will have no measurable effect on the price of heating oil or be of much help to heating oil users.
If this oil could be targeted to low-income users, where it would be of the most benefit, then this would have a more significant effect. With Maine, by far the state with the highest number of heating oil users in New England, targeting a proportionate amount of that oil to the Maine market would be more helpful. I wonder if Sen. Collins could have helped with that?
Michael Webber
Strong

title: Collins ad featuring retired broadcaster draws criticism in Maine Senate race
text:
MAINE (WABI) - Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson have released new ads in the final days of Maine’s U.S. Senate race, and the Collins campaign’s latest ad is making national headlines.
What the ad says
The Collins ad, “Cord of Wood,” features retired broadcaster Bill Green. Collins credited Green as being instrumental in her 2020 win over Sara Gideon.
In the ad, Green calls Collins one of the most decent and honest people he knows. He then references Jackson’s logging background, saying he knows both Collins and Jackson.
“We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Green says in the ad.
Critics say the ad talks down to Maine’s working class.
Political analyst weighs in
WABI asked UMaine’s Political Science Chair Mark Brewer if he thinks this could make a difference in the final days of the race.
“It certainly can have an impact in the race, and anytime you’re dealing with a race this close, any kind of an impact, even an impact say at the margins, could be enough to move the race in one direction or the other and help determine the outcome. I don’t know that this ad is that in this race. And I know that we’ll know until after the fact,” said Brewer.
Candidates respond
Jackson said, “This is about a cord of wood — and about Mainers struggling to afford to heat their homes this winter.”
The Collins campaign responded to a request for comment.
“Susan Collins would never talk down to any Mainer. And she wouldn’t tell anyone to shut up, like Troy Jackson said to her — or say that she kisses someone’s *** like Troy said. Troy spends all his time attacking Susan Collins, but never describes his plans for the future — because his whole campaign is based on trying to tear her down. The point of the ad is quite simple — Susan Collins is the most qualified person to represent Maine in the United States Senate,” the campaign said.

title: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream.
Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers.
Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city.
The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s.
“At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss.
Program details and requirements
- $10,000 in relocation cash
- $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations
Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years.
“The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said.
Tulsa leads the way
The website Make My Move lists more than 100 places advertising cash offers to attract potential new residents.
One of the largest programs is Tulsa Remote in Oklahoma, which started before the pandemic and pays remote workers $10,000 to move to Tulsa and rent or buy a home.
“We started the program really as an experiment to try to diversify the labor workforce here in Tulsa, which is often reliant on oil and gas,” said Justin Harlan, managing director of Tulsa Remote.
The program has grown from about 70 participants in 2019 to more than 3,500.
Tulsa Remote only requires a one-year residency but says it maintains a 90% retention rate beyond that requirement, with 75% of participants since 2019 still living in Tulsa.
“We work hard to meet with each individual in their first 90 days, understand what it is they’re wanting to get out of their commitment in Tulsa and really plug them in,” Harlan said.
Success stories and research
Faith Langevin moved from Atlanta to Tulsa in 2022, attracted by the lower cost of living and $10,000 incentive. Her husband is also a remote worker and also got paid to move there.
“I was looking for a place to move, looking for a lower cost of living, and that $10,000 -- there was that financial incentive and then what made it stand out was the social component,” Langevin said. “Absolutely not!” she said when asked about regrets three years later. “This is really home!”
Evan Starr, an associate professor at the University of Maryland’s School of Business, saw a need for more research around the idea of cities competing to attract remote workers.
“We wanted to study an early mover in that market to see what we can learn, that maybe other localities could benefit from,” Starr explained.
In studying the Tulsa Remote program, he found the program’s retention rate to be significant.
“You don’t want people only coming to your area for the money. They might come and just take the incentives and then as soon as any restrictions are up, then they might leave,” Starr said.
Starr believes remote work is here to stay.
“My sense is that it is here to stay. And so it’s really opened up this new level of geographic mobility. You’re not tied to where your employer is,” he said.
In Cumberland, longtime resident Gino Giatras, whose family has operated a hot dog shop since 1918, said he welcomes new neighbors.
“The reason I love it is because of the people, the weather, the actvities,” Giatras said.

title: Patrick Stewart: Where to Watch His Best Roles on Streaming
text:
Patrick Stewart: Where to Watch His Best Roles on Streaming
This one hurts. Patrick Stewart — Captain Picard on Star Trek, Professor X in the X-Men movies, the very embodiment of thoughtful heroism and leadership for several generations of pop culture fans — passed away this week at the age of 86.
It’s a terrible loss, but there is some small consolation in the fact that Stewart leaves behind a great body of work, much of which is currently available to stream at home. Here are a few of his many career highlights — and where to find them.
Dune (1984)
Currently streaming on Tubi
In one of his earliest Hollywood roles, Stewart plays Gurney, the mentor and trainer to Paul Atreides in David Lynch’s Dune. (Josh Brolin plays the role in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy.) Stewart’s most famous later roles were typically pacifists and statesmen; those who led with their words and their morals, rather than their fists. So it can be a little surprising to see him suddenly unsheathe a knife and go after a young Kyle MacLachlan. Lynch���s Dune can often bewilder viewers who aren’t familiar with Frank Herbert’s book or its terminology, but Stewart’s sturdy performance provides a steadying presence.
Star Trek: The Next Generation - “The Inner Light” (1992)
Currently streaming on Paramount+
Paramount+ is the home to all of Star Trek, so if you want to have yourself a full-blown Next Generation binge, that’s where to boldly go. If you only want to watch one episode to sample why Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard was so beloved, watch his work in the haunting Season 5 episode “The Inner Light,” in which the Captain of the Enterprise is mysteriously transported by an energy beam to a faraway planet, where he’s informed by everyone around him that he’s actually a humble agrarian worker. He pushes back, insisting he’s a starship captain, but gradually he comes to accept his life as “Kamin” — as years and then decades pass.
Star Trek: First Contact (1996)
Currently streaming on Paramount+
On the flip side of that quiet, contemplative episode, Stewart gave one of his most bombastic performances as Picard in the best of the Next Generation movies, 1996’s First Contact. The Enterprise crew travels back into the past, where they battle the techno-alien menace of the Borg and work to restore the timestream and the first-ever use of a warp drive for interstellar travel. Picard holds an understandable grudge against the Borg for the time they forcefully assimilated him. Stewart, in turn, gets to turn the typically stately Picard into a torrent of rage, giving us several very memorable scenes like this one.
A Christmas Carol (1999)
Currently available on YouTube
Stewart loved Charles Dickens A Christmas Carol and performed it on stage many times as a one-man show. Here he stars in a TV movie version of the classic holiday tale. In 2019, he said of his love of the show: “I believe that the world I’m in now has never been so troubled and dark a place. I’m a war baby. I was born in 1940, so I have some experience of the sounds of war. My father was away for the first five years of my life. I never knew who he was until he came home in 1945. But the times we’re living through now are exceptional and alarming. I felt that there was an opportunity here to say something about that.”
X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014)
Currently streaming on Disney+
Stewart did fine work in all of his X-Men movies, often in scenes opposite the great Ian McKellen as Magneto. But his most poignant moment in the franchise may be his encounter with his younger self (played by James McAvoy), where he pushes him to reject cynicism and to embrace the notion that peace can be achieved between humanity and mutantkind. “It’s not their pain you’re afraid of. It’s yours Charles,” Stewart whispers in that incredible voice of his. “And as frightening as it may be, that pain will make you stronger, if you allow yourself to feel it.”
Green Room (2015)
Currently streaming on Netflix
Stewart projected such innate goodness — or maybe he became so linked with heroic roles like Captain Picard — that he rarely strayed into more villainous territory in his later years. A rare exception is his work as the leader of a group of Neo-Nazis that try to kill the members of a punk band who witness a murder at a rock club. Talk about range; he is just as terrifying and sinister as Green Room’s Darcy as he is noble and dignified as Picard.
Logan (2017)
Currently streaming on Disney+
Logan was originally meant as the final farewell for Fox’s X-Men saga, and Stewart’s work as the aging Professor X — once the greatest telepathic mind in the world, now stricken with dementia — is one of the most moving performances in any superhero movie. Now that Stewart himself has passed away after, as his loved ones put it in their statement about his death, “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” this film, and Stewart’s work in it, becomes almost unfathomably sad.

title: ‘She just lit up the room’: Toddler dies after being hit by car at a pumpkin patch, family says
text:
SEVIERVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A Tennessee toddler died after being hit by a car at a pumpkin patch, according to her family.
The family of 21-month-old Nyxailia Hinton said they want answers after she died Tuesday.
The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said she fell and was hit by a car driven by a family friend at a pumpkin patch. However, details have not been given about how or where she fell.
“She just lit up the room,” said Peandra Hinton, the child’s mother. “If you were having a bad day, you see Zayla, she’s gonna turn it all around.”
Hinton said her daughter was with a babysitter who took her to the pumpkin patch without permission. She said her daughter was with a group of people she did not know.
Hinton rushed to the hospital, where her daughter died from her injuries Tuesday, according to the sheriff’s office.
Hinton said the past 48 hours have been a whirlwind, adding the hardest part has been waking up without her daughter.
“The fact that I couldn’t wake up this morning to my baby, it really tore me up,” Hinton said.
The family is planning funeral arrangements, and Nyxailia’s father said they want justice.
“We want justice for her. And we ain’t letting up, I don’t care if someone’s feelings get hurt, this has torn up her whole family. She wasn’t even 22 months old,” he said.
The sheriff’s office said the incident remains under investigation. No charges have been filed.

title: Milwaukee's William Contreras wins World Series MVP
text:
Milwaukee's William Contreras wins World Series MVP with .381 average, 10 ABS overturns
William Contreras became the eighth catcher voted the World Series MVP after lifting the Milwaukee Brewers to their first World Series championship.
The heart and soul of the small-market Brewers, Contreras batted .381 while guiding Milwaukee's pitching staff and capitalizing on the first Series with the Automated Ball-Strike challenge system by winning 10 of 13 appeals. He had an RBI double during Milwaukee's clinching 4-1 victory in Game 5 on Wednesday night.
“He posts every day," reliever Aaron Ashby said. "This team’s not what it is without this guy. He’s unbelievable.”
He joins Gene Tenace (1972), Johnny Bench (1976), Steve Yeager (co-winner in 1981), Darrell Porter (1982), Rick Dempsey (1983), Pat Borders (1992) and Salvador Perez (2015) as catchers to win the award.
At 28 a three-time All-Star, Contreras batted .270 with 18 homers and a career-best 94 RBIs as the Brewers won their fourth straight NL Central title.
He hit .444 with a pair of solo homers in the Division Series against San Diego, hitting a tiebreaking, seventh-inning drive in Game 1 and another homer in Game 3. He batted .357 with one homer and three RBIs in the Championship Series sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Contreras was on Venezuela’s team that won its first World Baseball Classic, though he was 0 for 13 with no RBIs.

title: Republican lawmakers call for MaineCare reforms after federal indictments
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -Republican lawmakers are calling for reforms to MaineCare following the federal indictments of six people tied to a South Portland home care agency. Defendants plead not guilty
According to court documents, six people associated with Community Home Health Care have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud.
Prosecutors allege the defendants submitted false visit records for services never provided, including more than $600,000 in fraudulent claims for one client.
Republican leaders outline requests
At a briefing Thursday, Republican leaders called for immediate oversight from Augusta.
“We’ve got three concrete actions we want to address. We want an independent, third-party review of MaineCare... We want a full public accounting from DHHS of when concerns about Community Healthcare were first raised... We want a status report on MaineCare providers under payment suspension or referred for investigation.”
House Minority Leader Billy Bob Faulkingham and Senate Minority Leader Trey Stewart argue state watchdogs failed to act on years of warnings until federal authorities stepped in.
DHHS response
Maine DHHS responded to our request for comment, saying:
“Maine DHHS takes fraud seriously and is committed to ensuring that every dollar managed by the Department is utilized lawfully, effectively, and in direct support of the programs and people they are intended to serve, which is why the Department engages in rigorous oversight and coordination with law enforcement and partners. The Department does not and cannot bring charges; when Maine DHHS identifies or is made aware of a credible allegation of MaineCare fraud, we refer the matter to appropriate law enforcement, including the Maine Office of the Attorney General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, for investigation and possible prosecution.”

title: Wiscasset Residents to Vote on Data Center Moratorium, Education Budget at Polls
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Wiscasset voters will decide on half a dozen items at the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, including a data center moratorium, a third attempt at validating an education budget, and the elimination of the ordinance review committee.
Residents will also consider a nonbinding referendum question about exploring a regional high school, a fire department cost recovery ordinance, and a mobile home lot rent increase moratorium.
The proposal comes after the town received pushback regarding the potential development of a data center last fall. Fred Robinson, CEO of international renewable energy company BayWa r.e. Americas, reached out to the town in November 2024 expressing interest in establishing a data center on the town’s Ferry Road property, according to town documents. Robinson and town staff exchanged questions and information regarding the town’s infrastructure capabilities for almost a year.
At the select board’s July 7 meeting, select board member Sarah Whitfield said the board has not heard from Boundless Power, the company Robinson has since founded, since the fall.
According to the findings and purpose section of the proposed moratorium, the town’s current ordinances do not address the potential impact a data center could have on the town’s infrastructure or character.
If approved, the moratorium would last six months and apply to data center development filed on or after Nov. 3. The language describes a data center as a facility primarily containing electronic equipment for the purpose of “data processing, data storage, cloud computing, or similar computing infrastructure services that uses environmental control equipment to maintain the proper conditions for the operation of electronic equipment.”
Town Manager Dennis Simmons proposed the fire department cost recovery ordinance after conversations with former Wiscasset Fire Chief Rob Bickford about recovering costs from certain emergency calls.
The fire department would bill recipients for services limited to hazardous material incidents, removing and disposing of hazardous waste discharges, vehicle crashes, vehicle fires, aircraft crashes, aircraft fires, a third and subsequent false fire or sprinkler alarm form the same location, water-related emergencies within a building, and providing standby for utility lines in a roadway due to a motor-vehicle crash.
The ordinance would not apply to house fires. The fire department cannot deny services to people because they are unable or refuse to pay. The proposed ordinance includes procedure for applying to the fire chief to seek reduction or forgiveness of the claim.
Wiscasset voters will consider enacting a moratorium on mobile home lot rent increases. The moratorium would be active for 180 days and would prevent increases in rent above 3% of the lot rent charged for the mobile home park as of Sept. 1. Violations of the proposed ordinance would result in $200 fines per infraction and a refund of the increase.
According to the findings and purpose section of the proposed ordinance, mobile home lot rent has been increasing beyond the capabilities of many renters to pay.
The select board first heard the proposal to create an ordinance controlling mobile home lot rent fees at its Aug. 25 workshop. At the Sept. 1 board meeting, Chair Alissa Eason said the board decided it needed time to review policy. In the interim, board members wanted to prevent lot rent increases, leading to the proposed moratorium.
There are three mobile home park lots in Wiscasset. According to the findings and purpose section of the proposed moratorium, rental rates have increased “rapidly” and increases are beyond the financial means of many renters, who are “uniquely vulnerable” to displacement.
If approved, the moratorium would be enacted under the town’s jurisdiction to protect the public health, safety, and general welfare of its residents under home rule authority, according to the draft.
An ordinance eliminating the ordinance review committee is also on the ballot. The ordinance was placed on the ballot on Sept. 1.
The ordinance review committee provides advice and recommendations on ordinance revisions or additions to the town. At the Sept. 1 meeting, Simmons said the town staff could handle the work of reviewing and proposing ordinance changes.
A third education budget is up for validation on the ballot. The budget of $10,630,432 was approved with a vote of 52-14 in a special town meeting on Sept. 29. It is a decrease of $113,687 or 1.06% from last year.
Voters failed to validate first budget, totaling $11,217,742, at the annual town meeting by referendum on June 9, 547-535. Voters failed to validate the second budget, totaling $10,736,486, at a special town meeting by referendum on Sept. 1, 250-228.
In the third budget, the amount to be raised from local taxes is $6,782,980, a decrease of $176,691 or 2.54% from last year’s subtotal of $6,959,671. Voters approved the budget at a special town meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 52-14.
Also relating to education, voters will consider whether the town should explore the possibility of a regional high school attended by students from multiple towns.
Whitfield said in an interview on July 21 the proposal came from a group who had prepared applications for state grants for a consolidated secondary school for Boothbay and Wiscasset. Wiscasset pulled out of the conversations regarding the grants in March, according to a superintendent’s report from the same month.
The question will be an attempt to keep the conversation about the merger going and to gauge public interest, Whitfield said.
“We have a general sense that we think both communities, particularly Wiscasset, they want to explore an option,” Whitfield said on July 21. “However, that may end up, we don’t have any data to support that.”
Polls will be open at the Wiscasset Community Center, at 242 Gardiner Road, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. For more information, go to wiscasset.gov or call 882-8200.

title: 92-year-old accused of trying to kill his wife at senior living home
text:
92-year-old accused of trying to kill his wife at senior living home in Kentucky
A man was arrested on Wednesday after police said he tried to murder his wife at a senior living home in Kentucky.
Bert Morris, 92, has been charged with attempted murder and strangulation.
According to court records, Morris was found pinching his wife's nose after putting a plastic bag over her head at StoryPoint Brownsboro in Louisville. Police said the incident was captured on video.
Morris put the bag over his wife's head "with the intent for the victim to pass away," according to arrest documents. Morris allegedly told police that she "needed to die."
He is scheduled to be arraigned Thursday.

title: Anne F. Wetzel | Obituaries
text:
Anne F. Wetzel slept her way into heaven on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at the age of 88. The cause of death was old age. (Heart failure.) She was a resident of Foulkeways in Gwynedd Valley, Penn.
Following a career in the administration of the Graduate School of Fine Arts at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, Anne turned to photography and moved to Maine, to Somesville, on Mount Desert Island. She was deeply involved in Episcopal Church activities at St. John’s, Southwest Harbor, where she served on the vestry and edited the church publication. She travelled to China, taking her camera along.

title: Washington County students serve up local seafood at Down East cookoff
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BEALS, Maine (WABI) — High school students in Washington County put their kitchen skills to the test Thursday, serving up fresh dishes straight from local waters.
Twelve students enrolled in culinary and aquaculture classes at Coastal Washington County Institute of Technology competed in a Seafood Cookoff at the Downeast Institute, organized by the Maine Aquaculture Innovation Center (MAIC).
“This is just bringing together chefs and students and seafood consumers, the general public, to celebrate seafood and the opportunities for diversification on the working waterfront,” said MAIC Executive Director Anne Langston Noll.
“What we’re trying to do is bring local seafood, both farm and wild-caught, having them be the next generation of seafood providers,” said Joshua Richards of MAIC.
Participating students worked in four separate teams to prepare and plate meals for a panel of judges, with dishes featuring salmon, mussels, and scallops. For many, it was their first time preparing seafood.
“I’ve never cooked any type of fish or anything like that,” said Gage Holland, a high school culinary student, “The most I’ve done is just like cook up a lobster.”
“They’ve been practicing for several months. It’s a great opportunity for them to really learn and express from what they’ve seen in the classroom,” said James Roberts, Executive Director at Coastal Washington County Institute of Technology.
The cookoff gives culinary students the chance to serve up dishes that are both local and innovative, showcasing cutting-edge aquaculture projects taking place right on Beals Island.
“Some of the products actually are born right here in our shellfish hatchery. We have deep sea scallops that were actually part of a project that we did with Maine Aquaculture Innovation Center and Mook Sea Farm to grow sea scallops in a shellfish hatchery. These are the world’s first ever consumed hatchery-reared scallops, which is pretty cool,” said Kyle Pepperman, Executive Director at Downeast Institute
Organizers and judges praised both the students and educators for their hard work and culinary creativity.
“The kids had to get up and talk about what they’re doing, and they were so proud of the food that they’ve created and kudos to the teachers, they are really killing it in there,” said Pepperman.

title: A Democratic victory will jumpstart America’s political engine
text:
The constant bombardment of political ads should be a warning to tune them out. A succession of negative advertisements cancels each other out and tells us nothing.
Look at where we are today. Economic difficulties, social unrest, a broken healthcare system, questioning of our election process, squelching our free press and the degraded integrity of the United States are mostly due to the current administration’s executive orders and policies, all exacerbated by the inability of Congress to follow our long-established rule of law.
I believe voting blue in this midterm election will get America’s political engine working to solve today’s real issues. Republicans, Democrats and independents working together, along with our system of checks and balances, could change today’s realities.
Tim Follo
Falmouth

title: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday.
June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014.
Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007.
His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors.
Jones’ teams captured two WAC titles, in 1999 and 2007, and his run-and-shoot offense produced record-breaking quarterbacks, most notably Heisman Trophy finalist Colt Brennan.
Jones coached five All-Americans, 52 all-conference performers and 16 NFL draft picks. He also started his coaching career at Hawaii as a graduate assistant in 1983 and played quarterback for the university from 1973-74.
Jones agreed to become the next offensive coordinator at Kapolei High School in 2016. He was most recently the offensive coordinator of the Seattle Sea Dragons.
Additionally, Jones coached for three years in the NFL.

title: County Community Players to Host Halloween Show
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - If you’re looking for some Halloween entertainment this weekend you could stop by the University of Maine at Presque Isle. The County Community Players will be presenting “An Evening of Halloween One-Acts” at the Gauvin Performing Arts Center. The show will feature 4 acts to give locals a frightful Halloween.
One cast member, Matthew Nonken said: “As someone who really has no experience in this field and just came in as a community member, I can only urge people to come and see because it’s enjoyable. I mean, you don’t get to see this every day. You’re gonna get to see a lot of, you know, dark and evil stuff and be able to enjoy that instead of your usual good tales all the time. So, I think it’ll be a bit of a different experience. At least for those who’ve come around and seen our shows a lot. So, it should be unique and fun. We’ve got 4 shows in total, two poems. We’ve got Lenore and The Raven. In the middle we have two plays. One of them is a bit of a bigger one, “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow”. Bigger cast, longer show, upwards of like an hour-ish and the next show is “To Burn a Witch”. Bit of a quick one but it’s a bit more of a dramatic play.”
The show will run on Friday Oct. 30th at 7pm, Saturday Oct. 31st at 2pm, and there will be a special showing at midnight Saturday night. Tickets can be purchased at thecountyplayers.org. Admission is $10 per child, $15 per adult, and free for UMPI students. Locals are encouraged to come out and join the Halloween fun.

title: Trump slams Peltola campaign over two Sullivans on Alaska ballot
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate.
Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that campaign staffers for Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman now running for the U.S. Senate, tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
The effort is not illegal. However, the reports have led Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, to order an investigation into alleged election manipulation.
Trump commented on the controversy Thursday before leaving for South Carolina.
“So nobody’s going to know what to do. That’s a fraud. And it shouldn’t be allowed to happen. And it was done in conjunction with Schumer and everybody else. It’s an absolute, it’s called voter fraud,” Trump said.
Vice President JD Vance echoed the president’s comments Thursday.
“It’s disgraceful, so whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her,” Vance said.
In a statement, Peltola’s campaign said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
Alaska’s highest state court earlier ruled that both men should remain on the ballot.
On the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan appears with no modifiers. Daniel S. Sullivan is listed with the labels incumbent and Republican next to his name.
Alaska’s elections are determined by ranked choice voting. If no candidate wins a majority in the Senate race after Tuesday’s midterm elections, the ranked choices will be tallied.
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) the chair of the House Oversight Committee announced Thursday he is launching an investigation into whether the Peltola campaign tried to intentionally confuse voters. He issued a letter requesting in-person testimony from key Peltola staffers next week.
