title: FTC orders Walmart, Delta and others to share how they use personal data to set prices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FTC orders Walmart, Delta and others to share how they use personal data to set prices and pay
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday it is ordering Delta Air Lines, Walmart and other companies to provide detailed information on how they use consumers’ data when they're setting prices.
The commission said it is also studying how ride-sharing and delivery companies like Uber use their independent drivers’ personal data when setting compensation rates.
“We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.
Orders were also issued to United, JetBlue, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart and Target, the FTC said.
Each company must share information that will allow the commission to assess whether pricing for tickets, rides, food delivery or other products and services varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data, the agency said.
The FTC said it is also examining whether companies compensate workers based on personal data like their phone usage or their history of accepting rides or deliveries. If the companies fail to turn over data, the FTC said it could compel compliance in federal court.
Delta said in response that it has “zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing” and fully complies with pricing and advertising laws.
“There is no fare product Delta has ever used, is testing or plans to use that targets customers with individualized offers based on personal data," the company said in a statement.
JetBlue said it doesn't use personal information or web-browsing history to set individual prices.
“Fares are determined by demand and seat availability, and all customers have access to the same fares,” the company said.
Instacart said compensation for its shoppers is based solely on job-related criteria, including the distance traveled, the number of items and expected shopping time. The grocery delivery company said it also doesn't use consumers' personal information to set prices. Prices on Instacart's website are set by the retailers the company serves.
“We appreciate the FTC's focus on this practice. We are committed to transparency and improving affordability for customers,” a spokesperson for Instacart said Wednesday. “We will continue engaging with policymakers and regulators to ensure they understand how pricing on our platform works.”
Walmart's CEO said in a statement last month that the retailer doesn't use personal information like income, shopping history or a customer’s willingness to pay to set prices, and it won’t be doing so in the future either. Target also said in a recent post on its website that it doesn't use personal information to raise prices for customers "based on who they are, where they live or when they shop.”
The FTC's actions reflect customers' increasing concerns about pricing technology and the use of artificial intelligence to collect vast amounts of data. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing-related bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
In August, the FTC announced a proposed policy that would require businesses to “clearly and conspicuously disclose” if they are engaging in personalized pricing and share the types of data they’re using to set those prices. The agency has extended the comment period on that policy until Nov. 21.
In a preliminary report filed in January 2025, the FTC found that grocers, clothing companies and others were using third-party companies to help them individualize online prices based on shoppers’ locations, browsing histories and other factors, including how long they left items in their virtual shopping carts.
But Ferguson, who assumed the chairmanship of the FTC when President Donald Trump took office, has said that report was rushed and should have asked the companies directly for data instead of focusing on third-party intermediaries.

title: 2 hospitalized after Harpswell house fire
text:
Two people were hospitalized after an early morning fire on Thursday in Harpswell.
The fire at a single-family home at 23 Smokehouse Road was reported at about 4:25 a.m.
Four people were in the house at the time, the state fire marshal’s office said on Thursday.
Two escaped uninjured. The other two were taken to a Portland hospital for injuries they sustained while trying to get out of the house to escape the fire, the office said. Their injuries were not considered life-threatening.
Two dogs also made it out of the house uninjured, the office said.
Investigators are still trying to determine the cause of the fire.

title: The woes at the root of UMaine football’s offensive issues
text:
Statistics can be misleading at times.
At other times, they accurately paint a picture of a team’s strengths and weaknesses and explain why a team is or isn’t successful.
When discussing his football team’s offensive woes during Monday’s Coastal Athletic Association coaches’ media zoom session, fifth-year University of Maine football coach Jordan Stevens reiterated a theme he has mentioned several times this season.
He said his offense’s ineffectiveness on first and second down has been an issue.
“We have to put ourselves in better situations on third down,” said Stevens in the wake of a 35-6 pummelling at the hands of nationally ranked Campbell University at UMaine’s Homecoming last Saturday. “There were too many third-and-9-plus distances, which are hard to get yourself out of.”
UMaine was in third-and-9 or longer situations 11 times in 17 third down plays vs. Campbell.
“We have to get better on first and second down to set up third down. We have to be more efficient,” he added.
The statistics validate his thoughts. UMaine’s third-down success rate of 30.6% is 110th among 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams, and the Black Bears are 103rd in fourth-down conversions at 39.1%.
The 1-7 Black Bears, losers of seven games in a row, have run 124 third down plays this season. In 66% of those plays, they have found themselves needing 5 or more yards. 
They have needed to pick up at least 10 yards 25% of the time. If you expand that to third-and-9 and third-and-8, that works out to needing 8 or more yards 40.3% of the time. They have had to pick up at least 6 yards 50% of the time.
UMaine has needed 3 yards or less only 22.6% of the time.
The Campbell game epitomized their struggles.
UMaine went 2-for-17 on third down against the Fighting Camels but only four of them required gaining 3 yards or less.
Stevens has always stressed the need to establish a running game in order to open up the passing game. That would make his offense less predictable and more difficult to defend.
But UMaine is averaging only 94.6 rushing yards per game, which is 113th in the country.
And the Black Bears are averaging only 3 yards per rush.
On first down, UMaine has run the ball 129 times and has gained 500 yards. That is a respectable 3.9 yards per carry.
However, 59 of those carries have garnered 2 yards or less. And they have four runs of between 26 and 34 yards.
In other words, UMaine needs to be more creative on first down.
Too often, the first down running plays are designed between the tackles and the offensive line hasn’t been able to create holes or seams for the undersized running backs. Rashawn Marshall and Nick Laughlin are both 5-foot-10 and in the 190-210 pound range.
That is a combination of the offensive line underperforming and opponents loading up the box and forcing one of UMaine’s inexperienced quarterbacks, either Caden Drezek or Eddie Buehler, to throw the ball.
Both have shown encouraging glimpses but they haven’t played with the consistency needed to move the ball down the field on a regular basis.
Having receivers drop balls at an alarming rate has hurt the offense, also.
UMaine is now 121st in the country in points per game (13.4) and 116th in total yards gained per game (281).
UMaine, which is 1-4 in the Coastal Athletic Association, has three games left, beginning with a Saturday game against Rhode Island (4-4, 1-3) at Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, which is serving as a temporary home for the Rams while Meade Stadium is undergoing a $42 million renovation.
The Black Bears will then travel to Albany (5-3, 3-1) before hosting an equally disappointing UNH team that is 2-7 and 1-4.
The battle for the Brice-Cowell Musket will supply either UMaine or UNH with the highlight of their season.

title: Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know
text:
Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know
What can federal agents legally do at polling places? Here’s what voters should know about federal law, election monitors and voter intimidation.
Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know
What can federal agents legally do at polling places? Here’s what voters should know about federal law, election monitors and voter intimidation.
With election day quickly approaching, questions about federal agents at polling places have left some voters wondering what is legally possible.
The Trump administration has said it does not plan to send immigration agents to patrol polling places. But Homeland Security officials have said agents could go to a location for specific reasons, such as serving a warrant or responding to a threat. President Donald Trump has also said he would do “anything necessary” to ensure honest elections, without ruling out deploying the National Guard.
Some civil rights groups have already filed a lawsuit asking a federal judge to block armed agents at polling locations.
What does the law say?
Federal law generally does not allow troops or armed personnel to be stationed at a place where an election is being held. The only exception is if an armed enemy of the U.S. is attacking a polling location and federal force is needed.
Voter intimidation is also illegal. Federal law prohibits threats, intimidation or coercion intended to interfere with someone’s right to vote or to choose how to vote. An agent’s presence alone does not establish intimidation. However, conduct that threatens or pressures voters, or deters them from voting, could raise legal concerns.
What about election monitors?
Election monitors and observers have different roles and rules. They can be congressional staff, Justice Department employees or private volunteers.
The Department of Justice has always sent monitors to polling locations in the past. Staff monitors can observe and report on possible violations of federal voting laws. They do not run elections, and in many states they need permission from state or local officials to enter a polling place. Congressional observers have broader access under federal law, but they cannot handle ballots or equipment, interfere with voters or disrupt election operations. Their presence does not give them authority to interfere with voting.
The Justice Department plans to send 1,000 monitors nationwide for this year's midterms.
What should you do if you feel intimidated?
Do not confront an agent or observer. Tell a poll worker or contact your local election office.
You can also call or text the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683) for help. The hotline provides voting information and assistance from trained volunteers.

title: Officials: Fire at US nuclear site results in no contamination found outside lab
text:
Officials: Fire at US nuclear site triggered emergency response, no contamination found outside lab
A fire at a South Carolina laboratory on a site that produces materials for US nuclear weapons triggered an emergency response, but the fire was extinguished and no contamination was reported outside of the facility, site officials said.
The emergency at the Savannah River National Laboratory near Aiken, located on the US Department of Energy’s Savannah River Site, was declared at 5:39 p.m. Wednesday, prompting a temporary shutdown of traffic at the facility’s entrances, the site’s emergency response organization said.
Related video: DHS grants permission to test heat ray weapon at border
Rail, river and air traffic in the area were also restricted out of precaution, a news release said. As of 9:18 p.m., there were no “operational emergencies or scheduled delays” at the facility and traffic at all entrance barriers resumed, a later update said.
The site emergency was terminated at 9:45 p.m.
All oncoming shift workers were allowed to report to work as usual, the update said.
Facility officials had directed emergency response efforts, as well as notified state and local government agencies, they said.
Earlier Wednesday, officials had advised residents to stay tuned to local news for updates on any actions they may need to take. Employees who were working in the impacted areas of the site had been sheltered “as a precaution” if they were not involved in the emergency response or shutdown operations, officials said.
The Savannah River Site contains both the national laboratory and a defense complex overseen by the semi-autonomous National Nuclear Security Administration. The site is managed by a pair of private contractors: the lab by Battelle Savannah River Alliance, and the defense site by Savannah River Nuclear Solutions, LLC. More than 13,000 contractors and federal employees work there.
The complex was built in the 1950s to produce tritium and plutonium for US nuclear weapons. Today, the site still produces tritium, and it also handles spent nuclear fuel and stores uranium and plutonium. The laboratory area of the site, where the fire occurred, focuses primarily on research, rather than large-scale nuclear material production and storage.
Savannah River Site is also at the heart of the US government’s push to reestablish mass production of US nuclear warheads. NNSA recently gave the site the green light to start full-scale construction on a major facility for producing plutonium pits — the explosive core of modern nuclear weapons — that is expected to cost roughly $23.5 billion, according to trade publication Exchange Monitor.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: 10 things to know about open enrollment for 2027
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Stacker) - This guide is for anyone who doesn’t have access to affordable health coverage through an employer. So, if you’re a 1099 worker (including self-employed or a gig worker) or if you’re between jobs, this guide from Intuit TurboTax is for you.
1. What is Open Enrollment?
The Open Enrollment Period, more commonly known as OEP, is the one time of year that you can buy or change your health insurance unless you experience a qualifying life event.
2. Who does Open Enrollment on marketplaces apply to?
OEP on federal or state-run marketplaces are mainly for people who aren’t covered by Medicaid, Medicare, or a parent’s health plan. You can still enroll if you have access to job-based coverage, but you likely won’t qualify for savings if the plan is considered affordable. So, for most people with a solid employer plan, sticking with that plan is the better deal.
3. When is Open Enrollment?
For the federal marketplace and many state-run marketplaces, OEP starts Nov. 1, 2026 and ends Dec. 15, 2026 for plans that start as early as Jan. 1, 2027, giving you six weeks to choose a health plan and get signed up. For plans with a later coverage start date, OEP does run through Jan. 15, 2027.
4. What can I expect for Open Enrollment 2027?
The original ACA premium tax credits (which help eligible households lower their payments towards premiums) are still in place. Many people still qualify for real savings, especially those without access to employer coverage.
Additionally, plans will continue to cover all the essential health benefits you’d look for in a health plan, such as emergency services, preventative care, prescription drugs, and more.
That said, premiums are higher this year for most marketplace shoppers. And the enhanced premium tax credits (which allowed more households to be eligible for the premium tax credit and provided larger subsidies to eligible households) expired in January 2026.
KFF, an independent source for health policy news, estimates that the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit combined with an increase in premiums charged by insurers means that ACA marketplace enrollees will pay about $780 more than last year (a 58% increase).
5. Where can I buy my health insurance?
You can buy health insurance directly through HealthCare.gov or your state’s own exchange, depending on where you live.
Most states use the federal marketplace at HealthCare.gov, but about 20 states (plus Washington, D.C.) run their own exchange instead. Use the links above to choose your state of residence and find the marketplace in your state.
6. Which states have extended enrollment windows?
Some states have different windows of dates available to buy health insurance. If you live in California, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, or Washington, use this link to take note of the enrollment window.
7. Do I have to sign up for all types of insurance during Open Enrollment?
No. Open Enrollment only applies to health insurance.
However, many people choose to enroll in dental, vision, disability, life, and accident insurance during OEP in order to protect their entire physical and financial wellbeing all at once.
8. How am I going to afford health insurance?
Subsidies (financial assistance) are offered to help people afford health insurance. These come in the form of an advance premium tax credit when you enroll in Marketplace insurance if you are eligible. Eligibility depends on your household income at the time you apply for Marketplace insurance. If your actual income reported on your taxes is higher than when you applied for insurance you may have to pay back some of the advance premium tax credit at tax time. If your income is lower you may be eligible for more premium tax credit at tax time.
Because the enhanced subsidies have lapsed, it’s more important than ever to run your specific numbers rather than assume you’ll qualify for the same discount as in past years. Also, if you have access to affordable employer coverage, you generally won’t qualify for a subsidy at all.
9. What if I already have a plan from last year?
If you purchased health insurance during last year’s OEP, you will be automatically re-enrolled for next year.
You should be aware that insurers often change their plans a bit from year to year. This is especially true in 2027. Several insurers have left the marketplaces, so your old plan may not exist.
If you don’t review your coverage during Open Enrollment, you may see your monthly health payments increase, your doctor may stop accepting your plan, or your prescriptions may no longer be covered. You should also make sure you update your income and household information since that information impacts how much subsidy you could receive.
Make it a habit to review your plan each year to make sure it still meets your needs. Also, check to see whether other plans have been added to your area. You could find an even better deal than your current plan offers, but you won’t know unless you look.
10. Why does Open Enrollment exist?
OEP restricts when you can buy health insurance in order to maintain a needed balance for health insurance companies. By constraining the time period in which you can purchase health insurance, the amount of money going into and coming out of insurance companies’ pockets remains relatively balanced. This allows insurance companies to maintain a balanced pool of sick and healthy people, keeping the marketplaces stable.
The amount individuals pay in premiums works to counteract the money insurance companies are paying out towards claims. If people could sign up for insurance at any point, this balance wouldn’t exist and would cause an unhealthy disruption within the health insurance industry.
This story was produced by Intuit TurboTax and reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump’s pressure
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.
As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.
Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.
Trump’s pressure campaign hasn’t worked
Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT.”
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”
An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year.”
The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump’s pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.
Previous laws have been repealed
In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.
An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year-round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.
“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”

title: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck.
Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing.
The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram.
The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita.
The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck.
The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

title: Indictment: 6 accused of filing 9,000 fraudulent tax returns seeking $177 million in refunds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) — A tax preparation service used a variety of bogus deductions to file thousands of returns seeking $177 million in fraudulent refunds, according to a federal indictment unsealed Wednesday.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Mobile said the investigation is part of an ongoing operation led by the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, the Internal Revenue Service and the FBI.
Defendants named in the indictment
The lead defendant is Jennifer Beverly, 47, who owned JB Accounting Tax Service LLC on Broad Street. She is charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud.
The indictment also names one of her employees, former University of Alabama basketball player Kennedy Lawrence Stovall Winston, 42. Winston, who attended Blount High School, also faces an unrelated federal fraud charge related to stolen Treasury checks.
Four other employees of the tax preparation service face conspiracy and wire fraud charges:
- Jadasha Bowman, 28
- Solida Lucille Green, 36
- Paris Lovett, also known as Paris Johnson, 30
- Shermeka Benjamin, 38
Allegations in the indictment
The indictment alleges that, from about 2021 through 2024, the defendants filed more than 9,000 fraudulent returns.
Of the $177 million in claimed refunds, the IRS issued $81 million, according to the indictment.
The indictment details a variety of tax deductions and credits that prosecutors allege the defendants improperly claimed. Those include COVID-19 credits, fuel tax credits, credit repayments, estimated tax payments and education credits.
Statements from federal agencies
Maisha Horton, acting special agent in charge of the Atlanta Field Office of the IRS Criminal Investigation Division, called the alleged abuse “staggering” in a prepared statement.
“Tax return preparers are entrusted with sensitive financial information and have a responsibility to uphold the integrity of our nation’s tax system, not exploit it for personal financial gain,” she said in the statement. “Those who seek to enrich themselves by manipulating tax credits and defrauding the American taxpayer should understand that IRS Criminal Investigation, along with the FBI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office, is committed to uncovering these schemes, following the money, and holding those responsible accountable.”
Christopher Flowers, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Mobile Field Office, said in a statement that the charges demonstrated a strong partnership among federal law enforcement agencies.
“These allegations involve a serious breach of trust, and our agencies worked closely to identify the extent of the fraudulent activity and ensure accountability,” he said in the statement. “Rebuilding public trust is one of the FBI’s core priorities, and we will continue to pursue anyone who exploits our financial and tax systems for personal gain.”
Court information
A court date has not been set for the defendants. If convicted, each faces a maximum of 20 years in prison.

title: Baby dies after 15-year-old girl gives birth at elementary school, reports say
text:
CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday.
Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene.
WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School.
The teen girl was reportedly in good condition when taken to an area hospital for treatment.
Officials from the elementary school did not immediately comment on the situation, WGN reported.

title: 11 Central In Bangor Is Looking For A New Owner: Turnkey Restaurant Includes Recipes, Bar Setup, And Established Clientele
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Longtime Bangor Entrepreneurs Look To Sell Popular Downtown Restaurant
Since opening its doors in 2012, the downtown Bangor restaurant 11 Central has become a popular spot for folks to meet up, grab a bite or a drink, and celebrate important milestones in the Queen City.
Read More: New Burger Restaurant Coming to Downtown Bangor This November
While the business has changed hands before, most recently in 2020 when local Bangor business owners Mike and Melissa Towle took the helm, its reputation for being a downtown destination has remained the same.
The Towles, who have connections with other businesses throughout Bangor in the past, including the Penobscot Pour House and Happy Endings. They cite their growing kids as the inspiration behind their desire to downsize their portfolio so they have more time to spend with family. They recently put the restaurant on the market.
They listed it as a turnkey business, according to a post by Caldwell Banker.
"The thoughtfully designed restaurant offers approximately 49 seats throughout the dining and lounge areas, plus an additional 12 seats at the bar. The space is well suited for dinner service, cocktails, private gatherings, and special events, with an established identity and customer base already in place. This is a complete business sale-not simply a restaurant space or equipment package. The 11 Central name and brand, recipes, website and social media presence, business phone numbers, owned POS system, furniture, fixtures, restaurant and bar equipment, food and liquor inventory, and other operating assets are included in the sale. The goal is a seamless transition, giving a new owner the opportunity to step into an established restaurant operation without building one from the ground up. "
It should be noted that the business is what's for sale, not the building, as the space is leased and the building is owned by someone else.

Mike Towle said in a post online this week that the decision was a bittersweet one, but that it was time for the couple to slow down a bit.
The 11 Central Facebook page said the establishment was closed Wednesday due to an "unforeseen mechanical issue" but that it would reopen Thursday the 29th, at 4 pm.

title: Republican Maine sheriff posts attack site against his own party’s nominee to replace him
text:
The bitter race for Hancock County sheriff came to a head this week, when outgoing Sheriff Scott Kane, a Republican, shared a website under his own byline accusing his party’s nominee to replace him, Corey Bagley, of steering a county contract to his father.
The site, entitled “Good Old Boys Exposed,” which Kane posted to Facebook on Monday, also takes aim at County Commissioner William Clark, the county’s longest-serving sheriff before his 2014 retirement and one of Bagley’s most prominent backers. Voters will choose between Bagley and Kane’s pick, Democratic sheriff’s Lt. Dakota Dupuis, in Tuesday’s election.
The candidates and their allies have been slinging misconduct allegations for weeks in one of the region’s most bitter contests in decades, and one that has scrambled the usual partisan lines. Kane, a staunch Dupuis ally who has featured in multiple controversies himself over 11 years as sheriff, has publicly battled Clark since Bagley’s 2023 departure as chief deputy.
“I think people can see through what this really is: a smear job from people who are desperate,” Bagley said. “Things aren’t going their way and they need to do what they can to try to make me look bad.”
The website shows images of Bagley and Clark smiling beside a banner reading: “Same people. Same circle. Same pattern?” Its central allegation dates to Bagley’s six-year assignment at the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency, where he supervised the Downeast Drug Task Force.
In 2014, Clark’s final year as sheriff, the county awarded a four-year drug seizure storage contract to Bagley’s father, Rudy Bagley. The seized assets, including a side-by-side, were moved from Ellsworth to Rudy Bagley’s Hancock property and stayed there until 2018.
The county paid Rudy Bagley $9,750 during that time, between $250 and $300 a month, according to invoices Kane published online and provided to the Bangor Daily News. Kane said neither he nor the drug agency authorized the arrangement.
“I believe it was a direct conflict of interest,” Kane said. “Bagley made the arrangement, his father benefited financially, and I was left not knowing about the arrangement until MDEA command staff alerted me to it.”
Bagley said Clark, while sheriff, made the arrangements with his father, and that Kane cherry-picked documents to imply misconduct. The property was moved because the Ellsworth location was compromised and cost $500 per month, which county officials discussed at a March 2014 public commissioners meeting, he said.
Drug agency officials wouldn’t comment on contract specifics, directing the BDN to the sheriff’s office because the county paid it.
Bagley was promoted twice after the alleged conflict of interest came to light, first to lieutenant and then to chief deputy. Kane, who picked Bagley as his chief deputy in 2022, said he had no hand in either promotion because they were contractually stipulated.
Whether Bagley made the storage arrangement for his family’s financial gain or didn’t recognize the conflict of interest, the deal is “significantly troubling,” Kane said.
The website’s other allegations revolve around Clark, who is accused of using inmate labor for landscaping at Woodbine Cemetery in violation of department protocols. Kane and the county’s jail administrator reported the arrangement to the Maine attorney general’s office in 2015, requesting a criminal investigation.
Because Clark had already left office, no probe was launched, according to Kane and documents uploaded to the site. Clark declined to comment on the accusations, saying they would likely be addressed in court.
A lawyer has reviewed the website, Clark said Tuesday, and sees a “strong likelihood that he [Kane] has not only committed a criminal violation of improper dissemination of that information, but he’s also put the county and himself at a personal civil liability.”
The bad blood between the current and former sheriffs runs deep. When Bagley left in 2023, Clark accused Kane of forcing him out to rehire his brother, Patrick Kane, as chief deputy. Kane said Bagley retired voluntarily.
The two have since clashed at commission meetings and on Facebook, including a 2025 spat over the sheriff’s police dog budget. Kane endorsed Dupuis over his fellow Republican and did not seek a fourth term himself. Clark endorsed Bagley.
Adding to the animosity, four Democratic state legislators made the extraordinary decision to cross party lines and back the Republican. Among them is Rep. Nina Milliken, D-Blue Hill, who has filed notice of a civil rights claim against Kane over a 2025 electioneering charge that his office pursued and a prosecutor later dismissed.
Sheriff’s office employees have also involved themselves in the acrimonious race. Lt. Brian K. Archer II posted an AI-generated meme of Clark with an elongated, Pinocchio-style nose, which he has since deleted and described as “political satire.”
Dupuis, 31, who registered as a Democrat in 2024, has tried to distance himself from Kane. He said Bagley’s supporters have repeatedly shared “inaccurate or misleading” claims about him. Once the election is over, he said, the department needs to look past politics.
“It’s unfortunate how divisive this race has become,” Dupuis said Wednesday.

title: Maine’s forest economy needs a friend in D.C.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mary Ignatiadis of Berwick has worked across Maine as a forest economist for the past eight years. After working for both large timberland managers and smallholder forest carbon projects in Maine, she now consults on forestry issues globally.
For 20 of the 24 years that Susan Collins has been Maine’s senator, some of our biggest mills have stood empty — Great Northern in Millinocket, Lincoln Paper and Tissue in Lincoln and many others. That’s not a coincidence.
Maine has lost many opportunities over the years to put these towns back to work with new forest product manufacturers, companies that would have refined our pulpwood into advanced fuels and turned our sawlogs into mass timber. A big part of the reason that we lost those opportunities was unfriendly and inconsistent federal policy from Collins and her colleagues.
Now, finally, there are new companies moving into these mills. The question is whether Maine will have a senator who will fight to keep those companies, and the thousands of jobs they could create here.
It’s true that Collins has brought a lot of grant money to Maine’s struggling forest economy — about $100 million since 2008. The first problem is that $100 million over 18 years is nothing compared to the $1.3 billion that Maine loses every single year from those closed mills.
The other problem is that Mainers don’t want government handouts. We want real economic growth for our heritage industries. And Collins has repeatedly voted against creating real demand and real advantages for Maine’s forest sector.
For example:
2002, 2005: Voted against the Renewable Electricity Standard, which would have given
biomass energy some of the same tax advantages as fossil fuel energy (Energy Policy
Acts of 2002 and 2005).
2008: Voted for long-term fossil fuel production tax credits, but not for long-term
biomass production tax credits (Emergency Economic Stabilization Act & Renewable
Tax Extensions).
2009: Voted against a national carbon market that would have promoted the use of
mass timber and other wood-based construction products (American Clean Energy and
Security Act).
2015: Voted against New England’s transition to cheap renewables, keeping Maine
manufacturers locked into the most expensive electric grid in the country (Clean Power
Plan).
2017: Voted to subsidize fossil-fuel-based resins and composites, using taxpayers’ own
money to destroy demand for Maine-made, wood-based resins and composites (Tax
Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017).
2021: Voted against federal procurement standards prioritizing US-grown mass timber
and other wood products over foreign steel and concrete (Build Back Better).
Another pain point for our industry is diesel prices. How much lower would diesel prices be if we had someone fighting for more cheap renewable energy, leaving a strategic diesel reserve for the heritage industries that really need it? There may have been a time when what was good for the fossil fuel industry was also good for the forest products sector, but that time passed decades ago.
Collins doesn’t seem to care that voting on behalf of her fossil fuel donors means taking opportunities away from Maine. Seeing our senator throw our future away in return for cash is, to say the least, frustrating.
I’m voting for Troy Jackson because I believe in the future of Maine’s forest industry. I believe that Maine’s mills should be producing world-leading forest technologies instead of sitting empty. I believe that Maine should be celebrated not just as “Vacationland,” but as a place where our heritage industries can thrive.

title: High school student accused of trying to make bombs for ISIS, deputies say
text:
GAINESVILLE, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) - A Florida high school student was arrested after an investigation into his contact with a terrorist organization revealed he was attempting to make bombs, authorities said.
Alachua County sheriff’s deputies said the 15-year-old is a student at Buchholz High School.
The sheriff’s office and FBI conducted a joint investigation on Friday at the teen’s home after investigators learned he was having online conversations with members and supporters of the Islamic State group, also known as ISIS.
Investigators say the teen asked for help to build drones and explosives to attack people at an unknown location.
Authorities spoke with the 15-year-old’s parents, who allowed them to search the boy’s phone. They reportedly found files containing instructions for making explosive devices and chemical compounds, as well as ISIS propaganda.
On Monday, investigators searched the teen’s home with his parents’ consent after they revealed the information found on the phone.
Inside, they found two jars in his bedroom. The 15-year-old reportedly told investigators the jars contained chemicals used to make “TATP,” or triacetone triperoxide, a dangerous explosive.
The Alachua County Bomb Squad unit responded to the home and secured the materials. Detectives then searched the home.
The 15-year-old was charged with making or attempting to make a destructive device. Additional charges could be added as the investigation continues.
Family members said off camera that they still had many questions about the investigation and declined to comment further.

title: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation.
“You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said.
Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis.
“And that was all while I was active,” he said.
Service dog provides daily support
Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline.
“You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said.
The dog helped Poggi regain his independence by taking care of tasks many people take for granted.
“His favorite thing is to retrieve, to help me carry things,” he said. “If I drop my keys or anything like that, I’ll pick them up for me. He can retrieve my cell phone for me and things like that.”
Poggi said Teddy brought back something harder to replace: joy.
“I love my children very, very much, but it is right up there with another child,” he said.
There’s growing evidence that service dogs can alleviate some symptoms. A 2024 study found the canines are associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression in veterans with PTSD.
Training prepares dogs for real-world scenarios
Poggi took Teddy to Dog Training Elite St. Louis, where they train dogs for everything from basic obedience to advanced therapy, protection and service work.
“The way DTE trains, it looks like a facility, but they turn this thing into like a real-world scenario,” Poggi said. “They prepare you and your service animal for real world experiences that you just you’re not going to get out of that book.”
Matt Willis, owner of Dog Training Elite St. Louis, said service dogs can be important for veterans, helping with both physical limitations and PTSD.
“Dogs just-they change your feeling, the chemical changes in your body with that interaction. And that’s exactly the uplift that these guys and ladies need,” Willis said.
Willis said veterans have been through traumatic things, both physically, emotionally and mentally.
“While you know our government and the system tries to do what they can, there’s obviously some gaps in that care for our veterans,” he said.
Grant to help veterans get service dogs
A private donor grant will help cover part of the cost for service dog training for 10 veterans or active military members in need.
“They wanted it to go towards veterans and military personnel for service dog training. So what we’ve done is divide that money up to where we are able to help 10 veterans in need. Can be active military or veterans. And so it basically pays 30% of their training costs for those 10 veterans,” Willis said.
“And that’s the kind of people that are out there that see the benefit of what these dogs can do,” he said.
Teddy will return to work with Poggi, resuming his job as a school crossing guard in Mascoutah.
“Next school year, I’ll be back full-time out on the corner every day, rain or shine. He’s out there with me. He’s got the got a little crossing guard hut and everything,” Poggi said.
A 2024 survey of about 600 veterans revealed about four in 10 never had a PTSD service dog but would like one.
It’s important to note the VA doesn’t provide service dogs for mental health conditions, including PTSD and is still studying the potential benefits of such interventions.

title: Device as small as 'grain of rice' offers hope for rare eye disease
text:
Device as small as 'grain of rice' offers new hope for rare eye disease
A tiny implant provides a groundbreaking treatment for macular telangiectasia
Device as small as 'grain of rice' offers new hope for rare eye disease
A tiny implant provides a groundbreaking treatment for macular telangiectasia
A new surgical implant tested in Boston is giving hope to patients with macular telangiectasia, or MacTel, a rare eye disease that impairs central vision and makes it difficult to see details.
Heather Harris-Keddy, a patient living with MacTel, said the disease has affected her vision dramatically over time.
"If I close this eye, all I'm seeing is your hair and the walls around you," said Harris-Keddy, a patient living with the disease for more than 20 years. "I can't see your face."
She said she noticed changes in her right eye first, then later in her left.
"And I was always doing this — like, can I see today?" Harris-Keddy said, holding her hand over one eye.
MacTel affects the macula, which is a round area at the back of the eyeball, in the center of the retina.
"The macula is what's responsible for fine, detailed vision — watching television, looking at faces, and especially reading," said Dr. Dean Elliott, director emeritus for the retina service at Mass Eye and Ear.
He has treated several cases of MacTel, despite its rarity.
Video below: 2027 Health Insurance: Check Before You Renew
"It starts out by causing some blurry vision, a few little small blind spots right around the center of vision," Elliott said.
Until recently, there was no treatment for the disease.
"People who had it were severely debilitated," Elliott said. "I mean, they had significant problems with their central vision, and most progressed to a point where they couldn't read. They had extreme difficulty watching television and seeing faces."
Harris-Keddy adapted to the changes as best she could.
"I have magnifying glasses around the house to make sure that I can read directions on boxes and stuff like that," she said.
But Harris-Keddy worried about the day her central vision would be gone for good.
"And you know, I won't be able to see again or drive again," she said. "My whole life will change. My husband's life will change because I will be more of a burden."
Her hope came in the form of a tiny implant called ENCELTO, which is the size of a single grain of rice.
Inserted into the eye, the implant generates and delivers proteins that the macula needs to function properly.
"The implant is like science fiction," Elliott said. "It is actually really hard to believe that this was developed."
Elliott participated in the clinical trials, which showed that while the implant cannot restore lost vision, it can significantly slow or even stop the gradual loss of central vision.
Last year, the Food and Drug Administration approved the device for patients like Harris-Keddy, who became the first person to receive it at Mass Eye and Ear.
"It's a very expensive device," Elliott said. "It's about $250,000, but it protects someone's eyesight for life."
Harris-Keddy said she is grateful — and relieved — to have it now while she still has some vision.
"At least we were able to stop it," she said.

title: Trump calls for prosecution of Democratic Alaska Senate candidate over spoiler candidate controversy
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — President Donald Trump called for the criminal prosecution of the Democratic candidate running for Senate in Alaska on Wednesday after revelations that her campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
“I think they should be prosecuted,” the Republican president said about Peltola and the other Sullivan, responding to questions about a report in The New York Times. He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”
Sen. Sullivan, appearing Wednesday night on Fox News, pressed Peltola to “come clean.”
He said he would tell Alaskans to “look Mary Peltola in the eye and ask her, ‘Did you cheat?’ She won’t even answer that question.”
The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Peltola’s campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. Sullivan. He made it through the state’s August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday’s general election.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
He did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.
Peltola calls report a ‘distraction’
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement, said: “Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.”
During a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction, it’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”
The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run.
Murkowski says Alaskans ‘deserve the honest truth’
Alaska Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has endorsed Sullivan and is a longtime friend of Peltola, said in a statement that Alaskans “deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials.”
Peltola’s campaign, in a statement, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan’s candidacy.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.
“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.
Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. Department of Justice. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s a good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”
Candidates in Alaska have raised questions, challenges before
It’s not the first time a candidate’s appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.
The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.
Through Tuesday, more than 61,000 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sen. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver.

title: 2 injured in Harpswell fire
text:
Two people were injured in an early morning fire at a home in Harpswell, according to officials.
Several local fire departments responded to the structure fire on Smokehouse Road around 4:30 a.m. Thursday, said David Mercier, Harpswell Neck Fire and Rescue chief.
The home was fully engulfed by the time first responders arrived, Mercier said.
Two occupants were injured while trying to escape the home, Maine State Police said in an update Thursday afternoon. They were taken to the hospital and their injuries were non-life threatening.
Two other occupants and their two dogs were unharmed in the fire, Mercier said.
The fire took a few hours to extinguish and the home was a total loss, he said.
Mercier added that, while responding, a fire hydrant ran dry due to drought conditions and crews had to connect to another.
Investigators from the state Fire Marshals Office also responded to the scene and are investigating the cause of the fire.

title: Janet Mills says she voted for Troy Jackson for US Senate
text:
Gov. Janet Mills said Thursday that she voted for Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
But Mills did not offer a direct endorsement for the 58-year-old former state Senate president, who is locked in a tight race against five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
“I encourage Maine people to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot who will stand up for our values and stand up to Trump,” Mills said in a social media post.
Mills’ announcement answered lingering questions about whether she would publicly endorse Jackson, who had used Mills as a foil during his unsuccessful bid for governor, saying she had vetoed many of his bills.
Mills had run unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, losing to political upstart Graham Platner in the June primary. The oyster farmer and military veteran from Sullivan had campaigned with Jackson before dropping out of the Senate race amid a sexual assault allegation that he denied.
Jackson was selected to replace Platner in July.
For months, Mills had said she would be open to talking with Jackson about a possible endorsement. But there had been little progress, at least publicly. And some political observers wondered whether an endorsement would benefit Jackson.
During a press event Thursday morning, Jackson was asked if he wanted Mills’ endorsement. He told reporters that he left the governor a message “about two or three weeks ago,” but that the two never spoke.
Jackson reached out to the governor after his fourth and final debate, according to a person close to the governor who asked not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak.
“I’ve got Republicans for me. I’ve got Democrats and independents. I don’t need high-ranking officials to support me,” Jackson said Thursday. “If they want, that’s great. In the end, it’s about the people on the ground that I care about.”
Jackson’s staff interrupted the candidate as he began responding to follow-up questions. And his campaign did not respond to follow-up questions.
During that debate, Jackson told Collins to “shut up” after she suggested a protester who interrupted the televised event was one of Jackson’s supporters.
The comment was quickly repurposed into an attack ad by Collins and her allies, who accused Jackson of being ill-tempered, especially with women.
Mills was away in Ireland when Jackson called, the person close to her said, but staff tried to arrange a meeting so they could talk when the governor returned. But the two never met.
Mills made her post on the last day of in-person, early voting.

title: Washington County residents raise nearly $34,000 in 22nd Annual Turkey-A-Thon to support local food pantries

text:
Thanks to the generosity of community members across Washington County, this year’s Annual Turkey-A-Thon raised $33,884.78 with donations still coming in. While the total fell short of the $40,000 goal, the results are especially meaningful amid today’s economic challenges. The strong response reflects the enduring spirit of neighbors helping neighbors and the community’s commitment to ensuring Washington County families have access to food this holiday season.
On Oct. 9, teams of enthusiastic volunteers from local schools, businesses, organizations and the community at large, together with employees from Classic Hits 92.7/95.3 FM Radio, Dunkin’ in Calais and Machias, V.L. Tammaro in Calais and Baileyville and Healthy Acadia, were stationed at seven sites across Washington County to collect donations for local food pantries. All funds from this annual event are distributed to community food security organizations.
Classic Hits 92.7/95.3 FM Radio, broadcasting live from the Dunkin’ studio at V.L Tammaro in Calais, kept the momentum throughout the day, encouraging a little friendly competition as collection sites reported their tallies hourly via phone.
Every dollar raised through the Turkey-A-Thon will be used to purchase gift certificates from local grocery stores to be distributed among the ten Washington County food pantries, emergency school backpack programs and other food cupboards. The gift certificates will help ensure that local families in need enjoy a healthy holiday meal. Community members can support their local food pantry by donating directly any time of the year.
Classic Hits 92.7/95.3, Dunkin’ in Calais and Machias, VL Tammaro in Woodland and in Calais and Healthy Acadia would like to thank all those who generously donated and/or volunteered their time during the event.

title: Two people injured after fire in Harpswell; home destroyed
text:
HARPSWELL, Maine (WMTW) - Two people were sent to the hospital with burn injuries after a fire at a home in Harpswell Thursday morning.
Several town fire departments, including Harpswell, Brunswick and West Bath responded to the fire on 22 Smokehouse Road. Officials say the call came in around 4:00 a.m.
According to responding fire crews, 4 people were at the home and 2 were taken to the hospital to be treated for burn injuries. One of the occupants had to jump out of a second-story window to escape the flames.
The fire destroyed the single-family home and also spread to the nearby woods. Crews were able to get the flames under control by around 6:30 a.m. but were still working to put out hot spots.
The State Fire Marshall’s office is now heading to the scene to investigate. Officials say it’s too early to determine a cause; the homeowner believes the fire started in a stairwell.

title: Ghost hunters certify paranormal presence in historic Freeport building
text:
When Kathy and Jim Welle opened their candy store What the Actual Fudge in the historic E.B. Mallett building at 7 Mill St. in Freeport, almost immediately they experienced strange occurrences they could not explain.
They would hear shuffling noises and footsteps coming from the third-story attic space.
They would hear the sound of a door opening and closing in areas where there was not one.
On two different occasions, pieces of parchment paper in a stack on the counter started flying around, one at a time, as if being flicked by a finger.
One entry door would be unlocked in the morning, even though everyone in the building the night before swore it was locked when they left.
And there were occasional voices that belonged to no one, including what sounded like a child sobbing.
So they made a call. No, not to the “Ghost Busters,” but to a Maine team of ghost hunters led by paranormal enthusiast Mike Greenleaf, of Litchfield.
Greenleaf founded G.H.O.S.T. (an acronym for Ghost Hunting & Occult Study Team) about a year ago. He said his team never charges for their time, but he does have a set of parameters they go by before agreeing to investigate a site.
“We are different from other ghost hunters,” he explained during an interview Oct. 19, a few hours before presenting the Welles with G.H.O.S.T.’s investigation results. “Some teams will go and try to prove that there is a paranormal presence.
“But we try to disprove it first,” Greenleaf said. “Are lights flickering? We look for wiring issues. Odd voices? Maybe there are people outside the building. We start by trying to debunk. When we can’t, that’s when we start reaching out to confirm the spirit.”
G.H.O.S.T. conducted its investigation of the Mallett building Sept. 18 from 6:30 p.m. until 5:30 a.m. the following morning. The equipment and investigators were staged on all three floors of the building.
It was not just spirits responding to the team. A Freeport police officer engaged with Greenleaf while patrolling around the building and after being invited inside see the work summoned officers to witness late-night ghost hunting.
Afterward, the investigators agreed they sensed odd sensations throughout the night. One example: while three people were in the attic they felt a physically close presence, or pressure, from one side of the room.
Throughout the night the team utilized their equipment to attempt communication with the presence.
Greenleaf presented video and audio clips to the Welles on Oct. 19. A few, he explained, contained flashes or glows that could not otherwise be explained by reflections coming through windows or lights in the building.
“They’re not, they’re not spectacular,” he said. “You’re not about to see it (a ghost). But they are things that we can’t explain. There was an orb-like light that moved around the bottom of a space and then across, which the team distinguished from dust because it did not move in a straight line.”
Listening with headphones, some recordings picked up sounds. Jim Welle heard what he said was a regular heartbeat in one segment, which Kathy and store employee Trinity Kangas concurred.
One voice captured was male, emphatically stating, “get out!” Another was childlike sobbing.
Investigator Tasha Michaud, G.H.O.S.T.’s lead interviewer, discerned from a piece of equipment called a cat ball that the spirit seemed to refer to a fire. “It’s possible that (E.B. Mallett’s) office may have served as a refuge during a fire,” she told the Welles.
There have been at least two notable fires in the past in Freeport, both at the same location a few blocks from Mill Street. In 1946, Clark’s Hotel at the corner of Main and Bow streets burned. The building was severely damaged in a fire four decades later that displaced a dozen people residing in second floor apartments.
In 1914, the Casco Castle hotel, a trolley car ride away in South Freeport, was destroyed in a massive blaze, although it was not open for business at the time.
With Mallett’s office the hub of Freeport manufacturing and mill trades, it would not be out of the question for an employee or neighbor to be taken to the building in the event of an accident.
Through the cat ball, a different presence spoke about being in prison and possibly being abused by officers or other authorities.
G.H.O.S.T.’s conclusion of the evidence was that a paranormal presence in the building is likely. Greenleaf characterized it as nonthreatening, though one entity in the attic appeared to just want to be left alone.
The Welles and Kangas confirmed that they had also felt the same sensation of a physical presence at their side while in the attic.
Greenleaf said the team was in agreement that it would certify the Mallett building as having paranormal activity.
From home Sept. 18, Kathy Welle had followed G.H.O.S.T.’s investigation using her webcam, picking up at least one image the same as the team’s video, and a couple other instances Greenleaf said they were able to debunk. She also saw the police officers trekking about with the team.
Even before the investigation she had placed security cameras inside the building, especially focused on the entry door that would unlock.
“Every time I wanted to go back to look for an oddity, I would get an error message that the SD card had to be reformatted,” she said. “It happened with two different cameras, and with brand new cards. I finally gave up and bought a service for 24-hour recording.”
She also said the unlocked door issue seemed to resolve itself, but only after she added another lock with a deadbolt and the owner of the first-floor business had a security gate installed so even if the door was opened from the outside no human would be able to enter.
Did the investigation make her a believer?
“I believe there are spirits, but I don’t know that they really talk,” she said.
What about the recorded man’s voice saying to get out?
“Are they trying to get us to leave? No, I don’t believe that.”
The evidence made her husband a believer.
Kangas believed there to be spirits from the start — it was she who made the call to G.H.O.S.T. to come investigate the Mallett building.
“People say there are several haunted buildings around town,” Kathy said. “I am having a good time with it. It’s been a fun experience.”
THE TEAM
Founder Mike Greenleaf, of Litchfield, is one of two lead investigators, along with Jason Coombs, a paranormal believer who grew up in nearby Brunswick and lives in Augusta.
Others on the team are craft specialists. Tasha Michaud, of Gardiner, interviews property owners, residents and staff of investigation sites.
Biddeford resident Shaun Miller is in charge of audio/visual equipment and operations. He has sensed otherworldly happenings since he was little.
Renee Clairmont, of Sabattus, is the team’s occult specialist focused on the metaphysical aspects of paranormal investigations. She counts herself as a believer in the supernatural, but also in the need to balance belief with evidence.
Claudette Tardif, who is from Auburn, assists with investigations, operates equipment and mentors new team members. She became a believer as a child experiencing the unexplainable and has sought answers ever since.
South Paris resident Curt Manchester is G.H.O.S.T.’s historical researcher, digging into relevant community information for each hunt, the focus property, and its previous inhabitants.

title: Collins highlights federal funding in closing pitch to voters
text:
As a bitter campaign nears its end, Sen. Susan Collins is making her role in Washington, D.C., central to her closing message.
Collins visited the Winthrop Police Department on Thursday afternoon to highlight new communications equipment — namely a massive radio tower — funded in large part with $1.1 million she secured through her role as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
At a news conference outside the police station, Collins reiterated what has been a core argument for her campaign: Her seniority in Congress gives her the ability to bring gobs of federal money to Maine.
“I’m the first Maine senator in nearly a century to chair the Appropriations Committee, and I’ve been able to bring $1.5 billion to Maine to support projects just like this one,” Collins told reporters.
Maine’s senior senator has touted several similar projects in the closing weeks of her campaign. On Monday, she made a trip to a mobile home park in Camden that received a $1.3 million federal earmark and on Wednesday, she traveled to Bath Iron Works, where she discussed the Pentagon’s support for the construction of a new destroyer.
Asked whether her seniority would matter if Democrats regain the Senate, Collins noted she would likely remain the committee’s vice chair. Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, would be hard-pressed for such a committee assignment if he is to win on Tuesday, she has said.
“I’m going to be the fifth-highest ranking senator if I’m elected. Troy would be number 100, or if he’s lucky, 99,” Collins said on WVOM Wednesday. “The difference that you can make for the people of Maine, because of your seniority, is enormous.”
The race between Collins and Jackson has in recent weeks devolved into attack ads and personal insults, fueled in large part by outside groups backing Collins.
But as Election Day nears and last-minute polling shows a tight race within the margins of error, each candidate has sought to put a more positive spin on their campaigns. While Collins has highlighted her seniority and local issues, Jackson has emphasized the importance of Maine’s election in determining the direction of the entire country.
On Thursday, Jackson campaigned in Westbrook with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree and the American Federation of Teachers, a national union that stopped in Maine as part of its get-out-the-vote tour.
Outside of the event at American Roots, union representatives held Troy Jackson signs while standing next to an inflatable fat cat with a diamond pinky ring in a suit and tie that was squeezing a worker in a hard hat.
“End the Republican squeeze on the American people,” a nearby sign read.
During a news conference, Jackson downplayed Collins’ leadership of the Appropriations Committee, saying that Alaska receives more federal earmarks (per capita) than Maine. Collins, at her news conference the same day, noted that Maine ranks No. 2 in terms of per capita earmarks.
Jackson also said Collins’ role will be diminished if the Democrats regain control of the Senate.
“Any amount of money that Sen. Collins brings to the state of Maine is a pittance compared to what we’re losing,” he said. “But in the end, she’s gonna be in the minority. Democrats are going to take this back over with or without me.”
When asked what he would do for the nation’s schools if elected, Jackson appeared to confuse the leadership of the U.S. Department of Education.
“Well, we’re not going to let DeVos get rid of the Department of Education,” Jackson said. “We’re gonna put money into education so that teachers can be paid more.”
The DOE is led by Secretary Linda McMahon, but Jackson was referring to Betsy Devos, who led the department during President Donald Trump’s first term from 2017-21.
His campaign said Jackson misspoke and that “he is fully aware that the current secretary of education is wrestling executive Linda McMahon, who wants to destroy the Department of Education.”

title: Smokers unite against Taxin’ Jaxin
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Taxin’ Jaxin is a perfect name for Troy Jackson. He loved to tax Mainers right out of their homes. He seemed to take pride in raising taxes.
One tax he raised that doesn’t garner much attention was the cigarette tax. There was a budget shortfall, so the Budget Committee asked Troy for a 50-cent increase on a pack of cigarettes. “Sure,” Jackson said, “here’s $ 1.50.” That was three times what they wanted.
History shows these “sin taxes” don’t work. People quit smoking, cut down or switch to other delivery methods — hence not as much money as projected. Therefore another shortfall in revenue.
Smokers unite, and get rid of this joker for good!
Kevin Noel
Portland

title: Patrick Stewart, of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dead at 86
text:
Patrick Stewart, of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dead at 86
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed English actor known for his roles in "Star Trek" and "X-Men," has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home following a brief battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, a statement on the actor's Instagram page reads.
“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," the post says.
Stewart's career spanned more than six decades in theater, television and film.
Stewart spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he became known for his performances in classical roles including Shakespeare’s “Coriolanus,” “Julius Caesar” and “Antony and Cleopatra.”
He won three Olivier Awards, Britain’s leading theater prize, and later returned to the stage in acclaimed productions including “Waiting for Godot” on Broadway.
He became internationally known as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” which aired from 1987 to 1994 and helped establish the series as one of television’s most enduring science-fiction dramas. He reprised Picard in four “Star Trek” films and the later series “Star Trek: Picard.”
Stewart also played Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, first appearing in the 2000 film “X-Men,” followed by “X2,” “X-Men: The Last Stand,” “X-Men: Days of Future Past” and “Logan.”
He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane’s Starz show “Blunt Talk” for two series and voiced Poop in “The Emoji Movie.” He made appearances on “Robot Chicken,” “Futurama” and “The Simpsons.”
His honors include a Grammy Award and nominations for Emmy and Tony Awards.
Stewart was also known for his philanthropy work. “His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties. He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life," a statement from spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said.
He is survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.

title: Milford father arrested in 1-year-old daughter’s death
text:
A Milford man has been arrested after a monthslong investigation into his 1-year-old daughter’s death.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, is accused of manslaughter in the death of Eleanora Ray McLaughlin, who was found dead in December 2025. State officials determined in April that the 13-month-old died of hypothermia.
Maine State Police arrested McLaughlin on Wednesday, according to a news release from the agency. A Penobscot County grand jury indicted him on charges of Class A manslaughter and three counts of endangering the welfare of a child.
McLaughlin is being held at the Penobscot County Jail on $250,000 bail, according to jail staff.
After Eleanora’s death, state lawmakers pressed the Maine Department of Health and Human Services for more information about recent child deaths.
Sen. Jeff Timberlake, R-Turner, wrote in a letter to the department that the toddler was found dead “while living in a home alongside her siblings with no heat and no running water in the middle of a Maine winter.”
The indictment, provided by the Office of the Maine Attorney General, says the Class D child endangerment charges stem from the day of Eleanora’s death. McLaughlin is accused of recklessly endangering the toddler, as well as two other unnamed children, “by violating a duty of care or protection,” according to the indictment.
McLaughlin is scheduled to attend his first court appearance via Zoom on Friday afternoon, according to a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office.
Months after the infant’s death, police arrested a Bangor woman who WMTW identified as Eleanora’s grandmother. Police said at the time the woman was taken into custody after responding to a custodial dispute. Penobscot County District Attorney Christopher Almy said Thursday that the woman’s case was declined.
State police ask anyone with information about the case to call Detective Jennifer Fiske at 207-973-3700, ext. 9, or submit tips online to the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit North.
