title: Maine Republicans call on state Auditor Matt Dunlap to release work hour records
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -Maine Republicans are calling on state Auditor Matt Dunlap to release records detailing his work hours.
Dunlap is running for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
About the position
The auditor is a salaried statutory officer elected by the Legislature. The auditor does not clock in for hourly shifts.
State law prohibits using public resources for political campaigns.
Republican leaders’ request
Republican leaders said Dunlap’s office is open 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday. They question whether he campaigned during work hours.
“Show Maine taxpayers that the job they’re paying you to do is truly getting done. Because at the end of the day, you work for us. We don’t work for you,” Scott King, Palmyra Selectman and State Committee Member of the Maine GOP said.
Dunlap’s office responds
Dunlap’s office responded with a statement.
“As state auditor, Matt Dunlap works long hours and is readily available during, before, and after the office’s stated business hours. The proof is in the pudding: this year, his work led directly to the arrest and conviction of the largest state employee fraud case in Maine history. He is regularly praised for his work as Auditor, including by current and former Republican legislators,” the statement said.

title: Man accused in Cornell rape lawsuit wants Letitia James removed from investigation over her posts
text:
Man accused in Cornell rape lawsuit wants Letitia James removed from investigation over her posts
Should social media posts disqualify New York’s attorney general from leading a criminal investigation into gang rape allegations at Cornell University?
That's the question before a state judge on Thursday as one of the accused men seeks to remove Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor overseeing the renewed criminal probe.
One of at least two cases against James contends she is biased because she posted messages expressing support for the accuser just days before she was appointed to the case.
The former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024. The former student said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent.
“What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James posted to X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order taking the case away from the local prosecutor, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024, and naming James as special prosecutor.
Within days, lawyers for two of the men named as defendants in Jane Doe's lawsuit filed challenges to James' appointment — one that Judge James R. Farrell is hearing on Thursday, and the other in Tompkins County, where Cornell is located.
James, a Democrat, is not expected to attend the hearing in Monticello, about 72 miles northwest of Manhattan.
A lawyer for the man whose case is being heard Thursday wrote that James' social media post “has unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants” named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit.
The lawyer, Andrew Miltenberg, asked that Farrell order Hochul to appoint a special prosecutor “who is free from actual or perceived conflicts of interest or bias.”
James' office argued in a court filing that the challenge is “procedurally defective and substantively meritless,” noting that courts have previously ruled that the governor is free to exercise her executive power as she chooses, such as in appointing a special prosecutor.
“While Petitioner relies on the AG’s remarks in a single social media post as proof that the various ills he fears will come to pass, such speculative and conclusory claims of harm — premised entirely on his own mischaracterization of the AG’s statements — are insufficient for hardship,” Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars wrote.
At a news conference to announce her appointment, James declined to comment when asked about the social media posts. But Hochul said she had no qualms about naming her as special prosecutor.
“I have every confidence in our attorney general to do what she has always done: Look at the facts, examine the record, draw the proper conclusions,” Hochul said. “That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case.”
James has been involved in a number of high-profile cases, most notably against the National Rifle Association and President Donald Trump. She labeled him a “con man” and “carnival barker” and pledged to shine a “bright light into every dark corner of his real estate dealings.” She also led a civil investigation that led to Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s resignation over sexual harassment allegations.

title: NH Man Charged After I-95 Construction Zone Crash Injures Maine DOT Worker
text:
Maine State Police Arrest a Suspect in an I-95 Hit-and-Run
A New Hampshire man is facing charges after allegedly causing an incident at an I-95 construction zone that seriously injured a Maine DOT worker.
New Hampshire Man Faces Charges for Crash on I-95 that Injured a Maine DOT Worker
Jonathan McDonald, 22, of Laconia, New Hampshire, is allegedly the driver in a crash on October 14, 2026, in Pittsfield.
He's charged with:
- Accidents involving death or personal injury, Class D
- Driving to endanger, Class E
- Accident reports, Class E
In Maine, a Class D or E crime carries a maximum sentence of less than one year.
Maine Police Charge a New Hampshire Man for a Crash on I-95 That Hurt a DOT Worker
The charges stem from a crash in the northbound lane of I-95 in Pittsfield, where construction had reduced traffic to one lane.
Investigators say it was just after 8 a.m. when a pickup truck towing a black dump trailer struck a concrete Jersey barrier, which caused a construction barrel to strike a Maine DOT worker.
Richard Smart, 56, of Westfield, was working in the construction zone when the barrel hit him, causing serious but non-life-threatening injuries.
Smart was treated at Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital and has since been released.
Maine State Police Say Tips from Residents Helped Them ID a Suspect in an I-95 Crash
Maine State Police released a photo of the pickup and trailer that's believed to be responsible for the incident.
Members of the public provided tips and information that assisted investigators and led them to McDonald.
State Police thank everyone who stepped up to help with this ongoing investigation.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: More than 2,000 Aroostook County voters have cast absentee ballots
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - More than 2,000 voters in four Aroostook County communities have cast absentee ballots ahead of Election Day, according to figures from local officials.
Sharon Nadeau voted absentee for the third year. She said the process is easier than voting on Election Day.
“It’s more relaxed and it’s just easier,” Nadeau said. “There’s not as many people and you get in and out a lot more quickly.”
Presque Isle and Easton
City officials said Presque Isle is processing about 60 absentee ballots a day. More than 1,000 voters have come in so far.
In Easton, Town Manager Cheryl Clark said absentee voting has become one of the main priorities at the town office, along with Election Day preparation.
“It has been very busy,” Clark said. “It’s pretty much the main priority of our office right now because Election Day is coming up and so many people are voting absentee.”
Easton has received about 142 absentee ballots. Clark said that number is unusually high for an election that is not presidential.
“A very large percentage have voted absentee,” Clark said. “Which is a little unusual. Like presidential elections, we expect it, and I guess governor elections also, but yeah, it’s been a very, very big turnout for absentee voting.”
Fort Kent, Houlton and statewide
Fort Kent town office officials said they also are seeing high numbers of absentee votes. As of Wednesday morning, the town had a count of 520.
Houlton has had 675 absentee ballot requests and 619 returns.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the trend is not limited to Aroostook County.
“More than 288,000 Mainers have requested an absentee ballot and most of them have already returned their ballot,” Bellows said. “That is record-breaking early voting.”
The last day to cast an absentee ballot is tomorrow.

title: Chicago-area Hindu community shaken but resilient after alleged mass shooting plan was thwarted
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — A thwarted mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago is stoking new fears for the area’s South Asian community, tainting a typically joyful season of faith and family gatherings.
Members of the targeted temple and others in the area said they are seeking comfort in preserving traditions, determined to celebrate the holidays without fear — and to press for ways to address hatred hurled at the community.
Earlier this month, as worshippers gathered in Hindu temples on Oct. 11 to kick off the festival of Navaratri, prosecutors said, Alexandros Paporakis showed up at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, and sat in the parking lot but fled before getting off a shot because his rifle jammed.
Paporakis, 19, was arrested later that day near his home in Palatine, Illinois, about 40 miles (64 kilometers) away after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his plan to “kill Indian people,” prosecutors said.
Paporakis faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a firearm. He is due back in court on Friday morning.
“A lot of us are just really appalled and just kind of disgusted,” said Asha Rao, executive director of The Chicago Kasam, a nonprofit aimed at bringing together the area’s South Asian community. “This is supposed to be a very peaceful time for our community, for all of us to come together and get time with our loved ones, our family, our friends, and be able to celebrate in a safe way.”
Safety concerns infiltrate joyful period
Navaratri is a nine-night celebration of the Goddess Durga, which culminates in Dussehra or Vijayadashami; Diwali, the major Hindu holiday, comes about three weeks later. Avatans Kumar, a freelance columnist who occasionally attends the temple that was targeted, said people often break the nine-night fast with a huge celebration on the 10th day that features outdoor fairs and gatherings with friends and family.
This year, those events have been shaped by discussions about how to increase security.
“People are more vigilant now,” Kumar said. “People are looking for any signs of disturbance, keeping eyes and ears open.”
Rao said some people were “more hesitant” to leave home and celebrate. But the threat had also sparked a renewed resilience and resolve to honor the holiday without fear, she said.
She hoped South Asians could “recognize how far we’ve come, all the great things that are happening in our community, the friends and the people,” she said. “That’s what it means to curate resilience in community in times like this.”
Calls for prosecution and attention to hateful language
South Asian local and congressional leaders are pushing for law enforcement to investigate whether the thwarted attack was a hate crime, and to pursue additional charges against Paporakis if it was. Prosecutors say Paporakis described himself as a white supremacist and neo-Nazi, and used slurs and hateful language to refer to Indians and other minority groups.
U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat whose district includes the temple that was targeted, previously told The Associated Press that he is “calling on the FBI to investigate and prosecute this particular matter as a hate crime.”
The planned attack has stirred painful memories of hateful comments. Use of anti-South Asian slurs online rose by 109% from 2023 to 2025, and nearly half of all South Asian adults said they experienced a hate act due to their race, ethnicity, or nationality last year, according to Stop AAPI Hate, which collects reports of hate crimes against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders.
Illinois’ South Asian population rose from more than 242,000 in 2010 to more than 337,000 in 2020, to comprise around 2.5% of the state’s total population, according to the South Asian American Policy and Research Institute. Some said bullying and race-based harassment were a regular part of life.
After Paporakis’ arrest, authorities said they recovered weapons, ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians and several items depicting Nazi symbols from his home. Officials said Paporakis wrote a lengthy note in which he fantasized about mass murder and expressed his desire to kill as many non-white people as he could.
Rishab Chatty, who leads the Chicago chapter of Hindus for Human Rights, said hatred directed at Hindus and South Asians was once “thought to be something that namely existed in chat rooms and in school lunch cafeterias” but was recently “becoming more and more violent.”
“A lot of folks within my community are really questioning what it means to belong in a country that exercises hate and violence against them,” he added.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Bruins belted by Blues, drop second straight
text:
ST. LOUIS — Robert Thomas and Philip Broberg each had a goal and two assists to lead the St. Louis Blues to a 4-1 win over the Boston Bruins on Thursday night.
Before the win, the Blues were 0-3-3 in their last six games against Bruins at home since Game 4 of Stanley Cup Final on June 3, 2019.
Jimmy Snuggerud and Jake Neighbours scored power-play goals for St. Louis and Joel Hofer recorded 31 saves.
James Hagens scored for the Bruins, while Jeremy Swayman stopped 14 shots.
St. Louis went ahead 2-1 on a wrist shot from the top of the slot by Broberg at 5:17 of the second period. Connor McMichael passed from behind the net to an open Broberg, whose shot went just inside the right post.
The Blues extended the lead to 3-1 on a goal by Thomas at 12:08. He took the puck from Justin Barron at the blue line, skated to the high slot and fired a wrist shot high to beat Swayman.
Neighbours scored a power-play goal at 12:42 of the third period.
Hagens deflected a shot by Casey Mittelstadt, giving the Bruins a 1-0 lead at 5:28 of the first period.
Snuggerud tied it 1-1 when he scored a power-play goal on a one-timer from the left faceoff circle. The goal at 15:43 snapped a 138:38 scoreless skid for the Blues.
Thomas assisted on the goal. He passed Brian Sutter for sole possession of fourth place on the Blues’ all-time list with 334 assists.

title: Westbrook 12-year-old reported missing
text:
The Westbrook Police Department has located a 12-year-old girl who went missing after leaving Westbrook Middle School on foot Thursday afternoon.
She was located on Main Street around 9:45 pm Thursday by a Westbrook Police Officer who was investigating a report of suspicious activity, police said in a news release.

title: Meet one of the student winners of South Portland's 'I Voted' sticker contest
text:
Meet one of the student winners of South Portland's 'I Voted' sticker contest
For the first year, South Portland held a competition for students to design "I Voted" stickers for this year's election. Three different winners were ultimately chosen.
Meet one of the student winners of South Portland's 'I Voted' sticker contest
For the first year, South Portland held a competition for students to design "I Voted" stickers for this year's election. Three different winners were ultimately chosen.
It's arguably one of the most fun parts of voting: walking away with an "I voted" sticker. This year, South Portland made it extra special by giving out stickers designed by local children.
For the first year ever, South Portland's City Clerk's Office held a competition for kids 18 and under to design the "I Voted" stickers. The entries were divided into three different age groups.
"We had to wait until after school got out because we wanted to call them when the kids were home to share the news, and they were very excited," said Jessica Hughes, South Portland's city clerk.
That's exactly how 1st grader Phillip Sobey reacted when he got the call.
"I was so happy. I was like, I was shocked," he said.
Phillip said he found out about the sticker contest through school, so his family took him to a local library to participate. He just submitted one sticker and the design showcases an American flag and a chickadee flying through the air underneath the words "I voted."
"I was trying to draw an eagle, and I was like, wait a minute, this looks like a chickadee. So, I made it a chickadee," he said.
His librarian was a big fan of the sticker.
"I showed it to my librarian. Her name is Mrs. Anderson, and she is the best one. I like her," he said. "Then, one day in the hallway, she was like, 'Love your sticker. I think it's going to win.' And she was true. I did win."
Hughes said that there were more than 50 entrants this year between all of the age categories. She hopes it becomes the start of a new yearly tradition with participation from teachers.
"It's important for everybody to understand the process of democracy and we can start that at a young age, from designing a sticker to going to the polls with their parents to vote. I think that's a great opportunity for them," Hughes said.
Phillip said he's looking forward to the day when he turns 18 and can walk away with his own "I Voted" sticker.

title: Patrick Stewart, stage giant also of 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86
text:
Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a “Star Trek” franchise and the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said.
While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen.
Story by Mark Kennedy, AP Entertainment Writer

title: ‘I rape little girls like you’: Former councilman arrested after allegedly making terrorist threats at Hooters
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A former Alabama city councilman was charged after allegedly making terrorist threats at a Hooters, according to authorities.
Former Mobile City Council member William Carroll, 56, was arrested Wednesday night on two counts of second-degree making terrorist threats.
Mobile police said the incident stems from an encounter on Oct. 14.
Officers responded to Hooters after receiving reports of a man making inappropriate and threatening comments toward an employee.
According to a Mobile County District Court complaint, Carroll told an employee, “I rape little girls like you,” and “I dig ditches and kill people before.” The complaint said the employee feared for her safety.
Another complaint said Carroll told a second employee, “I kill people for a living and rape little girls like her.”
Police said officers arrived and issued a trespass warning to Carroll.
Carroll was booked into the Mobile County Metro Jail shortly before 8 p.m. Wednesday.
Each charge carries a $3,000 bond. He was released shortly after 9 p.m. and has a bond hearing scheduled for Friday.

title: Space heaters under recall after units reportedly catch fire
text:
(Gray News) - Almost 340,000 space heaters are under recall throughout the United States due to the risk of fire and burns.
DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported.
About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026.
According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. DREO said they received 17 reports of ignition, three resulting in property damage and one burning a person’s hand.
Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one.
Consumers will be instructed to cut the electrical cord of the old space heater after it’s been unplugged and to send in a photo of it.

title: Average price of heating oil in Maine reaches record high for second time in 2 weeks
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Average price of heating oil in Maine reaches record high for second time in two weeks
Maine DOER says average statewide price of heating oil hit $6.05 per gallon, up one cent from last week
Average price of heating oil in Maine reaches record high for second time in two weeks
Maine DOER says average statewide price of heating oil hit $6.05 per gallon, up one cent from last week
The Maine Department of Energy Resources (DOER) announced Thursday that the average statewide price of heating oil hit a new record high, marking the second straight week this has happened.
The DOER's latest weekly fuel survey shows the price of heating oil reached $6.05 per gallon on Monday, Oct. 26, which was up one cent from the previous record high of $6.04 that was set the week before.
According to the DOER, the average statewide price of $6.05 per gallon marked an 82% increase in price from this time last year. The department also said that based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, Maine residents are estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank to capacity than they would have one year ago.
"Heating oil prices in Maine are now breaking records week after week, putting growing pressure on Maine families as temperatures continue to drop," DOER Acting Commissioner Celina Cunningham said in a statement. "I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief."
The DOER also said that kerosene reached a statewide average price of $7.06 per gallon on Oct. 26.
State officials said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and consumes significantly more per capita than other New England states. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, but the DOER noted that figure has declined steadily from 70% in 2010.
Last month, projections from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association indicated that Maine households are expected to spend an average of $2,939 to heat their homes with heating oil this winter.
Last Wednesday, Oct. 21, the U.S. Department of Energy announced that it will make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in an effort to increase supply and bring down prices.
The latest heating fuel prices are available to view on the DOER website and are updated weekly during the heating season. The DOER is encouraging Maine residents to review the department's Winter Heating Guide for helpful tips and resources related to winter heating, including information about financial assistance for home heating and cost-saving home efficiency incentives.

title: Cooper Flagg scores 26 points in Mavs’ win over Thunder
text:
DALLAS — Cooper Flagg had 26 points and eight assists and P.J. Washington scored 18 points as the Dallas Mavericks beat the injury-depleted Oklahoma City Thunder 120-96 on Wednesday night.
The Mavericks (3-2) led by 12 in the first half and by 27 in the fourth quarter to move over .500 for the first time since Flagg joined the team last fall.
Dallas’ Kyrie Irving scored 15 points, 13 in the first half when he hit his first four shots, including three behind the arc. It was Irving’s first home regular-season game since March 3, 2025, when he suffered a torn ACL in his left knee. Irving sat out Dallas’ home opener last week on the second half of a back-to-back.
Ajay Mitchell scored 29 points and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander had 21 for the Thunder (4-1).
Oklahoma City played its second game of the extended absences of Jalen Williams (broken leg, dislocated ankle) and Cason Wallace (torn labrum) and also the second without Chet Holmgren (patellar tendinitis in his right knee). Alex Caruso also sat out with patellar tendinitis that sidelined him during a home win over Phoenix on Monday.
It was the first home victory for first-year Mavericks coach Dusty May.
The Mavericks dominated from downtown. They sank a season-best 16 3-pointers on 45 attempts, with 11 made in the first half. The Thunder were a season-low 5 of 32 behind the arc for a season-worst 15.6%. Those were also lows for a Mavericks opponent this season.
Dallas’ accuracy from distance included center Daniel Gafford’s first 3 in eight NBA seasons on his 2,384th career shot. Gafford missed one 3-point try previously, on March 29, 2022 with Washington.
Up next
Both teams will face the Houston Rockets next, Dallas at home on Friday and Oklahoma City on the road on Saturday.

title: ‘She just lit up the room’: Toddler dies after being hit by car at a pumpkin patch, family says
text:
SEVIERVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A Tennessee toddler died after being hit by a car at a pumpkin patch, according to her family.
The family of 21-month-old Nyxailia Hinton said they want answers after she died Tuesday.
The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said she fell and was hit by a car driven by a family friend at a pumpkin patch. However, details have not been given about how or where she fell.
“She just lit up the room,” said Peandra Hinton, the child’s mother. “If you were having a bad day, you see Zayla, she’s gonna turn it all around.”
Hinton said her daughter was with a babysitter who took her to the pumpkin patch without permission. She said her daughter was with a group of people she did not know.
Hinton rushed to the hospital, where her daughter died from her injuries Tuesday, according to the sheriff’s office.
Hinton said the past 48 hours have been a whirlwind, adding the hardest part has been waking up without her daughter.
“The fact that I couldn’t wake up this morning to my baby, it really tore me up,” Hinton said.
The family is planning funeral arrangements, and Nyxailia’s father said they want justice.
“We want justice for her. And we ain’t letting up, I don’t care if someone’s feelings get hurt, this has torn up her whole family. She wasn’t even 22 months old,” he said.
The sheriff’s office said the incident remains under investigation. No charges have been filed.

title: Trump slams Peltola campaign over two Sullivans on Alaska ballot
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate.
Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that campaign staffers for Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman now running for the U.S. Senate, tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
The effort is not illegal. However, the reports have led Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, to order an investigation into alleged election manipulation.
Trump commented on the controversy Thursday before leaving for South Carolina.
“So nobody’s going to know what to do. That’s a fraud. And it shouldn’t be allowed to happen. And it was done in conjunction with Schumer and everybody else. It’s an absolute, it’s called voter fraud,” Trump said.
Vice President JD Vance echoed the president’s comments Thursday.
“It’s disgraceful, so whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her,” Vance said.
In a statement, Peltola’s campaign said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
Alaska’s highest state court earlier ruled that both men should remain on the ballot.
On the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan appears with no modifiers. Daniel S. Sullivan is listed with the labels incumbent and Republican next to his name.
Alaska’s elections are determined by ranked choice voting. If no candidate wins a majority in the Senate race after Tuesday’s midterm elections, the ranked choices will be tallied.
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) the chair of the House Oversight Committee announced Thursday he is launching an investigation into whether the Peltola campaign tried to intentionally confuse voters. He issued a letter requesting in-person testimony from key Peltola staffers next week.

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.
As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.
Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.
Trump’s pressure campaign hasn’t worked
Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT.”
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”
An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year.”
The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump’s pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.
Previous laws have been repealed
In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.
An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.
“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”
___
Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed to this report.

title: Worker rights pioneer Dolores Huerta wanted others to feel seen
text:
Dolores Huerta had spent decades advocating for labor rights and marginalized people when she went to a central California college and met a group of farmworkers’ descendants — many of them students who choked back tears over the then-94-year-old taking the time to listen to them.
That was the effect Huerta had on young people, said Ana Padilla, executive director of the Community and Labor Center at the University of California, Merced, which had hosted Huerta for the event.
“It was transformative,” Padilla said. “Something that I heard a lot from students in particular was just how accessible she was. That’s just what made Dolores a natural organizer, just an ability to connect immediately with really anyone.”
The activist and icon who helped improve the lives of laborers in farming and other industries died Wednesday from cancer at 96. She was surrounded by family at her home in Bakersfield, California.
While most people would spend their golden years enjoying retirement, Huerta never stopped fighting. Living up to her famous rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” (“Yes, it can be done”), the civil rights activist marched alongside protesters, spoke on countless panels and lent her voice to progressive causes well into her 90s. And it wasn’t just on issues impacting Latinos but also African Americans, the LGBTQ+ community and women. Not just an organizer, Huerta during every major election encouraged voters and endorsed candidates. She also pushed more Latinos to consider running for office.
Even after Huerta revealed in March that she was among the women and girls who say they were sexually abused by César Chavez, the labor leader she was inextricably linked to in history, admiration for her only strengthened.
Huerta once said she simply wanted encourage younger generations, particularly women, to use their voice.
“I hope that they know they have a place,” Huerta told The Associated Press in August while attending the Los Angeles premiere of the documentary, “American Pachuco.”
“Never be afraid to take the leadership,” she said.
A living Latina legend who continued to show up
From the United Farm Workers union to the Latino Victory Project, many groups said they would not exist if not for Huerta. She co-founded with Chavez the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. It would become the United Farm Workers of America a few years later and then join with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee.
The movement fought for better wages and working conditions for agricultural workers such as fair hours and access to bathrooms. Her work has garnered her accolades including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2012.
Her leadership has made Huerta almost a mythical figure especially in Latino households. Anabelle Sanchez, 20, of Lansing, Michigan, texted her parents when she learned of Huerta’s death. Sanchez, who is Mexican American, was a child when her mother taught her about Huerta.
“I’ve always looked up to her. She was very civically involved throughout her life and just using her voice even when things were scary,” said Sanchez, a Michigan State University political science and public policy major who hopes to emulate Huerta’s “strength and her courage.”
“She was a part of everyday life and she would always go to events like pretty much up until her last breath,” Sanchez said. “Always being an advocate, thinking of others who may not have that opportunity. That’s just something that will always stay with me about her.”
Irasema Coronado, director of Arizona State University’s School of Transborder Studies, became friends with Huerta over 20 years ago when they met at a feminist-centered conference on a cruise ship. She remembers Huerta as someone with boundless energy who showed up for people. She recalls Huerta attending a protest in Phoenix and then leaving immediately after to make appearances at demonstrations in New Mexico and Texas.
“She was everywhere,” Coronado said. “She never missed an opportunity to be on the right side of something. I never saw her with a script. It was from the heart.”
An unapologetic feminist
During the farmworkers movement of the 1960s, Huerta put up with a great deal of sexism being the only woman in the room.
“She was expected to be quiet and stay in the background and instead, she was out in front and demanding change,” said Kathy Spillar, executive director of the Feminist Majority Foundation, of which Huerta served on the board.
The two women met at a conference for the National Organization for Women in the late 1980s. Spillar approached Huerta with the idea of launching the foundation.
“It was the only way that the issues Dolores was talking about could be addressed,” Spillar said. “She said, ‘Sign me up. I’m with you.’ And that was the beginning of almost 40 years.”
Spillar met Huerta around the time that a police officer attacked and beat Huerta. On Sept. 14, 1988, while protesting outside an appearance by then-Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush in San Francisco, she was beaten with a baton. Huerta was hospitalized with broken ribs, a ruptured spleen and other injuries. She later won an $825,000 settlement from the city.
But, that ordeal also got Huerta thinking about how to help others besides farmworkers, Spillar recalls. Huerta noticed the women caring for her at the hospital as she recovered from the police assault were under-appreciated.
“They all would talk with her about the struggles that they faced,” Spillar said. “And she decided, I think then, that she was going to become very active in the feminist movement.”
A larger-than-life figure who connected with people
Many schools in California bear the name Dolores Huerta. The state also joins Washington, Oregon and New Mexico in marking her legacy on her April 10 birthday.
However, after the revelations about Chavez’s abuse, Huerta rejected pledges by some to use her name as a replacement for his on streets, schools and other sites. Instead, those places “should not be renamed after her, but the UFW martyrs, organizers, farmworkers, and families who sacrificed everything to build something bigger than any one person,” a spokesperson for Huerta told The San Francisco Standard earlier this year.
Huerta used her influence when it felt needed. That’s how the labor center in Merced was officially founded in 2020, Padilla said, after the labor rights pioneer lobbied state lawmakers to fund it.
Talking to students there was among Huerta’s favorite things.
“She would want to spend as much time as she could with you and regardless of your standing,” Padilla said. “She treated folks the same.”
___ Associated Press writers Leslie Ambriz in Los Angeles and Fabianna Rincon in New York contributed to this report.

title: Brewers beat Rays in Game 5 to win first World Series title in franchise history
text:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers playing in the smallest market in the majors are World Series champions for the first time.
Hey, Milwaukee: grab a brat, raise a beer and prepare for that parade.
To borrow a line from Bob Uecker, your title drought is up, outta here, gone.
Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings, rookie Cooper Pratt had two more hits and two RBIs, and Milwaukee beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 on Wednesday night to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.
“It’s the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city’s waited a long, long time for this,” said captain Christian Yelich, who got hugs from franchise icon Robin Yount on the field when it was over. “We’re so happy to bring it home to them.”
World Series MVP William Contreras hit an RBI double and Misiorowski allowed just two hits before leaving the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee’s dugout for the last three games.
They filled the entire infield section of the ballpark for the trophy presentation and were still chanting “Let’s go Brewers!” almost two hours after the final pitch.
The 22-year-old Pratt set a Series rookie record with six straight hits before his sacrifice fly in the sixth. Jackson Chourio set a five-game Series record with 11 hits.
“This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real,” said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June. “This is surreal. It only took four months!”
The championship comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers’ only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.
But this team displayed the toughness and resilience of 67-year-old manager Pat Murphy, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.
“This group of guys right here, the 2026 team, will be remembered forever — and they deserve that because they were a team,” Murphy said. “They’re not worried about their own stats. No one cares about that. They care about coming together and winning tonight.”
With their flame-throwing, 24-year-old two-time All-Star on the mound, the Brewers rebounded from a heartbreaking, 4-3 extra-inning loss in Game 4 when they were three outs from a sweep in the 12th before a stellar bullpen finally faltered.
Pitching on four days’ rest for only the fifth time in 34 starts this year, The Miz had his longest outing since throwing 6 1/3 innings against the Cubs on Sept. 8. Leg cramps also forced him out of two outings earlier in the season.
“I don’t even have words,” Misiorowski said. “It’s amazing, just watching my guys celebrate. And the city — I know they’re going crazy in Milwaukee. It’s awesome.”
Misiorowski, who broke the World Series velocity record with a 103.5 mph fastball on the first pitch last Friday, opened with 12 straight four-seamers between 100.9-103 mph. He topped out at 103 twice among his 86 pitches, 58 strikes.
The 6-foot-7 right-hander didn’t record a strikeout in the first three innings for the first time in his two-year career and finished with two, matching his career low. But he was fired up after Yandy Díaz missed a cutter to end the fifth: The Miz pumped his fist twice and punched the air walking off the mound.
The NL Cy Young Award favorite allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter in a 3-2 victory in the opener. He was 2-0 with a 0.84 ERA in the best-of-seven Series.
JoJo Romero got two outs, Abner Uribe recorded two more and closer Trevor Megill pitched the last two innings, allowing an RBI double to Chandler Simpson with two outs in the ninth.
Megill retired Richie Palacios on a grounder to end it, threw his arms in the air and was mobbed by teammates near the mound while Brewers fans celebrated in the stands.
First baseman Jake Bauers tucked the ball in his back pocket before piling on and later gave the souvenir to Murphy, saying the skipper “deserved it.”
“Milwaukee has waited 44 years, and Milwaukee, you have your world championship!” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said from the postgame stage on the field.
Pratt, who was 4 for 5 with a tiebreaking solo homer in the 12th inning of Game 4, gave the Brewers a 1-0 lead with an RBI single against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in the second. Pratt singled for his sixth straight hit in the fifth and scored on David Hamilton’s single off Kevin Kelly.
Contreras hit an RBI double off Garrett Cleavinger in the sixth and Pratt added a sac fly to make it 4-0.
The teams combined for just four home runs in the Series, three by Milwaukee. The Brewers scored a major league-low 32.1% of their runs on homers this season and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Brewers led the majors with 103 wins in the regular season and went 11-2 in the postseason, including seven comeback wins and a sweep of the mighty Dodgers in the National League Championship Series.
“That’s the best team I’ve ever played against,” Rasmussen said.
Making history
Milwaukee’s only other MLB championship was won in 1957 by the Braves, who moved to Atlanta for the 1966 season.
Murphy’s team finished what Harvey Kuenn’s star-studded crew couldn’t accomplish 44 years ago as the American League champions. Harvey’s Wallbangers had five Hall of Famers: Yount, Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers, who missed the postseason with a forearm injury.
They also had a Hall of Fame broadcaster in the booth. The beloved Uecker died in January 2025 at age 90 after announcing Brewers games for 54 years.
“Cooperstown will remember the 2026 Brewers,” Murphy said.
Still seeking a title
The Rays, an expansion team that debuted in 1998, dropped to 0-3 in the World Series after defeats in 2008 and 2020. They’re one of four MLB franchises that have never won one. Colorado, San Diego and Seattle are the others.
“They’re banged-up and hurting right now, but just grateful for the way they carried themselves all season long, winning a bunch of games. It’s as close-knit of a group as I’ve ever been around,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said.
Lockout looming
This might have been the last Major League Baseball game for an extended period.
The Brewers won the World Series at a time when owners are pushing the players’ association for a salary cap because they maintain small-market teams can’t regularly succeed. A management lockout is likely to start Dec. 2 and could threaten the 2027 season.
This was the first Series since 1991 between teams in the bottom half of payrolls. The Brewers ranked 19th as of Aug. 31, and the Rays were 25th.

title: Bowdoinham Community School receives $300K donation
text:
The Bowdoinham Community School recently received a donation of $300,000.
The gift came unexpectedly, said Superintendent Heidi O’Leary. The district had been aware that a donation was coming, but they had no idea it would be such a large amount.
The money will be able to be used for a wide variety of projects, and is intended to support both students and teachers. Rachel Ledbetter was the donor.
The school board accepted the gift on Oct. 8. “I’m a little overwhelmed by that generosity, that’s a big moment,” said Hutson Hayward, school board chair.
Bowdoinham Community School Principal Chris Lajoie said in an email that Ledbetter was supportive of plans to use the money to revitalize the nonfiction section of the school’s library, and fund opportunities for field trips and outdoor learning. Ledbetter also requested in a letter that the money be used to celebrate teachers efforts, and support their professional development.
Lajoie wrote that he plans to create a small committee, which will evaluate proposals for projects from staff at the school that this money could be used to fund.
The gift will be kept in a newly established trust fund, called the VC Dunlap Fund. At the school board meeting, Lajoie said that Rachel Ledbetter’s stepfather was Vining Campbell Dunlap, and he went to school in one-room schoolhouse in Bowdoinham, later graduating from Bowdoinham High School in 1910. Dunlap was a botanist, who among other achievements, discovered a wilt resistant banana variety. According to the Donor Intent and Gift Agreement, establishing the fund with his name is intended to recognize him.
The original gift will stay in the trust, and the interest can be used to fund school projects in perpetuity, said O’Leary. Lajoie said that the school will leave the gift be for the first year, and then begin to spend the interest.

title: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for $17 billion
text:
DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for $17 billion
DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for $17 billion
DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17 billion acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 "shoppers" — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.
Related video above: DoorDash uses delivery drones in Georgia
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation's largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart's expertise in grocery with DoorDash's expertise in logistics and delivery.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said in a statement. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
DoorDash's aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash's share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats' share held steady at just under 20%.
It's not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.
"The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash's delivery network and Instacart's grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores' own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built," DoorDash said in a news release on Thursday morning. "On either app, customers pick a store in their own community, and the store makes the sale. Consumers will have more stores to choose from, more savings opportunities when they choose to shop with a local business, and faster delivery options, while Dashers and Shoppers will have more ways to earn."

title: Naples man arrested after 100 mph police chase in New Hampshire
text:
Naples man arrested after 100 mph police chase in New Hampshire
Police say the 20-year-old driver crossed the concrete median before his pickup truck became disabled on Interstate 93
Naples man arrested after 100 mph police chase in New Hampshire
Police say the 20-year-old driver crossed the concrete median before his pickup truck became disabled on Interstate 93
A 20-year-old Maine man was arrested early Thursday morning after leading New Hampshire State Police on a high-speed pursuit that reached speeds exceeding 100 mph, authorities said.
Shortly before 2 a.m., a trooper spotted a 2005 GMC Sierra traveling northbound at 100 mph on Interstate 93 in Bow, New Hampshire, according to state police.
The trooper attempted to stop the pickup, but the driver did not pull over and continued north.
Police said the driver exited the highway at Exit 13 in Concord, crossed a concrete median on Manchester Street and reentered I-93 northbound. The pursuit continued at speeds exceeding 100 mph.
Between exits 16 and 17 in Concord, the truck became disabled due to damage sustained while crossing the median.
The driver, identified as Jacob Lemery, 20, of Naples, Maine was taken into custody.
Lemery was arrested on charges of reckless conduct with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled drug, aggravated driving while intoxicated, disobeying a police officer, and reckless operation.
He was released on personal recognizance bail and is scheduled to appear in Concord District Court on Nov. 17.

title: Man indicted after allegedly stabbing, kidnapping mother in Old Town, officials say
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A man accused of attacking and kidnapping his mother before leading police on a manhunt has been indicted by a Penobscot County grand jury.
Nathan Lagasse, 28, faces charges of assault and kidnapping in connection with the August incident.
Authorities said Lagasse’s mother woke up to her son striking her in the head with a 25-pound barbell weight plate and stabbing her with a butter knife.
Police said Lagasse then forced his mother into a vehicle and took her on a drive. After returning to the residence, he allegedly stole her wallet, phone and keys before fleeing the home a second time. Officers were subsequently called to the scene.
Authorities later located and arrested Lagasse as he walked along a road in Orono.
Lagasse alleged that he attacked his mother in self-defense.

title: Caretaker charged for recording 92-year-old man suffocating his wife with plastic bag in senior living center, police say
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A Kentucky woman’s designated caretaker was arrested after allegedly recording an incident in which her 92-year-old husband allegedly tried to suffocate her instead of helping the victim.
Bert Morris, 92, was charged Wednesday with attempted murder and first-degree strangulation.
According to Morris’ arrest citation, Louisville Metro Police officers responded to a senior living center after a report of a domestic violence incident.
Police said Morris was found pinching his wife’s nose after “placing a plastic bag over her face.” The citation said the bag could be seen sealing around her mouth and continued to tighten around her head while Morris held her nose.
According to the citation, Morris made a statement that his wife “needed to die.”
Terrence Gabie, 41, was also arrested Wednesday and is facing charges of knowingly abusing or neglecting an adult.
Court documents state Gabie recorded a 71-second video of the incident instead of helping the victim.
Another nurse had to intervene and separate the victim and Morris, court documents state.
Gabie was the victim’s designated caretaker during her time at the assisted living facility.
Morris’ wife was taken to a local hospital, where she was unconscious.
Morris pleaded not guilty in court Thursday. His bond was reduced from $250,000 to $150,000. He is scheduled to appear in court Nov. 6 for a preliminary hearing.
Gabie was also arraigned in court Thursday, where he pleaded not guilty and his bond was set at $10,000. He was released on a personal recognizance bond.
His preliminary hearing is scheduled for Nov. 6.

title: Maine Savings commits $1 million to expand St. Joseph Healthcare’s Emergency Department
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gift brings Called to Care campaign commitments to $4.2 million — nearly halfway to its $8.5 million fundraising goal
BANGOR — St. Joseph Healthcare has received a $1 million gift from Maine Savings Federal Credit Union to support the expansion and modernization of its Emergency Department, a significant investment in emergency care for Bangor and surrounding communities.
The gift helps bring community commitments to the hospital’s Called to Care campaign to $4.2 million, nearly 50% of its $8.5 million fundraising goal. Together with $6.8 million in Congressionally Directed Spending secured by U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, philanthropic support will help make possible a redesigned Emergency Department that better serves patients, families and care teams.
“We are overwhelmed by the generosity of Maine Savings and deeply grateful for this extraordinary commitment,” Greg LaFrancois, president of St. Joseph Healthcare, said. “Maine Savings has shown what it means to invest in the well-being of its members and the community we share. When someone comes through our Emergency Department doors, they may be experiencing one of the most frightening moments of their life. This gift brings us closer to providing a space that matches the exceptional care and compassion our team delivers every day, and its impact will be felt by patients and families for years to come.”
Expanding capacity and improving the care experience
St. Joseph Healthcare’s Emergency Department cares for as many as 30,000 patients each year. The expansion and modernization will address limitations in the existing space while preparing the hospital to meet future community needs.
Plans include additional patient treatment spaces, a new entrance and lobby, a dedicated fast-track area for less acute emergencies, an improved environment for patients experiencing behavioral health needs and a redesigned nursing station to support care delivery.
These improvements are intended to help patients move more efficiently through care, create a more supportive environment during stressful situations and give clinical teams a space better suited to the needs of the people they serve.
Construction is anticipated to begin in October 2027, with the project completed in three phases through March 2029.
“At Maine Savings, we believe our role reaches well beyond banking. It means showing up for the communities our members and employees call home,” Vanessa Madore, president and CEO of Maine Savings and chair of the St. Joseph Healthcare Board of Trustees, said. “St. Joseph’s Emergency Department is there for our neighbors during some of the hardest moments of their lives, and right now, that care is being delivered in a space the region has outgrown. We’re proud to help create an environment that matches the compassion and skill of the people who work there, and we hope our commitment encourages others across Maine to join us.”
Building momentum toward the campaign goal
The Called to Care campaign will help close the funding gap between the federal investment and the resources needed to complete the Emergency Department project. Maine Savings’ extraordinary $1 million gift marks a major milestone for the campaign and provides powerful momentum as St. Joseph Healthcare invites the broader community to help bring this vision to life.
“Maine Savings has made an extraordinary investment in the future of local healthcare,” Brad Coffey, senior vice president and president of Covenant Health Foundation, said. “Their generosity brings us nearly halfway to our fundraising goal and demonstrates what is possible when local businesses help meet a shared community need. We hope their leadership inspires other businesses and individuals to join us in answering this call to care.”
For more information about the Emergency Department project, the Called to Care campaign, or opportunities to contribute, please contact the St. Joseph Healthcare Foundation office at 207-907-1740.
Maine Savings, founded in 1961, is a modern financial institution with state-of-the-art technology offering members a full range of financial services, including RedWallet Checking. With more than 42,000 members, 11 branches and over 170 employees, Maine Savings is one of Maine’s largest credit unions. Maine Savings is committed to providing in-person services paired with modern conveniences. Branches are located in Bangor, Brewer, Corinth, Ellsworth, Hampden, Milo, North Vassalboro, Old Town and Portland. Maine Savings continues to serve its membership as a federally insured not-for-profit credit union.

title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections, AP sources say
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.
Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by U.S. diplomats and defense officials.
President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.
The White House and U.S. officials declined to comment.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.
The U.S. has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran’s response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
It’s unclear how soon the US military would be ready
While the U.S. has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated.
The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the U.S.
It’s unclear how soon after Election Day that the U.S. military would be ready to potentially resume strikes.
The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the U.S. military in the region.
At the time, one U.S. official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003.
Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran.
The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that’s driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy.
The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress.
While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes.
During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.”
“Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then -- especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank.
“Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said.
___
Magdy reported from New York. AP writers Konstantin Toropin and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

title: Why Medicare Advantage plans fluctuate annually and vary based on location
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Why Medicare Advantage plans fluctuate annually and vary based on location
Thousands of Mainers are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered next year
Why Medicare Advantage plans fluctuate annually and vary based on location
Thousands of Mainers are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered next year
As 8 Investigates has reported, more than 13,111 Mainers are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that won’t be offered next year.
Thousands of others will see reduced benefits or higher premiums, and costs can vary depending on location.
When an insurance company is approved to offer a Medicare Advantage plan, the government agrees to pay a certain fixed amount for each enrollee the insurer covers.
Companies submit bids based on a benchmark rate for each county that's set by the government. Those rates are predictions based on historical data, estimates of how much each enrollee will cost.
For 2027, the benchmark is highest in Piscataquis County and lowest in Washington County.
"It’s like throwing darts at a dartboard blindfolded," said Michael Cannon, director of health policy studies at the Cato Institute.
The benchmarks are shaped by a range of factors, including the overall health of patients living in a county and the local cost of care.
"If you only have one hospital in a rural area, and a Medicare Advantage plan has to have that hospital in-network in order to attract enrollees in that area, then that hospital might have the insurance companies over a barrel," Cannon said. "They might be able to charge very high prices, and the insurance companies don't have a lot of negotiating room."
The benchmarks aren't always accurate. If Medicare overpays, insurance companies make a profit, especially if the majority of their enrollees are healthy.
"When Medicare is setting the prices that it pays to insurance companies too high, then the insurance companies are making lots of money off of Medicare enrollees, and they compete to enroll as many of them as they can by offering these optional benefits like dental and vision and hearing, but also gym memberships and even groceries, and in some cases, pet care," Cannon said.
If Medicare underpays, or if a high percentage of enrollees require costly medical care, companies are left with a deficit.
"If the insurance companies are backing away from a county, it's because Medicare is not paying them enough to provide the coverage that Medicare requires, to the people who end up enrolling," Cannon said.
This year, many plans are scaling back on extra benefits such as vision, dental and wellness reimbursements.

title: What’s the Most Snow Bangor Has Ever Received on Halloween?
text:
What’s the Most Snow Bangor Has Ever Received on Halloween?
Halloween in Maine can call for an extra layer, but Bangor’s snowfall record for the holiday might surprise you.
👇 KEEP READING: The Most Popular Halloween Costumes for Boys and Girls from 1980 - 2025 👇
According to the National Weather Service’s Halloween history, Bangor’s holiday snowfall record is only a trace, observed on Oct. 31st, 2010.
That means less than one-tenth of an inch, too little to count as measurable snowfall.
For comparison, Caribou recorded 7.6 inches of snow on Halloween in 1959.
Even there, measurable snowfall on the holiday is uncommon, with a 2024 Northeast Regional Climate Center review finding it occurred on approximately 6% of Halloweens in Caribou’s historical records.
While that may be the case for Bangor, the city has still had its share of snowy, wintry weather around Halloween.
For example, a nor’easter brought 6 inches of snow to Bangor on Oct. 30th, 2011, just one day before the holiday. Bangor’s weather station reported 1 inch of snow on the ground on Halloween morning that year, with no new snowfall during the day.
Halloween has also brought unusually warm weather to Bangor.
On Oct. 31st, 2024, the city reached 78 degrees, breaking the previous holiday record of 71 degrees set in 1956.
And there you have it! A snowy Halloween in Bangor could involve snow left on the ground from an earlier storm, which is measured separately from snowfall on the holiday itself.

title: Lincoln Girls Soccer Shut Out By Freeport
text:
The Lincoln Academy girls soccer team lost to Freeport 1-0 in a Class B South quarterfinal match on Tuesday, Oct. 27 in Freeport.
The playoff game was a defensive battle from the start, with both teams playing a conservative style focused on avoiding mistakes and keeping the ball out of their own net.
The Falcons scored the only goal of the game with 17 minutes left in the first half. Keeley Furtney booted a long direct kick from 40 yards that took a huge bounce over the head of Lincoln Academy goalie Natalie Hanna, who leaped and got a hand on the ball. It wasn’t enough to stop the ball, as it barely crossed the goal line to give Freeport the lead.
The Falcons controlled possession for the majority of the game, leaving the Eagles with few chances to knot the score. One of the best scoring chances for the Eagles came with 16 minutes remaining in the game. Rowan Coffin banged a shot off the cross bar but the ball bounced out of bounds. Brea Lafrenaye created a scoring chance with less than a minute remaining when she got free from a defender and blasted a shot beyond the outstretched Freeport goalie Karleigh Costello, but the shot bounced wide of the post by a foot.
“We played more defensively today, with the idea to keep the score low and then capitalize on our scoring chances,” said coach Lauren Ober, whose team lost to the Falcons 6-2 earlier this season in a wide-open, high-scoring game. “Heading into the rematch, we practiced being more thoughtful about where we played the ball. Unlike the last time we played them and it was a little more kickball, we wanted to play balls in certain spaces, and the girls executed the plan well.”
The Eagles had to shuffle the lineup to account for the loss of starting defender Leanne Lord, who was not available to play. Offensive players including Dory Westhaver and Yzze Bhe had to take on defensive roles to mark the dangerous Freeport scorers.
“The girls competed hard and played great defense all game, but the trade-off was that our offense had a little less potency without them up front,” said Ober. “I am so proud of the girls for pushing a great team like Freeport to the limit.”
Hanna stopped eight Freeport shots for the Eagles during the game, including six in the second half to keep the Eagles in striking range. Costello made three saves for the Falcons.
Ober expressed sadness that the team, which had 11 seniors, could not advance further in the playoffs.
“I showed the seniors some video of them playing as freshmen the other day, and it was amazing how much they have grown up and improved their game over the years,” said Ober. “This was a big year for us, and we came so close to advancing deep in the playoffs. Class B South is the toughest league in the state, for sure.”
The No. 5 seed Eagles finished the season with a 9-5-1 record. The No. 4 seed Falcons advanced to face top seed Cape Elizabeth in a Class B South semifinal on Friday, Oct. 30.

text:
More than 300,000 space heaters sold at popular retailers recalled over fire risk
As temperatures drop, many people turn to space heaters to warm their homes—but one popular model is now subject to a major safety recall.
About 338,800 DREO space heaters sold at Costco and several major online retailers are being recalled because they can overheat and catch fire, officials with the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said Thursday.
Related video above | Recalls, explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The recall covers black ceramic electric heaters with model number DR-HSH015, made from April 2025 through January 2026.
The heaters are about 11.5 inches wide and 13 inches tall and come with a remote. The model number and manufacture date are printed on a label on the underside, federal officials said.
Officials with DREO say they have received 17 reports of the heaters igniting. Three reports involved property damage, and one involved a burn to a person’s hand.
Consumers should stop using the heaters immediately and contact DREO for a free replacement, federal officials said.
The company says customers will need to unplug the unit, cut its power cord, and send a photo of the destroyed heater according to its instructions.
The heaters were sold from September 2025 through October 2026 for between $70 and $110 at Costco stores and online at Dreo.com, BestBuy.com, Kohls.com, Lowes.com, QVC.com, HomeDepot.com, B2BRenew.com and Costco.com.
