title: Trump plans for golf course are in the works, DOJ announces. What to know about the park
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that President Donald Trump’s announcements that there are plans for renovating the East Potomac Golf Course and there are plans to close the park beginning Nov. 15 are accurate.
“On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events—such as the U.S. Open” and other events.
“Thereafter, on November 15, 2026, the National Park Service will close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive, including the Golf Course, consistent with the President’s directive,” the filing said.
The planning commission will consider the plan at its Dec. 3 meeting.
The announcement is the latest move in a 10-day period that started with a social media posting by Trump Oct. 18 that the park would be closed Nov. 15 for the next 15 months while the park undergoes renovation into what the president has called a world-class facility.
Trump’s social media postings touched off a series of court hearings in the lawsuit filed by the DC Preservation League and two golfers challenging the plans. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction Oct. 26, due in part to the discrepancy between the president’s public announcements and the testimony from various National Park Service, Interior Department and Justice Department officials who testified that they had no knowledge of the plans Trump was announcing.
The current preliminary injunction temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active.
Reyes was planning another hearing to bring officials back to court to explain why the president continued to announce plans that officials said they had no knowledge of.
Wednesday’s filing explained that the National Park Service entered into a new lease agreement with the National Links Trust — the company currently responsible for operating the East Potomac Golf Course — under which the National Links Trust will cease operating the East Potomac Golf Course as of the close of business on or before Nov. 15, but will continue to operate two other public golf courses.
Trump’s social media posts on the renovation of the historic golf course had put Justice Department lawyers in the uncomfortable position of explaining whether the president of the United States should be believed or not.
On Tuesday, Reyes said the department should clarify “whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026.” She ordered Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. to appear in court Friday or Monday for a status hearing. On Wednesday, she then issued an order for Woodward to appear on Friday, along with at least one person from the Department of the Interior’s Office of the Solicitor “with pre-existing experience on this case.”
Tuesday’s order came in response to Trump’s social media post late Monday criticizing Reyes’ temporary injunction stopping work at East Potomac Park.
That injunction, issued Monday, was in large part due to previous Trump announcements — via social media — that plans had been completed for the golf course and construction would begin next month. Trump said the facility would be closed for 15 months. The following day he set the timetable to “immediately.”
Much of the activity in the court has accelerated this month, after the government gave the plaintiffs in the case short notice on plans to cut down hundreds of trees at the course.
The plaintiffs challenging the project claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. Critics say Trump’s plan will make playing there unaffordable for the general public and destroy the site’s other uses.
In a Wednesday night posting on Truth Social, Trump called the golf course “highly dangerous, dilapidated, and absolutely disgusting.” He added that Reyes would be held responsible for anyone injured or killed at the course.
“No one will be more thrilled by our plans to renovate the Course and Driving Range than the Local Golfers who have played there for years, and have begged to have their Home Course brought into pristine condition,” he wrote.
The course renovation project is part of Trump’s aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape.
Those plans include construction of a huge ballroom at the White House, a massive arch and the creation of a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. The DC Preservation League is part of a coalition of organizations, including the Cultural Landscape Foundation and one D.C. resident, who have filed lawsuits challenging those plans.
There are several cases where judges have taken actions and issued injunctions or restraining orders because of the Trump administration’s push to begin work despite the pending lawsuits.
The golf course is one of two major and controversial projects with imminent starting dates in court this week.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan will hold a hearing Friday on a motion from plaintiffs in a lawsuit asking she call a temporary halt to plans to begin construction as early as Friday on the arch in the Memorial Circle. The arch is opposed by a small group of veterans and an architectural historian who sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. Chutkan had already said the administration must give the court 48 hours before undertaking any activities related to or in preparation for construction of the arch. The administration has announced plans to begin construction as early as Nov. 5, pending the approval of the construction by the National Capital Planning Commission.
Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex.”
Although plans submitted to the National Capital Planning Commission did not include defensive structures, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin submitted court filings Wednesday supporting the president’s comments that the defense structures would help combat the threat of drones.
The lawsuit Chutkan is overseeing is one of two filed challenging the construction of the arch. Earlier this month, the Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit opposing the construction, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against Trump’s planned monument.
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process.

title: Auto Loan Debt Is Rising Faster in Maine Than in Almost Every Other State
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While everything seems more expensive in 2026, we have concrete numbers showing that auto loan debt is on the rise here in Maine.
👇 KEEP READING: 25 Maine Thrift Stores and Antique Shops Mainers Love 👇
WalletHub compared all 50 states using three metrics from its consumer debt data to measure changes in auto loan debt, average balances and monthly payments.
Each metric was graded on a 100-point scale and weighted to calculate an overall score used to rank the states.
Maine ranked second overall in WalletHub’s study of states where auto loan debt is increasing the most.
The state ranked third for its change in auto loan debt from the first to the second quarter of 2026 and 26th for its average auto loan balance and monthly payment in the second quarter.
According to the study, Maine’s average auto loan balance was $20,865, relatively low compared with most states, but it increased by more than 2.6% between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Residents paid an average of $523 per month toward their auto loans, and Maine ranked 27th nationally for its increase in auto loan delinquency.
And there you have it! Maine drivers carry a relatively modest average balance compared with much of the country, but that debt grew at one of the fastest rates in the nation during the second quarter.

title: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide.
It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations.
But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes.
“Every day, almost every hour” battle
Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight.
Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35.
“Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said.
Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor.
Tucker said at the time of his diagnosis, he weighed about 250 pounds, while juggling graduate school and long hours — along with what he now calls a diet full of junk food.
He said he followed medical advice, changed how he ate, and started exercising. He lost more than 30 pounds — but the diabetes remained.
“What I learned, it was also hereditary,” Tucker said. “My father had it, grandfather had diabetes.”
And even with better habits, the grind can be exhausting.
The “diabetes belt”
Novant Health endocrinologist Dr. Adam Spitz said North Carolina is part of what’s often called the “diabetes belt,” a region where rates tend to be higher.
Spitz said diagnoses have continued to climb, even as medications improve.
“We’ve got about a million people in NC with diabetes,” Spitz said. “But we have another quarter million people who have undiagnosed diabetes. And that is very scary because they can start to develop all the complications without even knowing it.”
Those complications can include heart disease, advanced kidney disease, and eye disease. The American Diabetes Association said Type 2 diabetes is the leading cause of amputation in the United States.
Spitz said newer medications — including GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy — have helped many patients, but other challenges remain.
“We’ve got more people, especially in rural or under-served communities who don’t have access to health care,” Spitz said. “And don’t have good education on healthy lifestyle.”
Millions more have prediabetes
Spitz said the stakes are even bigger because an estimated 3 million people in North Carolina have prediabetes.
“They are at a fork in the road where they can either go on to get diabetes, or they can prevent it,” Spitz said.
Doctors say prevention often requires major, sustained changes — improving diet and adding regular exercise — and many people struggle to keep those changes long-term.
Tucker said he’s committed to those changes. He bikes, stays active, and uses technology to help manage his condition, including a continuous glucose monitor that shows his blood sugar in real time.
He even recorded a recent doctor’s visit in which he was told his numbers are improving.
“Your average sugar is 129, which is also improved from our last time,” the doctor said in Tucker’s video.
For Tucker, the motivation is simple: stay healthy long enough to enjoy life — and avoid the worst outcomes he’s seen in others.
What to look for
The most common signs associated with undiagnosed diabetes include excessive thirst, extreme fatigue, and frequent urination.
You should consult your doctor for further testing.

title: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
text:
(AP) - Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.” The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and The New York Times said it was “a must-see.”
“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”
Starship commander grew up without a toilet
Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
In his memoir, “Making It So,” Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. “Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”
The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard
“The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time,” he would write.
Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. “People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?‘” he told the AP. “Telly?”
Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film “Excalibur.” He had just done a production of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. “I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail.”
It didn’t, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the “Star Trek” franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”
His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in ‘Henry IV,’ which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.
Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series “Star Trek: Picard.”)
Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another “Star Trek” icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
The show gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films “Conspiracy Theory,” “L.A. Story” and on Broadway, where he starred in “The Tempest,” “The Caretaker” and David Mamet’s “A Life in the Theater.” He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.
A brave and commanding persona. But sexy?
In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide’s “Top Turn-Ons,” based on a readers’ poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: “Absurd.”
Stewart was first introduced as the character Xavier in the original X-Men trilogy, appearing in three films from 2000 to 2006. He later returned in four more movies before Professor X’s death in 2017’s “Logan.” He reappeared in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” in 2022 and is reprising the role in the upcoming “Avengers: Doomsday.”
He also showed off his comedic chops aboard Seth MacFarlane’s Starz show “Blunt Talk” for two series and voiced Poop in “The Emoji Movie.” He made appearances on “Robot Chicken,” “Futurama” and “The Simpsons” (in one episode, Homer loses his hair, and Stewart tells him it’s great to be bald.)
Later in life, he proved internet-savvy and found new fans with his humor, posing in a bath in a lobster suit and triggering memes when he posted a photo of him picking apples. When he was mistakenly outed as gay by a British newspaper, he said it was a nice change. “At least I didn’t wake up to the internet telling me I was dead again,” he tweeted.
He married Brooklyn songwriter and singer Sunny Ozell in 2013, with the actor’s “X-Men” co-star McKellen officiating. Stewart later tweeted a photo of the newlyweds in a ball pit.
He also is survived by two children, a daughter, Sophia, and a son, Daniel.

title: 'Dixie' map that divided the US into North and South fetches nearly $1 million at auction
text:
ASHEVILLE, N.C. (AP) — The hand-drawn map showing the Mason-Dixon Line that eventually divided free from slave states in the U.S. sold Thursday for $950,000.
Forty-five bidders battled for just under three minutes for ownership of what is perhaps the most consequential map in American history.
Bidding started at $400,000 for the survey of states divided by the Mason-Dixon Line, finished in 1768 by Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon. The sale was held online and in person at Brunk Auctions in Asheville, North Carolina.
While it didn’t fetch the hoped-for $1.2 million high estimate, auction house Vice President Lauren Brunk said she was pleased.
“It’s a very high price for a map,” she said.
Brunk said the buyer asked to remain anonymous, at least for the time being.
The survey was originally commissioned to settle a border dispute between what were then the colonies of Maryland and Pennsylvania. It was used in the 1820 Missouri Compromise to establish the limits of human bondage in the still adolescent United States and became synonymous with the fundamental divisions that exploded into the Civil War four decades later.
The late publisher Malcolm Forbes bought the map in 1982 for $360,000, beating out the Library of Congress. The document was resold in 2002 for $556,000.
Brunk said the Library of Congress was not among Thursday’s bidders.
“I would like to say I’m thrilled that this is going to a good home and we are so happy to have had it in our presence for these last months,” Brunk said. “It also feels like a privilege to have been entrusted to steward this from one owner to the next.”
A vertical section of the map showing the Delaware-Maryland border is housed at Princeton University.

title: James Gunn Says Casting the New Batman ‘Isn’t Very Far’
text:
James Gunn Says Casting the DCU’s Batman ‘Isn’t Very Far Away’
The DCU’s Batman hasn’t been chosen yet, says James Gunn. But he also notes the next Dark Knight “isn’t very far away.”
That’s what Gunn said on the The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon? The Official Podcast saying “it won’t be too long before we’re casting, you know, Batman. We haven’t cast yet, by the way — all the people thinking he’ll show up in this or that, it’s all bulls—.”
Gunn then added that unlike prior Batmen, he intends to cast “the best actor” for the role, explaining..
...if I gave somebody a day role in [The] Suicide Squad that is going to be the best Batman, I’m not going to rule him out from that. I want to get everybody into account. One of the things that excites me about casting Batman is being able to pick a Batman who’s actually the best actor for that role. Superman’s have always been chosen based on who the best actor for that role is. And for some reason, Batman’s are always chosen as movie stars.
You can watch Gunn’s full quote in the video below.
READ MORE: Every DC Comics Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
Gunn also said that whoever is cast as Batman will need to be “contemporaries” with the DCU’s Superman, David Corenswet, who is 33 years old.
“Roughly, Batman and Superman are around the same age. I don’t think they’re drastically different ages,” Gunn explained. So that means you’re out, Al Pacino. You will not be the next Batman. My apologies.
The Batman Part II — which stars Robert Pattinson, not whoever Gunn picks for the same role — is currently scheduled to open in theaters on February 18, 2028. The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon? The Official Podcast will be available on HBO Max tomorrow.

title: Maine heating oil prices hit another record high
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Department of Energy Resources announced Thursday that heating oil prices in the state have hit another record high.
The average statewide price of heating oil is $6.05 per gallon this week, up one cent from last week and three cents from a record $6.02 set in September.
Costs are up 82% over this time last year, according to the department. At this price, Mainers will spend about $750 more filling a standard 275-gallon oil tank than they did last fall.
“Heating oil prices in Maine are now breaking records week after week, putting growing pressure on Maine families as temperatures continue to drop,” Celina Cunningham, the department’s acting commissioner, said in a written statement. “I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and to contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief.”
Since the war with Iran began in late February, Maine heating oil prices have spiked roughly 57%.
Mainers consume more residential heating oil per capita than any other state, according to the department, and significantly more than other New England states. Roughly half of Maine households rely on heating oil.

title: Sandy Hook families urge Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on AR-15-style rifles
text:
Sandy Hook families urge Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on AR-15-style rifles
Families whose loved ones were killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting are making an impassioned plea to the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold state and local bans on certain semiautomatic rifles, citing the high body counts and devastating injuries the weapons can inflict.
The parents of five of the 20 first-graders killed in the 2012 Connecticut shooting and relatives of one of six educators who died filed a “friend of the court” brief on Wednesday, weighing in on two cases challenging bans in Connecticut and the Chicago area. Justices are scheduled to hear oral arguments in both cases on Dec. 2.
“The assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School, carried out by an untrained, 112-pound youth armed with an AR-15-style rifle, is graphic proof of the unusual and extreme lethality of that firearm and the harm it is capable of inflicting on American communities,” the relatives' filing says. They added that they “seek to protect other American families from becoming casualties in another AR-15 killing spree.”
Gun rights advocates and groups whose lawsuits led to the two Supreme Court cases are arguing that it's unconstitutional under the Second Amendment to ban semiautomatic rifles, which are legally owned by millions of Americans. Supporters of the bans say such rifles were designed for military use, are too dangerous for civilians and should be regulated like machine guns.
More than 40 other people and groups — most in favor of the rifle bans — also filed “amicus curiae” briefs on Wednesday. Such filings are submitted by parties who are not directly involved in the litigation.
Sandy Hook shooter killed 26 people with AR-15-style rifle
The 20-year-old Sandy Hook gunman, Adam Lanza, shot his way into the locked school in Newtown, Connecticut, and fired more than 150 bullets in about four minutes with a Bushmaster AR-15-style rifle fueled by high-capacity ammunition magazines. The massacre led Connecticut to ban such rifles in 2013 — the same law now before the Supreme Court.
Jennifer Hensel, whose 6-year-old daughter Avielle Richman was killed in the shooting, was quoted in the relatives' brief saying Avielle was shot multiple times in the face and authorities told her that she would not recognize her daughter if she saw her body.
“A moral imperative is truly at hand,” Hensel said in supporting weapons bans. “Please, do not allow more blood to soak our Connecticut soil from assault-style weapons. A fundamental duty to protect all in Connecticut is at stake.”
A similar brief filed Wednesday by Sandy Hook Promise, the gun violence prevention group started by Newtown families, said another victim, 6-year-old Dylan Hockley, was shot five times — “his body destroyed so completely, his mother was told not to touch him to say goodbye as he lay in his coffin.”
“The effects of these weapons on children’s bodies are catastrophic and obscene,” the filing said.
Dylan's mother, Nicole Hockley, a co-founder of Sandy Hook Promise, urged the Supreme Court to consider children's safety.
“I know firsthand the devastation a semiautomatic rifle can inflict in minutes on the bodies, hearts, and minds of children — and the families who love them,” she said in a statement. “No family should have to live with that pain. As the Court considers this case, the consequences being experienced by children and communities cannot be an afterthought.”
Gun rights advocates filed suit to block rifle bans
Gun rights supporters say that while they sympathize with gun violence victims' families and condemn mass shootings, the solution isn't to curtail Second Amendment rights. They say school shootings happen despite bans on so-called “assault weapons.”
“Solving or at least mitigating school shootings is not about banning a type of gun,” said Konstadinos Moros, director of legal research and education for the Second Amendment Foundation, a plaintiff in the challenges to both the Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, bans.
“While some guns are obviously more capable than others, school shooters inflict harm not because of the capability of their firearms, but because of the helplessness of their targets,” he said in an email to The Associated Press. “The real solution lies in proper school security, which can both more quickly respond to shootings, and deter attacks from happening in the first place, given that the depraved individuals who commit these sorts of crimes tend to pick ‘soft targets.’”
Justices to weigh whether bans violate Second Amendment
The current Supreme Court, which has expanded gun rights, announced in June that it would hear appeals challenging bans on the AR-15 and similar semiautomatic firearms in Connecticut and the Chicago area. The ban in Cook County was first passed in 1993. Lower courts have upheld both laws.
Similar laws are in place in about a dozen states, covering major cities like New York, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. Congress allowed a national assault weapons ban to expire in 2004, but Democrats have supported renewing it in response to mass shootings. States have also continued to pass their own laws, including recent measures in Virginia and Rhode Island.
It is the latest high-profile dispute over guns to reach the court since its conservative majority handed down a landmark ruling in 2022 that expanded Second Amendment rights and spawned challenges to firearm laws around the country. The court said that any gun laws must have a strong grounding in the nation’s historical traditions.

title: Humanitarian aid set to enter Oleshky as a localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds for a third day
text:
Humanitarian aid set to enter Oleshky as a localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds for a third day
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky on Friday, a Ukrainian official said, as a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, despite remaining locked in war since Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
But elsewhere, a jet-powered Russian drone hit two trains stopped at a station in central Ukraine, killing at least 13 people and injuring 10 others, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it in a post on X as a “horrific attack” that struck passenger trains in Dnipro.
Also, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
Ukraine said Russia fired 112 drones at seven locations across the country.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has also brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
The Oleshky ceasefire has held for 54 hours, officials say
Both sides thanked U.S. first lady Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so that food and medical supplies can reach some desperate 2,000 people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
“The ceasefire has been in place for 54 hours now,” Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day. “The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported.”
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on de-mining Oleshky roads.
“Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded,” she said. “This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy.”
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work were unclear.
Russian leader Putin says Elon Musk is ‘a genius’
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talksnext month between Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but U.S. President Donald Trump has recently indicated that he is disengaging with Kyiv as he waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are currently sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the U.S. for a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow’s invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotageacross the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communications.
Putin said that Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
“Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius,” Putin said late Wednesday.
“We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together,” he added.
___
AP journalists Vasilisa Stepanenko and Volodymyr Yurchuk in Kherson, Ukraine and Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Ukraine contributed to this report.

title: Maine can lead the effort to restore America
text:
Donald Trump is a rogue president who lies, displays erratic behavior, relies on insulting rhetoric, illogical executive orders and phony legal battles with his perceived enemies. More troubling, we have a sycophantic Republican-controlled Senate willing to do Trump’s bidding.

As Colby professor Dan Shea detailed in his excellent Oct. 3 op-ed (“There is no ‘bipartisan’ way to organize the Senate”), reelecting Sen. Nothing else matters!

title: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
text:
NEW ORLEANS (InvestigateTV) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street.
The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship.
“The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen.
Four men with four different careers create one sound.
Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead.
“Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said.
Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong.
“It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne.
One of the city’s most famous native sons sang before he played.
“Louis Armstrong was in a vocal quartet before he ever started playing a horn,” Matherne said.
Matherne is an award-winning barbershop quartet singer who also performs with a larger vocal group, NOLA Vox, which spawned The Dreamers, a coed barbershop quartet.
Quartet aficionados said female voices are a welcome addition to this traditionally male art form.
“It’s a lot of fun to see where you stack up against somebody else,” said Sarah Todd.
“We need the ladies to hit the high notes,” said Matt Ridley. “We do have some gentlemen, but they’re not as attractive.”
The singers do it for love, not money, though New Orleans has a long history of hosting thousands of singers for international competition.
“The most recent one in New Orleans international was 1992 in the Superdome,” Matherne said.
But for these local quartets, it’s more about harmony and camaraderie.
“I think it’s beautiful, when you learn the parts really well and it all comes together it’s really amazing,” Ridley said.
The groups join voices every couple of weeks. In a city built on music, their harmony still has a place.

text:
Which races could determine control of Congress?
With five days until the midterm elections, both parties are making their final push, with key figures like President Trump and former President Obama rallying voters in critical states.
Which races could determine control of Congress?
With five days until the midterm elections, both parties are making their final push, with key figures like President Trump and former President Obama rallying voters in critical states.
With five days remaining until the midterm elections on Nov. 3, Democrats and Republicans are ramping up their efforts to secure votes in key races across the country.
Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who is running for reelection in Arkansas, told reporters on Wednesday that he is confident the GOP will maintain control of both chambers of Congress. title: In Maine, you can lose your home to your oil bill
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Matt Pouliot is a real estate broker and entrepreneur who served six terms in the Maine Legislature, including a leadership role on the Housing Committee. He is co-founder and CEO of ATLAS Building Composites. Martin Grohman is the former mayor of Biddeford and a former executive director of E2Tech.
You can lose your home to the bank. In Maine, you can also lose it to your oil bill.
That sounds like a stretch until you look at how people decide whether they can afford a home. It isn’t just the rent or mortgage. It’s rent plus heat plus electricity.
A family might be able to swing $1,800 a month for a place. Then January’s oil bill arrives. Maine depends on heating oil more than any other state, and our electric rates are among the highest in the country. Energy costs can mean the difference between keeping a home and losing it.
So when we talk about Maine needing roughly 84,000 more homes by 2030, we should be talking about energy costs in the same breath. It’s the same affordability crisis showing up on different bills.
The two of us come at this from different places. One is a Republican who spent a career in real estate and the Legislature. The other is an independent who has worked in manufacturing, served as mayor and led Maine’s clean-energy business group. We don’t agree on everything. But we agree on this.
First, stop picking winners in energy.
Solar and batteries make sense where the numbers work. One of us has solar on his building and an electric car in the driveway. But we shouldn’t rule out pipelines, fuel infrastructure or transmission projects simply because they don’t fit a preferred energy strategy.
Restricting supply or limiting options often means Maine families and businesses pay the price, especially the retiree in a drafty farmhouse who can’t afford new heating equipment or the tenant whose landlord passes along rising energy costs.
What helps keep prices down is reliable supply and competition. Solar, hydro, wind, natural gas, renewable fuels, propane and energy storage all deserve consideration. Judge them on cost, reliability and environmental impact, not ideology. And start with efficiency. The cheapest energy is the energy you never have to buy.
Second, make it easier to build things.
That goes for apartments and it goes for power lines. A good project in Maine can spend years navigating reviews that overlap, stall or start over. Every month of delay adds carrying costs, and somebody pays them, usually the renter or the ratepayer. We need clear standards, firm timelines and decisions someone is accountable for. Protect the environment, absolutely. But an unpredictable process that takes years to reach a decision serves nobody well.
We also need to build differently. Most homes still go up much the way they did 50 years ago: stick by stick, in the weather, with a shortage of skilled tradespeople. Prefabricated panels and newer methods like large-format 3D printing of structural components, which ATLAS Building Composites is developing here in Maine, offer ways to build faster, waste less and create tighter, more energy-efficient homes. They’re not a silver bullet, but they belong in the plan.
Third, Washington has a role.
Federal permitting requirements can add years to major projects. Sen. Susan Collins has a long record of backing Maine’s economy, and this year helped secure nearly $25 million for housing projects across the state, including workforce and senior housing in Springvale and student housing at York County Community College in Wells. That’s welcome progress.
We’d like to see that same leadership applied to permitting reform: clear standards, predictable timelines and strong environmental protections. Few things Congress could do would help Maine’s housing and energy challenges more.
No single fuel, technology or law will fix this. But if we want young people to stay and employers to grow, Mainers need homes they can afford to live in, not just move into. That means making it faster and easier to build and keeping all energy options on the table.

title: Dunlap ties rising heating oil costs to Iran war, targets LePage over energy donations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Matt Dunlap challenged opponent Paul LePage during a Thursday press conference in the final stretch of the campaign, connecting surging home heating oil prices directly to the war in Iran and criticizing the former governor’s stance.
Dunlap noted that heating oil is now $6.00-7.00 per gallon across parts of Maine.
He called the war in Iran an unauthorized conflict driving up local energy costs.
Dunlap pledged to vote for a War Powers Resolution if elected and accused LePage of dodging questions while taking campaign donations from the oil and gas sector.
“Paul LePage has taken nearly $48,000 from the oil and gas industry in this campaign. Oil and gas investors, refiners, industry lobbyists. The big players whose profits go up every time your heating oil bill does. Those are the people writing his checks. Of course, he won’t tell you where he stands on the war that’s padding their bottom line. And I’m not talking about the family oil company down the road. They’re getting squeezed, too,” Dunlap said.
The LePage campaign responded by defending the former governor’s record and criticizing Dunlap’s voting history.
“Matt Dunlap is lying to the people of Maine because he is desperate to win and get another government paid job. Governor LePage has said repeatedly he wants the war in Iran to end, and to end quickly. Governor LePage cut the gas tax so Mainers pay less at the pump. It was Matt Dunlap who voted to increase the gas tax so Mainers pay more for fuel and Dunlap said this year he would do it all over again, he would raise prices again,” said a spokesperson with the LePage campaign.

title: TSA confiscates Wolverine-style claws at airport checkpoint
text:
SEATTLE (Gray News) - Transportation Security Administration officers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport recently stopped a suspicious carry-on item that looked more like something out of a Marvel movie.
According to the TSA, officers Douglas Linn and Dennis Oishi teamed up to identify and stop a dangerous item in a carry-on bag.
Officials said while reviewing X-ray images, Linn spotted the item and immediately recognized it required additional attention.
“I saw three blades and distinct claw-like features,” Linn said. “I was amazed, and even more so when it came out of the bag. I have never seen anything like this during my two years at TSA.”
Officials said the item resembled a mix between Wolverine-style claws and Freddy Krueger blades, noting that some accessories are better suited for movie screens rather than airplane cabins.
As the property search officer, Oishi conducted a bag search, confirmed the prohibited item and was said to handle the situation with the professionalism expected during checkpoint operations.
The passenger immediately remembered the items after Oishi removed them from the bag and voluntarily abandoned them at the checkpoint.
“In my seven years with TSA, this is one of the most unusual items I have encountered,” responding supervisory TSA officer Ann Rhoades said. “When Dennis asked the passenger if there was anything sharp in the bag, he said he wasn’t sure. Obviously, there was.”

title: Obama doubles down on ‘Cheesecake Factory’ joke after criticism from Trump
text:
(AP) — Former President Barack Obama is pushing back on Republicans’ reactions to a recent quip he made about President Donald Trump’s White House renovations and decor.
Obama said Trump’s gold accents looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
“These are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems,” Obama said in Georgia, pushing back on criticism he received for his comments. He said Republicans would rather have “phony outrage” and “talk about the Cheesecake Factory.”
Republicans painted Obama’s comment as insulting to middle-class Americans who enjoy the restaurant.
But Obama name-checked middle-class establishments he’s patronized with his daughters, including the California Pizza Kitchen, Cheesecake Factory and Chuck E. Cheese.
He said it’s telling that the White House did not dispute his main argument that Trump cares about trivialities, not helping Americans.
“The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” Obama said. “That part didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory.”

title: Man in wheelchair fatally struck by city-owned garbage truck, police say
text:
ROCHESTER, N.Y. (WHAM) — A man was struck and killed Tuesday by a city-owned and -operated garbage truck, and police are investigating.
Rochester police said they responded around 3:30 p.m. Tuesday to the city’s North Side and found a man dead at the scene.
What police say happened
Officers said a garbage truck was traveling eastbound on Warsaw Street and was attempting to make a left turn onto Hudson Avenue. At the same time, the man, who was operating a motorized wheelchair, was on the west shoulder of the road.
Witnesses said the wheelchair was pinned under the front end of the truck.
Police said the driver of the truck, a man in his 50s, was not hurt.
Officers do not believe drugs or alcohol played a role in the incident.
Bystander describes scene
Carl Canty came upon the scene minutes after the crash, as first responders worked to secure the area.
“You could see the wheelchair up under the garbage truck, and there were people that were there that were really pretty distraught at the situation in the scene,” Canty said.
Canty also said he feels for the driver of the truck.
“It was just kind of devastating to drive by and see that, and think someone just probably left, went to the store, wherever. They’re not going to return home,” he said.
City response
Rochester Mayor Malik Evans offered condolences and said the city is committed to conducting a thorough investigation to determine how the crash happened and what can be done to prevent further tragedies like this one.
The victim had not yet been identified.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion in big consolidation for grocery delivery
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17 billion acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains by have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

title: CNN, MSNOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent
text:
Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge’s orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press “pool.”
CNN, MSNOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly’s previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president.
Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in “the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press,” Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets’ attorney, said in a statement.
The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent.
At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is “viewpoint discrimination” forbidden by the First Amendment’s free-speech protections.
Trump insists that he doesn’t have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning.
“Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable,” the outlets wrote in their filing, “and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government.”
The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him.
In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.
Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.
“Simply put,” Kelly wrote in the opinion, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.

title: Ukraine war continues despite Trump’s promise to end it
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The war in Ukraine has lasted more than four-and-a-half years, and fighting continues despite repeated efforts by President Donald Trump to end the conflict.
Trump made a pledge on the campaign trail dozens of times during the last presidential campaign.
“Before I even arrive at the Oval Office shortly after I win the presidency, I will have the horrible war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump said at a July 7, 2023, rally in Council Bluffs, Iowa. “Somebody said, are you on Russia’s side? Are you on Ukraine’s side? You know what? The side — I want people to stop dying. That’s the side I’m on.”
That campaign promise has not been fulfilled.
Trump has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice at the White House. He met once with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in August 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
“I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting,” Trump said. “There were many, many points that we agreed on. Most of them, I would say. A couple of big ones that we haven’t quite got there, but we’ve made some headway. So, there’s no deal until there’s a deal.”
On Sept. 18, Trump signed bipartisan legislation named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) that imposes sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia. On Oct. 16 Trump signed an executive order waiving those sanctions.

title: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation.
“You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said.
Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis.
“And that was all while I was active,” he said.
To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog.
Service dog provides daily support
Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline.
“You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said.
The dog helped Poggi regain his independence by taking care of tasks many people take for granted.
“His favorite thing is to retrieve, to help me carry things,” he said. “If I drop my keys or anything like that, I’ll pick them up for me. He can retrieve my cell phone for me and things like that.”
Poggi said Teddy brought back something harder to replace: joy.
“I love my children very, very much, but it is right up there with another child,” he said.
There’s growing evidence that service dogs can alleviate some symptoms. A 2024 study found the canines are associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression in veterans with PTSD.
Training prepares dogs for real-world scenarios
Poggi took Teddy to Dog Training Elite St. Louis, where they train dogs for everything from basic obedience to advanced therapy, protection and service work.
“The way DTE trains, it looks like a facility, but they turn this thing into like a real-world scenario,” Poggi said. “They prepare you and your service animal for real world experiences that you just you’re not going to get out of that book.”
Matt Willis, owner of Dog Training Elite St. Louis, said service dogs can be important for veterans, helping with both physical limitations and PTSD.
“Dogs just-they change your feeling, the chemical changes in your body with that interaction. And that’s exactly the uplift that these guys and ladies need,” Willis said.
Willis said veterans have been through traumatic things, both physically, emotionally and mentally.
“While you know our government and the system tries to do what they can, there’s obviously some gaps in that care for our veterans,” he said.
Grant to help veterans get service dogs
A private donor grant will help cover part of the cost for service dog training for 10 veterans or active military members in need.
“They wanted it to go towards veterans and military personnel for service dog training. So what we’ve done is divide that money up to where we are able to help 10 veterans in need. Can be active military or veterans. And so it basically pays 30% of their training costs for those 10 veterans,” Willis said.
“And that’s the kind of people that are out there that see the benefit of what these dogs can do,” he said.
Teddy will return to work with Poggi, resuming his job as a school crossing guard in Mascoutah.
“Next school year, I’ll be back full-time out on the corner every day, rain or shine. He’s out there with me. He’s got the got a little crossing guard hut and everything,” Poggi said.
A 2024 survey of about 600 veterans revealed about four in 10 never had a PTSD service dog but would like one.
It’s important to note the VA doesn’t provide service dogs for mental health conditions, including PTSD and is still studying the potential benefits of such interventions.
